66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary:
House Bill 752, signed by Governor Brad Little and effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match their sex assigned at birth. The prohibition reaches government buildings and public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail. Idaho's measure is the only state law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses and, according to the ACLU, carries steeper penalties than other states' bans.

Six transgender Idahoans filed suit on 30 April 2026 to block HB 752 before its effect date, arguing the law is unconstitutional and violates due process, equal protection and privacy, and noting it targets no actual criminal conduct. The ACLU of Idaho filed a parallel challenge the same day. National wire reporting covered the legislature's passage of the ban and the jail penalties it carries, along with a lawsuit that has partially blocked it. U.S. District Judge Amanda Brailsford narrowed the law on 16 June 2026, two weeks before it took effect, barring enforcement against single-stall use and against multi-user use where no unoccupied single-user restroom is available on the same floor.

Idaho bans any change of sex on birth certificates. A 2018 implementation law, allowed into legal effect in January 2026, permits only biological male or female sex at birth, reversing a period from 6 April 2018 when trans people could change birth certificates following a 2017 lawsuit. Governor Brad Little's HB 509, signed 30 March 2020, was ruled moot and unenforceable on 7 August 2020 by District Judge David C. Nye, with $321,000 in attorneys' fees awarded to Lambda Legal and approved in August 2022.

Since March 2019 Idaho has offered an "X" third-gender option on driver's licences and state IDs. Under the 7 August 2020 ruling, however, applicants changing a gender marker must submit a physician letter certifying sex reassignment surgery. In November 2019 the Board of Health and Welfare removed the doctor-approval requirement for gender change by transgender minors, retaining parental permission, emancipation or court order.

Gender-affirming medical care for minors is a felony for doctors under HB 71, signed 4 April 2023, which bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgeries; the ban was upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in April 2024. HB 668, effective 1 July 2024, further restricts care for minors and adults when provided by state, local or county professionals, through Idaho Medicaid, or on state property including hospitals, public colleges and prisons, excluding counselling and mental health but limiting hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery and barring tax deductibility. An earlier bill, HB 675, which passed the House in March 2022 proposing felony liability and life imprisonment for parents taking children out of state, was blocked by the Senate.

Transgender prisoners were permitted hormone therapy under a September 2024 federal judge ruling that nullified a 1997 law banning it. In August 2024 the Governor signed an executive order barring application within Idaho of any federal laws, regulations and guidelines regarding gender identity or gender ideology.

Under a March 2026 law, schools, childcare providers and medical professionals must out transgender minors to their parents within three days of learning the minor's trans status. An April 2024 law bars teachers and education agencies from using pronouns not based on birth certificates for students. Transgender athletes are barred from public school and university sports teams matching their gender identity under legislation signed 30 March 2020.

No Idaho state law explicitly prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. Federal Title VII protection under Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) covers workplace discrimination, and roughly 40% of the population is covered by county and city ordinances in Ada County, Bellevue, Boise, Coeur d'Alene, Driggs, Hailey, Idaho Falls, Ketchum, Lewiston, Meridian, Moscow, Pocatello, Sandpoint, Victor, plus Latah County employee protection. Idaho's hate-crime law excludes gender identity, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009 allows federal prosecution of gender-identity-motivated crimes.

Texas in 2003, remaining formally in Idaho Code until the Legislature passed repeal in March 2022 signed by the Governor effective July 1, 2022, after history including an 1864 sodomy statute punishing anal intercourse with five years to life, 1916 extension to fellatio in State v. 66186276B48953429733047.tangentialFactors:
Idaho's HB 752 is the most far-reaching of the state bathroom restrictions now in force nationally, because it reaches private businesses as well as government buildings and attaches jail time to a first offence. The partial injunction issued by Judge Brailsford on 16 June 2026 narrows but does not void the statute, so the operative scope on any given day should be checked before travel.

The state's document regime runs in two directions at once: an X marker remains available on driver's licences and state IDs, while birth certificates are locked to sex assigned at birth and licence gender-marker changes require a physician letter certifying sex reassignment surgery. A visitor relying on an out-of-state licence with an X marker is not governed by Idaho's marker rules, but presentation of documents that do not align with appearance may invite scrutiny in settings where HB 752 applies.

Idaho's August 2024 executive order directing that federal gender-identity law and guidance not be applied within the state sits alongside federal measures that are themselves being litigated, so the interaction between the two layers is unsettled in practice.
66186276B48953429733047.localsOnly:
Idaho residents face a birth-certificate regime that permits no change of sex, a felony exposure for doctors providing gender-affirming care to minors, and additional restrictions on care delivered by state or local professionals, through Idaho Medicaid, or on state property. HB 668 also bars tax deductibility for that care.

A March 2026 statute requires schools, childcare providers and medical professionals to disclose a transgender minor's status to parents within three days of learning it. Transgender minors therefore cannot rely on professional confidentiality in educational or clinical settings.

Workplace and housing protection rests on federal Title VII under Bostock and on local ordinances covering about 40% of the population; Idaho has no statewide gender-identity nondiscrimination statute, and its hate-crime law excludes gender identity. Enforcement of gender-identity-motivated crimes can proceed federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Act.

Transgender prisoners won hormone-therapy access through a September 2024 federal ruling nullifying a 1997 ban, but the Governor's August 2024 executive order rejecting application of federal gender-identity guidance within Idaho creates conflicting authority on how that right is administered.

66186276B41335105066757.name: Louisiana
66186276B41335105066757.summary:
Louisiana has no state law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, or public accommodations. As of 12 October 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scores the state's gender-identity policy at -8.75/25, with recourse limited to federal EEOC processes and the June 2020 Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County for employment claims only. Local ordinances provide partial cover: New Orleans and Shreveport prohibit gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Alexandria, Baton Rouge, Lafayette, Lake Charles and Jefferson Parish extend protection only to public employees.

The 1997 state hate-crime statute, which provides penalty enhancements, covers sexual orientation or perceived sexual orientation but does not include gender identity. Hate crimes motivated by gender identity therefore fall to federal prosecution under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009.

Physical safety data for Louisiana is severe. A July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams Institute data reports Louisiana with the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state, 24.7 per 100,000 per year (19 recorded killings), against 23.5 for the state ranked safest on this measure, drawn from a base of 428 US victims recorded 2008–2025. The source cautions that every figure is an undercount floor and that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, with the worst-law states holding the highest rate.

Trans-specific violence has been documented with direct legal consequences. In August 2026 a mob attacked trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton over restroom use; Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who sustained a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested. Rush was denied hospital care, jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. Reporting on 5 August 2026 notes the plea deal was not signed and that the Sheriff's Office confirmed no other arrests that day; the same municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances.

Trans people in state custody face documented harm. Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates on 2 April 2024. This was at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person killed in the United States in 2024 that the Human Rights Campaign had learned of, and the fifth in April alone; such deaths are systematically under- or mis-reported.

Identity documents in Louisiana are changed only through surgery. A driver's licence gender marker may be changed on submission of a physician-signed statement confirming successful sex reassignment surgery. A new birth certificate requires a certified court order confirming surgical gender change, proof of diagnosis as transsexual or pseudo-hermaphrodite, and evidence of anatomical change.

Transition-related healthcare for minors is banned. In July 2023 the Legislature overrode the Governor's June 2023 veto to prohibit puberty blockers, hormones, and surgeries for minors, formally effective 1 January 2024. Surgery, puberty blockers, hormone replacement therapy and other transition-related care are excluded from health insurance and state Medicaid coverage.

Facilities and sport rules restrict trans participation. In June 2022 Louisiana banned transgender girls from sports in public schools, passed with more than two-thirds support in both chambers after a similar 2021 bill (House 77-17, Senate 29-6) was vetoed and the override failed by two votes. The Benton incident above shows restroom restrictions being enforced by mob violence and subsequently codified in municipal ordinance.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by the 2003 Lawrence v. Texas ruling and a 2005 Fifth Circuit decision, though an unenforceable sodomy law carrying up to five years imprisonment, a $2,000 fine and sex-offender registration remains on the books after repeal failed 66-27 in April 2014. Same-sex marriage has been recognised since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with compliance confirmed two days later; married same-sex couples are entitled to full joint adoption and parental rights following Costanza v. Caldwell of 22 September 2014. A June 2017 domestic-violence amendment removed opposite-sex language, ensuring identical treatment irrespective of sexual orientation where same-sex offenders previously received lesser sentences. Louisiana also maintains a no-promo-homo law barring sex education classes from discussing male or female homosexual activity.

66186276B29106115751815.name: Texas
66186276B29106115751815.summary:
Texas law restricts trans people's use of sex-separated facilities. Governor Abbott signed the Women's Privacy Act on 22 September 2025 and it took effect on 4 December 2025, requiring restrooms to match the sex recorded on a person's birth certificate and applying to public schools, universities, prisons and Texas government buildings. Facilities face a $25,000 fine for a first violation and $125,000 for subsequent violations. The most recent gender-placements statute reaches prisons only as to restroom use; it does not govern cell assignment or the housing placement of trans prisoners.

Enforcement has begun and has been uneven. On 6 December 2025 Department of Public Safety troopers checked identification at women's restrooms outside the state capitol in Austin, admitting trans women whose identity documents carried female markers. Opponents of the law warn that unclear guidance produces inconsistent and invasive checks, and protests followed at the capitol. The Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent.

The state has also moved against a school district over facility policy. In April 2026 Attorney General Paxton filed a second complaint escalating the state investigation of Austin Independent School District, with a renewed demand for records following a tip-line complaint. It is the first state enforcement inquiry into a school district under a Texas bathroom law.

Gender markers on state documents are closed. House Bill 229, the Women's Bill of Rights, passed in May 2025, signed in June 2025 and effective from September 2025, legally defines female as a person who can biologically produce ova and male as a person who can biologically fertilize ova, requires people with disorders of sex development to select one of two genders with no third-gender recognition, and applies across state statutes, regulations and rules that use gendered terms. It explicitly bans any change of sex on Texas driver's licences and birth certificates. Before that, changing the gender indicator on a birth certificate required a court order, with judicial discretion often referring to WPATH Standards of Care and to a narrative statement from a doctor or therapist that the change was appropriate and in the person's best interest. On 30 January 2025 Governor Abbott separately directed state agencies to recognise only two genders.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. Senate Bill 14, signed in June 2023, prohibits such care for young people, following a February 2022 opinion from the Attorney General classifying the care as child abuse and directives ordering the Department of Family and Protective Services to investigate parents who facilitate it, with criminal penalties for a knowing failure to report. Five district attorneys publicly refused to apply that position. A temporary injunction issued in March 2022 was reinstated by the Third Court of Appeals after a suit by the ACLU and Lambda Legal on behalf of providers and a family with a 16-year-old transgender girl on puberty blockers. Investigative supervisors testified that cases involving trans children were handled under different rules, with mandatory investigation regardless of evidence and a prohibition on discussing them by email or text.

Texas offers trans people no statewide statutory protection against violence or discrimination. The state hate-crime statute enhances penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, and it is rarely prosecuted. As of 2021 no state law barred discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or insurance; Texas courts recognised federal employment protections in March 2021. Municipal ordinances fill part of that gap: Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio prohibit gender-identity discrimination in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations, with narrower protections limited to city employment or public accommodations in Denton, El Paso, Arlington, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Irving, Lubbock, Mesquite and Waco.

Violence against trans women in Texas is recorded at the highest absolute level of any state: 44 killings between 2008 and 2025, a rate of roughly 7.6 per 100,000 per year on the source's count, which is described as an undercount floor. The ranking is by raw tally, and raw tallies track population size; the per-capita figure is the better comparison across states, and the source provides no per-capita ranking of its own.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places Texas in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier for adult trans travellers, alongside Florida, Idaho and Kansas, graded state by state across care bans, facility bans and enforcement posture using five years of legislation tracking.

Trans prisoners in Texas have limited access to medically necessary care through the courts. In Gibson v. Collier, Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and incarcerated by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the agency's treatment policy excluded that procedure. The federal district court rejected the state's immunity defences but ruled against her on the Eighth Amendment claim. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding no deliberate indifference and holding that refusing the surgery was a permissible medical choice, with Judge Barksdale dissenting on summary-judgement procedure.

Austin Current (27 Apr 2026): Attorney General Paxton's second complaint escalated the state probe of Austin ISD over bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint — the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry against a school district.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Texas carries the highest absolute toll of any state — 44 recorded killings of trans women 2008–2025, about 7.6 per 100k per year (undercount floor) — within the map's 'Do Not Travel' grading.

Senate Bill 14 signed June 2023 effectively bans gender-affirming care for minors, following a February 2022 Attorney General opinion classifying such care as child abuse and Governor Abbott directives ordering the Department of Family and Protective Services to investigate parents who facilitate it and imposing criminal penalties for knowing failure to report, which five district attorneys refused to follow and which was blocked by a March 2022 temporary injunction reinstated by the Third Court of Appeals after ACLU/Lambda Legal suit on behalf of providers including Dr. Megan Mooney and a family with a 16-year-old transgender girl on puberty blockers. Investigative supervisor testimony stated trans-child cases faced different rules with mandatory investigation regardless of evidence and prohibition on email/text discussion; earlier legislative efforts included 2021 House Bill 1399 and Senate Bill 1311 passed 18-13 to revoke licenses of doctors providing blockers to minors, while House Bill 1106 excludes a parent's refusal to affirm a child's gender identity or sexual orientation from child-abuse definition. Texas hate-crime statute enhances penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity and is rarely prosecuted; as of 2021 no state law bars employment, housing, public-accommodations or insurance discrimination based on gender identity, though March 2021 Texas courts recognized Bostock federal employment protections and cities including Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio prohibit gender-identity discrimination in private/public employment, housing and public accommodations with narrower city-employment or public-accommodation protections in Denton, El Paso, Arlington, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Irving, Lubbock, Mesquite and Waco. June 2025 Parents' Bill of Rights bars school employees from teaching/discussing gender identity, bans LGBT-related student organizations, mandates deadnaming and misgendering of trans students and expands parental authority; prefiled November 2022 House Bill 643 would expand sexually oriented business definitions to restrict any performance where a performer uses clothing, makeup or other markers to exhibit a gender variance from birth-assigned sex while singing, lip-syncing, dancing or otherwise performing, thereby capturing transgender performers in any role and cisgender portrayals of diverse/ambiguous genders and criminalizing minors' attendance at drag shows. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by Lawrence v. Texas in June 2003, but as of 2023 Texas remains one of three states retaining a dormant same-sex-only sodomy law termed deviate sexual intercourse; a 2025 House-passed repeal failed in the Senate, and Texas retains a same-sex-exclusionary Romeo-and-Juliet affirmative defense allowing a defense only if the actor is not more than three years older than a child under 17 or is a spouse and not of the child's same sex, with no published constitutional challenge since Obergefell and sole retention since Kansas struck a similar law in 2005 after 2013 repeal bills died. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide by Obergefell on June 26, 2015 with about 2,500 licenses issued within months, following 1973 HB 103 limiting licenses to a man and a woman effective January 1, 1974, a 1997 licensing ban, 2003 non-recognition of marriages/civil unions, and a 2005 constitutional referendum, plus 2014 federal and state rulings striking the ban; the 2022 federal Respect for Marriage Act requires Texas to recognize lawfully performed out-of-state same-sex marriages but does not obligate issuance, with identical licensing requirements of age 18, unrelated, and unmarried/single. There is no statewide recognition of domestic partnerships for same- or opposite-sex couples, though Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, El Paso, Houston and San Antonio provide health insurance to domestic partners of city workers, Dallas County paid $300 per month cash subsidies in October 2012, Travis, El Paso and Bexar Counties allow partner participation, and Pflugerville ISD allows inclusion at full worker cost, while 2001 Houston Proposition 2 barred city domestic-partner benefits except legal spouses later interpreted in November 2013 to require spousal benefits for legally married same-sex couples, and an April 2013 Attorney General opinion held the constitution bars political-subdivision benefits based on domestic-partnership status as similar to marriage. Any adult may adopt regardless of sexual orientation with legally married same-sex couples able to adopt jointly and obtain supplemental birth certificates listing both parents, lesbian couples may access IVF/assisted insemination though health-plan IVF coverage requiring fertilization only with the spouse's sperm restricts access, and even federally funded adoption agencies may discriminate per religious beliefs. The hate-crime statute enhances penalties for sexual-orientation-motivated crimes but is rarely prosecuted; as of 2021 no state law bars sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodations or insurance with bills dying in committee since at least 1999 including 2009 HB 2215 and 2013 HBs 238, 1146, 206, 541 and SBs 237, 73, though federal Bostock 2020 employment protections apply and were recognized by Texas courts in March 2021 even as Texas joined a 2022 federal suit to overturn some LGBT protections, and cities Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio bar sexual-orientation discrimination in private/public employment, housing and public accommodations with limited city-employment protections elsewhere and Houston's 2014 broad ordinance repealed by voters in 2015. Since September 1, 2025 a law explicitly listing banned DEI school and certain workplace programs for sexual orientation is in effect and under court challenge, November 2025 voters passed a constitutional parental-rights amendment, June 2019 SB 1978 bars adverse government action for supporting religious organizations that may refuse LGBTQ service, and effective 2025 judges refusing same-sex weddings on religious grounds face no punishment.

66186276B52324970173776.name: Tennessee
66186276B52324970173776.summary:
Visitors to Tennessee face state law that regulates gender presentation in public, restricts access to sex-segregated facilities by birth sex, and criminalises some categories of performance. The Adult Entertainment Act of 2023 (SB 3/HB 9) defines "adult cabaret entertainment" to include male or female impersonators and prohibits it on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony with 1 to 6 years and fines to $3,000.

The drag ban has survived challenge. A federal judge held it vague and overbroad in June 2023, but the appeals-court ruling upholding the Act now stands and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear challenges to it. A separate suit remains ongoing.

Facility use is governed by birth sex. Under the Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act passed in April 2026, transgender people must use only facilities matching their sex assigned at birth, trans women are barred from women's shelters, and transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons by sex assigned at birth. A 2019 statute separately defines a transgender person using the bathroom corresponding with their gender identity as indecent exposure. The 2021 requirement that small businesses post warning signs in such circumstances was struck down in May 2022 on First Amendment grounds and is not in force; the 2021 ban on transgender students using public-school bathrooms matching their identity has been in litigation since August 2021.

Identity documents are effectively closed. Change of sex on an original birth certificate has been prohibited under Tenn. Code Ann. § 68-3-203(d) since 1977, and a 2023 law signed by Governor Lee defines sex by anatomy and genetics existing at birth. The Department of Safety refused a legally transitioned transgender woman a gender change on her driver's licence, prompting an ACLU suit filed in Davidson County on 23 April 2024; the outcome of that suit is not sourced here.

Gender-affirming care is barred for minors. Senate Bill 1, signed 1 March 2023, makes it illegal to provide such healthcare to anyone under 18 in state or through out-of-state telehealth, banned new care after 1 July 2023 and required existing care to be withdrawn by 31 March 2024, authorises regret suits against parents, guardians and physicians, and permits $25,000 actions by the Attorney General against providers. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld it as not violating equal protection on 18 June 2025 in United States v. Skrmetti. A May 2024 law adds civil penalties for adults who help a minor obtain such care, and April 2024 legislation bans the care for inmates.

Violence against trans women is documented at a high rate. A July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams data records 10 killings of trans women in Tennessee between 2008 and 2025, a rate of 7.8 per 100,000 per year, and treats that figure as an undercount floor rather than a complete count; the same analysis places Tennessee in its worst tier for laws passed.

The gay and trans panic defence remains available to lower or eliminate punishment for fatal attacks, and reporting from April 2021 describes police and legal officials turning a blind eye to assaults on LGBTQ people while treating attractions as sin. LGBTQ people in the state are reported to be discriminated against, refused service and beaten.

Tennessee's hate-crime statute has covered bias based on sexual orientation since 2001 but does not list gender identity. A February 2019 Attorney General opinion concluded that selecting a victim because they are transgender qualifies for enhancement under § 40-35-114(17) as a crime committed because of gender. The state Bureau of Investigation recorded 0 anti-transgender incidents in 2019, 1 in 2020 and 2 in 2021; these are raw recorded counts with no population denominator and reflect recording and reporting practices rather than incidence.

Marriage is available on the same terms as elsewhere in the United States, but HB 878, signed 21 February 2024, allows government employees to refuse to solemnise marriages that conflict with their personal beliefs.

Advocate: the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to Tennessee's drag ban, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 Adult Entertainment Act in place; a separate suit remains ongoing, with performers saying they refuse to be silenced.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Tennessee's killing rate of trans women runs at 7.8 per 100k per year (10 recorded deaths, 2008–2025, an undercount floor), and the state is graded in the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier.

66186276B52324970173776.tangentialFactors:
The state's relative position is measured consistently low. The Human Rights Campaign's 2024 State Equality Index records that Tennessee lacked statewide non-discrimination protections in employment, housing and public accommodations and was among the states most likely to have religious-refusal or other anti-LGBTQ+ laws; a 2024 Human Rights Campaign assessment also classified Tennessee among the lowest-ranking states for LGBTQ rights.

The July 2026 national analysis that produces the 7.8 per 100,000 killing rate ranks jurisdictions by state-level tallies of killings of trans women; its own figure for Tennessee rests on 10 recorded deaths across 18 years, a count small enough that a single additional year moves the rate substantially.

Drag-law litigation has a longer history than the current position suggests. The 2023 adult-cabaret law was halted before enforcement in March 2023 and declared vague and overbroad in June 2023 by Judge Parker, with the Attorney General appealing and oral argument held 1 February 2024. In Blount County, a district attorney's August 2023 threat against a Pride event was enjoined on 1 September 2023 by Judge Greer. The Supreme Court's refusal to hear challenges left the appellate ruling upholding the Act as the operative position, with a further suit still running.

Reporting from April 2021 compared the economic and social effects of Tennessee's bathroom legislation to the 2016 backlash in North Carolina, where similar laws produced corporate and event withdrawals.

66186276B64014601259366.name: Kansas
66186276B64014601259366.summary:
Kansas visitors are subject to Kansas law as well as to the United States federal framework, which the national profile carries. Kansas Senate Bill 244 was enacted on 26 February 2026 through a legislative override of Governor Laura Kelly's veto and took effect immediately.

SB 244 confines trans people to sex-segregated facilities matching sex assigned at birth. The Human Rights Campaign records that the restriction covers public buildings including schools, universities, airports and government offices. The ACLU of Kansas states that the law creates new civil and criminal penalties, and the statute sets fines of up to $1,000 for using a gender-segregated facility in a publicly owned building when the user's gender does not match sex assigned at birth. It also authorises any private individual to sue for at least $1,000 over a bathroom or locker-room encounter with a trans person, a private-enforcement provision that has no parallel in neighbouring jurisdictions.

A legal-risk assessment published on 20 February 2026 moved Kansas from its "Worst Laws" tier to "Do Not Travel", the first state added to that tier in a year. The reclassification follows the private-suit provision and the exposure it creates for a trans person moving through the state, including interstate transit through Kansas airports and government buildings.

Identity documents are the second exposure. SB 244 bars trans people from updating a driver's licence or state ID and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. Documents must be reissued at the holder's expense with no grace period, and holders receive surrender letters warning of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential. The ACLU of Kansas reports that the Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice and that many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.

Two trans men filed Doe v. State of Kansas within days of SB 244's enactment, represented by the ACLU of Kansas and Ballard Spahr in Douglas County District Court, citing fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation provisions. The challenge was still pending as of the sources' reporting, so the operative position of the law should be checked before travel.

The document restrictions follow three years of litigation. Senate Bill 180, enacted in April 2023 over Governor Kelly's veto, defined biological sex in state law and barred agencies from recognising genders beyond sex assigned at birth; the attorney general then directed that new or updated driver's licences and birth certificates reflect only sex assigned at birth. A temporary restraining order blocked gender-marker changes, the Kansas Court of Appeals reversed unanimously on 13 June 2025 for lack of evidence of irreparable harm to law-enforcement identification, and the Kansas Supreme Court declined an appeal in October 2025, allowing the Department of Revenue to continue processing changes until SB 244 ended them.

Discrimination protections survive at state level. Kansas law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020, following Bostock v. Clayton County and Kansas Human Rights Commission action in August 2020 covering businesses with four or more employees. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, so a bias-motivated assault against a trans person carries no state-level enhancement.

Gender-affirming care for minors under 18 has been banned since Senate Bill 63 was overridden on 18 February 2025. In May 2026 State District Judge Carl Folsom III granted a temporary injunction blocking enforcement in an ACLU-backed parental lawsuit, so the ban is not being enforced while that case proceeds.

Marriage is not restricted by gender. Same-sex marriage became available after U.S. District Judge Daniel D. Crabtree ruled the state ban unconstitutional on 4 November 2014, effective 12 November 2014, and became fully legal under Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, replacing the prior statutory and constitutional bans on same-sex marriage and other unions. A trans visitor's marriage is recognised on the same terms.

66186276B69138566591314.name: Mississippi
66186276B69138566591314.summary:
Mississippi stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Within Mississippi itself, the state's own legal regime is among the most restrictive in the country: the Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its "Worst Laws Passed" category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people, using a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

Facilities access is restricted by statute. Mississippi enacted public bathroom and facilities bans in 2024 and 2025, and a law signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth." The Movement Advancement Project's equality map tabulates these bans. A 2024 Harrison County dress code requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event.

Earlier legislative attempts went further and failed: in 2024 the "SAFER Act," which would have restricted transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories, and the "Women's Bill of Rights," which would have codified a binary definition of sex determined at birth into state law and curtailed legal recognition of transgender gender identities, both died in the legislature after House and Senate lawmakers failed to reach a compromise by the 29 April 2024 deadline.

Identity documents are a live constraint. From 1 November 2021 to March 2026, a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist allowed driver's licence marker changes; a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth. The Vital Records office issues an amended birth certificate with a new name and gender marker upon certified court order, a medical statement attesting to gender reassignment and a fee, but lists both the updated and original information.

Judicial posture is documented and adverse. On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the trans boy as a "minor female" and cited the 2023 REAP Act as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest. A separate enacted measure prohibits inmate name changes.

Care for minors is banned. The Regulate Experimental Adolescent Procedures (REAP) Act, signed 28 February 2023, bans gender-affirming care for individuals under 18. After its passage, the University of Mississippi Medical Center's TEAM Clinic closed on 30 June 2023, leaving Spectrum: The Other Clinic in Hattiesburg operating virtually as the only LGBTQ+-specializing clinic in the state.

School sports are restricted. SB 2536, signed 11 March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021, bars transgender students from school sports consistent with their gender identity and requires any athlete whose sex is disputed to provide a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA and hormone levels.

Violence against trans women is documented at a rate above the national general-population homicide rate. A July 2026 state-by-state analysis by The Needle, measuring killings of trans women per 100,000 trans women per year from 2008 to 2025 and adjusted for undercounting, records 6.6 such killings per 100,000 annually for Mississippi, above the US general-population homicide rate of 6.0 per 100,000 printed as a comparison line. The analysis's headline finding is that law tiers do not sort violence: both worst-law and safest-law states carry high rates.

Federal prosecution has reached a bias-motivated killing in Mississippi. Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale, prosecuted under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act because Mississippi's 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity.

State non-discrimination law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Federal Title VII, per Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020), prohibits employment discrimination based on gender identity, but that federal floor does not extend to housing or public accommodations. The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523) protects refusal of services based on belief that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics, effective after the Fifth Circuit lifted an injunction on 23 June 2017.

Local ordinances offer partial cover. Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville protect city employees only.

Marriage and relationship recognition follow the national position: same-sex marriage has been recognised since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, overriding Mississippi's 1996 executive order, 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 1, which remain unrepealed. Mississippi's sodomy statute originating in 1839, carrying up to ten years' imprisonment, remains on the books unenforceable since Lawrence v. Texas (2003), and persons convicted before 2003 are still required to register as sex offenders under the 1995 registration law.

The state/province enacted public bathroom and facilities bans in 2024 and 2025, and a law signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth." 66186276B83300161667341.summary:
Oklahoma is a state within the United States, so a visitor stands under the federal framework described in the national record. Within that framework, Oklahoma's own laws are among the most restrictive in the country for a transgender visitor. The Movement Advancement Project's national tracker (25 March 2026) lists Oklahoma among states banning transgender people from bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity in K-12 schools, with enactments in 2022 and again in 2025. Senate Bill 615, signed in May 2022, requires transgender students and staff to use school bathrooms, changing rooms and similar facilities matching sex assigned at birth per original birth certificate rather than gender identity; this law is linked to the 2024 death of 16-year-old non-binary student Nex Benedict shortly after being beaten in a school bathroom.

On 1 August 2023 Governor Kevin Stitt signed an executive order defining male and female as biological sexes assigned at birth for all state and legal purposes, expressly applying to bathrooms and changing rooms in state-owned facilities, sports, domestic violence shelters, rape crisis centers, incarceration, and statistics collection. The order requires state agencies to define female, woman, girl and mother as a person whose biological reproductive system is designed to produce ova and male, man, boy and father as a person whose biological reproductive system is designed to fertilize the ova of a female, restricting legal recognition of transgender people for state agency purposes including women's spaces.

Identity documents are tightly restricted. Transgender Oklahomans could previously change birth certificates upon court order and driver's licenses upon notarized physician statement of permanent and irreversible transition, and in October 2021 Oklahoma became the 14th state to allow a non-binary birth-certificate option in Kit Vivien Loreleid v. Oklahoma State Department of Health, but in November 2021 Stitt ordered the health department to block any gender-marker changes, and in April 2022 Senate Bill 1100 limited birth certificates to male or female only and banned any other markers effective immediately. House Bill 1225, requiring a male or female designation on Oklahoma birth certificates and prohibiting changes with very little exception, passed its most recent vote 70-17 and headed to Governor Kevin Stitt's desk as of 6 May 2026, still pending his signature; authors said it is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in federal court by transgender plaintiffs including Tulsa resident Rowan Fowler, and the state Attorney General's office confirmed the bill clarifies that Oklahoma never permitted gender birth-certificate changes, while critics called it further discrimination. In October 2026 the Oklahoma Supreme Court ruled retroactively that changing a birth certificate gender marker was never legal, even to correct a cisgender person's error.

Healthcare access is restricted. An October 2022 law bans government funding to Oklahoma hospitals providing any gender transition services to minors. An April 2023 law signed in May 2023 explicitly bans any gender-affirming healthcare practices on minors, making Oklahoma the 16th restricting state, with a judge declining to block it in October 2023. Senate Bill 904, passed at the end of the 2026 session (77-14 House, 39-8 Senate) and signed 14 May 2026 effective immediately, prohibits use of public funds, Oklahoma Medicaid (SoonerCare) coverage or reimbursement, and state-owned properties and healthcare facilities for gender-affirming surgeries, puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and other medications to delay puberty or develop secondary sex characteristics when affirming a gender identity different from sex assigned at birth, for both minors and adults. Intentional violations by state employees are punishable as a criminal misdemeanor; patients face no penalties. The ban exempts mental health counseling, anxiety and depression medications, precocious puberty treatment, intersex care, treatment of complications from prior gender-affirming care, and emergency treatment to prevent death or major impairment, leaving gender-affirming medical care available only at privately owned facilities paid by private insurance or out-of-pocket without Medicaid. A February 2023 House-passed bill to bar publicly funded entities from providing or allowing gender-affirming care to transgender people of any age and to ban insurance coverage did not pass the Senate and did not become law.

Sports and athletics are restricted: in March 2022 Governor Stitt signed a law barring transgender women and girls from women's and girls' athletic teams at public schools and universities, and in 2022 he signed S.B. 2 prohibiting transgender students from playing school sports consistent with their gender identity and excluding all transgender girls from school athletics.

State statutes provide no discrimination protection based on gender identity. Norman prohibits discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations on gender identity and sexual orientation, while Edmond, Oklahoma City and Tulsa prohibit it only for public (city) employment. Under the June 15, 2020 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County workplace discrimination based on gender identity is illegal under Title VII, though practice may continue because Oklahoma is at-will employment allowing firing without stated reason. State hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act signed October 2009 provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity prosecutable in federal court.

On violence, in 2018 a school in Achille shut down for days after a 12-year-old transgender student received death threats including threats of mutilation, whipping and castration from classmates' parents.

The Erin In The Morning / Stonewall News 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map' (July 2026) assigns Oklahoma a per-state traveller risk grade alongside the other states; the July 2026 edition added a fourth 'Do Not Travel' state and tracked changes to the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier, though the specific grade assigned to Oklahoma is not stated in the source inventory.

66186276B98021244841737.name: Alabama
66186276B98021244841737.summary:
Alabama is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework. Federal passport and visa rules, entry screening, federal custody and detention policy, and federal healthcare and funding measures apply in Alabama as they do elsewhere in the country.

Facility rules are the first thing a trans visitor encounters. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map tabulates state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and records Alabama as enacting such bans in 2022 and 2024. The 2022 statute, House Bill 322, signed on 8 April 2022 as Act No. 2022-290, requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with the gender recorded on their birth certificate, and the state Board of Education codified that rule in September 2022. A March 2024 measure extends the restriction to university facilities. Senate Bill 79, signed in February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and authorises separate single-sex spaces where biology, privacy, safety or fairness are implicated.

The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, citing a bathroom ban carried by the state's 'Don't Say Gay' legislation that reaches college campuses.

Gender-affirming care for minors is a felony in Alabama. The Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act, Senate Bill 184, signed on 8 April 2022 and effective from 8 May 2022, makes it a Class C felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison for a medical provider to supply gender-affirming care, including puberty blockers, hormones or surgery, to anyone under 19. The Eleventh Circuit allowed enforcement on 21 August 2023, and the ban remains in force after the plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025. A trans visitor accompanying a minor, or seeking care for one, is exposed to that prohibition.

Identity documents are closed to most trans people. Alabama permits amendment of birth certificates and driver's licences to a person's current sex only with documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" together with a name change. A January 2021 federal ruling in Corbitt v. Taylor invalidated the surgery requirement, but the Eleventh Circuit reversed it and the requirement stands. On 20 September 2024 the same court ruled that refusal to issue accurate licences did not violate the federal constitution; rehearing was denied on 13 November 2024 and judgment entered on 10 December 2024. Most transgender people cannot obtain an accurate licence and must carry daily identification showing the wrong gender, which the ACLU describes as exposing them to a high risk of harassment and violence during ID checks.

No statewide law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment and bullying. Alabama also has no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare and no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees. A trans visitor has no statewide public-accommodations recourse.

Alabama's hate-crime statute, in force since 1994, covers offences motivated by race, colour, religion, national origin, ethnicity, or physical or mental disability. Gender identity is not covered. Attempts to add sexual orientation failed: House Bill 533 passed the House 46 to 41 in April 2009 but received no Senate vote before adjournment on 15 May 2009, and House Bills 413 in 2016 and 8 in 2017 also failed.

Partner recognition is settled statewide. Eight counties were still refusing all marriage licences in 2017, but the Legislature required recording of marriage certificates in May 2019 and every county began recording for all couples, including couples read as same-sex under birth-sex status, on 29 August 2019. The 1996 Executive Order Number 24, the 1998 statute at Alabama Code § 30-1-19 and the June 2006 constitutional Amendment 774 remain unenforceable.

Violence data for Alabama is incomplete. A July 2026 national analysis drawing on TGEU and Williams Institute data records a killing rate of trans women in Alabama of 3.8 per 100,000 per year, a figure the source itself describes as an undercount floor, calculated on a 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025. Alabama's general homicide rate does not appear in the source material, so the comparison that would show whether this exceeds background violence cannot be made, and the figure should not be read as a measure of severity on its own.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alabama (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since May 8, 2022, Alabama makes it a Class C felony punishable by 10 years in prison for a medical provider to provide gender-affirming care including puberty blockers, hormones, or surgeries to anyone under age 19 under the Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act (SB 184) signed April 8, 2022, enforceable after the 11th Circuit allowed enforcement on August 21, 2023, with the ban remaining in force after plaintiffs withdrew challenge on May 1, 2025. Alabama permits amendment of birth certificates and driver's licenses to current sex only with documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" and name change, after a January 2021 federal ruling invalidating the surgery requirement in Corbitt v. Taylor was reversed by the Eleventh Circuit leaving the requirement standing. Since July 1, 2021, public schools must assign single-sex sports teams by "biological sex," and House Bill 261 signed May 30, 2023 prohibits college and university competition on a team differing from sex assigned at birth even after gender-affirming hormone therapy except co-ed sports. HB322 signed April 8, 2022 as Act No. 2022-290 requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with gender on birth certificate as codified by the Board of Education in September 2022, while a March 2024 bill would ban university bathroom use not aligned with sex assigned at birth, and Senate Bill 79 signed February 2025 declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and allows separate single-sex spaces where biology, privacy, safety or fairness are implicated. State law provides no prohibition on discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment/bullying, no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare, and no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees, with only Birmingham since September 2017 and Montevallo since April 2018 prohibiting all such discrimination and Huntsville, Tuscaloosa and Montgomery providing public-employment protections. Alabama's hate-crime law since 1994 covers only race, color, religion, national origin, ethnicity, or physical or mental disability and does not apply to crimes based on gender identity, though gender identity has been applied to sex under Title VII since 2011 in Eleventh Circuit jurisdiction and the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act signed October 2009 bans such hate crimes federally. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the 2003 Lawrence v. Texas decision striking down sodomy laws, with Alabama Senate Bill 320 passed by the House May 23, 2019 by 101 yes with 3 absent and by the Senate May 28, 2019 by 32 yea with 3 absent repealing the ban on "deviate sexual intercourse" effective September 1, 2019, and the age of consent is 16 with a within-2-years exception extended to same-sex contact in 2019. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide June 26, 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, but eight counties still refused all marriage licenses by 2017, until the Legislature in May 2019 required recording of marriage certificates and all counties began recording for all couples including same-sex couples on August 29, 2019, leaving the 1996 Executive Order Number 24, 1998 statute Alabama Code § 30-1-19, and June 2006 constitutional Amendment 774 unenforceable. Alabama permits adoption by same-sex couples, though the Supreme Court of Alabama in 2002 held homosexual conduct created a strong presumption of parental unfitness as "abhorrent, immoral, detestable," and the May 2017 Child Placing Agency Inclusion Act signed by Governor Kay Ivey protects faith-based agencies refusing placements on religious beliefs. State law does not address discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment/bullying, with only Birmingham and Montevallo ordinances and public-employment protections in Huntsville, Tuscaloosa and Montgomery, though sexual orientation has been applied to sex under Title VII since 2020. Alabama's hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation, after HB533 adding sexual orientation passed the House April 2009 by 46 to 41 but received no full Senate vote before adjournment May 15, 2009 and later HB413 (2016) and HB8 (2017) failed, though the federal Matthew Shepard Act of October 2009 applies. From 1992 to 2021 Alabama law required sexual education to emphasize "that homosexuality is not a lifestyle acceptable to the general public and that homosexual conduct is a criminal offense," repealed in April 2021 after Governor Kay Ivey signed repeal of archaic references to homosexuality and HIV/AIDS.

66186276B82803899326534.name: Indiana
66186276B82803899326534.summary:
Indiana is a state within the United States, and a visitor to Indiana stands under the national framework on travel documents and entry. Indiana's own identity-document regime has tightened sharply. The Bureau of Motor Vehicles' ban on gender-marker changes to driver's licenses and state identification cards took effect on 1 February 2026, ending the long-standing route of obtaining such a change through a court order or physician statement. LGBTQ advocates who testified against the administrative rule change warned that it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents whenever their documents are checked.

Birth certificates are closed as well. Transgender people could change the gender designation on an Indiana birth certificate by court order from 2014 until 2025, when Governor Mike Braun's March 2025 executive order defining sex solely as assigned sex at birth directed the Department of Health to stop updating markers. In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court had already declined, in split votes, to hear two cases seeking birth-certificate changes, leaving in place appeals-court rulings that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One of those cases involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose male birth-certificate designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access. The state's X marker on identification was offered only between March 2019 and January 2020 before rejection following a March 2020 Attorney General opinion that only the General Assembly could authorize non-binary designations.

Facilities access is contested but, as of April 2026, Indiana law imposes no restriction on transgender people using restrooms aligned with their gender identity. Indianapolis and Bloomington ordinances expressly protect such use, and repeated criminal-ban proposals since 2021 have died in committee. An August 2023 Seventh Circuit decision upheld a preliminary injunction barring schools from limiting transgender students' bathroom use pending litigation. Senate Bill 182, which would designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in public K-12 schools and state universities for use only by males or females based on reproductive biology at birth, passed the Indiana Senate on 27 January 2026 by a 37-8 party-line vote; it would also define sex and gender in statute, permanently bar birth-certificate amendments, restrict housing in prisons by birth sex, and restrict school and university sleeping facilities. The bill received no House hearing. Opponents including GenderNexus argued that its private right of action for anyone "directly or indirectly injured" would encourage harassment-style enforcement.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. Senate Bill 480, signed in April 2023 under an emergency clause, prohibits physicians from providing gender transition procedures to anyone under 18 or aiding such care, with a phase-out for existing patients; it was temporarily enjoined on 16 June 2023, took effect 27 February 2024 after a stay, and was upheld in November 2024 as a ban on surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy. House Bill 1569, signed April 2023 and effective 1 July 2023, bars use of state or federal funds for sexual reassignment surgery for incarcerated patients, exempting approvals granted before that date.

Indiana's hate-crimes law, enacted 3 April 2019, makes intent to harm or intimidate based on perceived or actual characteristics, including gender identity, an aggravating circumstance permitting enhanced sentences; before it, Indiana tracked bias crimes without sentencing enhancement. Employment protection for state workers on gender identity rests on 2004 and 2005 executive orders rather than statute, supplemented by county and city ordinances in Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe and Vanderburgh counties. The April 2015 RFRA clarification bars denial of services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation based on gender identity. Same-sex marriage has been recognized in Indiana since October 2014.

Erin In The Morning's February 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map places Indiana among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, citing the 2026 identification policy and bathroom-ban escalation as drivers of adult risk.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indiana (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender persons could change legal gender on Indiana birth certificates with a court order from 2014 until 2025, when Governor Mike Braun's March 2025 executive order defining sex solely as assigned sex at birth directed the Department of Health to stop updating gender markers, a policy extended by the Bureau of Motor Vehicles in February 2026 to prohibit gender-marker changes on driver's licenses despite pushback and challenged by an ACLU lawsuit. An "X" marker is no longer offered, having only been available from March 2019 to January 2020 upon presentation of an amended birth certificate or physician's statement confirming permanent gender change before rejection after public hearing and a March 2020 Attorney General opinion that only the General Assembly could authorize non-binary designations. As of April 2026 state law imposes no restriction on transgender people using restrooms aligned with gender identity, with Indianapolis and Bloomington ordinances expressly protecting such use, while repeated criminal-ban proposals since 2021 died in committee and an August 2023 Seventh Circuit decision upheld a preliminary injunction barring schools from limiting transgender students' bathroom use pending litigation. A 2026 Senate Bill 182 to define gender as sex assigned at birth, permanently ban birth-certificate changes, bar placement in prisons misaligned with birth sex, and restrict school and university bathrooms and sleeping facilities passed the Senate but received no House hearing. Senate Bill 480 passed March 2023 and signed April 2023 by Governor Eric Holcomb under emergency clause prohibits physicians from providing gender transition procedures to persons under 18 or aiding such care, with a phase-out for existing patients, temporarily enjoined June 16, 2023 but effective February 27, 2024 after stay and upheld November 2024 to ban surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors. House Bill 1569 signed April 2023 effective July 1, 2023 bans use of state or federal funds for sexual reassignment surgery for offender patients in prisons, exempting approvals before that date. House Bill 1608 signed May 2023 prohibits classroom instruction on human sexuality in kindergarten through third grade and compels schools to notify a parent in writing if a non-emancipated minor requests use of a different name, pronoun or title. Employment protection for state workers based on gender identity and expression rests on 2004 and 2005 executive orders rather than statute, supplemented by county and city ordinances in Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe, Vanderburgh and numerous cities, an April 2015 RFRA clarification barring denial of services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation based on gender identity, and an April 2019 hate-crimes law allowing enhanced sentences for crimes motivated by perceived or actual characteristics including gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1976 effective July 1, 1977 with age of consent 16 after history including death penalty for sodomy and later 2-14 year penalties, and a 1977 House committee rejected 6-4 reinstating consensual sodomy as felony. Same-sex marriages have been recognized and performed since October 2014 when a federal district ruling declaring the ban unconstitutional took effect after the U.S. Supreme Court refused appeal in Baskin v. Bogan on October 6, 2014, ending annual amendment efforts since 2004. On April 4, 2017 the Seventh Circuit ruled 8-3 in Hively v. Ivy Tech that employment discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the prohibition on sex discrimination in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, binding in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin, though Indiana statutes still omit sexual orientation as a protected category. State-level workplace protection rests on 2004 and 2005 executive orders covering state employees, while Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe, Vanderburgh counties and many cities prohibit employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and Lake County, Fort Wayne and Whitestown do so on that basis alone. The March 26, 2015 Religious Freedom Restoration Act drew boycott threats and protests alleging targeting of LGBT rights and was clarified April 2, 2015 to provide that it does not authorize providers to refuse services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation based on sexual orientation. Indiana tracked bias crimes including sexual-orientation bias since 2003 without sentencing enhancement until the April 3, 2019 hate-crimes law making intent to harm or intimidate based on perceived or actual characteristics an aggravating circumstance allowing harsher sentences for sexual-orientation-motivated crimes, also covered federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act. In May 2023 the governor signed a law barring city and county governments from enacting conversion-therapy bans by ordinance or executive order, effectively keeping the practice legal statewide.

66186276B31593004124297.name: Utah
66186276B31593004124297.summary:
Utah regulates where transgender people may use restrooms and locker rooms. HB 257, signed by Governor Spencer Cox on 30 January 2024, requires people to use bathrooms and locker rooms in public schools and government-owned buildings according to sex assigned at birth. The law does not apply to private businesses. A person challenged under the statute may defend themselves by presenting documentation: a birth certificate, and, where the marker has been changed, proof of gender-affirming surgery. New government buildings must include single-occupant bathrooms. By the time of signing, at least 10 other states had enacted comparable bathroom-regulation laws.

Utah operates a reporting mechanism under HB 257. A state form allows residents to report transgender people using 'privacy spaces' such as changing rooms and restrooms; complainants may choose whether their names are included while the state investigates each reported violation. A May 2024 procedure permits officials and individuals to file formal complaints about suspected incorrect bathroom use in schools and government buildings. The ACLU of Utah opposed the bill on the ground that it risks discriminatory enforcement.

Utah restricts transgender students' housing. In 2024 the state passed a bill banning transgender students from dorms aligned with their gender identity, following an incident in which a transgender woman was assigned to a girls' dorm at Utah State University.

Utah bans gender-affirming care for minors. Legislation passed by the House on 26 January 2023 and the Senate 20-8 on 27 January was signed on 28 January 2023 with immediate effect. Continuation of care was permitted only for youth already receiving it in January 2023. Doctors may provide such care to persons aged 18 to 24, but those patients retain a retroactive right to disaffirm consent and sue. A legislative legal review found the ban potentially unconstitutional for targeting transgender people. A two-year systematic review released in May 2025, commissioned under the ban, concluded that the treatments are effective for mental health and psychosocial outcomes and for body changes consistent with affirmed gender, and safe regarding bone density, cardiovascular risk, metabolic changes and cancer; the legislature dismissed the findings and kept the ban in place.

Utah restricts transgender athletes' participation in sport. House Bill 11, banning transgender athletes from sports, athletics and the Olympics, passed in March 2022 and was vetoed by Governor Spencer Cox on 22 March 2022; the Legislature overrode the veto to take effect 1 July, and a judge partly reversed it on 19 August, allowing transgender girls to be considered case-by-case for girls' sports in 2022-2023. On 3 October 2024, Southern Utah University and Utah State University forfeited matches against San Jose State University amid litigation over a transgender player under NCAA sport-by-sport eligibility and testosterone standards.

Utah restricts display of LGBTQ+ flags. On 7 May 2025 the state became the first to explicitly prohibit flying LGBTQ+ flags at government buildings and schools, with fines of $500 a day; a March 2025 law had already banned LGBTQ pride flags on public schools and government buildings. Utah Pride's executive director said the state 'leads the nation in anti-LGBTQ legislation.' In May 2025 Salt Lake City adopted the Sego Visibility Flag, based on the transgender pride flag, as an official city flag.

Identity documents in Utah are comparatively open. Transgender people may amend the gender marker on a birth certificate by submitting a certified court order changing name and gender, without requiring sex reassignment surgery; an 'X' descriptor is available subject to judicial approval. In May 2021 the Utah Supreme Court held 4-1 that judges must grant such sex and name changes when clinical requirements are met.

Utah provides statutory non-discrimination and hate-crime protection with gaps. SB 296, passed by the Senate 23-5 on 6 March 2015, approved by the House 65-10 on 11 March and signed 12 March 2015, bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment and housing but not public accommodations, and exempts religious organizations and affiliates including schools and hospitals. The hate-crime statute amended in 2019 (Senate 18-11 on 5 March, House 64-9 on 12 March, Senate concurrence 22-3, signed 2 April) criminalizes hate crimes based on gender identity and requires collection and publication of hate-crime statistics.

Utah prohibits conversion therapy on minors. The prohibition was established by Governor Gary Herbert's executive order of 21 January 2020 and codified by legislation passed in February 2023 covering LGBT minors, while exempting clergy, religious counselors, parents and grandparents unless acting as psychologists.

66186276B22881275445497.name: North Dakota
66186276B22881275445497.summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework in every respect that governs a trans visitor's documents, screening and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F according to supporting documents, and leaves previously issued X-marker passports valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. On 5 February 2025 an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Within North Dakota itself, the legislative record is among the most restrictive for transgender adults. Erin Reed's July 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessment map, built from five years of daily legislative tracking, lists North Dakota among "the worst states" for legislation targeting transgender adults and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates, forcing trans people to out themselves when showing documents.

North Dakota's 2023 law bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states; the Movement Advancement Project marks North Dakota a "negative law" state on its identity-document tracker. Accompanying regulations to the May 2023 bill were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation. By contrast, the North Dakota Department of Transportation updates driver licence and state ID gender markers upon receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating the applicant completed a permanent gender role transition.

Facilities and schools are also regulated. An April 2023 law, signed by the Governor and effective 1 July 2023, explicitly allows restriction of transgender individuals' public bathroom usage in many state-run facilities. House Bill 1522 (2023), an act creating new sections of the North Dakota Century Code relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student, carries a penalty provision and an emergency clause; it was signed by the governor with the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023. A May 2023 law effective 1 July forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use but requires disclosure and outing of transgender students to parents in state-run schools.

Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a North Dakota bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023. Transgender girls were targeted by 2021 legislation banning participation in girls' school sports teams, passed 69 to 25 in the House and 27 to 20 in the Senate and vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on 21 April 2021, followed in April 2023 by two bills signed into law banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and higher education respectively.

Discrimination protections are thin. North Dakota statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, though Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) established that Title VII protects employees from workplace discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Limited city-level protections exist in Grand Forks for city employees and applicants and in rental housing from 2013. An April 2021 state law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students. State hate crime law does not cover gender identity, though federal law since the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act allows federal prosecution for crimes based on gender identity. A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counselors.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, and adoption by individuals is permitted with no express ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, though state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate based on sincerely held religious belief. A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found 78 percent of residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity while 22 percent were opposed.

66186276B38006515706420.name: South Dakota
66186276B38006515706420.summary:
South Dakota stands under the national framework of the United States, and that federal layer carries the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad.

State law now restricts facility use as well. Governor Larry Rhoden's office announced on Friday 21 March 2025 that he had signed House Bill 1259 the previous day, barring trans people from restrooms matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings. The measure took effect on 1 July 2025 and marks the first time a restriction of this kind has been placed on the books in South Dakota; comparable legislation failed in 2016, in 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022.

House Bill 1259 passed the South Dakota House of Representatives by a 49-21 vote and limits restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in state-run facilities to the same 'biological sex.' Its institutional scope reaches K-12 schools and state colleges, including off-campus activities, as well as prisons and other state facilities. The bill's 'reasonable accommodation' clause and the floor debate over it raised the prospect that incarcerated trans people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply with the law.

South Dakota is listed among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults in Erin Reed's July 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessment for transgender travellers, compiled from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric identifying the most damaging bills. Federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.
