sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Dakota (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: South Dakota law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination on the basis of gender identity, though federal Title VII protection was established by Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020, and Oglala Lakota County and the cities of Sioux Falls, Vermillion and Brookings provide limited public-employee or comprehensive employment, housing and public-accommodations protections, with Brookings acting in March 2018. A March 2021 law signed by Governor Kristi Noem allows businesses to deny goods or services to LGBTQ people based on owners' purported religious beliefs, and in 2024 the Transformation Project won a discrimination lawsuit against the state. South Dakota hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, but federal prosecution has been available since the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act, and in September 2019 the Oglala Sioux Tribal Council passed hate-crime legislation protecting LGBT and two-spirit individuals by 14-2-1. For identity documents, the article states both a March 2026 Supreme Court of South Dakota ruling banning change of sex on a birth certificate unless an error was made at birth and a procedure allowing legal gender change via court order, photo ID, application and fee for birth certificates and via court order or physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery for driver's licenses and state IDs. Gender-affirming healthcare for persons under 18 was banned by House Bill 1080 passed in February 2023 and signed February 13, 2023, requiring prior puberty-blocker or hormone treatment to be systematically reduced ending no later than December 31, 2023, and authorizing suits by affected persons until age 25 or within three years of discovering injury. A March 2016 bill requiring transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching birth sex was vetoed by Governor Dennis Daugaard, while House Bill 1108 barring K-7 instruction on gender identity and expression passed the House February 12, 2019 but failed in the Senate on March 29, 2019 adjournment. Transgender participation in female school sports was restricted by executive order in March 2021 after Governor Noem declined to sign a broader legislative ban over college-sports concerns, followed by a statutory ban signed February 4, 2022 effective July 1, 2022, with ACLU federal litigation threatened. Private adult consensual non-commercial same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976 after prior Dakota Territory criminal bans dating to 1862 with penalties up to life imprisonment, later ten years, expanded in 1910 in State v. Whitmarsh to include fellatio, with current age of consent at fifteen after initial thirteen. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since June 26, 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, superseding a November 2006 constitutional amendment and statutes defining marriage as man-woman and barring other recognition, following Rosenbrahn v. Daugaard filed May 22, 2014 where Judge Karen Schreier ruled for plaintiffs January 12, 2015 but stayed pending appeal. Adoption law does not specify rules for single individuals or married same-sex couples, lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilization with non-genetic married mothers recognized after donor insemination, gay male couples may use surrogacy with pre-birth orders, but S.J. 746 enacted May 2017 permits agencies to refuse placements violating religious or moral convictions. No state provision explicitly bars sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations, though Oglala Lakota County, Sioux Falls, Vermillion, Minnehaha County, Spearfish, Watertown and Brookings provide limited public-employee or, in Brookings' March 2018 ordinance, comprehensive protections, while federal Bostock protection applies from June 15, 2020 and a March 2021 law permits religious-based denial of goods or services. State hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation, but federal coverage has existed since 2009 allowing federal prosecution. A 2022 PRRI poll found 63% support for same-sex marriage, 67% support for anti-discrimination laws covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and 62% opposition to religious-based refusal to serve gay and lesbian people.

66186276B10933057601622.summary:
Wyoming has no state law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or credit. As of 12 October 2026 the Movement Advancement Project rates the state's gender-identity policy score at -9 out of 25 and its overall score at -6.5 out of 47, a Negative rating, with the only noted protection being federal recourse for employment discrimination under the June 2020 Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County, pursued through the EEOC and federal courts. Three cities, Jackson, Casper and Laramie, have local ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations; Cheyenne and Gillette prohibit discrimination in city employment on the basis of sexual orientation only.

Facilities access is restricted by statute. On 3 March 2025 Governor Mark Gordon signed House Bill 72, the Protecting Privacy in Public Spaces Act, which passed the House 52-8 on 7 February 2025 and the Senate 25-6. It defines male and female by biological sex, requires public facilities to reserve multi-occupancy restrooms, changing areas and sleeping quarters exclusively for one sex, prohibits entry into a facility not matching biological sex, and took effect 1 July 2025. The only permitted accommodation is one that does not involve opposite-sex access to multi-occupancy facilities. The law creates a private cause of action for a person who encounters an opposite-sex person in a sex-designated restroom or changing area where the facility permitted it or failed to prohibit it, and for a person required by a correctional or educational facility to share sleeping quarters with the opposite sex.

The same day, Governor Gordon signed Senate File 62, Sex-Designated Facilities and Public Schools, which requires public school children from pre-kindergarten upward, including charter school students, to use restrooms and facilities aligned with sex assigned at birth. SF 62 requires districts to provide a reasonable accommodation to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records both facility bans as enacted in March 2025.

Sports participation is barred. Senate File 133, approved by the Wyoming Legislature on 1 March 2023 and becoming law without the governor's signature or veto, bans transgender athletes from competing on any female sports and athletics teams; it took effect 1 July 2023.

Gender-affirming care for minors is prohibited. A bill passed by both houses in March 2024 and signed by the governor bans sex reassignment surgery and gender-affirming care on children, taking effect 1 July 2024.

Changing identity documents is possible but onerous. A gender-marker change on a Wyoming birth certificate requires sex reassignment surgery and a court order stating that sex has been changed, submitted to Vital Statistics Services with a letter requesting the change, a photocopy of current identification, a certified copy of the court order, and a doctor's letter confirming the surgery was performed. Correcting the gender marker on a driver's licence or state ID requires a completed Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and by a physician, therapist, counsellor, psychiatric social worker or other medical or social service provider confirming gender identity.

Wyoming has no state hate crime law. Federal coverage under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009 does extend to crimes motivated by gender identity. A state obscenity-material law affecting certain LGBT books was enforced in October 2021, when the district attorney and sheriff's office in Gillette charged a librarian.

A July 2026 legal-risk assessment by Erin Reed, based on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric identifying the worst bills, lists Wyoming among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults; it was republished on 27 August 2026 by a regional LGBTQ outlet.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wyoming (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Wyoming state statutes do not address discrimination based on gender identity, but the United States Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v Clayton County protects LGBT employees from workplace discrimination under federal law, and the cities of Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations. Wyoming has no state hate crime law, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009 expanded the federal definition to include gender identity. Changing the gender marker on a Wyoming birth certificate requires undergoing sex reassignment surgery and obtaining a court order stating sex has been changed, with submission to Vital Statistics Services of a letter requesting the change, a photocopy of current ID, a certified copy of the court order, and a doctor letter confirming surgery was performed. Correction of the gender marker on a driver's license or state ID requires a completed Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and a physician, therapist or counselor, psychiatric social worker or other medical or social service provider confirming gender identity. A bill passed in March 2023 explicitly bans transgender athletes from playing on any female sports and athletics teams, which became law without the governor's signature or veto and took effect July 1, 2023. A bill passed by both houses in March 2024 explicitly bans sexual reassignment surgery and gender-affirming care on children, which the governor signed to take effect July 1. House Bill 72 signed in April 2025 requires all public restrooms in the state to be segregated by biological sex and takes effect July 1, 2025. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since Wyoming decriminalized consensual sodomy in February 1977, with common-law liability for anal intercourse abrogated in 1982, and the age of consent for all consensual sexual activity is 17. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since October 21, 2014 after state officials declined to appeal the October 17 federal decision in Guzzo v Mead finding the ban unconstitutional, replacing a statutory ban in place since 1977 and made more explicit in 2003, under which legal relationships of same-sex couples had been recognized only for divorce. A 2013 domestic partnership bill to provide immediate-family rights was approved 7-2 in House committee on January 28 but rejected 24-35 by the full House on January 30. Married same-sex couples are permitted to adopt and lesbian couples can access in vitro fertilization, with state law recognizing the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status. State law does not authorize or prohibit gestational surrogacy contracts leaving review case-by-case, and an August 2021 law explicitly legalizing surrogacy contracts uses the terms mother and father instead of parent or parents to exclude single people and same-sex couples. State statutes do not address discrimination based on sexual orientation, with prohibitory bills rejected by the House on January 31, 2011 and by the Senate 15-13 on January 31, 2013, and bill SF 115 approved 24-6 by the Senate and 6-2 in House committee in February 2015 but rejected 26-33 by the House on February 24, 2015. Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering sexual orientation in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Cheyenne and Gillette prohibit city employment discrimination on sexual orientation only, and federal Bostock protections apply to sexual orientation in the workplace. Wyoming has no state hate crime law following hot debate after the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard near Laramie, but the federal 2009 Act covers sexual orientation, and a state obscenity-material law affecting certain LGBT books was enforced in October 2021 when a Gillette librarian was charged by the district attorney and sheriff office.

66186276B64762166704956.name: West Virginia
66186276B64762166704956.summary:
Every visitor to West Virginia stands first under the federal travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. A trans or nonbinary visitor can therefore arrive holding papers that do not match their presentation, with airport screening and visa decisions following the same national rules, including the February 2025 State Department policy refusing visas to trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud.

West Virginia's own facility restriction is statutory. Governor Patrick Morrisey signed Senate Bill 456, the 'Riley Gaines Act,' on 12 March 2025, after the state Senate passed it on 3 March and the House of Delegates passed it on 6 March. The statute defines 'woman' as an adult human of the female sex and 'man' as an adult human of the male sex and aims to preserve women's single-sex spaces, covering locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centers, dormitories, prisons, and domestic violence shelters. At the signing, Morrisey said bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centers 'should be kept private for women only.' The Movement Advancement Project equality map cataloguing state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity is the source for West Virginia's facility-ban enumeration.

National risk gradings place West Virginia near the top of the risk scale. The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map (Erin In The Morning, published 27 August 2026) places West Virginia in 'The Worst States' group (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY), one tier below 'Do Not Travel' (FL, ID, KS, TX), within a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'. Idaho was promoted to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban, which carries up to 5 years and is partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in West Virginia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since March 2025 West Virginia law recognizes only male and female exclusively under the enacted Riley Gaines Act, which does not recognize transgender or non-binary persons after genital-examination language was deleted before signing by Governor Morrisey. Transgender individuals may change gender markers on birth certificates upon submitting a Birth Certificate Request Form with a court order for gender change and fees to Vital Registration, and on driver's licenses and IDs upon submitting a Gender Designation Form signed by a licensed physician without required surgery or sterilization, though in July 2020 the West Virginia Supreme Court upheld Wood County Circuit Court's denial of a marker change even after sexual reassignment surgery. House Bill 3293 passed March 2021 and effective July 1 restricts transgender athletes from teams aligning with gender identity by defining male and female solely on reproductive biology and genetics at birth, with a July 2021 federal order allowing a transgender girl to join cross-country, a January 5 2023 federal ruling upholding the ban, April 2023 Supreme Court declination, April 2024 Fourth Circuit holding the ban unconstitutional in West Virginia v. B.P.J., and July 2025 Supreme Court agreement to hear the case. A March 2023 law effective January 1 2024 bans puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery for transgender minors except for severe dysphoria diagnosed by at least two physicians, while a 1997 Medicaid ban on sexual reassignment surgery was ruled unconstitutional in August 2022 requiring coverage, overturned in 2026 by the Fourth Circuit as not irrational to refuse funding, with Anderson v. Crouch challenging adult Medicaid exclusion argued December 9 2025. An April 2025 bill passed by both houses and awaiting gubernatorial action would require teachers and principals to immediately out transgender, non-binary and intersex students to parents and guardians. State statutes provide no discrimination protection on gender identity, though Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15 2020 protects LGBT employees under Title VII, fifteen listed cities maintain ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations plus county and city employee protections in Kanawha County, Buckhannon and Elkins, while a March 2023 religious-refusal law permits businesses to refuse LGBTQ customers with qualified immunity and a March 2025 Senate 25-8 bill to nullify all city and county LGBTQ anti-discrimination ordinances awaits House vote. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since repeal of the sodomy law in March 1976, after an 1863 inherited buggery law punishing anal intercourse with one to five years, a failed 1917 House-passed extension to oral sex, and a 1930 revision creating crimes against nature punishing homosexual or heterosexual sodomy with one to ten years without distinguishing consensual status or privacy, enforced in only four recorded cases with three overturned. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since October 9 2014 when Attorney General Patrick Morrisey ceased defending the ban and Governor Earl Ray Tomblin directed agencies to comply with federal rulings, despite an unrepealed statute defining marriage as between a man and a woman, failed constitutional bans voted down 67-30 in 2009 and on discharge 68-30 in 2010, a 2011 civil-unions bill dying in 2012, and McGee v. Cole filed October 1 2013 by Lambda Legal and stayed June 10 2014 pending Bostic v. Schaefer. Married same-sex couples may adopt, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization, state law recognizes a married non-genetic non-gestational mother after donor insemination, and gestational and traditional surrogacy are valid with equal treatment of different-sex and same-sex couples. State statutes address no discrimination on sexual orientation, with a Senate-passed March 2009 bill killed by the House and reintroductions stalled in 2010, 2011 and 2013 and a February 2021 bill sent to House Judiciary, while federal Bostock protection applies and fifteen cities plus county and city employee policies provide sexual-orientation protections subject to the 2023 religious-refusal law allowing refusal of LGBTQ customers and the 2025 nullification effort. Same-sex couples receive hospital visitation through a designated visitor statute. There are no statewide conversion-therapy laws, with Charleston banning the practice by 14-9 in August 2021 and Morgantown by 7-0 in October 2021.

66186276B86295910312663.name: Arkansas
66186276B86295910312663.summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents, and adds its own state-level restrictions. A bathroom bill became law on 11 April 2023 as Act 619, making Arkansas the fourth state to restrict transgender students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender identity; the law was amended and extended in 2025, and the Movement Advancement Project's equality-map citations record HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025. Act 619 of 11 April 2023 separately creates a misdemeanour for transgender use of public bathrooms, locker rooms or changing facilities where a minor is present, dependent on intent of arousing or gratifying sexual desire.

Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026 places Arkansas in 'The Worst States' group, one tier below the 'Do Not Travel' designation given to Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas. The grading reflects the state's own body of anti-trans law rather than any federal measure.

Arkansas was the first state, in 2021, to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, after the legislature overrode the governor's veto. HB 1570, banning puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery for under-18s, was vetoed on 5 April 2021 as overbroad and extreme but overridden on 6 April 2021; it was blocked and then struck down on 20 June 2023 by Judge James M. Moody Jr. for discrimination and constitutional violations, before the Eighth Circuit overturned that ruling on 12 August 2025 and allowed enforcement, citing United States v. Skrmetti. Litigation over the 2021 care ban continues, and a federal judge enjoined it for 'irreparable harm' to minors while litigation was ongoing.

Identity documents at state level have narrowed. Arkansas has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981, when Senate Bill 256, the Arkansas Vital Statistics Act, passed 34-0 in the Senate and 92-0 in the House on 19 February 1981, codifying a surgery-based pathway requiring court order verifying sex reassignment surgery and a name change. Identity documents with an X sex descriptor were available from December 2010, but in March 2024 the Department of Finance and Administration rescinded X descriptors for driver's licences.

Arkansas law does not address discrimination based on gender identity, leaving protection only through the 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County nationwide ban. Little Rock, Conway, Hot Springs, North Little Rock and Pulaski County bar gender-identity discrimination in public employment, while the comprehensive ordinances in Eureka Springs and Fayetteville are unenforced under the Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act; the Arkansas Supreme Court struck down Fayetteville's ordinance in February 2017.

Arkansas has no hate-crime penalty-enhancement statute, and its civil remedy for intimidation, harassment, violence or property damage covers only racial, religious or ethnic animosity, not gender identity. The April 2021 state hate-crimes law, signed effective immediately, excludes sexual orientation or gender identity explicitly or implicitly. Federal law has covered gender identity since October 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Act.

SB 289, signed 26 March by Governor Asa Hutchinson and effective immediately, allows medical practitioners to cite religious beliefs to deny healthcare to LGBT patients. In March 2021 the Legislature passed a ban on transgender athletes in sports, signed 25 March and effective immediately; ESPN records it as enacted 25 March 2021, prohibiting transgender women and girls from competing on school sports teams consistent with their gender identity across K-12 and collegiate sports, and allowing a student or school claiming harm to sue a school for violation.

In March 2023 the Legislature passed a gender-affirming litigation bill, signed 13 March 2023 by Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, allowing those who received such care as minors to sue providers 15 years after turning 18, versus two years for other care. On 21 March 2023 a law prohibiting trans people from using public school bathrooms matching gender was signed, making Arkansas the fourth such state.

66186276B76680759932915.name: Ohio
66186276B76680759932915.summary:
Ohio is one of sixteen states placed in the second-highest risk tier, "The Worst States," in Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026, below the four "Do Not Travel" states. The assessment grades Ohio under a national frame of "Worst Policies In Effect."

Ohio's facility law, Senate Bill 104, the "Protect All Students Act," was signed by Governor Mike DeWine on 27 November 2024 and took effect 25 February 2025. It requires all K-12 schools, colleges and universities, public and private, to designate bathrooms, locker rooms, changing rooms, shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females based on sex assigned at or near birth, with single-occupancy restrooms with controlled use as the only exception. The governor signed the bill out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil-rights groups; the sponsor was Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino. The law contains no enforcement mechanism.

House Bill 8, signed 8 January 2025, requires educators, counselors and other school staff to out LGBTQ students to parents and bars "sexual content," including undefined "gender ideology," from kindergarten through third-grade curriculum, with parental opt-out.

Ohio statutes do not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, but gender-identity discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since 19 December 2018, and 33 Ohio cities and counties have ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations. The Sixth Circuit held on 7 March 2018 that transgender-status discrimination is sex discrimination under Title VII.

Amendment of the gender marker on an Ohio birth certificate was barred under the 1987 In re Ladrach decision, challenged by four transgender Ohioans in March 2018, and invalidated as unconstitutional by federal Judge Michael H. Watson in Ray v. McCloud in December 2020. Corrections have been officially allowed since 1 June 2021 after no appeal, though some counties continue to refuse them.

Transgender people can change name and gender on Ohio driver's licences via court order and a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist, with an X option available since April 2022. In August 2026 the Bureau of Motor Vehicles announced rules allowing only male or female markers and requiring an exact-matching birth certificate or passport.

HB68, the Saving Adolescents from Experimentation Act, passed 13 December 2023, bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bars transgender girls and women from women's high-school and college sports. It was vetoed on 29 December 2023, then enacted by House override on 10 January 2024 and Senate override on 24 January 2024. It was blocked in April 2024, allowed to take effect in August 2024 after a court found the regulation of transgender individuals a legitimate state interest, and re-enjoined on 18 March 2025 by the 10th District Court of Appeals, with Attorney General Dave Yost vowing an appeal. The operative position should be checked before travel.

Adult-care rules adopted in January 2024 would have required perpetual psychiatric counseling, an endocrinologist relationship, bioethicist approval and 30-day reporting of gender dysphoria; they were dropped in February 2024.

In January 2024 transgender candidate Vanessa Joy was stripped from the ballot for failing to disclose her deadname under a seldom-enforced law, and three of four transgender state-office candidates were challenged or disqualified.

Same-sex marriage has been legally recognised in Ohio since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, invalidating the 2004 Defense of Marriage Act and 2004 Issue 1 constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman.

There is no statewide conversion-therapy law after failed bills in 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2021, but seven or more cities ban it for minors, including Cincinnati (December 2015), Toledo, Columbus, Dayton and Athens (2017), Lakewood and Kent (2018), and Cleveland, Cleveland Heights, Akron and Reynoldsburg (2022).

sources.summary: Ohio statutes do not address discrimination on account of gender identity, but gender-identity discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since December 19, 2018, discrimination on the basis of transgender status was held to be sex discrimination under Title VII by the Sixth Circuit on March 7, 2018, workplace discrimination on the basis of gender identity was barred nationally by Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020, and 33 Ohio cities and counties have ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations. Senate Bill 104 signed November 27, 2024 bans transgender students from sex-segregated bathrooms, locker rooms and overnight accommodations except for single-occupancy restrooms with controlled use. House Bill 8 signed January 8, 2025 requires educators, counselors and other school staff to out LGBTQ students to parents and bans "sexual content" including undefined "gender ideology" from Kindergarten through 3rd grade curriculum with parental opt-out. Amendment of gender marker on Ohio birth certificates was barred under 1987 In re Ladrach, challenged by four transgender Ohioans in March 2018, invalidated as unconstitutional by federal Judge Michael H. Watson in Ray v. McCloud in December 2020, and officially allowed after June 1, 2021 after no appeal, though some counties continue to refuse corrections. Transgender people can change name and gender on driver's licenses via court order and a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist with an X option since April 2022, but in August 2026 the BMV announced rules allowing only male or female markers and requiring an exact-matching birth certificate or passport. HB68 Saving Adolescents from Experimentation Act passed December 13, 2023 bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bans transgender girls and women from women's high-school and college sports, was vetoed December 29, 2023 and enacted by House override January 10, 2024 and Senate override January 24, 2024, was blocked in April 2024, allowed to take effect in August 2024 after a court found the regulation of transgender individuals to be a legitimate state interest, and re-enjoined March 18, 2025 by the 10th District Court of Appeals with Attorney General Dave Yost vowing appeal, while January 5, 2024 adult-care rules requiring perpetual psychiatric counseling, endocrinologist relationship, bioethicist approval and 30-day reporting of gender dysphoria were dropped in February 2024. In January 2024 transgender candidate Vanessa Joy was stripped from the ballot for failing to disclose her deadname under a seldom-enforced law, with three of four transgender state-office candidates challenged or disqualified. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1974 after Ohio became the eighth state to repeal its sodomy statute in 1972, the Supreme Court of Ohio unanimously overturned conviction for same-sex solicitation as facially invalid in May 2002, Ohio repealed its anti-gay importuning law in 2003, and Lawrence v. Texas abolished remaining sodomy laws June 26, 2003. Same-sex marriage has been legally recognized since June 26, 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, invalidating the 2004 Defense of Marriage Act and 2004 Issue 1 constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman. Ohio statutes do not address discrimination on account of sexual orientation, but sexual-orientation discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since January 21, 2011, workplace discrimination was barred nationally by Bostock on June 15, 2020, and 33 cities and counties plus additional housing-only jurisdictions provide sexual-orientation protections. Domestic partnerships for same-sex couples exist in Yellow Springs and Cuyahoga and Franklin counties with Cleveland's registry upheld in October 2010, court-approved custody agreements between lesbian parents were affirmed enforceable in December 2008 and shared custody ordered in August 2010, but a non-biological mother was denied shared custody 4-3 in July 2011. 66186276B63937528568220.name: Iowa
66186276B63937528568220.summary:
Iowa enacted two restrictions on 22 March 2023. Senate File 538 bars doctors from providing gender-affirming care to anyone under 18, covering puberty blockers, hormone therapy and transition-related surgeries, with a 180-day wind-down for existing patients. Senate File 482 restricts restroom and locker-room use in schools: multiperson restrooms and changing areas at public and private elementary and secondary schools are limited to the sex listed on a person's birth certificate, and the rule applies to everyone on school grounds, including students, staff, parents and visitors. Single-person facilities remain available to trans students who obtain written consent from legal guardians.

Since 1 July 2025, Senate File 418 prohibits transgender people from altering legal gender on government identification or documents and requires legal recognition to match sex assigned at birth, defined by gametes expected to be produced later in life. The law stripped the gender-transition language added to Iowa's civil rights statutes in 2007.

In February 2025 the Iowa Legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing gender identity from the state's anti-discrimination laws, signed by Governor Kim Reynolds and effective 1 July 2025. Iowa became the first state to remove anti-discrimination protections for any class. In 2026 the state passed a bill barring localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state's, after several cities had enacted their own.

Iowa's hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but not gender identity. A Senate bill adding gender identity passed 27-21 on 8 March 2016 but died in the House.

On Medicaid coverage, the Iowa Supreme Court ruled unanimously on 8 March 2019 in Good v. Iowa Department of Human Services that excluding coverage for gender-affirming surgery violated the Iowa Civil Rights Act. The General Assembly responded by passing, and Governor Reynolds signing, a ban on state funding within a month. A Polk County District Court ruled that ban unconstitutional in November 2021. In June 2025 Governor Reynolds signed another law banning Medicaid coverage for transgender surgeries and hormone treatments, effective 1 July 2025.

Since March 2022, Iowa has limited women's sports to females based on sex at birth at all accredited public or private educational institutions, including colleges and universities, effective 1 July 2022, with a civil cause of action for harm resulting from a violation.

Since 2007 Iowa prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations; that protection was removed effective 1 July 2025. Sexual orientation remains a protected class in employment, housing and public accommodations, with Des Moines protected since 1991.

The Movement Advancement Project equality map catalogues Iowa's enacted facility ban and groups Iowa among states that do not define sex by birth in statute. Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map (July 2026) places Iowa in 'The Worst States' tier, one level below 'Do Not Travel'.

sources.summary: The Movement Advancement Project equality map catalogues state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity. It is cited for Iowa's enacted facility ban and for an 18-state group defining sex as biological sex. Iowa is not listed among the states that define sex by birth in statute.

Erin In The Morning's 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map: July 2026' (Stonewall News, published 27 Aug 2026) grades every state's legal risk under anti-trans law within a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'. Iowa sits in 'The Worst States' group (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY), one tier below 'Do Not Travel' (FL, ID, KS, TX). Idaho reached that top tier after a felony bathroom ban carrying up to 5 years, partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists; Kansas is there for its bounty-hunter civil-suit regime.

'Safe states don't make safer people' (The Needle, July 2026) overlays the state legal-risk map on Trans Murder Monitoring killings data. Legal-risk grades predict how a state behaves, not how people behave toward trans people, and rates do not line up with the map. Every count is an undercount. Iowa is not named in the essay, which bears on Iowa's mid-map legal-risk position.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Iowa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2007 Iowa prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations, but in February 2025 the Legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing gender identity from anti-discrimination laws, signed by Governor Kim Reynolds and effective July 1, making Iowa the first state to remove anti-discrimination protections for any class and the first to take a protected group away from civil rights protections. In 2025 Iowa stripped nondiscrimination protections from trans people and in 2026 passed a bill banning localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state government, after several cities passed their own protections. As of July 1, 2025 under Senate File 418 transgender people may not alter legal gender on government IDs or documents or be legally recognized differently from assigned sex, stripping 2007 gender-transition language and imposing an unchangeable binary legal definition of sex determined at birth based on gametes expected to be produced later in life. Iowa hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation but not gender identity; a March 8, 2016 Senate bill to add gender identity passed 27-21 but died in the Republican-controlled House, though federal law has covered gender identity since October 2009. In March 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court required Medicaid coverage of sex reassignment surgery, but the General Assembly passed and Reynolds signed a ban on state funding a month later, a Polk County District Court ruled that ban unconstitutional in November 2021, and in June 2025 Reynolds signed another law banning Medicaid coverage for transgender surgeries and hormone treatments effective July 1, 2025. In March 2022 Iowa limited women's sports to cisgender females based on sex at birth, effectively barring transgender girls and women at all accredited public or private educational institutions including colleges and universities effective July 1, 2022, with civil lawsuit cause for any direct or indirect harm from violation. In March 2023 Senate File 538 banned provision of any gender-affirming healthcare to transgender minors effective immediately with 180-day wind-down for existing patients, and a separate March 2023 bill required written parental permission for students to use a single-person restroom at school. In May 2023 Iowa banned sexual orientation and gender identity lessons in Kindergarten through grade 6 classrooms, and only Davenport has banned conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 council vote April 22, 2020 after statewide Senate and medical and psychology board efforts failed. Iowa Territory adopted Wisconsin anti-sodomy law in 1838 punishable by up to three years, omitted sodomy in its 1843 code making it legal as noted in 1860 Estes v. Carter, re-criminalized sodomy in 1892 with one to ten years for heterosexual or homosexual consensual activity with first conviction in 1900 State v. Todd and fellatio criminalized in 1902, limited prosecution of heterosexual sodomy in a divided 5-4 1976 Supreme Court ruling requiring compelling state interest for private consensual adult opposite-sex conduct, and repealed same-sex criminalization in a 1978 comprehensive code with no mention of sodomy and age of consent 16 regardless of gender and sexual orientation. Iowa provided benefits to same-sex partners of state employees since 2003, recognized same-sex marriages since April 3, 2009 after unanimous Iowa Supreme Court affirmance in Varnum v. Brien, issued licenses from April 27, 2009 as fourth U.S. state to legalize same-sex marriage, defeated constitutional amendment and convention attempts to ban it, and removed three participating justices in November 2010 retention elections while retaining a fourth in November 2012. Joint adoption by married same-sex couples has been legal since a 2008 Supreme Court ruling with individuals and married couples allowed to adopt regardless of sexual orientation, state courts ordered listing of married lesbian non-birthing mothers on death certificates in December 12, 2012 Buntemeyer v. Iowa DPH and on birth certificates in Gartner v. Newton unanimously affirmed May 3, 2013 to ensure support and fundamental legal rights at birth, lesbian couples have IVF access with non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized if married, and courts are generally favorable to gestational or traditional surrogacy despite no defined surrogacy laws. Since 2007 Iowa has outlawed discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing and public accommodations with Des Moines protected since 1991, and hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation. On March 17, 2015 the Senate voted 26-24 to ban sexual orientation change efforts on LGBT minors but the bill died in the Republican-controlled House, the Board of Medicine and Board of Psychology declined in 2016 to ban conversion therapy by rule, and Davenport became the first city to ban conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 vote April 22, 2020. In March 2020 the House unanimously passed 95-0 a bill to abolish the gay panic defence twice, but the Republican-controlled Senate twice refused to take it up.

sources.title: Iowa Supreme Court March 2019 Medicaid ruling and legislative reversal
sources.summary: In March 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled Iowa Medicaid cannot deny coverage for medically necessary gender confirmation surgery for transgender recipients under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and in late April 2019 the Iowa House and Senate passed a health and human services appropriations bill containing the Costello amendment allowing state and local government units to refuse taxpayer and Medicaid funds for sex reassignment surgery and any other cosmetic reconstructive or plastic surgery procedure related to transsexualism, hermaphroditism, gender identity disorder, or body dysmorphic disorder to overturn that ruling with the bill sent to Governor Kim Reynolds to sign or line-item veto.

sources.title: Iowa hate crime law and March 8, 2016 Senate bill
sources.summary: On March 8, 2016 the Iowa Senate voted 27-21 to pass a bill adding gender identity and gender expression to Iowa's hate crimes law to provide legal protection from hate crimes for transgender people, advancing the bill to the Iowa House of Representatives.

66186276B79689460185872.name: South Carolina
66186276B79689460185872.summary:
A trans visitor to South Carolina enters under the United States federal document and screening regime before state law applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, issuing new passports only as M or F, while previously issued X-marker passports remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening adds exposure. The State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flags visa applicants with an internal marking, and treats a declared gender other than the one assigned at birth as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures can involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that risk outing a trans traveller.

Facilities are the sharpest South Carolina-specific exposure. Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on 15 May 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth. The Senate amended the bill before passage, and the ACLU of South Carolina issued a response on 18 May 2026 framing it as discrimination against trans students in both K-12 and higher education.

The measure extends a pre-existing restriction on school restrooms into campus settings. A July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, which ranks states on the severity of adult and youth law by reading bills, places South Carolina among the escalating states rather than in the harshest tier.

Custody carries a further state-layer restriction: South Carolina operates a "freeze-frame" policy limiting the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. Federal custody is separately affected by the Bureau of Prisons adoption of Florida-based policies for transgender inmates from 2026, which mandate short haircuts, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs, and by the Bureau's cessation of reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025.

The assessment ranks states on the severity of adult and youth law by reading bills. South Carolina's expansion places it among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier.

ACLU of South Carolina (May 18, 2026): Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on Friday May 15, 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth; ACLU frames it as discrimination against trans students in K-12 and higher education and notes the Senate amended the bill before passage. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Carolina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Changing legal gender on the birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery. State anti-discrimination law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination on the basis of gender identity, but 2020 federal workplace protections against LGBT discrimination apply in South Carolina, with additional local employment protections for gender identity in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees only in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina has no state hate crime law, while hate crimes motivated by gender identity are prohibited federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2016 Governor Nikki Haley said she opposed a transgender bathroom-restriction bill introduced in the Legislature and viewed it as "unnecessary". On May 17, 2022 the governor signed a transgender sports ban. In May 2024 legislation signed into law and effective immediately banned gender-affirming healthcare for individuals under 18 and banned federal funding going directly or indirectly toward gender-affirming care for adults, after which providers including the Medical University of South Carolina stopped providing such care regardless of age. The 2024-25 and 2025-26 budget appropriations bills require students to use bathrooms based on sex "at the time of birth", though on September 10, 2025 the U.S. Supreme Court allowed trans student plaintiff John Doe to continue using the boys' bathroom while his challenge proceeds, with all other trans students required to follow state law. Same-sex sexual activity is legal under the 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Lawrence v. Texas, which invalidated South Carolina's sodomy law making "buggery" a felony punishable by five years in prison or a $500 fine, though the legislature has not repealed it. Voters adopted a November 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman, which was overturned in Condon v. Haley on November 12, 2014, with stay denials by the Fourth Circuit on November 18 and by the U.S. Supreme Court on November 20, the first same-sex marriage on November 19, 2014 and general recognition and performance from the next day. South Carolina permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibition on adoption by same-sex couples or on stepchild adoptions, and since a February 15, 2017 federal order the state must list both same-sex parents on children's birth certificates without the adoption or Family Court order previously required only of same-sex couples. No state anti-discrimination provision explicitly covers sexual orientation, though 2020 federal workplace protections apply, supplemented by local employment protections in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina is the only state not to include same-sex couples in domestic violence statutes, which explicitly cover only opposite-sex couples, and it has no state hate crime law, though crimes motivated by sexual orientation are covered federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In March 2020 a federal judge declared unconstitutional the 1988 law "banning homosexual or gay topics within school classrooms".

sources.title: South Carolina May 2024 gender-affirming healthcare ban - Legislature bill signed by Governor
sources.summary: In May 2024 South Carolina enacted a law signed by Gov. Henry McMaster prohibiting healthcare workers from prescribing puberty blockers or hormone treatments or performing gender-affirming surgeries for transgender people under age 18, with an exception permitting puberty blockers for cisgender conditions such as precocious puberty, thereby denying trans youth visitors legal access to gender-affirming medical care in the state.

sources.title: U.S. Supreme Court order September 10, 2025 in trans student John Doe lawsuit
sources.summary: South Carolina's 2024-25 and 2025-26 budget laws require students to use bathrooms corresponding to biological sex "at the time of birth," and on September 10, 2025 the U.S. Supreme Court denied South Carolina's August 26, 2025 request to pause a Fourth Circuit order requiring a school district to allow transgender student John Doe to use the boys' bathroom while his equal-protection and federal education anti-discrimination challenge to the law continues, leaving the law unenforceable against Doe during the litigation without ruling on its merits.

sources.title: Medical University of South Carolina cessation of gender-affirming care
sources.summary: South Carolina H4624 took effect May 21, 2024 prohibiting gender transition procedures for persons under 18 and prohibiting direct or indirect use of public funds for gender transition procedures, and because MUSC Health funds are public funds MUSC ceased gender transition services for patients of all ages, stopping new trans patients after August 1, 2024 and transitioning existing patients out by end of January 2025, displacing roughly 500 trans adult patients in the Lowcountry to limited alternative providers while continuing other primary, behavioral and complex care for transgender patients.

sources.title: March 2020 federal judge ruling striking down 1988 anti-gay school classroom law
sources.summary: On March 11, 2020 the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina in Gender and Sexuality Alliance v. Spearman declared S.C. Code § 59-32-30(A)(5), the 1988 provision barring any discussion of same-sex relationships in public-school health education except in the context of sexually transmitted diseases with dismissal for violating teachers, unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause for discriminating against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer students and barred its enforcement.

sources.title: Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act (federal) / SC hate-crime law gap
sources.summary: As of 26 March 2007, South Carolina had no hate crimes law, so gender identity had no hate-crime protection.

South Carolina sits within a wider facilities pattern. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, and some states make trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances, while 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law, an arrest civil-rights attorneys described as the first known under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Document and care measures at other state level show the direction of travel. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described such care for minors as mutilation, with the Department of Justice subpoenaing more than 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19.

Several federal measures in force or in litigation, including the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth, have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

66186276B65591139260314.name: Florida
66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Florida stands under the United States national framework, and adds its own layer of state-level restrictions that a trans visitor will encounter on the ground.

Facilities are the sharpest Florida-specific exposure. Under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act, in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity at any state school, state university, or government building, including publicly owned or leased airports, convention centres, parks, school campuses, stadiums, toll-road plazas, state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails. An authority figure may order departure under internal disciplinary procedures, and a person who does not leave can be charged with criminal trespass. The ACLU notes the statute reaches all schools, public and private, but does not cover private businesses.

Enforcement has produced a prosecution. On 19 March 2025 Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was arrested at the Florida State Capitol after police, alerted in advance, found her washing her hands in a women's restroom; she had declared an intention to break the law. She was charged with misdemeanour trespass carrying up to 60 days in jail, in what was believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw the case out, holding that as a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested.

Identity documents are closed at state level. In January 2024 the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles stopped issuing any driver's licence with a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, treating holders or applicants as criminally guilty of fraud with licence suspension and revocation. In July 2024 trans people born in Florida could no longer update or change sex on birth certificates despite legislation that expressly permitted it; previously an amended birth certificate required an application, notarised affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment without requiring surgery or sterilisation.

Care for trans minors is banned. Rules approved on 4 November 2022 and effective 16 March 2023, codified 17 May 2023, prohibit puberty blockers, hormone therapy and confirming surgeries for anyone under 18 unless intersex, and a state memo stated that social transition should not be a treatment option. Adult barriers include a 24-hour waiting period before sexual reassignment surgery, a ban on insurance coverage for gender-affirming care, and a requirement that treatment be administered by a physician rather than a nurse practitioner. Senate Bill 254's Physicians Only provision bars nurse practitioners and physician assistants from providing gender-affirming care to trans adults, which the Human Rights Campaign states disrupted care for an estimated 80 percent or more of transgender clinic patients. A May 2023 conscience law allows medical practitioners to refuse treatment on religious or belief grounds.

Custody is a site of documented harm. Senate Bill 254 of 17 May 2023 permits child custody modification on the basis that a child received or might receive gender-affirming care, and April 2023 legislation allows modifying or nullifying out-of-state parental custody agreements if the child is allowed or threatened with access, which opponents describe as permitting removal across state lines. Three plaintiffs obtained a preliminary injunction on 6 June 2023 limited to themselves, stayed by the Eleventh Circuit on 26 August 2024, and a federal judge permanently blocked the provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024.

Sports and education restrictions date from 2021. A law effective 1 June 2021 excluded transgender girls and women, defined as students of the male sex based on sex assigned at birth, from female school sports. In early 2023 the Florida High School Athletics Association recommended that female athletes supply menstrual cycle information to a school-accessible database. The Attorney General threatened competitions including an Irish step dancing competition and Miss America for allowing transgender competitors.

Facility rules were extended to private campuses. On 23 August 2023 the Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter a forbidden bathroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply similar restrictions to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof due by 1 April 2024. This followed the Eleventh Circuit's January 2023 reversal of an August 2020 ruling that a Ponte Vedra Beach high school violated the law by refusing a transgender student consistent restroom use; the ban was codified 17 May 2023.

Protection machinery is thin. Florida statutes do not address gender identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations, and hate-crime penalties cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. The Florida Commission on Human Relations announced in February 2021 that it would enforce Bostock v. Clayton County in employment, housing and public accommodations, and Glenn v. Brumby (December 2011) holds that employment discrimination based on transgender status is sex discrimination. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population, including Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, Orlando, St. Petersburg, Tallahassee and West Palm Beach, prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations. Nursing home and hospital protections since 2000, amended 2007, cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. Conversion therapy bans in a number of cities, mainly in the Miami metropolitan area, have been struck down by the Eleventh Circuit.

Official posture is hostile. Equality Florida issued a travel advisory on 12 April 2023 warning of risks to health, safety and freedom for those considering travel or relocation, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans; the Human Rights Campaign joined in May 2023. On 23 April 2026 HB 1001/SB 1134, effective January 2027, prohibits state and local funding or promotion of diversity, equity and inclusion as defined to include gender identity, with lawsuits and removal of officials available as remedies, and has been interpreted as barring government support for LGBTQ organisations and events.

Violence risk does not track the legal climate. A national analysis of 2008 to 2025 data scores Florida 8.0 on the anti-trans law scale with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100,000 per year, and its core finding is that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates across the 26 states with data. Legal climate and street-level violence are independent risks for a visitor.

Stat. 553.865): refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can be criminal trespass, but the law only applies in buildings owned or leased by the state or local government — state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons/jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas — and purports to cover all schools, public or private. Private businesses are outside its scope; the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

NBC News (2025): Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was arrested at the Florida State Capitol after declaring 'I am here to break the law' and entering a women's restroom — believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. She faces a misdemeanor trespass charge punishable by up to 60 days in jail; at least 14 states have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

Metro Weekly (July 6, 2025): On June 20, 2025, Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw out the trespass case against Marcy Rheintgen. As a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested. She had been charged March 19, 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the Statehouse.

Equality Florida travel advisory (April 12, 2023): the organization took the 'unprecedented step' of warning about risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people, reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks, and book bans/curriculum censorship. The advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries; EQFL reports events and conferences cancelling and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.

sources.summary: Since 2021 the state has seen significant erosion especially in transgender rights: on June 1, 2021 a law excluded transgender girls and women defined as students of the male sex based on sex assigned at birth from female school sports, in early 2023 the Florida High School Athletics Association recommended female athletes supply menstrual cycle information to a school-accessible database speculated to enforce abortion restrictions and detect trans women, and the Attorney General threatened competitions including an Irish step dancing competition and Miss America for allowing transgender competitors as deceptive and depriving women of fair competition. Since July 1, 2023 under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act it is illegal for a trans person at any state school, state university, or government building e.g. beach or airport to use a bathroom or changing facility consistent with gender identity, requiring gender labels and internal disciplinary procedures where an authority figure may order departure and a non-member who does not depart can be charged with criminal trespass; on August 23 the Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on October 18, 2023 voted to apply similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing with compliance proof by April 1, 2024, after an August 2020 Eleventh Circuit ruling that Ponte Vedra Beach high school violated the law by refusing transgender student Andrew Adams consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the Eleventh Circuit sided with the district to uphold the ban, codified May 17, 2023. For identity documents, in January 2024 the Department of Highway Services and Motor Vehicles unilaterally banned issuing any driver's license with a gender marker different from assigned sex at birth, treating holders/users or applicants as criminally guilty of fraud with suspension and revocation, and in July 2024 transgender individuals born in Florida could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it; previously an amended birth certificate required an Application to Amend a Florida Birth Record, notarized Affidavit, physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition without requiring surgery or sterilization, and after 2011 driver's license/ID changes required a court order for name and physician statement of appropriate clinical treatment, while in January 2022 the first sex-unknown birth certificate was reported. For healthcare, after August 2022 rule-change citing state guidance against gender-affirming care, on October 31, 2022 the Medical Board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery and banned minors from gender-affirming healthcare approved November 4, 2022 and effective March 16, 2023, codified May 17, 2023 to prohibit hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and create adult barriers including banning insurance coverage and requiring a physician rather than nurse practitioner to administer treatment; minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy, or confirming surgeries unless intersex and a memo stated social transition should not be a treatment option, opposed by HHS, the Endocrine Society and other major medical organizations. On custody, May 17, 2023 Senate Bill 254 allows child custody modifications on the basis the child received or might receive gender-affirming care, and April 2023 legislation allowed modifying or nullifying out-of-state parental custody agreements if the child is allowed or threatened with access, described by opponents as allowing kidnapping across state lines amid protests where trans children were detained and one arrested for disturbing the peace; three plaintiffs obtained a June 6 preliminary injunction limited to them, stayed August 26, 2024 by the 11th Circuit, before a federal judge in June 2024 permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults. On discrimination and protection, statutes do not address gender identity discrimination in employment, housing or other areas and nursing home/hospital protections since 2000 amended 2007 cover sexual orientation but not gender identity, but counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of population prohibit private and public employment, housing and public accommodations discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity, the February 2021 Commission on Human Relations announced enforcement of Bostock v. Clayton County June 15, 2020 holding workplace discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination under Title VII to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations, and Glenn v. Brumby December 2011 held employment discrimination based on transgender status is sex discrimination, while hate-crime law provides harsher penalties based on sexual orientation but not gender identity. In May 2023 a medical practitioner law allows discrimination in doctors surgery, medicine and hospitals on conscience, religion or belief effective immediately by emergency clause criticized as preventing PrEP, gender-affirming care and abortion access, a May 2023 law bans adult live performances anywhere a minor might view under criminal penalty which DeSantis said was about drag shows but was preliminarily enjoined June 23 as not all drag is obscene, and on April 23, 2026 HB 1001/SB 1134 effective January 2027 prohibits state and local funding or promoting diversity, equity and inclusion defined to include gender identity with suits and removal of officials, interpreted as banning government support to LGBTQ organizations/events as in Palm Beach County denying a HUD grant to repair Compass headquarters air conditioning; in April 2023 Equality Florida issued a travel advisory to avoid visiting or moving to the state joined in May by the Human Rights Campaign citing DeSantis-signed legislation. Same-sex sexual activity became legal after Lawrence v. Texas June 26, 2003 striking all sodomy laws, though the 1868 felony crime against nature law punishable up to 20 years and 1917 misdemeanor unnatural and lascivious act law punishable by up to $500 or 6 months remained unenforced and unrepealed as of 2020, with the 1955 psychopathic offender law labeling sodomy convicts criminal sexual psychopathic persons for periodic examination repealed in 1979; in 2026 the legislature passed CS/CS/HB 1525 repealing §800.02, House 108-0 March 3, 2026 and Senate 38-0 March 10, 2026, signed June 16, 2026 effective October 1, 2026, and in October 2018 during a gay sex sting a judge ruled gay sex is not illegal in a public space so long as within a room. Scott August 21, 2014 held Florida's ban violated the U.S. Constitution as marriage is a fundamental right under Fourteenth Amendment Due Process and Equal Protection subject to strict scrutiny, superseding the 1977 same-sex marriage ban law and November 2008 Amendment 2 adding Article I Section 27 banning same-sex marriage, civil unions and substantial equivalents; nine counties, thirty cities and one town offer domestic partnership benefits, and a 2016 repeal of the 1868 unmarried cohabitation ban passed House 112-5 and Senate 38-0, signed April 6, 2016 effective July 1, 2016. Clayton County June 15, 2020 outlawed workplace discrimination on sexual orientation as sex discrimination under Title VII, which the Florida Commission on Human Relations announced in February 2021 it will enforce for employment, housing and public accommodations, though statutes otherwise do not address sexual orientation discrimination; counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of population including Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, Orlando, St. Petersburg, Tallahassee and West Palm Beach prohibit private and public employment, housing and public accommodations discrimination on sexual orientation, nursing homes and hospitals since 2000 amended 2007 cannot discriminate on sexual orientation, the Department of Agriculture added sexual orientation to workplace policy in January 2019, and hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation.
