66186276B65591139260314.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework, and adds its own layer of state-level restrictions that a trans visitor will encounter on the ground.

Facilities are the sharpest state/province-specific exposure. Under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act, in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity at any state school, state university, or government building, including publicly owned or leased airports, government buildings, convention centres, parks, school campuses, stadiums, toll-road plazas, state/province offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails. An authority figure may order departure under internal disciplinary procedures, and a person who does not leave can be charged with criminal trespass. The statute reaches all schools, public and private, but does not cover private businesses.

Enforcement has produced a prosecution. On 19 March 2025 a 20-year-old trans college student was arrested at the state capitol after police, alerted in advance, found her washing her hands in a women's restroom; she had declared an intention to break the law. She was charged with misdemeanour trespass carrying up to 60 days in jail, in what was believed to be the first arrest under the state's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 a Leon County judge threw the case out, holding that as a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested.

Identity documents are closed at state level. In January 2024 the state's motor-vehicle department stopped issuing any driver's licence with a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, treating holders or applicants as criminally guilty of fraud with licence suspension and revocation. In July 2024 trans people born in the state could no longer update or change sex on birth certificates despite legislation that expressly permitted it; previously an amended birth certificate required an application, notarised affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment without requiring surgery or sterilisation.

Care for trans minors is banned. Rules approved on 4 November 2022 and effective 16 March 2023, codified 17 May 2023, prohibit puberty blockers, hormone therapy and confirming surgeries for anyone under 18 unless intersex, and a state/province memo stated that social transition should not be a treatment option. Adult barriers include a 24-hour waiting period before sexual reassignment surgery, a ban on insurance coverage for gender-affirming care, and a requirement that treatment be administered by a physician rather than a nurse practitioner. Senate Bill 254's Physicians Only provision bars nurse practitioners and physician assistants from providing gender-affirming care to trans adults, which disrupted care for an estimated 80 percent or more of transgender clinic patients. A May 2023 conscience law allows medical practitioners to refuse treatment on religious or belief grounds.

Custody is a site of documented harm. Senate Bill 254 of 17 May 2023 permits child custody modification on the basis that a child received or might receive gender-affirming care, and April 2023 legislation allows modifying or nullifying out-of-state/province parental custody agreements if the child is allowed or threatened with access, which opponents describe as permitting removal across state/province lines. Three plaintiffs obtained a preliminary injunction on 6 June 2023 limited to themselves, stayed by the Eleventh Circuit on 26 August 2024, and a national judge permanently blocked the provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024.

Sports and education restrictions date from 2021. A law effective 1 June 2021 excluded transgender girls and women, defined as students of the male sex based on sex assigned at birth, from female school sports. In early 2023 the state high school athletics association recommended that female athletes supply menstrual cycle information to a school-accessible database. The national justice department threatened competitions including an Irish step dancing competition and Miss America for allowing transgender competitors.

Facility rules were extended to private campuses. On 23 August 2023 the Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter a forbidden bathroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply similar restrictions to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof due by 1 April 2024. This followed the Eleventh Circuit's January 2023 reversal of an August 2020 ruling that a high school in the state violated the law by refusing a transgender student consistent restroom use; the ban was codified 17 May 2023.

Protection machinery is thin. State/province statutes do not address gender identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations, and hate-crime penalties cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. The state human-relations commission announced in February 2021 that it would enforce the national workplace-discrimination ruling in employment, housing and public accommodations, and a 2011 national appellate holding states that employment discrimination based on transgender status is sex discrimination. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations. Nursing home and hospital protections since 2000, amended 2007, cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. Conversion therapy bans in a number of cities have been struck down by the Eleventh Circuit.

Official posture is hostile. The state's largest LGBTQ advocacy organisation issued a travel advisory on 12 April 2023 warning of risks to health, safety and freedom for those considering travel or relocation, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans; a national advocacy group joined in May 2023. Legislation passed 23 April 2026, effective January 2027, prohibits state/province and local funding or promotion of diversity, equity and inclusion as defined to include gender identity, with lawsuits and removal of officials available as remedies, and has been interpreted as barring government support for LGBTQ organisations and events.

Violence risk does not track the legal climate. A national analysis of 2008 to 2025 data scores the state 8.0 on the anti-trans law scale with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100,000 per year, and its core finding is that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates across the 26 jurisdictions with data. Legal climate and street-level violence are independent risks for a visitor.
66186276B65591139260314.outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of Florida's restroom statute as applied to private businesses is stated by the ACLU as outside the law's terms, but the ACLU itself advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel rather than a categorical answer.

Whether the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act has been substantively tested on the merits remains unresolved: the June 2025 dismissal rested on the defendant's standing to challenge the statute, not on its constitutionality.

The Eleventh Circuit's June 2024 permanent block of the provisions banning gender-affirming care for minors and adults is recorded alongside the state's codified ban; the operative position for a given patient is not resolved by the sources.

The claim that the January 2024 licence policy treats applicants as criminally guilty of fraud, and the July 2024 birth-certificate closure despite permissive legislation, are sourced to a single encyclopedic compilation and are not independently corroborated in this inventory.

The Florida-specific homicide figure of 3.7 trans women murdered per 100,000 per year derives from a national analysis using 2008 to 2025 data; the underlying methodology and the annual denominator are not stated in the source.

The interpretation of HB 1001/SB 1134 as barring government support for LGBTQ organisations and events is described as an interpretation, not a court holding; the law takes effect January 2027 and its application is unresolved.

66186276B73402293045483.name: Nebraska
66186276B73402293045483.summary:
Nebraska is a state within the United States, and its own measures shape what a trans visitor encounters on the ground. Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023, established a Women's Bill of Rights that defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms; opponents have questioned its scope and legality.

Identity-document changes in Nebraska are procedurally demanding. Changing the gender marker on a birth certificate requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the name. Driver's licences and state IDs require a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A legal name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, reduced to two weeks for minors.

Trans athletes face documented exclusion. The Nebraska School Activities Association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery to compete. In June 2025 Legislative Bill 89 banning transgender athletes from any sports passed the unicameral legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by Governor Pillen; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming care for minors is prohibited. In May 2023 the Nebraska Legislature passed a ban on such healthcare for individuals under age 19 by a vote of 33-15; Governor Pillen signed it and it took effect immediately. The Nebraska Supreme Court upheld the ban 6-1 in July 2024.

Custody and prison conditions are a documented site of harm. In August 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for Nebraska prison officials in a suit brought by a transgender inmate identified only as Jane Doe, who was diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in Nebraska's men's prison. Nebraska housed her by assigned birth sex among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge dismissed her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her, writing that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and finding she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault.

State-level hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Nebraska's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation and enhances sentences for offences including manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing, but does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity in hate crimes since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.

Protections against discrimination are uneven across the state. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became unlawful under Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020), and in August 2020 the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Omaha has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both public and private sectors since 2012, following a 4-3 City Council vote on 13 March 2012 that added sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes with an exemption for religious institutions. Lincoln passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the Nebraska State College System voted 4-2 to include gender identity in policy.

Conversion therapy restricting gender identity is outlawed only in Lincoln, where the practice has been banned since 2021; it remains lawful elsewhere in the state, and statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025.

Clayton County decided June 15, 2020, and in August 2020 the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission announced it will investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity. 66186276B22971435435932.name: Kentucky
66186276B22971435435932.summary:
Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 after the Kentucky General Assembly overrode Governor Andy Beshear's veto, is the single 2023 statute carrying the state's restriction on which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools, and it also bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map lists Kentucky's 2023 K-12 facility ban among its state-by-state entries cataloguing restrictions on transgender people using public bathrooms according to their gender identity.

The Kentucky Department of Education released implementation guidance in April 2023, advising school districts to tread cautiously with the bathroom-ban provisions and to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum. School districts carry out the facility restriction, so the practical rule a trans visitor or student encounters is applied locally rather than uniformly.

The ban on gender-affirming care for minors took effect on 14 July 2023, when U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month. Transgender minors in Kentucky are barred from puberty blockers and hormone therapy, with no phaseout for those already receiving care. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law; the ACLU of Kentucky called the ruling a temporary setback. On 28 September 2023 federal appeals judges allowed the ban to remain in effect while legal challenges proceed.

Kentucky permits post-operative transgender people to amend the sex recorded on a birth certificate by sending a doctor's letter stating that gender-affigning surgery was performed directly to the Department of Vital Statistics in Frankfort, replacing an earlier requirement of a court order for a Kentucky-born person. The amendment route is therefore conditioned on surgery rather than on identity documentation alone.

Senate Bill 83, banning transgender athletes from female sports teams, passed the General Assembly in March 2022, was vetoed by Governor Beshear in April 2022 on constitutionality and vagueness grounds, and the veto was overridden the same month, with the law taking effect immediately.

Kentucky's hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation but expressly do not cover gender identity. An assault motivated by a victim's gender identity therefore falls outside the state's hate-crime enhancement, even though comparable assaults motivated by sexual orientation are covered.

Conversion therapy on minors has been illegal statewide since Governor Beshear's executive order of 18 September 2024, following earlier city bans adopted in Covington in March 2020 by a 5-0 vote, Louisville in September 2020 by 24-1, and Lexington in May 2021 by unanimous vote.

Workplace protection rests on two layers. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit held on 7 March 2018 in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes, a decision covering Kentucky, that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits firing an employee for being transgender or transitioning, because such a firing penalises failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes and necessarily takes sex into account, and that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act does not permit a private employer to dismiss a transgender worker on the belief that sex is immutable. The case followed the 2013 dismissal of funeral director Aimee Stephens after she disclosed her planned transition.

State government is additionally barred from hiring or or firing employees based on sexual orientation or gender identity under an executive order of 2 June 2008 that restored protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006, and 19 Kentucky cities maintain Fairness Ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations.

The 2013 Religious Freedom Act requires the state to show clear and convincing evidence before burdening sincerely held religious beliefs. Governor Beshear vetoed the measure over vagueness and the risk of overriding local non-discrimination ordinances; it was enacted by override votes of 79-15 in the House and 32-6 in the Senate.

66186276B6801956407400.name: North Carolina
66186276B6801956407400.summary:
North Carolina is a state within the United States, and a trans visitor stands under the federal framework before any state rule applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The same order required federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender," mandated removal of materials promoting what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces. The facilities bar reaches federal buildings in North Carolina.

The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker had been available since 2022. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the restriction remains challenged in federal courts. The ACLU sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. An executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued on 5 February 2025, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Gender-affirming care is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described such care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and in October 2025 proposed health-department rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.

Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

At state level, facility rules are the defining North Carolina question. After the Charlotte city council passed an ordinance in March 2016 allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity, the North Carolina General Assembly met in emergency session and passed House Bill 2, which barred cities from passing anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people and required people to use public bathrooms corresponding with the sex listed on their birth certificate. The law drew global backlash, with companies including Google and Disney pledging to pull back business, and the U.S. Justice Department called it "state-sponsored discrimination" and sued, while North Carolina filed its own suit. Legislators repealed House Bill 2 on 30 March 2017 in the face of the boycotts.

Facility use remains an active legislative subject in North Carolina. In the 2025 session Republican lawmakers were again pushing a transgender bathroom bill, years after the HB 2 boycotts forced the repeal, so a visitor should expect facilities access to be contested rather than settled.

Lethal violence against trans people in North Carolina does not track the state's protective posture. A July 2026 investigative data analysis comparing legal-risk tiers with Trans Murder Monitoring records found that protective statutes do not predict lower lethal risk for trans women; its state rate chart places North Carolina at 3.0 killings per 100,000 trans women, on a recorded base of three or more victims that the analysis acknowledges is an undercount, and characterises the state as moderate-risk. That rating describes recorded killings and should not be read as an assurance of safety for an individual visitor.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in North Carolina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In March 2016 the Public Facilities Privacy & Security Act (HB2) barred local governments from enacting contrary hiring and bathroom-facility policies and required bathroom use according to gender listed on birth certificate, with the birth-certificate bathroom-use portion repealed by the legislature March 30, 2017. A prior state ban on local non-public-employment ordinances prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity expired December 1, 2020, and Charlotte (August 2021) and Wake County (October 2021) ordinances explicitly covering gender identity took effect January 1, 2022, with the article reporting about 30% of the state population covered by local sexual-orientation and gender-identity ordinances. For public employment, an April 12, 2016 executive order barred LGBT discrimination including gender identity and an October 2017 extension applied protection to state contractors, while the University of North Carolina system and most listed campuses maintain gender-identity non-discrimination policies for employment and students. On August 16, 2023 three veto-overridden laws took effect requiring educators to notify parents if a student requests a different name or pronouns, banning trans girls from team sports, and banning gender-affirming care for transgender minors, with House Bill 574 specifically banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. Since August 2023 minors cannot be prescribed puberty blockers or hormone therapy or receive gender-affirming surgery, and under HB 805 veto-overridden July 29, 2025, effective January 1, 2026 the state recognizes only male and female sexes and disallows state funds for gender transition care for minors and people in prison. On gender-marker documents, a June 26, 2022 federal ruling removed the undefined sex-reassignment-surgery requirement for North Carolina birth-certificate changes following a November 2021 Lambda Legal suit, but the July 29, 2025 HB 805 override requires amended certificates to continue displaying originally assigned sex alongside any change. Effective August 15, 2023 SB49 Parents' Bill of Rights bans K-4 instruction on gender identity, requires parental notification if a child requests a different name or pronoun in records or by personnel, and grants inspection and objection rights over instructional materials, while the state hate-crime statute does not cover gender identity. Private consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by Lawrence v. Texas (2003), but N.C. G.S. section 14-177 remains unrepealed and unenforceable for that conduct after State v. Whiteley (2005) upheld it facially only for minors, non-consensual or coercive conduct, public conduct, and prostitution. A prior state ban on local municipalities prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination outside public employment expired December 1, 2020, while Durham and Guilford counties and Bessemer City, Durham, and High Point prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination in local public employment or discrimination and Charlotte and Wake County ordinances effective January 1, 2022 explicitly ban sexual-orientation discrimination. In public employment, the April 12, 2016 executive order and October 2017 extension bar sexual-orientation discrimination for state employees and contractors, with University of North Carolina campuses and the Housing Finance Agency maintaining sexual-orientation non-discrimination policies. The state hate-crime statute does not cover sexual orientation. In January 2021 a federal judge struck down North Carolina's exclusion of same-sex couples from domestic-violence protection, extending protections to them, and a 2008 Patients' Bill of Rights provision granted hospital visitation via designated visitor statute. In November 2021 a law banning sexual-orientation discrimination in foster-parenting placements was signed effective January 1, 2022, and on August 3, 2019 an executive order banned state funding of conversion therapy on minors.

66186276B80192890672447.name: Montana
66186276B80192890672447.summary:
Montana stands under the United States national travel-document regime, and separately under a state legal environment in which courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans legislation under the Montana Constitution. In the July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment, Montana is the only state to improve its ranking; laws that would ordinarily place it among the worst states have not taken full effect because of that court record. Adult restrictions that were passed remain unenforced pending litigation, while federal policy shifts and litigation keep the youth-side picture unstable.

On 24 March 2026 Montana enacted Senate Bill 437, defining sex as a binary of male or female based on primary sexual anatomy and reproductive system (female defined as ova-based, male as sperm-based), and defining man, woman, mother and father on that basis. The statute provides that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role. The definitions apply across more than 60 sections of state law, including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, and applicants for driver's and marriage licences must list sex as so defined. Plaintiffs sought in April 2026 to add SB 437 to ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to Senate Bill 458, which was struck down in February 2025 by District Judge Leslie Halligan for violating the equal-protection clauses of the Montana Constitution.

Identity-document changes remain contested. On 9 September 2022 Montana prohibited changing sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of data-entry error or a DNA test; a court order blocked that rule on 15 September 2022 and the Department of Public Health and Human Services complied. A February 2023 bill prohibiting gender-marker changes on all identity documents was signed on 19 May 2023 and blocked by a December 2024 injunction from District Judge Mike Menahan. After an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update driver's licences and birth certificates, Judge Menahan issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 pending trial on sex-discrimination grounds, upheld 15 April 2026 by the Montana Supreme Court, which held that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. The December 2024 Helena district court order also enjoined the 2022 health department rule barring gender-identity-based changes to birth-certificate sex and the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate to change driver's-licence sex.

Facilities rules have been repeatedly restrained. In February 2025 the legislature passed HB 121 requiring bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth; the ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta temporarily restrained the law, finding it motivated by animus and unsupported by evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A 2018 Montana Family Foundation initiative to require public bathroom use corresponding to birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures, and on 3 December 2024 the Montana House voted down a proposal to forbid trans people from using Capitol bathrooms aligned with gender.

Gender-affirming care for trans minors was prohibited by SB 99, signed 28 April 2023 and described as the most comprehensive such prohibition in the United States. District Judge Jason Marks preliminarily enjoined it on 27 September 2023, ruling that discrimination against a person for being transgender constitutes sex discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County and served no compelling governmental interest; the Montana Supreme Court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class. Judge Marks permanently struck the law down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly.

A 2021 law banning transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Greg Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.

Montana hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed religious-belief legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people. In May 2023 HB 359 prohibited sexually oriented or obscene performances in public spaces where minors may be present and explicitly barred drag story hours at publicly funded schools and libraries, leading a Butte-Silver Bow library to cancel a transgender woman's reading; District Judge Brian Morris issued a temporary restraining order in July 2023, extended October 2024, blocking enforcement as vague and overbroad with risk of disproportionate enforcement against trans, Two-Spirit and gender-nonconforming people. A March 2025 bill, HB 675, defining drag as inherently sexual was defeated with 13 Republicans joining Democrats.

Discrimination protections exist at state-executive and local level. By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules by Governor Marc Racicot, broadened by Executive Order 41-2008 in November 2008 under Governor Brian Schweitzer, and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016 by Governor Steve Bullock. Federal Title VII protections for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County apply in Montana. Ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations; Missoula County's ordinance covers county employees only.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined enforcement of the state ban, later mooted by Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015; the Montana Supreme Court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019. Montana permits adoption with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, with Kulstad v. Maniaci affirmed 6-1 on 7 October 2009. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997.

On 6 March 2025 House Bill 819 was debated and signed by Governor Gianforte in May 2025 with immediate effect, prohibiting flags representing political party, race, sexual orientation, gender or political ideology on government property and public schools, thereby banning Pride and other LGBTQ flags while permitting specified historical and official flags. Missoula adopted a rainbow pride flag as its municipal flag, effectively exempting it statewide.

66186276B13694661525286.name: Missouri
66186276B13694661525286.summary:
Missouri's Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a judge denied a preliminary injunction sought by Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, who had filed in Cole County Circuit Court on behalf of three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. The law bars under-18s from starting hormones or puberty blockers, though those already in treatment may continue, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The SAFE Act also bars Missouri HealthNet Medicaid from covering gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes violating providers to medical-licence revocation. Doctors who breach the ban can also be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment.

The ban has been upheld twice. Judge Robert Craig Carter ruled it constitutional on 25 November 2024 after a September 2024 trial in the 44th Judicial Circuit Court, with plaintiffs announcing an appeal; on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court upheld the ban unanimously, citing the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court decision upholding Tennessee's similar law. The statute sunsets on 28 August 2027, but lawmakers seek to make it permanent and a November 2026 ballot initiative also aims to extend the ban indefinitely.

Trans inmates in Missouri state prisons face a separate care cutoff. Effective 2 July 2026, an appropriations law signed by Governor Mike Kehoe bars state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban such care for incarcerated people; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while federal courts blocked comparable Idaho and Georgia measures.

Missouri restricts sports participation by sex assigned at birth. Senate Bill 39, signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to limit sports to sex assigned at birth, and a May 2023 law bans transgender athletes from female sports with a sunset clause repealing it on 28 August 2027.

Changing identity documents in Missouri requires surgery or a court order. Under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9), a birth certificate sex change requires a court order supported by certified proof on hospital letterhead stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible. Two 2013 cases that had allowed exceptions were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no workaround to the surgical requirement. Between 2016 and 2024 the Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 for gender designation changes on licences or IDs, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Missouri's hate-crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," but the state's non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity. The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations of the SAFE Act and complaints about "gender transition intervention." Kansas City declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals in May 2023, and Columbia voted in February 2024 to include LGBT protections in its sanctuary ordinance.

sources.title: Missouri Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act
sources.summary: On June 7, 2023, Missouri enacted S.B. 49 effective August 28 banning gender-affirming treatments including puberty blockers for minors until August 2027 with license loss for violating providers while allowing minors already receiving care to continue, and S.B. 39 requiring public and private schools through college to restrict sports participation to sex assigned at birth.

The state's Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a judge denied a preliminary injunction sought by national and state/province civil-rights organisations representing three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. The law bars under-18s from starting hormones or puberty blockers, though those already in treatment may continue, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The SAFE Act also bars state/province Medicaid from covering gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes violating providers to medical-licence revocation. Doctors who breach the ban can also be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment.

The ban has been upheld twice. A trial judge ruled it constitutional on 25 November 2024 after a September 2024 trial, with plaintiffs announcing an appeal; on 13 January 2026 the state supreme court upheld the ban unanimously, citing the 2025 national supreme court decision upholding a neighbouring jurisdiction's similar law. The statute sunsets on 28 August 2027, but lawmakers seek to make it permanent and a November 2026 ballot initiative also aims to extend the ban indefinitely.

Trans inmates in state prisons face a separate care cutoff. Effective 2 July 2026, an appropriations law signed by the governor bars state/province funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. The state became the seventh in the country, and the second in 2026 after a neighbouring jurisdiction, to ban such care for incarcerated people; several other state/provinces have near-identical laws, while national courts blocked comparable measures elsewhere.

The state restricts sports participation by sex assigned at birth. A 2023 law requires public and private schools through college to limit sports to sex assigned at birth, and a companion measure bans transgender athletes from female sports with a sunset clause repealing it on 28 August 2027.

Changing identity documents in the state/province requires surgery or a court order. Under state/province statute, a birth certificate sex change requires a court order supported by certified proof on hospital letterhead stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible. Two 2013 cases that had allowed exceptions were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no workaround to the surgical requirement. Between 2016 and 2024 the Department of Revenue accepted a standard form for gender designation changes on licences or IDs, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

The state's hate-crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," but its non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity. The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations of the SAFE Act and complaints about "gender transition intervention." One city declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals in May 2023, and another voted in February 2024 to include LGBT protections in its sanctuary ordinance.

66186276B62688952876525.name: Alaska
66186276B62688952876525.summary:
Alaska falls in the Moderate-Risk group of Erin In The Morning's July 2026 legal-risk assessment, alongside Kentucky and North Carolina. That tier is defined as states that have passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults, enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly. It sits above the assessment's worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below its protective groupings.

No statewide statute bars a transgender adult from using a public restroom or changing room matching their gender identity, and no statewide law bans gender-affirming care for adults. Pressure has reached Alaska through appointed regulatory boards rather than the legislature. Gov. Mike Dunleavy's earlier attempt to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, while boards he appoints have restricted transgender girls' participation in girls' sports.

The State Medical Board, whose members Dunleavy appoints, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation that would classify providing gender-transition care to anyone under 18 as unprofessional conduct, exposing clinicians to disciplinary action. A board member had proposed the resolution in June 2025. The draft must be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then pass a 30-day public comment period before it can take effect.

The Alaska Board of Education voted 7-1 in September 2023 to bar transgender students from female sports and athletics statewide. Facilities policy below that level is set district by district. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to require transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex assigned at birth or a private alternative such as the nurse's office, replacing guidance that had stood for more than seven years; the policy was described at the time as an apparent first for Alaska. It binds one district's schools and does not extend to adult facilities anywhere in the state.

Alaska's statewide nondiscrimination law does not cover gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the 2002 executive order protecting state employees from discrimination addresses sexual orientation only. Four municipalities, Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, home to about 46% of the state's population, prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, public accommodations and housing. Ketchikan's ordinance passed unanimously in July 2020 and took effect in mid-August 2020. Anchorage's ordinance passed 9-2 in September 2015 and survived a repeal attempt on 3 April 2018, when voters rejected Proposition 1 by 53% to 47%; that measure would have required people in public spaces to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching their sex assigned at birth. In Fairbanks, a February 2019 City Council ordinance covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations was vetoed by Mayor Jim Matherly.

Alaska's hate-crime statute does not list gender identity, so bias-driven violence against a transgender person does not trigger a state-level penalty enhancement. A visitor outside the four municipalities with local ordinances has no state or municipal recourse against discrimination in a hotel, restaurant or workplace.

Document changes are available and leave a record. An amended Alaska birth certificate with a corrected name and gender marker requires a Birth Certificate Request Form, a photocopy of identification, a letter from a medical or mental health provider attesting appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex, plus a fee. The amended certificate keeps the previous legal name printed at the bottom with a notation that it was originally issued under the former name and amended because of a change of name. Changing the gender marker on an Alaska driver's licence requires a letter from a licensed provider attesting clinical treatment, or an already-updated birth certificate or a court order for gender change.

Marriage licences have issued without regard to the sex of the spouses since 13 October 2014, after the federal district court in Hamby v. Parnell struck down the state's statutory and constitutional bans; the statutory ban had been allowed to become law without Gov. Tony Knowles' signature in 1996, and a constitutional amendment passed on 3 November 1998. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status can therefore marry in Alaska.

Private consensual sex between adults is not criminalised. Alaska repealed its sodomy law with effect from 1 January 1980; the 1899 statute had punished the crime against nature with up to ten years in prison.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alaska (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Alaska state law provides no protection against discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, or public accommodations, and the 2002 executive order covering state employment addresses sexual orientation only with no gender identity provision. Four municipalities — Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, covering about 46% of the state population — ban discrimination based on gender identity in public and private employment, public accommodations and housing, with Ketchikan's unanimous ordinance passed in July 2020 effective in mid-August, and Anchorage's September 2015 ordinance (9-2) retained after voters rejected Proposition 1 to strip protections from transgender individuals on April 3, 2018 by 53% to 47%. In Fairbanks, a February 2019 City Council ordinance banning discrimination on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations was vetoed by Mayor Jim Matherly. Under federal law, the June 15, 2020 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County holds workplace discrimination on gender identity is sex discrimination prohibited by Title VII, and the October 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act provides federal penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity prosecutable in federal court, while Alaska state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Transgender persons may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and gender marker by submitting a Birth Certificate Request Form, ID photocopy, letter from a medical or mental health provider attesting appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition or certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex, plus fee, but the amended certificate retains the previous legal name at the bottom with notation it was originally issued under the former name and amended due to change of name. Changing the gender marker on a driver's license requires a letter from a licensed provider attesting clinical treatment or an already-updated birth certificate or court order for gender change. In September 2023 the Alaska Board of Education voted 7-1 to ban transgender individuals from participating in female sports and athletics statewide, while in August 2020 Anchorage voted 9-2 to ban conversion therapy on minors, the first such city ban in Alaska. Same-sex sexual conduct has been allowed since January 1, 1980 when Alaska repealed its sodomy law, which under the 1899 Alaska-specific statute had punished crime against nature with up to ten years in jail. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 12, 2014 via the Hamby v. Parnell district court ruling declaring statutory and constitutional bans unconstitutional, with licenses accepted from October 13, 2014, following a 1996 statutory ban allowed to become law without Governor Tony Knowles' signature on May 6, 1996 and a constitutional amendment approved November 3, 1998. Alaska law does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing, or public accommodations, except for a 2002 executive order prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in state employment and a 1975 Human Rights Commission stance; a 2015 bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation died without a vote. Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, representing about 46% of the population, ban sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations; Anchorage first passed an ordinance 7-4 in 2009 vetoed by Mayor Dan Sullivan, voters rejected Proposition 5 in April 2012 with 57% opposed, then passed an ordinance 9-2 in September 2015, and Ketchikan passed an ordinance unanimously in July 2020 effective mid-August, while Fairbanks limits protection to sexual orientation discrimination against city employees after mayoral veto of a broader 2019 ordinance. Federal protections apply via Bostock on June 15, 2020 holding workplace discrimination on sexual orientation violates Title VII, and the October 2009 Matthew Shepard Act providing federal penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation prosecutable in federal court, while Alaska state hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation. Alaska permits adoption by married same-sex couples and recognizes the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent for a child born via donor insemination only if the parents are married, with lesbian couples having access to in vitro fertilization and courts generally favorable to surrogacy despite no surrogacy laws; Anchorage banned conversion therapy on minors in August 2020 by a 9-2 vote.

sources.summary: The Anchorage Assembly approved nondiscrimination protections covering trans people in 2015, Proposition 1 on the April 2018 Anchorage ballot would have required people in public spaces to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching their sex assigned at birth rather than gender identity, and Anchorage voters rejected Proposition 1 by 53-47% so the 2015 protections remained in place.

66186276B75419826371250.name: Georgia
66186276B75419826371250.summary:
Georgia stands under the national framework of the United States; the federal document, entry and screening rules set out in the national record apply in this state without modification. The state-specific layer adds three things a trans visitor should weigh: documented street violence concentrated in Atlanta, a statutory ban on gender-affirming care for minors, and a measurable contraction of adult surgical care under federal funding pressure.

Violence is the sharpest documented risk. In April 2023 the Atlanta Police Department said it was actively investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, following the fatal shootings of two Black transgender women a week apart. A January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open at that point. The department publicly acknowledged the epidemic-level violence that Black and Brown transgender women face in the United States. The incidents are Atlanta's, and Atlanta is one city in the state, but it is the state's largest urban centre and the point at which the available record concentrates.

The recorded killing rate for trans women in Georgia is 4.8 per 100,000 per year. That figure is an acknowledged floor drawn from a monitoring project known to undercount, so the true rate is at least this and probably higher; it should be read as a minimum exposure level rather than a measured ceiling.

Care access is restricted by state law. Governor Brian Kemp signed Senate Bill 140 on 23 March 2023, barring licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or gender-transition surgery to patients under 18, with licence revocation available as a penalty. The ban took effect on 1 July 2023. Minors who had begun hormone replacement therapy before that date may continue under the law. The ACLU of Georgia said at the time of signing that it would sue.

Adult care has also narrowed in practice. On 13 February 2025 Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man, citing a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations. The Savannah Pride Center reported that at least two other area residents were denied care in the same period. A trans adult seeking surgical care in Georgia should therefore expect providers to test each case against current funding rules before scheduling.

66186276B86627915353587.name: New Hampshire
66186276B86627915353587.summary:
Visitors to New Hampshire stand under the United States national framework in every respect that touches identity documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department no longer processes the X marker, and passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application. The Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue this treatment, and the ACLU litigation on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending.

Entry rules add a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Within that national regime, New Hampshire carries an unusually high recorded incident load. GLAAD's 2025 national census documents 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in New Hampshire during 2025, the second-highest count of any state after California's 198, and ahead of Texas at 66, Ohio at 50 and Washington at 50. The figure exceeds counts recorded in states with several times New Hampshire's population, which is the strongest single indicator in the sourced material of what a trans visitor may encounter on the ground.

Against that, the state's courts have applied existing civil-rights machinery to a trans victim. On 17 July 2026 the Merrimack County Superior Court found that a Concord man violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman. The case establishes that assault against a trans person in New Hampshire can be pursued as a civil-rights violation and adjudicated in state court, rather than going unremedied.

Checkpoint and screening exposure follows national procedure: the National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can disclose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation. Multiple foreign governments, including at least eight European countries such as Finland and Denmark, have issued or adjusted travel advisories for trans and nonbinary citizens travelling to the United States.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Hampshire (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gender identity has been protected against discrimination in housing, employment and public accommodations since June 2018, extended to health care, public accommodations and jury selection effective January 1, 2020, and to public schools effective September 17, 2019, with anti-bullying law covering gender identity and expression including cyberbullying. Hate crimes based on gender identity have been covered since 2019 with penalty enhancements effective October 15, 2019, and the gay and trans panic defence was abolished effective January 1, 2024 after passage in June 2023. Legal change of gender marker on a birth certificate requires sex reassignment surgery, legal since 1990, plus a certified court order stating a "sex change," application form, photograph and fees after a July 2019 veto of reform, while driver's licenses offer male, female and X since January 1, 2020 implemented in August 2021 with X unavailable on birth certificates, and the Medicaid ban on surgery coverage was lifted October 20, 2017. A June 30, 2016 executive order prohibited gender identity and expression discrimination in public employment, state programs and contracting, and a 2022 parental bill criticized as forcing schools to disclose gender identities died after a veto threat. July 18, 2024 laws banned trans girls from girls sports in grades 5 to 12 effective August 19, 2024 requiring a birth certificate for eligibility, banned gender-affirming medicine for minors, and allowed parental opt-out from instruction on gender identity or expression, while a fourth bill allowing discrimination against trans people including adults was vetoed. An August 2024 Supreme Court 3-1 ruling protected transgender individuals in schools on privacy and autonomy grounds, and a judge granted a temporary stay of the sports ban pending investigation and appeals. From January 1, 2025 reassignment surgery was banned for trans minors while retained for intersex people and circumcisions, and August 2025 House Bill 377 and House Bill 712 effective January 2026 banned puberty blockers, hormone therapy and chest surgeries for under-18 gender-affirming care with a grandfather clause for treatment ongoing as of January 1, 2026, disciplinary action for violating providers and a right to sue, alongside a conversion therapy ban for LGBT minors effective January 1, 2019. Same-sex sexual activity is legal after sodomy repeal in June 1975, with age of consent at 16 regardless of sexual orientation and at 18 where one party is under the care, guardianship or authority of the other. Sexual orientation has been protected in anti-discrimination law since 1998 covering public accommodations, housing and private or public employment, extended to public schools effective September 17, 2019 with anti-bullying coverage including sexual orientation and cyberbullying. Hate crimes based on sexual orientation have been covered since 1991 with penalty enhancements for actual or perceived orientation. The gay panic defence was abolished effective January 1, 2024. Conversion therapy on LGBT minors was banned effective January 1, 2019 after 2018 passage, with a 2022 repeal attempt dying in the House. Sexual orientation was explicitly listed within expectation of privacy legislation effective January 1, 2025, and same-sex marriage has been legal since January 1, 2010 after civil unions from January 1, 2008, with same-sex adultery recognized by an April 2021 Supreme Court ruling reversing the 2003 Blanchflower rule. A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found that 88% of New Hampshire residents supported discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The same poll found that 11% were opposed to those protections. The article states that "New Hampshire became regarded as the least safe New England state for transgender citizens" following August 2025 laws restricting transgender care and other changes in transgender protections. Those August 2025 laws eliminated access for transgender youth to receive gender-affirming care even when deemed medically necessary by a physician, with effect from January 2026.

Arizona has not enacted restrictions on transgender adults' use of public facilities or on their participation in public life. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment placed it in a low-risk group of eight states and the District of Columbia, described as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults, and named Arizona with Virginia as a state whose youth-targeting policies were judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Bathroom and school measures have been stopped at the executive stage rather than enacted. In June 2023 the governor vetoed legislature-passed bills on bathroom use and on classroom pronoun use, and in April 2023 vetoed a bill aimed at LGBT safe spaces in schools. No state law bars a trans visitor from using a restroom or changing facility that matches their gender.

Statewide non-discrimination protection rests on executive action rather than statute. A January 2023 gubernatorial executive order bars discrimination based on gender identity in state employment and state contracts, and a June 2023 attorney general opinion treats gender identity as within the state's sex-discrimination prohibition. Municipal ordinances in Phoenix, Flagstaff, Tempe, Sedona, Winslow, Mesa, Scottsdale, Glendale and Tolleson prohibit gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with exemptions for religious organisations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses. Outside those municipalities and the state employment context, a trans visitor has no state statutory remedy for discrimination in a shop, hotel or restaurant.

The state hate-crime statute does not list gender identity among its protected categories, so bias-motivated violence against a trans person is neither recorded nor sentenced as a hate crime under Arizona law. A panic defence resting on a victim's sexuality or gender identity remains available at common law, and reform bills have lapsed without a vote.

Identity documents can be changed, on conditions. A driver's licence or state identification change requires a signed physician statement attesting that the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process; surgery is not required. Birth-certificate changes were permitted without surgery by a federal court order in August 2024, following a November 2020 suit brought by three families against the Department of Health Services.

Adult health coverage is uneven. A 1982 state regulation excludes sex reassignment surgery from Medicaid, and two transgender teenagers challenged it as unconstitutional in August 2020. A June 2023 executive order extended full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming health care to state government employees over the age of 21.

For younger trans people the state has legislated. A March 2022 law, effective March 2023, bans surgery on transgender minors while permitting it on intersex children. A second March 2022 law bars transgender girls from female school sports. In March 2023 the Department of Education opened a hotline for reporting schools that expose children to topics including gender ideology.

Partner recognition is settled in practice. Marriages between people of the same sex have been recognised since a federal district court ruling on 17 October 2014; the statutory and constitutional bans remain on the books and are unenforceable under Obergefell v. Hodges and, for marriages entered elsewhere, the Respect for Marriage Act. Phoenix, Bisbee, Tucson and Flagstaff have enacted domestic-partnership or civil-union registries. The Arizona Supreme Court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that married same-sex spouses hold equal parental rights and may both be listed on a birth certificate.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Arizona (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal rulings in Bostock v. Clayton County, Altitude Express v. Zarda and Harris Funeral Homes v. EEOC in 2020 protect gender-identity discrimination in employment under Title VII, reinforced by a January 2023 gubernatorial executive order banning state employment and contract discrimination based on gender identity and a June 2023 Attorney General affirmation that state sex discrimination includes gender identity, plus municipal ordinances in Phoenix (revised February 2013), Flagstaff (March 2013), Tempe (February 2014), Sedona (2015), Winslow (November 2018), Mesa (March 2021), Scottsdale (April 2021, effective May 20), Glendale (May 2021) and Tolleson (June 2021) banning gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations with exemptions for religious organizations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses. A 1982 regulation provides Medicaid cannot cover sex reassignment surgery, challenged in August 2020 by two transgender teenagers with NCLR, NHeLP and co-counsel as unconstitutional after 2019 lawsuits sought to void the ban, while a June 2023 executive order granted Arizona government employees over age 21 full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services. In March 2022 the Legislature passed and Governor Doug Ducey signed a ban on sex reassignment surgery on transgender children with an exception allowing surgery on intersex children effective March 2023, while the Arizona Supreme Court ruled April 25, 2019 that family courts may determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances when divorced parents reach impasse, authorized to decide disputed parenting-plan elements and other factors necessary for emotional and physical health narrowly tailored on evidence of imminent harm. In November 2020 three families with transgender children sued the Department of Health Services to allow birth-certificate gender change without sex reassignment surgery, litigation ongoing as of August 2023 with all resident transgender individuals joined, resulting in an August 2024 federal judge order permitting change without surgery, while driver's license and state ID change requires a signed physician statement attesting the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process without requiring surgery. A second March 2022 bill signed by Ducey legally bans transgender children from female sports, athletics and/or Olympics effective 30 days after enactment. In March 2023 the Department of Education introduced a hotline to report schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology for investigation, while in June 2023 the Governor vetoed legislature-passed anti-trans bathroom and classroom pronoun-usage bills and vetoed an April 2023 bill targeting LGBT safe spaces in schools. Arizona hate-crime law does not include gender identity though the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act since October 2009 covers gender identity, a gay and trans panic defence remains under common law with reform bills lapsing without action, and conversion therapy was banned by Pima County in August 2017 by 3-2 vote with fines up to 2,500 dollars alongside a June 2023 executive order banning government funding for conversion therapy. Same-sex sexual activity is legal, after sodomy was first criminalized under Spanish Empire, Mexico and then Arizona Territory with an 1863 code imposing five years to life, extended to fellatio in 1912 with penalty reduced to one to five years, changed in 1951 to five to twenty years plus requirements to register with the sheriff and report address changes, with Arizona Supreme Court rejecting vagueness challenges, until the Arizona Equity Act of 2001 repealed sodomy laws and legalized homosexuality. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since a U.S. district court decision October 17, 2014 forced end to enforcement of statutory and constitutional bans, though bans remain textually in the constitution and Arizona Revised Statutes and on the Legislature website as unenforceable under Obergefell v. Hodges and, for out-of-state recognition, the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act, after voters rejected Proposition 107 in November 2006 banning marriage and marriage-like status but approved Proposition 102 in 2008 banning recognition, prompting cities including Phoenix, Bisbee, Tucson and Flagstaff to enact domestic partnerships or civil unions. Adoption is permitted by individuals with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions but with primary consideration to married couples unless in the child's best interest or no married couple available, lesbian couples have IVF access, state law recognizes a non-genetic, non-gestational married mother via donor insemination, the Arizona Supreme Court ruled unanimously September 2017 that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights under Obergefell and Pavan v. Smith to list both names on birth certificates with October 2020 Appeals implementation, surrogacy gestational or traditional is prohibited and contracts unenforceable though Soos v. Superior Court (1994) allows pre-birth orders for biological parents requiring second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent, and an April 2022 emergency law signed by Ducey allows religious organizations to legally discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster. Workplace sexual-orientation protections apply via 2020 Bostock/Zarda Title VII rulings, a 1992 Phoenix ordinance for city and contract workers, 1999 Tucson ordinance, 2003 Governor Napolitano order for state employees, and expanded 2013-2021 city ordinances in Phoenix, Flagstaff, Tempe, Sedona, Mesa, Scottsdale, Glendale and Tolleson plus the January 2023 executive order and June 2023 Attorney General interpretation covering sexual orientation. Hate-crime law includes sexual orientation as a protected category providing additional penalties for bias-motivated crimes. A 1991 law prohibiting AIDS/HIV instruction promoting, portraying positively, or suggesting safe methods of homosexual sex was repealed April 2019 by House 55-5 and Senate 19-10 effective July 1, 2019 amid court challenges, Governor Ducey vetoed SB1456 April 20, 2021 requiring parental opt-in for sex, gender identity and sexuality teaching after 31-28 House and 16-14 Senate passage, with a watered-down successor advancing June 2021, and Governor Brewer vetoed a February 2014 religious-freedom bill widely reported as targeting LGBTQ people. The article describes thousands of years of indigenous inhabitation with traditions of cross-dressing and gender variance and perceptions of gender and sexuality different from the Western world with no legal or social punishments for same-sex activity, including Navajo recognition of four roles asdzáán (feminine female), hastiin (masculine male), dilbaa (masculine female) and nádleehi defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature whose identity is fluid. It states nádleehi were perceived as balanced between sexes and typically chosen for communal roles such as spiritual healers, traditionally wearing female clothes and doing female work with some having sexual relations with men accepted by the tribe, with parallel transgender and gender-variance terms including wi:k’ovat among Tohono O’odham, hova among Hopi, alyha and hwame among Mohave, ilyaxai’ and kwiraxame’ among Maricopa, and others now increasingly called two-spirit. It states the relative openness to these different gender identities mostly disappeared after European settlement and colonization as introduced stringent beliefs made nádleehi subject to ridicule, citing a Franciscan missionary stating the abominable vice would be eliminated with Catholic faith and Hopi Christian converts prohibited from the snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. It documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically by quoting Will Roscoe’s work that the "prevalence of sodomy" and the tolerance or even respect of transgender people fueled the Spanish explorers' argument for the colonization of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity, alongside Jonathan Ned Katz that Christianization included attempting to eliminate traditional Indian homosexuality as cultural genocide. It states today LGBT Navajo may find it difficult being accepted by family with 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempting suicide. It notes Phoenix and Tucson are home to prominent LGBTQ communities with Tucson Pride founded 1977 as first in the state and first Phoenix Pride parade in 1981 now attracting thousands yearly, and cites 2019 Public Religion Research Institute polling that 71% of Arizona residents supported LGBTQ non-discrimination legislation, with 2017 PRRI finding 63% supported same-sex marriage, 73% supported anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and 59% opposed religious refusals to serve LGBTQ people.

66186276B89395128410123.tangentialFactors:
Tucson Pride cancelled all of its 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; the reporting grouped Tucson with Tampa, Florida and Arlington, Texas as affected cities.

Phoenix and Tucson hold established LGBTQ communities. Tucson Pride was founded in 1977 as the first in the state, and the first Phoenix Pride parade was held in 1981; both now draw thousands annually.

Public opinion polling has been permissive. A 2019 Public Religion Research Institute survey found 71 per cent of Arizona residents supported LGBTQ non-discrimination legislation; its 2017 survey found 63 per cent supported same-sex marriage, 73 per cent supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and 59 per cent opposed religious refusals to serve LGBTQ people.

Indigenous nations in the state historically recognised gender-variant roles, including the Navajo nádleehi and parallel terms among the Tohono O'odham, Hopi, Mohave and Maricopa, many of them now described as two-spirit. Missionary and colonial pressure suppressed these roles. Reporting cited in state-level accounts holds that 70 per cent of LGBT Navajo youth have attempted suicide, a figure presented without a stated source or method.
66186276B89395128410123.localsOnly:
Adoption is open to individuals with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions, but statute gives primary consideration to married couples unless that is not in the child's best interest or no married couple is available. An April 2022 emergency law signed by the governor allows religious organisations to refuse adoption and foster placements to same-sex couples. Gestational and traditional surrogacy are prohibited and contracts unenforceable, though Soos v. Superior Court (1994) allows pre-birth orders for biological parents, and a non-biological parent in a same-sex couple must complete a second-parent adoption. Lesbian couples have access to IVF, and state law recognises a non-genetic, non-gestational married mother via donor insemination.

On custody, the Arizona Supreme Court ruled on 25 April 2019 that family courts may determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances, when divorced parents reach impasse, and only on evidence of imminent harm, with any order narrowly tailored.

Conversion therapy is banned by Pima County under an August 2017 ordinance passed 3-2, with fines up to 2,500 dollars, and a June 2023 executive order bars government funding for the practice. No statewide ban exists.

Workplace protection for state and municipal employees rests on a 1992 Phoenix ordinance covering city and contract workers, a 1999 Tucson ordinance, a 2003 gubernatorial order for state employees, and the city ordinances expanded between 2013 and 2021, alongside the January 2023 executive order and the June 2023 attorney general interpretation.
