66186276B53580985925186.summary:
Virginia stands under the United States federal framework, and the national layer of exposure is carried at country level; what follows is the state-specific position. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Virginia in its Low-Risk States group with Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, and names Virginia alongside Arizona as a state that has enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on that assessment, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

State civil-rights law is protective. The Virginia Values Act, passed 6 February 2020 and signed 11 April 2020, prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit with effect from 1 July 2020, replacing the earlier position in which protection covered state employment only. A statute of 4 March 2020, effective 1 July 2020, allows Virginia localities to enact their own protections covering gender identity and sexual orientation, so the standards a visitor meets vary between cities and counties.

Violence against a person because of gender identity is addressed by Virginia hate-crime law under a bill signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020. HB 2132, repealing the gay and trans panic defence, was signed by Governor Northam in March 2021 and took effect 1 July 2021, removing that line of mitigation from prosecutions over assaults on LGBTQ people.

State identity documents are comparatively open. An X gender marker has been available on Virginia driver's licences since 1 July 2020. Since 1 September 2020 changing the sex designation on a Virginia birth certificate has required only "appropriate clinical treatment," dropping the sex reassignment surgery requirement that had stood since 1979.

Facility access in Virginia schools was litigated to a favourable result for the trans student: a Gloucester County case, in which a transgender high school student was denied use of the boys' bathroom, produced a ruling that the school board had acted unlawfully, and the U.S. Supreme Court left that outcome undisturbed in 2021.

School sport is closed. In February 2025 the Virginia High School League banned transgender athletes from girls' sports, following the federal executive order on the subject.

On care, Virginia prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of a minor.

Partner recognition is settled in practice but not fully in the state's own text. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 6 October 2014, when the Supreme Court refused appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer and marriages began at 1 p.m. that day; the defunct statutory ban was repealed on 3 March 2020 and a codifying protection signed in March 2024 took effect 1 July 2024. The 2006 constitutional ban, however, remains on the books pending repeal resolutions approved in January 2025 and January 2026 for a voter referendum. A designated-visitor statute signed 26 March 2007 and effective 1 July 2007 extended hospital visitation rights to same-sex couples after unanimous House and Senate votes.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Virginia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Effective July 1, 2020, Virginia law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, and credit under the Virginia Values Act passed February 6, 2020 and signed April 11, 2020, and a March 4, 2020 law allows localities to enact their own protections on sexual orientation and gender identity. Virginia hate crime laws address violence based on gender identity under a bill signed March 4, 2020 and effective July 1, 2020, and HB 2132 repealing the gay and trans panic defense passed in March 2021, signed by Governor Northam, and went into effect July 1. Since September 1, 2020, changing sex on a birth certificate requires only “appropriate clinical treatment” rather than sex reassignment surgery required since 1979, and effective July 1, 2020 Virginia offers an “X” gender marker on driver’s licenses. A 2014 Gloucester County case denying a transgender high school student use of the boys’ bathroom resulted in a court ruling that the school board acted unlawfully, which the U.S. Supreme Court let stand in 2021, while in July 2023 the Department of Education passed policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender individuals in schools, intended to be reversed in 2026. In February 2025 the Virginia High School League banned transgender athletes from girls’ sports following Trump’s executive order, and Virginia prohibits health care providers from trying to change the gender identity of minors. In September 2021 the Virginia Supreme Court upheld reinstatement of a teacher suspended for speaking out against transgender children and not using their pronouns on Christian-belief grounds, and in May 2024 Governor Youngkin vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity. Virginia statutes criminalizing sodomy and crimes against nature were effectively invalidated by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003, with §18.2-361 struck down March 12, 2013 and revised to remove criminalization of consensual same-sex relations by Senate vote 40-0 on February 7, 2014 and House vote 100-0 on March 6, 2014 signed into immediate effect, while §18.2-345 on lewd cohabitation was repealed in 2013 and §18.2-344 on fornication was repealed March 4, 2020. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 6, 2014 after the Supreme Court refused appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer with marriages beginning at 1 p.m. October 6, the defunct statutory ban was repealed March 3, 2020, and a codifying protection was signed in March 2024 effective July 1, while the 2006 constitutional ban remains pending repeal resolutions approved January 2025 and January 2026 for voter referendum. Effective July 1, 2020 the Virginia Values Act passed February 6, 2020 and signed April 11, 2020 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations, replacing prior limited state-employment-only protections, and a March 4, 2020 law effective July 1, 2020 added sexual orientation to hate crime laws. The 1934 ABC ban on gay bars was declared unconstitutional in 1991 in French Quarter Cafe v. Virginia Alcoholic Beverage Control Board, and hospital visitation rights were extended to same-sex couples through a designated visitor statute signed March 26, 2007 effective July 1, 2007 after unanimous House and Senate votes. Virginia allows single persons to adopt with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples, but HB 189 and SB 349 signed April 9, 2012 effective July 1, 2012 authorize adoption agencies to refuse for religious reasons, while surrogacy contracts for same-sex couples were legalized by a bill passed February 2019 signed March 2019 effective July 1, 2019 and a February 2021 bill banned taxpayer dollars to religious organizations discriminating in adoption. Virginia prohibits health providers from attempting to change sexual orientation of minors, SB 1138 decriminalizing and modernizing HIV laws was signed March 31, 2021, a PrEP insurance anti-discrimination bill was vetoed in March 2025, and an archaic Code reference defining homosexuality as sexual conduct discovered August 2022 bars explicit sexual conduct materials from classrooms as a criminal offence since July 1, 2022.

A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places the District of Columbia on its Low-Risk list alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, while cautioning that the District may no longer warrant its prior reputation as the most protective jurisdiction, because District law can be overridden by congressional action and by executive orders.

Because the District has no state government of its own in the ordinary sense, the federal measures described in the national record — passport marker restrictions, entry screening markings, federal facility bans, custody policies, and care restrictions — operate on visitors in the District without any intervening state layer to soften them.

66186276B78821008370123.name: Maine
66186276B78821008370123.summary:
Maine is a comparatively low-risk state for a transgender visitor within the United States. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group, while separately flagging that Maine's risk has increased because the University of Maine system capitulated to federal restrictions on trans sports participation.

The University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation on 21 March 2025 (updated 24 March), following suspension by the US Department of Agriculture of federal funding for research and programs while it investigated possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes.

Maine law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity or expression in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education opportunity. The protection was added in 2005 and retained after a November 8, 2005 veto referendum; LD1688, signed 17 June 2021, explicitly extends gender identity throughout state statutes. Maine's hate crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity. The gay and trans panic defense was banned by legislation passed in June 2019 (House 132-1, Senate 35-0), effective 1 July 2019.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since November 2019 no medical provider certification is required to change the gender marker on driver's licences and state IDs; a completed Gender Designation Form with male, female and X options suffices. Birth certificates reflecting gender identity, including X, have been available since July 2020 upon notarized affidavit, though X requires a declaration from a licensed physician or mental health provider and minors require parental consent.

Facilities access is protected. In January 2014 the Maine Supreme Court ruled in Doe v. Regional School Unit 26 against a district that denied a student bathroom use aligned with gender identity. Beginning 1 October 2026, healthcare facilities must mandate and include sexual orientation and gender identity data.

Gender-affirming care is protected rather than banned. A law effective since July 2023 allows 16 and 17 year olds to access hormone therapy for gender-affirming healthcare, and an April 2024 law explicitly protects, defends and safeguards gender-affirming healthcare. A bill that would have provided sanctuary protections to trans minors was unanimously struck down by Maine Democrats in January 2024 following backlash.

On sports, in June 2025 the Maine Senate rejected Legislative Document 233, which would have prohibited transgender women from competing in women's sports in state-funded schools; it was the only one of eight anti-trans bills in 2025 to pass the House.

Correctional placement is documented. Andrea Balcer, a 27-year-old transgender woman and convicted double murderer, is housed in the women's facility at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham, where she has been held for at least a year as of April 2026, meaning placement by current gender identity rather than birth sex. On 3 April 2026 inmate Katie Mountain (41) filed a 30-page complaint against MDOC Commissioner Randall Liberty, Warden Ben Beal and Balcer, alleging chronic harassment and assault by the trans prisoner; attorney Cynthia Dill filed it. No ruling has been reported. The harassment and assault claims are allegations, while the placement of a trans woman in the women's prison is documented.

66186276B31549545599635.name: Delaware
66186276B31549545599635.summary:
Delaware is a state within the United States, so entry rules, passport and visa policy, and federal identity screening are governed by federal measures rather than Delaware law; the national record carries that layer.

Delaware imposes no ban on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, per the Movement Advancement Project equality map (the archived equality-map URL returned HTTP 404 at the time of checking).

Since 2013 Delaware law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and other areas under SB 97, which passed the Senate 11-7 on 6 June 2013, passed the House 24-17 with amendments, passed the Senate on amendments 11-9 on 18 June, was signed the next day and took effect immediately.

Since 2013 Delaware imposes additional penalties for a violent crime motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity.

HB142 to formally repeal the common-law gay and trans panic defense and ban its usage was introduced in May 2023 and passed both houses of the Legislature in June 2023, with the Governor yet to either sign or veto it.

Transgender people may change their legal gender on state-issued identification with only the signed statement of a licensed medical provider, and as of 11 February 2017 sex reassignment surgery is no longer an explicit requirement for an amended birth certificate, which instead requires a signed affidavit of surgical, hormonal, psychological or other treatment appropriate for gender transition.

A 2015 law signed 25 June 2015 and effective immediately allows inmates to access and change the name on birth certificates to reflect gender identity, where previously inmates could only change names due to religious beliefs.

Since 26 March 2016 Delaware has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity within insurance contracts, including sex reassignment surgery.

As of April 2020 Delaware does not offer a gender X option on drivers licenses.

An 11 August 2009 executive order protects employees of state executive branch departments and agencies from discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

Since 26 July 2018 (SB 65, signed and effective 23 July 2018 as Laws of Delaware 81:340, introduced 26 April 2017), Delaware defines conversion therapy to include practices seeking to change gender identity, behaviors or gender expressions and makes it unprofessional conduct subject to discipline for physicians, nurses, mental health and chemical dependency professionals, psychologists and clinical social workers to perform it on a minor or refer a minor out-of-state for it, while prohibiting the Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families from performing or recommending it for a minor.

A July 2026 national legal risk assessment lists Delaware in its Low-Risk States group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC), described as states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection.

66186276B6628180846672.name: Pennsylvania
66186276B6628180846672.summary:
Pennsylvania stands under the United States federal framework, and the federal layer of travel-document, entry-screening and facilities risk is carried by the national record rather than restated here. Within the state, Erin Reed's anti-trans legal-risk map places Pennsylvania in its low-risk tier in its July 2026 update, covering states that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without specially protecting them, while documenting continued national degradation of trans rights through the 2026 legislative season.

State-level discrimination protection is explicit. Since June 2023, discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been banned statewide, building on executive-order protection for state employees since 2003 and for state contractors since April 7, 2016, and on the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission's interpretation since August 2018 that the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act's ban on sex discrimination covers gender identity, with complaint investigation and remedies including stop orders, training and economic damages. Legally binding regulations signed in December 2022 define sex to include gender identity. The June 15, 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County decision supplies parallel federal Title VII workplace protection.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since August 2016 a transgender person can change the gender on a Pennsylvania birth certificate with a physician note of appropriate clinical treatment, without sex reassignment surgery; parental request is required under age 18, and there is no X option on birth certificates. Driver's licences and state IDs have offered the X marker since July 23, 2020.

The live legislative pressure is concentrated on school and collegiate sports rather than on trans adults or public-facility access. The Pennsylvania Senate approved Senate Bill 9, the Save Women's Sports Act, on May 6, 2025, reserving teams designated for women for "biological females" in K-12 and collegiate sport and sending it to the House; the Senate Republican Caucus release, with sponsors including Sens. Judy Ward and Kristin Phillips-Hill, confirms repeated upper-chamber backing for such restrictions. The Senate passed a further measure, Senate Bill 1293, on April 22, 2026, which would ban transgender female athletes from girls' and women's teams in the commonwealth; the Pennsylvania Capital-Star reports Gov. Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers "extremists," and it was unclear whether the House would take the bill up. A June 2022 bill to bar transgender athletes from female teams passed both houses but was vetoed on July 11, 2022 by Gov. Tom Wolf, who rejected legislation that would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed with female-designated sports restricted to athletes assigned female at birth.

Facilities access in Philadelphia is affirmatively protected. November 2019 ordinances require at least one gender-neutral bathroom in every city-owned building, prohibit youth-serving organizations from discriminating against trans, nonbinary and gender-nonconforming youth, and clarify that the city's Fair Practice Ordinance covers nonbinary and gender-fluid people. In December 2021 Philadelphia added X alongside male and female in all virtual public schools.

Philadelphia operates as a sanctuary jurisdiction for gender-affirming care. On October 17, 2023 Mayor Jim Kenney issued an executive order banning use of city resources to investigate or punish in-state and out-of-state residents seeking gender-affirming care in the city, deprioritising enforcement of any future state or federal restrictions, and shielding travellers from out-of-state enforcement. In October 2023 the city also became, by executive order, a sanctuary for transgender and non-binary individuals for access, health and safety to services.

Care and conversion-therapy restrictions are locally entrenched. Sex reassignment surgery is legal in Pennsylvania. Conversion therapy on minors is banned by local ordinances including Pittsburgh (passed December 14, 2016, effective January 1, 2017), Philadelphia, Allentown, Reading, Doylestown, State College, Yardley, Bellefonte, Bethlehem, Newtown Township and York, alongside a May 2024 ban by five health boards applying to statewide healthcare policies and an August 2022 executive order barring state government funding for conversion therapy. A statewide conversion-therapy ban, including an April 2015 bill with 20 sponsors, has repeatedly died without action.

Hate-crime protection for LGBTQ people is not in force. The 2002 hate-crime law covering LGBTQ people was struck down in 2008 on a technicality over its insertion into an agricultural terrorism bill, and reinstatement never left committee. An April 2021 Pittsburgh mayoral proposal for a city ordinance explicitly including gender identity is the local counterweight.

Education and family law carry specific rulings. In October 2024 a district court ruled that Mt. Lebanon School District must allow parents to opt children out of lessons or activities about transgender identity. The state Supreme Court ruled in March 2025 that same-sex couples must have equal legal parentage obligations for IVF children as heterosexual couples within an established household agreement regardless of marital status; a single person may adopt without regard to sexual orientation, stepchild adoption by a same-sex partner was established by a 6-0 Supreme Court ruling in 2002, and no statute prohibits joint adoption by a same-sex couple. Same-sex marriage has been legal since May 20, 2014 under Whitewood v. Wolf, which struck the statutory ban after a suit filed July 9, 2013 that Attorney General Kathleen Kane refused to defend; Philadelphia offers life partnerships and Pittsburgh domestic partnerships for same-gender couples, and Luzerne County defines a domestic partnership as between people of the same gender.

66186276B91272823970344.name: Wisconsin
66186276B91272823970344.summary:
Wisconsin is a state within the United States and stands under the country's national framework, which is carried by the national record. What follows is the Wisconsin-specific layer only.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Wisconsin in its low-risk group alongside Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Arizona and the District of Columbia, describing jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them. Wisconsin sits in that middle position: no state restriction on transgender people's use of facilities, no state ban on gender-affirming care, and no statewide nondiscrimination protection on gender identity.

As of May 2025 Wisconsin had no law barring transgender people from government-building bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender identity, no law defining sex to exclude transgender people, and no restriction on drag performance. The Equality Map, which tracks state-level facility bans, records no such ban in Wisconsin.

Gender-affirming care for minors is not banned in Wisconsin. Governor Tony Evers vetoed Assembly Bill 465 on 6 December 2023 and, later the same month, a second legislature-passed bill barring such care for under-18s; a 2021 bill barring insurers from covering the procedures failed in committee. Wisconsin also did not enact a trans-athlete ban: Evers vetoed the bill on 2 April 2024, having promised the veto since its introduction, and the bill's sponsor called the decision disgusting.

Care access nonetheless narrowed under federal funding pressure. On 13 January 2026 UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced a pause on gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18 after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care to minors. Mental and behavioural health services continued. Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul joined a coalition of states seeking to block the HHS declaration. The pause flows from federal pressure rather than any state ban, and Wisconsin has no shield law.

Wisconsin has no statewide nondiscrimination law covering gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. As of May 2025, 21% of the population was covered by full local ordinances in 10 cities and 12% by partial ordinances, so in most of the state a refusal of service or accommodation on grounds of gender identity has no state or local statutory remedy. The state hate-crime law covers sexual orientation but not gender identity, though prosecutors have used perceived sexual orientation as the medium to charge crimes motivated by a victim's gender identity.

State employment is covered. Executive Order #1, issued 7 January 2019, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in state employment, state contracting and the provision of state services, and directs state agencies to adopt and enforce nondiscrimination policies carrying those protections.

Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department has stopped publishing the gender of crime victims, a change made to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in future reporting.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wisconsin (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Wisconsin has no statewide anti-discrimination law covering gender identity and gender identity is not covered in the state's hate crime law, though perceived sexual orientation is often used as a medium to prosecute crimes based on the victim's gender identity; Executive Order #1 in January 2019 prohibited gender-identity discrimination in government employment, while Dane and Milwaukee counties and the cities of Appleton, Cudahy, De Pere, Janesville, Madison, Milwaukee and Racine ban gender-identity discrimination and Oshkosh and Stevens Point ban discrimination against transgender city employees only. A person born in the state who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend their birth certificate upon documentation of surgery and name change, while persons on Wisconsin's sex offender registry are not allowed to change their names with no exception if the person is transgender. Sex reassignment surgery had to be explicitly included in Wisconsin Medicaid for government employees from January 2019 and was ordered extended to non-government employees in May 2019 under the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, while a June 2023 budget bill passed by both houses banning Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming healthcare to all individuals regardless of age was vetoed under line-item veto power. People in prison are entitled to hormone therapy after the 2005 Inmate Sex Change Prevention Act denying hormone therapy to prisoners undergoing sex reassignment was ruled unconstitutional unanimously in Fields v. Smith by the Seventh Circuit on August 5, 2011, with Supreme Court denial of the state's appeal on March 26, 2012. Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department no longer lists gender as well as race of victims to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in the future. On sports, a 2021 Republican bill banning transgender women from teams aligning with their gender passed the Assembly on party lines but was never voted in the Senate, was re-introduced in 2023, and a 2024 legislature-passed bill banning transgender individuals from female sports and athletics teams was vetoed by the Governor. On medical care, a 2021 Republican bill prohibiting insurers from covering gender-affirming care procedures for minors failed in committee, a re-introduced bill passed the Assembly October 12, 2023 and Senate October 17, 2023 and was vetoed December 6, 2023, and in December 2023 the Governor also vetoed a legislature-passed bill explicitly banning gender-affirming healthcare to individuals under 18. Consensual sodomy prohibitions originating in Michigan Territory in 1836 and retained at 1848 statehood, expanded to fellatio in 1897 and to cunnilingus with five-year penalties for sexual perversion in the 1950s, were reclassified as a misdemeanor punishable by nine months jail and/or 10,000 dollars in 1977 and legalized for private, non-commercial acts between consenting adults in 1983 with a statement that Wisconsin did not approve of any sexual conduct outside marriage. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 6, 2014 when the Supreme Court refused appeal in Wolf v. Walker, lifting Judge Crabb's stay, while the Chapter 770 domestic partnership registry established in 2009 providing 43 of 200-plus spousal rights without stepchild adoptions was upheld unanimously in Appling v. Walker on July 31, 2014 and ended April 1, 2018, with same-sex partner benefits for state employees since 2009. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned statewide in employment, housing, education, credit and all public accommodations since 1982, making Wisconsin the first U.S. state to do so, and sexual orientation is a protected class in hate crime law and under a 2001 law prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination in schools. Parenting provisions allow individuals to adopt without respect to sexual orientation and married same-sex couples to adopt, allow lesbian access to IVF and artificial insemination with state recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother only if married, required recording of both same-sex parents on birth certificates under a September 2016 federal ruling, and from July 1, 2021 provide gender-neutral spouse and spouse or parent 1 and parent 2 birth certificate options for children of same-sex couples. Conversion therapy on minors is banned in 14 communities including Milwaukee in March 2018, Madison in July 2018, Eau Claire in October 2018, plus Cudahy, Shorewood, Racine, Glendale, Sheboygan, Superior, West Allis by 6-3 in September 2020, Kenosha by 14-1 in October 2020 with maximum 1,000 dollar fine plus costs and 90 days in Kenosha County Jail and possible suspension of driving privileges up to five years, Sun Prairie, Appleton and La Crosse, while a June 2021 executive order banned state taxpayer dollars funding conversion therapy on LGBT minors, statewide ban efforts were blocked in June 2020 and January 2023, and in July 2025 the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled 4-3 that bans can be enacted by regulation and executive order. A 2017 PRRI poll found 73% supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity with 20% opposed, distinct from 66% support for same-sex marriage with 26% opposed and 8% unsure. In October 2023 Governor Evers, speaking to "LGBTQ folks — especially our trans kids", said he would "veto any bill that makes Wisconsin a less welcoming, less inclusive, and less safe place for you to be who you are". Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department has omitted victim gender to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in the future. Introductions of the transgender athlete and medical-care bills sparked significant backlash from organizational and community advocates, including Fair Wisconsin, GSAFE, and the ACLU of Wisconsin.

66186276B37442548568489.summary:
Michigan stands under the national framework of the United States. The July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map places Michigan in the 'Low-Risk States' tier, noting that Michigan has enacted fairly robust non-discrimination policies but falls short in ensuring healthcare equity and providing protections for incarcerated transgender individuals. The same map designates the United States 'Do Not Travel' for transgender people overall, so the state-level tier does not offset the national warning.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is unlawful under Michigan's Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act. The Michigan Supreme Court affirmed this in a July 2022 ruling on the Attorney General's appeal, and the protection was codified by legislation signed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer on 8 March 2023. The ruling built on the Michigan Civil Rights Commission's 5-0 interpretation of 21 May 2018 and the Sixth Circuit's 7 March 2018 decision in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes holding that Title VII bars employment discrimination against transgender people.

Insurance companies and corporations are explicitly barred from discriminating on the basis of gender identity under a bill passed by both houses in October 2023 and signed by Governor Whitmer. State government employment protections cover gender identity through the 2007 extension and a January 2019 executive order covering state employment, contractors and grantees.

Gender identity is implicitly included under Michigan's 1992 hate-crime law via the term 'gender', per an August 2021 court declaration. A hate-crime package explicitly adding 'gender identity or expression' passed the House in June 2023 and the Senate in December 2024, and was signed in January 2025 with effect 90 days after signature. Federal hate-crime coverage has applied since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.

The gay and trans panic defence was abolished by law passed, signed and implemented in July 2024. Conversion therapy is banned statewide by a bill passed by both houses in June 2023 and signed in July 2023, following a June 2021 executive order barring taxpayer funding for conversion therapy on minors and local ordinances including an August 2020 Royal Oak ban punishable by up to 90 days jail and a $500 fine.

Sex on Michigan birth certificates can be changed without sexual reassignment surgery, following a 30 June 2021 court ruling declaring the 1978 surgery and physician-statement requirement unconstitutional; this was certified and codified by a bill passed in December 2024. Changing sex on a driver's licence or state ID requires a signed statutory declaration and a fee under the system introduced in November 2019. An 'X' marker was announced as forthcoming in January 2020 and described as 'soon' in November 2021; whether it is now available is not confirmed in these sources.

In March 2025 the Michigan House adopted a bipartisan, non-binding resolution urging the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) to ban transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports. The measure is advisory only and does not change state law or the state's non-discrimination protections. 66186276B98615608994420.name: Nevada
66186276B98615608994420.summary:
Nevada is one of the more protective US states for a trans visitor, though it sits below the most-protective tier. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, crediting the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while finding it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

State anti-discrimination law covers gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public accommodations under statutes effective 1 October 2011 and extended throughout state codes effective 1 July 2017. In November 2022 voters approved Question 1 by 58%, writing sexual orientation and gender identity or expression into the state Constitution's equal protection clause.

Nevada's hate-crime law adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived characteristics; gender identity or expression was added by a May 2013 amendment effective 1 October 2013, and a hate-crime reporting hotline opened in January 2025.

Identity documents are among Nevada's most permissive features. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with no sex reassignment surgery required; the DMV makes similar changes to driver's licences and state IDs. The state offers an X third-gender designation on licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation (2019). A 2017 law signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that trans people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes.

Facilities access is not restricted by state law: the Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map, which tracks state-by-state rules on whether trans people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, does not record a Nevada ban.

Care access has a mixed record. Health insurers are barred under state law from discriminating against transgender patients. The state Medicaid agency announced in March 2018 it would cover sex-reassignment surgery. A bill passed June 2023 and effective 1 January 2024 requires insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments. The governor vetoed the broader SB 302 omnibus in 2023, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and mandated Medicaid surgery coverage.

In May 2023 the governor signed legislation explicitly protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, one of the areas the July 2026 assessment still flags as under-protective in practice.

School sport moved the other way. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth. A governor-supported 2026 ballot initiative to generally determine school sports eligibility by sex assigned at birth failed to reach the November 2026 ballot.

Anti-bullying law SB 504, effective 1 July 2015, expressly lists gender identity or expression as a protected ground and directs school policies, reporting, parent notification and staff training. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 1 January 2018.

sources.title: Transgender rights in the United States (Wikipedia)

California stands under the United States national framework on travel documents, entry screening and federal facilities policy; that national layer is not repeated here. What is specific to California is a statutory and administrative posture that is protective on care access and on custody, alongside a documented record of anti-LGBTQ hostility.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 107 in September 2022, the first law of its kind in the country: out-of-state youth can obtain hormones and puberty blockers here, and the statute shields families from child-abuse investigations and criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care. Recorded anti-LGBTQ hostility in California is documented at scale. The GLAAD ALERT Desk recorded more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, of which California accounted for 198, the highest state count in the dataset. That ranking is by raw count only: the source gives no per-capita or population denominator, so it does not establish that California is more dangerous per resident than smaller states, and it does not diminish the volume of incidents recorded here.

Law-enforcement data for Los Angeles shows a "dramatic increase" in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports over the same period, which the analysis places alongside Governor Gavin Newsom's platforming of anti-trans figures. Los Angeles is one city within the statewide count, and the source does not break the 198 incidents down by offence type or by whether targets were transgender.

66186276B35012827062242.name: Colorado
66186276B35012827062242.summary:
Colorado's own law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage that dates to 2008 and was expanded again in 2025 through the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act. The Kelly Loving Act, signed by Governor Jared Polis on 16 May 2025, requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, bars deadnaming and misgendering, requires schools with dress codes to allow any uniform option, and simplifies gender-marker changes on birth certificates and driver's licences from 1 October 2026. As of 12 October 2026, the state's gender-identity policy score stood at 23.25 out of 25 in the Movement Advancement Project's equality mapping.

Identity documents are comparatively open. The surgical requirement for changing the gender marker on a birth certificate was removed unanimously by the Board of Public Health and Environment in February 2019; a Change of Sex Designation form suffices for licences and IDs through the Division of Motor Vehicles, and Birth Certificate Correction and Sex Designation forms go to the Department of Public Health and Environment. Birth certificates offer M, F and X markers, and IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus a medical or mental health professional's involvement.

Hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001 with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a Greeley jury convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in what was described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The anti-bullying statute also prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the Colorado Civil Rights Division ruled that transgender six-year-old Coy Mathis could use the girls' bathroom at her elementary school in Fountain, and in 2023 Colorado implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. There is no state bathroom ban of the kind in force in nine states and one territory.

Care access is contested on two fronts. The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on 18 May 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law by suspending gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, ordering an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy; Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denied petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity, and two justices dissented citing federal threats to the hospital system. Separately, Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning 13 October 2026 because a federal rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care under 18 (and under 19 under the CHP+ child programme); about 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25, patients already on hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period, behavioural healthcare is unaffected, and the state Medicaid agency said resuming coverage will require legislative action.

Insurance coverage is comparatively broad. Basic health insurance in Colorado must explicitly include sexual reassignment surgery as a basic policy from 2023, and a July 2026 national assessment counts Colorado among the states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. The same assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people.

Conversion therapy on minors was banned statewide by a bill signed 31 May 2019. Following the U.S. Supreme Court's 31 March 2026 ruling in Chiles v. Salazar by 8-1 requiring strict scrutiny of that ban, Colorado passed HB 26-1322 on 8 May 2026, which redefines conversion therapy as direction toward a pre-determined gender identity or sexual orientation outcome and removes the statute of limitations for claims.

Prison conditions are governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged the Colorado Department of Corrections subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care. A court-approved 2024 consent decree in Denver District Court (Raven v. Polis) required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing (a 100-bed unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison), and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. A 2019 settlement (Lindsay Saunders-Velez, $170,000) addressed the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief achieved through litigation and consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

State-level school sports policy is moving in the opposite direction. In April 2025 the D49 school board voted 3-2 to advance a policy banning biologically male students from female sports and vice versa, the D-11 Board voted 6-1 in June 2025 for a similar policy with Academy District 20 following suit, and in December 2025 an undisclosed lawsuit settlement was reached over banning trans individuals from playing on female sports teams within some association governing districts. 66186276B10610315112087.summary:
Minnesota stands under the United States federal framework, and the state's own law runs in the opposite direction from several other states. Minnesota Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (HF 146) provides that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied" in pending cases, and the law amends provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions related to out-of-state laws on gender-affirming health care. House File 146, the "Trans Refuge Bill," passed the Minnesota House on 24 March 2023 by 68-62 and was signed by Governor Tim Walz effective immediately; it protects transgender patients and providers of gender-affirming care that is legal in Minnesota from legal action in states where such care is banned, prohibiting enforcement in Minnesota of out-of-state subpoenas, arrest warrants and extradition requests related to such care and barring compliance with out-of-state court orders to remove children from parental custody for obtaining such care. The shield followed a March 2023 executive order and a Department of Health review of the scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care, and providers may bill insurance for such care.

Minnesota has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity since 1993 in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation rights. A May 2023 omnibus community justice bill explicitly added "gender identity" separately from sexual orientation and repealed exemptions for nonpublic service organizations, effective immediately. Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes committed based on gender identity since its 1993 expansion to include that category.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Changing legal gender on a Minnesota birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery; it requires a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a court order for gender change, plus a notarized Birth Certificate Application and fee, with the old certificate kept confidential. Driver and Vehicle Services updates a driver's license or state ID upon individual request with no documentation required, and since October 2018 licences and state IDs allow M, F, or X upon request with no documentation for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex people. No X option is available on Minnesota birth certificates.

Care access is protected at state level. State Medicaid policy covers transgender-related care, and Minnesota law prohibits health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients. Conversion therapy was banned statewide effective 1 August 2023 after a July 2021 executive order and prior city ordinances; the ban covers medical and mental-health practitioners, prohibits advertising that describes LGBTQ identities as a mental disease or promises to change sexual orientation or gender identity, makes violations subject to discipline by health licensing boards, and bars insurers and health plans from paying for it. The "trans panic defense" was abolished in the omnibus justice reforms bill signed 29 May 2024, effective 1 August 2024, after a 34-33 Senate vote.

A July 2026 national legal risk assessment lists Minnesota among the most protective states, the tier that assessment treats as strongest. The Minnesota high school transgender athlete policy has been challenged in court by attorneys representing three school softball players, so the operative position on school sport should be checked before relying on it.

The Minnesota Department of Corrections placed her in an adult male facility, Minnesota Correctional Facility - St. Cloud, after a state gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility; despite a later transfer to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment (a petition during her imprisonment led DOC to administer the correct hormone regimen). She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial, and in May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound requiring eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation.

66186276B73434888205604.name: New Jersey
66186276B73434888205604.summary:
A trans visitor to New Jersey is bound first by United States federal rules, which apply identically in every state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passport applications are decided only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted. Passports already issued with an X marker stay valid until expiry, but travellers whose papers no longer match their presentation can expect questions at issuance and at the border. The ACLU's lawsuit on behalf of seven plaintiffs and Lambda Legal's documentation guidance are the outstanding points of challenge, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, followed by the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, requires refusal of visas to trans athletes seeking to enter to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement treats a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth as potential fraud, carrying a permanent bar. A visitor travelling for sport should assume the rule is applied mechanically.

Checkpoint procedures risk involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as steps that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Inside New Jersey the measured legal environment is among the most protective in the country. The July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, places New Jersey in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier whose laws have, in the assessment's words, gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. On the separate state-by-state dataset of killings of trans women covering 2008 to 2025, New Jersey records 3.4 per 100,000 per year, four recorded deaths in total, and is labelled 'Safest States'.

sources.summary: State-by-state dataset of killings of trans women 2008-2025 (TGEU Trans Murder Monitoring / Williams Institute): New Jersey = 3.4 per 100k per year (4 recorded deaths), labelled 'Safest States', against 428 US trans women confirmed killed since 2008. Central finding: state anti-trans law hostility does not correlate with where trans women are killed (trendline nearly flat over the 26-state comparison) - law predicts government treatment (ID, healthcare, bathroom access), not private violence.

July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills (youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate/driver-license restrictions, end of legal recognition): New Jersey sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier (CA, CO, CT, HI, IL, MA, MD, MN, NJ, NM, NY, OR, RI, VT, WA), whose laws have 'gone above and beyond in safeguarding' trans rights. Contrast tier: worst-law states carry up to 5-year prison terms (Idaho) or arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use (Florida).

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Jersey (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination was amended in 2006 to include gender identity and expression as prohibited categories for employment, housing and public accommodations. Enhanced penalties apply for crimes with bias based on gender identity or expression with sensitivity-training sentencing options, the FBI New Jersey division reports gender X since June 2021, bill A-4833 on bias and intimidation based on gender identity passed the lower house 71-0 in March 2021, and July 2022 laws created a police licensing system with gender-identity protections and protected sexual orientation and gender identity data in state-run hospital patient records. Since February 1, 2019 transgender persons may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and sex without surgery or medical procedures under three 2018 laws signed in June 2018 by Governor Phil Murphy that established a Transgender Equality Task Force, repealed the surgery requirement, created an X marker on official documents, and included transgender and intersex people on death certificates effective July 4, 2018. Since February 2020 no doctor's note is required to change driver license/ID sex marker M to F or F to M, since April 2021 X, M and F markers are available, and a November 2022 executive order provides privacy, dignity and confidentiality for legal name changes. An April 2023 executive order protects and defends gender-affirming healthcare within New Jersey borders including interstate access. The New Jersey State Interscholastic Athletic Association allows sports participation according to gender identity, and September 2018 school guidance promotes transgender-friendly policies on names and pronouns, participation in activities, use of facilities and student records. In June 2023 school boards in Middletown, Marlboro and Manalapan-Englishtown adopted parental notification policies outing transgender and non-binary students described as potentially violating discrimination and hate-crime legislation with a lawsuit by the Attorney General's office to block them, and the January 2020 law banning the gay panic defense provides provocation is not objectively reasonable if based on actual or perceived gender identity or expression including unwanted non-forcible romantic or sexual advance. Same-sex sexual activity is legal after State v. Ciuffini (1978) struck down sodomy laws as violating personal privacy and autonomy and the legislature repealed the sodomy law in 1978. LGBT persons were allowed to gather in drinking establishments after One Eleven Liquors, Inc. vs. Division of Alcoholic Beverage Commission in 1967 invalidated license revocations under the rule against serving female impersonators or persons of ill repute, with an official apology by Attorney General Gurbir Grewal in June 2021. Same-sex marriages have been recognized and performed since October 21, 2013 following a September 27 court decision whose appeal was rejected October 19, 2013, and were codified by legislation passed December 2021 and signed January 10, 2022 by Governor Phil Murphy effective immediately. The Law Against Discrimination was amended in 1991 to include affectional or sexual orientation prohibiting discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations including based on perceived orientation. Enhanced penalties apply for bias-motivated crimes based on sexual orientation with sensitivity-training sentencing options, and bill A1796 banning the gay panic defense for provocation based on affectional or sexual orientation including unwanted non-forcible advance passed 73-0 and 39-0 and was signed in January 2020 effective immediately. Sexual orientation change efforts directed at minors were banned by legislation passed June 2013 and signed August 19, 2013, upheld November 8, 2013 in District Court and September 11, 2014 in the Third Circuit with Supreme Court review declined in May 2015 and again April 15, 2019 in King v. Murphy, with a Hudson County ruling that claiming to cure a disorder is fraud. Knowing HIV nondisclosure in sexual activity was a third-degree offense versus fourth-degree for other STIs until bill S3707 signed January 18, 2022 reduced engaging in sex while infected with any STI including HIV to a disorderly persons offense.

sources.title: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (amended 1991, 2006)
sources.summary: New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination was amended in 1991 to prohibit discrimination based on affectional or sexual orientation and in 2006 to prohibit discrimination based on gender identity or expression. For trans visitors this bars denial of goods, services, facilities or lodging based on gender identity or expression in places of public accommodation including hotels, restaurants, stores and transportation and in housing, enforceable through complaints to the Division on Civil Rights for investigation and relief.

sources.title: 2018 transgender rights package - birth certificates, death certificates, Transgender Equality Task Force

Connecticut is one of fifteen states placed in the 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition. Connecticut's hate-crime statute covers gender identity or expression and carries additional penalties; that legislation was consolidated and strengthened by a law signed in June 2026, effective 1 October 2026.

Connecticut operates a healthcare shield or refuge law, in force since 2022, which protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal here has been banned in the patient's home state. This is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a state that prohibits gender-affirming care.

Since 1 October 2015, under H.B. 7006, the sex marker on a Connecticut birth certificate can be changed without surgery, on a notarised applicant affidavit plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. 66186276B99594608635082.name: Hawaii
66186276B99594608635082.summary:
Hawaii is a state within the United States and stands under the US federal framework; the findings below concern Hawaii's own laws and their application on the ground.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition, places Hawaii in a fifteen-state Most Protective tier. The assessment describes the laws of that tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding transgender rights.

Hawaii operates a transgender healthcare shield law. As of 27 September 2026 the MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map lists Hawaii as a state holding a shield law or 2026 executive order, protecting patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Hawaii has been banned in the patient's home state. This bears directly on visitors travelling from states with youth-care bans, and on residents of Hawaii whose care could otherwise be pursued across state lines.

State law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public accommodations since 2006 and in housing since 2005, in employment since 2011, and in insurance contracts since 1 July 2016. A visitor who is refused service, lodging or an insurance-related benefit on grounds of gender identity has a state statutory claim.

Hawaii's hate-crime law covers conduct motivated by actual or perceived gender identity or expression. The statutory definition expressly includes a person's actual or perceived gender, gender identity, gender-related self-image, appearance or expression, whether or not that differs from the gender traditionally associated with the person's sex at birth. The law took effect immediately on 14 July 2015.

The gay and trans panic defences were abolished in 2019, signed 26 June and effective immediately, removing a defence strategy that had allowed defendants in assault cases to rely on the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 5 July 2015 a transgender person may change the gender marker on a Hawaii birth certificate or state identification without sex reassignment surgery, simply by request: an updated birth certificate requires an Application for Amendment to Birth Record with an affidavit from a licensed physician, and a driver's licence or state ID requires a Gender Designation Form completed by a medical or social professional confirming gender identity. An X sex option on both driver's licences and birth certificates has been available since 1 July 2020, changeable by request with no medical documentation required.

Marriage is not restricted to opposite-sex couples under the state constitution. The 1998 provision authorising the legislature to reserve marriage to opposite-sex couples was replaced by the Hawaii Marriage Equality Act of 2013 and repealed by voters on 5 November 2024 with 55.94 per cent voting to delete the opposite-sex limitation from Article I Section 23. State law separately prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and of gender and gender identity.

State-regulated health insurance must cover sex reassignment surgery, with mandatory coverage effective 1 January 2023 under the nondiscrimination rule in insurance contracts that took effect 1 July 2016, and transgender individuals must be included in health insurance planning under a bill signed in 2022 with an emergency clause, effective immediately.

Hate-crime law protects actual and/or perceived gender identity or expression, defined to include a person's actual or perceived gender, gender identity, gender-related self image, appearance, or expression regardless of whether different from that traditionally associated with the person's sex at birth. Since the law passed May 5, 2015, signed July 14, 2015 and effective immediately, transgender people may change the gender marker without sex reassignment surgery simply by request, with an updated birth certificate requiring a completed Application for Amendment to Birth Record and affidavit from a licensed physician and an updated driver's license or state ID requiring a Gender Designation Form completed by a medical or social professional confirming gender identity. An X sex option on driver's licenses and birth certificates was passed in May 2019, signed June 26, 2019 and effective July 1, 2020, with change by request and no medical documentation required. Health care provisions include insurance coverage of sex reassignment surgeries under the 2016 insurance nondiscrimination rule, mandatory coverage effective January 1, 2023, and inclusion of transgender individuals in health insurance planning under a bill passed May 2022 with emergency clause signed a month later effective immediately, replacing male- and female-only planning since 1980. The gay and trans panic defenses were abolished by a bill passed April 2019 through conference committee April 26, signed June 26, 2019 effective immediately, while anti-bullying law covering gender identity and expression including cyberbullying in public elementary and secondary schools and a July 2018 Title IX law effective January 1, 2019 ensure students are not denied programs or extracurricular activities because of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the beginning of 1973 following repeal in April 1972 with sex offences revised in 1986, replacing the 1850 anti-sodomy statute that punished both heterosexual and homosexual consensual adult conduct with up to 20 years' hard labor and a $1,000 fine and was last enforced in the 1958 case Territory v. Bell. The age of consent was lowered to 14 in 1986 regardless of gender or sexual orientation and raised to 16 in 2001. Same-sex couples have been allowed to marry since the Hawaii Marriage Equality Act passed the Senate 20-4 on October 30, 2013, the House 30-19 on November 8, 2013 and final Senate approval 19-4 on November 12, signed November 13 with marriages beginning December 2, 2013, following the May 1993 Hawaii Supreme Court finding of unconstitutional restriction, a 1994 statutory ban, November 1998 Constitutional Amendment 2 passed with 70 percent to allow legislative ban leading to dismissal, and repeal by November 5, 2024 referendum with 55.9 percent. Reciprocal beneficiary relationships for same- and opposite-sex couples were established in 1997, a civil union law vetoed in 2010 was signed February 23, 2011 effective January 1, 2012, and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1997. Adoption is allowed for same-sex couples, lesbian couples can access IVF and artificial insemination with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized if married, surrogacy is legal with courts ruling for gay male gestational surrogacy, HB1096 passed April 2021 and signed July 2021 recognized unmarried same-sex parentage effective immediately, and Act 298 effective January 1, 2026 implements gender-neutral parentage by voluntary acknowledgment or court adjudication. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited in employment since 1991 and in housing since 2005 and public accommodations since 2006, hate-crime law covers actual and/or perceived sexual orientation defined as heterosexuality, homosexuality or bisexuality including history or identification, and conversion therapy on minors has been banned since July 1, 2018 after House and Senate passage in April 2018 and conference agreement in May 2018 signed by Governor David Ige. The gay panic defense was abolished with the trans panic defense in 2019 effective immediately, and 2023 FDA rules permit gay and bi men to donate blood on condition of being monogamous.

66186276B15934532614691.name: Massachusetts
66186276B15934532614691.summary:
Massachusetts sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and loss of legal recognition. The assessment records that the tier's laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding transgender rights, in contrast to the worst-law states, which carry up to five-year prison terms or arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use.

Massachusetts prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in credit, public and private employment, union practices and housing under legislation enacted 23 November 2011 and effective 1 July 2012, following a 17 February 2011 executive order protecting transgender state government employees and contractors. Public-accommodations coverage was added by Senate vote 33-4 on 12 May 2016 and House vote 117-36 on 7 July 2016, signed by Governor Charlie Baker and effective 1 October 2016, and was retained by popular vote on 6 November 2018 with 67.8% voting to uphold it against 32.2% opposed, the first statewide ballot question of its kind in the United States.

Gender identity was added to the hate-crime statute effective 1 July 2012. The framework defines a hate crime as any criminal act coupled with overt actions motivated at least in part by prejudice including gender and sexual orientation, and requires collection, summary and public reporting of incidents through the 1990 Hate Crimes Reporting Act, the Crime Reporting Unit, State Police, Attorney General and legislative committees, alongside a 1991 Governor's Task Force on Hate Crimes.

Transgender people may amend birth certificates to reflect gender identity without sex reassignment surgery, and may select a non-binary 'X' marker on driver's licences and state IDs by RMV regulation effective November 2019 and on birth certificates. Gender may be amended on marriage certificates under law signed 29 July 2024 as part of the FY25 budget, and Boston marriage licence forms have carried no gender or sex fields since August 2023. Confidential name changes without public notice became available under 'An Act Protecting Personal Security' signed 25 November 2025.

A July 2022 bill codifying reaffirmed gender-healthcare protections passed both houses, was signed by the Governor and took effect immediately under an emergency clause bypassing the usual 90-day period. The state operates a healthcare shield law, listed as 'State has shield law or executive order 2022' in MAP's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map as of 27 September 2026, which protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal in Massachusetts was banned in the patient's home state. Nationally, 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none.

Conversion therapy on LGBT minors was banned by legislation passed by the House 147-8 on 13 March 2019 and the Senate 34-0 on 28 March 2019, enacted 4 April 2019 and signed 8 April 2019 effective immediately, making Massachusetts the 16th state to do so. Discrimination against LGBTI individuals within nursing homes was prohibited by a bill passed by the General Court in August 2024 and signed 6 September 2024.

Private consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the 1974 Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decision in Commonwealth v. Balthazar, which held the 'unnatural and lascivious act' prohibition inapplicable to private consensual adult conduct; current private behaviour is permanently enjoined by that decision and Lawrence v. Texas. Sections 34 and 35, criminalizing the 'abominable and detestable crime against nature' and 'any unnatural and lascivious act', remain on the books unrepealed. Legislative repeal efforts repeatedly stalled in committee and through the 2018 session, followed by unanimous Senate passage of repeal in January 2024, House advancement in June 2025 and Senate committee scheduling for floor consideration 24 July 2025, leaving Massachusetts as the only New England state and one of two northern states still legislatively criminalizing same-sex activity.

Same-sex marriage has been authorized following the 18 November 2003 Goodridge v. Department of Public Health ruling, with licences issued from 17 May 2004 after a 180-day legislative window, unsuccessful constitutional-amendment attempts culminating in 2007, repeal on 31 July 2008 of the 1913 non-resident marriage bar, and 2012 rulings treating out-of-jurisdiction civil unions and California registered domestic partnerships as equivalent to marriage. Same-sex couples may adopt through second-parent adoption allowed since In re Adoption of Tammy in 1993, with visitation rights recognized July 1999, after 1985 foster-parent exclusionary regulations were rescinded April 1990 in settlement of suit by Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders and the ACLU. Birth-certificate forms were changed from mother/father to mother/parent and father/parent under Governor Deval Patrick in 2007, with standardized electronic hospital forms announced February 2011, and legal parentage from IVF and surrogacy regardless of marital status was passed unanimously 1 August 2024, signed 8 August 2024 and effective 1 January 2025.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1989 in credit, public and private employment, union practices, housing and public accommodation, the second such state law after Wisconsin in 1982, with sexual orientation added to the 1983 hate-crime law in June 1996 and recognized as a protective class for jury selection by an August 2021 Supreme Judicial Court ruling, alongside May 2010 anti-bullying legislation requiring schools to adopt reporting, investigation and anti-retaliation procedures. Catholic Charities of Boston ceased adoption services in March 2006 rather than comply with the law prohibiting discrimination against homosexuals.

66186276B2592965416524.name: New Mexico
66186276B2592965416524.summary:
New Mexico stands under the national framework of the United States, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry and screening follow national rules regardless of which state the visitor lands in. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, according to the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide, which sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Facility use and identity documents are regulated state by state, so the rules encountered inside New Mexico differ from those in states that restrict them. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances in some jurisdictions, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed after using a women's restroom at a state capitol, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following. Multiple foreign governments, at least eight European countries including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens after the federal document and data rules, and a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies four states now designated do-not-travel for trans people.

Within that national picture, New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of the July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The ranking is built from a rubric applied over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, and it records that the laws of the protective-tier states have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

New Mexico also operates a shield or refuge law, listed by the Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map as 'State has shield law or executive order 2023'. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in New Mexico has been banned in the home state of the person travelling for it. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state with a care ban, and it applies alongside, not instead of, the federal document and entry rules.
