sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Mexico (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, later expanded by repeal of the 15-or-more-employees exemption effective July 1, 2019 and by 2023 legislation explicitly covering local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under emergency clause, with Albuquerque amending its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align. Since 2003 hate-crime law explicitly covers violence committed based on actual or perceived gender identity, and March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies effective July 1, 2019. Since November 1, 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery under legislation repealing the 1984 surgery requirement and providing male, female and X neutral designation on birth certificates, driver's licenses and state IDs, passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. Applicants need only submit a completed Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, and a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licenses and IDs, replacing the prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician of surgical change plus certified name-change order. Since July 1, 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex under legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and signed by the Governor. In March 2023 HB7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sexual reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions even for interstate travellers, making New Mexico a sanctuary state for transgender youths, while HB31 repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper that risked privacy, safety and lives of transgender individuals, and in 2026 the health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule to exclude it. In February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed March 9, 2022, and there is no state law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation with eligibility determined by birth certificate original or amended and no further guidance from the New Mexico Activities Association. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since repeal of the anti-sodomy law in 1975, with a 1986 attempt to reinstate it failing. Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the December 19, 2013 state Supreme Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making New Mexico the 17th state to recognize same-sex marriage, with benefits for same-sex partners of state employees since 2003 and statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019, signed in April by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham effective July 1, 2019. Single persons, same-sex couples and second-parent adoptions are permitted with no prohibition, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization and donor insemination regardless of sexual orientation or marital status with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent, and no statute or case law prohibits gestational or traditional surrogacy which courts generally recognize. State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, supplemented by a 1985 executive order barring sexual-orientation discrimination in public employment, with enforcement upheld unanimously in Elane Photography v. Willock in 2013 for refusal to photograph a same-sex commitment ceremony. Since 2003 hate-crime law explicitly covers violence based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, and March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of sexual orientation effective July 1, 2019. Sexual orientation change efforts on minors are prohibited under SB121 passed 32-6 in the Senate and 44-23 in the House, signed April 7, 2017 by Governor Susana Martinez effective July 6, 2017. The common-law gay panic defence was repealed through omnibus crime bill HB68 passed in February 2022 and signed March 9, 2022 after unanimous Senate-only passages in 2019 and 2021 that died without House action. Historically the Navajo recognized four gender roles including nadleehi defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature, who due to perceived balance between sexes were typically chosen for certain societal and communal roles such as spiritual healers. They would traditionally wear female clothes and do female work, and some would have sexual relations with men which was accepted by the tribe, with similar recognized roles including Zuni lhamana and katsotse and equivalents among Mescalero Apache, Tiwa, Tewa and pueblos. As a result of colonization much of this cultural acceptance has disappeared, Navajo nadleehi became the subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among the Hopi were prohibited from attending the traditional snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. Will Roscoe is documented as writing about the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" as fueling Spanish explorers' argument for colonization of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity. Today LGBTQ Navajo may find it difficult being accepted by family, with 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempting suicide. Statewide polling showed 73% supported anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people in 2018 and 64% supported a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity in 2017, while Santa Fe is cited as a gay capital and Albuquerque including its metropolitan area as a gay-friendly city.

Against that federal backdrop, New York sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions, and the end of legal recognition. The ranking places New York alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington as states whose laws have, in the assessment's terms, gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New York (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gender identity or expression has been explicitly included in statewide credit, housing, employment, education, and public accommodation protections since GENDA was signed in January 2019 and took effect in February 2019, following a 2009 executive order banning gender-identity discrimination in state employment and Division of Human Rights regulations issued November 4, 2015 and effective January 20, 2016 banning transgender harassment and discrimination in those domains, plus a 2024 constitutional amendment explicitly banning discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since November 1, 2019 with further anti-bias reform bills signed November 2022, the gay and transgender panic defense was repealed in June 2019 effective immediately making New York the 6th state to abolish it, and conversion therapy on minors was banned effective January 25, 2019. Since 2014 transgender adults could change gender on birth certificates with a notarized medical affidavit verifying surgery or gender dysphoria diagnosis, updated in 2020 to allow self-affirmation if 17 or older and parental consent if younger, while the June 2021 Gender Recognition Act allowed X on driver's licenses and eased sealing of name and gender-change records, X on New York City birth certificates took effect January 1, 2019 and on death certificates from January 2, 2020, X was reported for state court and jury documents in November 2019 and in healthcare data from August 2020, X on all state forms was approved in April 2022 for 2023 with some organizations until 2024 plus updatable marriage certificates, and a November 2021 law effective January 1, 2022 requires utilities and municipalities to use preferred names and pronouns. Shield protections include a June 12, 2023 New York City executive order barring city resources to detain, prosecute or investigate provision or receipt of gender-affirming care, and a June 25, 2023 state law barring courts from enforcing out-of-state laws taking custody for youth gender-affirming care, barring treating such care as child abuse, and barring law enforcement cooperation with out-of-state agencies, making New York the 12th shield state, with a September 2023 Ithaca ordinance and April 2025 City Council bills expanding provider protections. Former Penal Law Section 240.37, in effect since 1976 and used by police to harass and arrest transgender individuals, was repealed in February 2021 effective immediately, and gender-neutral bathrooms were mandated by a law signed in December 2020 effective March 23, 2021. The anti-bullying law covers gender including gender identity and expression including cyberbullying in all public elementary and secondary schools with a 2019 loophole closure, a June 2023 law explicitly includes gender identity in drug treatment and addiction programs, a November 2020 law requires annual judiciary statistics by gender identity, while Nassau County remains the only county banning transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities with a 2025 ruling of no clear violation of anti-discrimination laws and an NYCLU lawsuit for inclusion. Consenting adult same-sex sexual activity was legalized by New York v. Onofre in 1980 except laws affecting National Guard employees with defunct sodomy provisions repealed effective 2000, adultery was repealed in November 2024, and a 2019 law granted state veterans benefits to those dishonorably discharged under Don't Ask, Don't Tell from 1993 to 2011. Same-sex marriage became legal statewide under the Marriage Equality Act passed June 24, 2011 and effective July 24, 2011 after a May 2008 directive recognizing out-of-jurisdiction marriages, with state-employee same-sex partner benefits since 1995 and New York City domestic partnerships since 1998. Adoption non-discrimination for gay and lesbian applicants was adopted in 1982, second-parent adoptions regardless of sexual orientation were protected by 1995 rulings in Matter of Jacob and Matter of Dana, joint same-sex adoption was allowed by 2004 In re Adoption of Carolyn B., though an October 2020 district court order allowed religious-affiliated agencies to turn away gay, single and unmarried heterosexual couples. Commercial surrogacy banned from 1992 to 2020 was legalized effective February 2021, with a February 2021 announcement requiring insurance to cover same-sex couples for IVF, surrogacy and fertility treatments amid an April 2022 lawsuit by a male same-sex couple alleging only heterosexual and female same-sex couples receive coverage. SONDA effective 2003 prohibits actual or perceived sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodations, education, credit and civil rights and explicitly includes asexuality, the Hate Crimes Act covered sexual orientation since July 1, 2001, conversion therapy on minors was banned effective January 25, 2019, and the 2024 constitution bans sexual orientation discrimination. Defamation law under Yonaty v. Mincolla on May 30, 2012 holds labeling someone gay or homosexual is no longer defamation, St. Patrick's Day parade bans ended September 2014 in New York City and November 2024 in Staten Island, and the 1985 law enabling municipalities to close gay bathhouses and saunas where high-risk sexual activities occur remains in effect as of August 2026. The article states New York has generally been seen as socially liberal regarding LGBTQ rights and New York City is now regarded as one of the most LGBTQ-friendly cities in the world. The article states societal and public attitudes toward the LGBTQ community evolved from general antipathy and hostility to tolerance and acceptance alongside reforms including 1980 legalization, 2003 sexual orientation and 2019 gender identity protections, relaxed transition rules, hate-crime law, and 2011 marriage equality. The article reports New York City is home to the largest transgender U.S. population estimated at 50,000 in 2018 concentrated in Manhattan and Queens, within broader 2005 estimates of 272,493 self-identifying gay and bisexual individuals in the city and 568,903 LGB residents in the metropolitan area. Cited polls show support for discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity at 75% in 2017 with 19% opposed and 82% in 2022 with 14% opposed, alongside same-sex marriage support at 69% in 2017 and 75% in 2022. The article provides no transgender-specific societal tolerance quote distinct from LGBTQ-general language; its tolerance descriptions quoted as "generally been seen as socially liberal in regard to [LGBTQ] rights" and attitudes going "from general antipathy and hostility to tolerance and acceptance" refer to the LGBTQ community generally, not transgender people specifically.

The July 2026 ranking that places New York in the top tier is a rubric-based assessment rather than a court finding, and its 'Most Protective' label describes statutes on the books rather than enforcement in practice or the behaviour of individual officers at a checkpoint.

The federal measures driving visitor risk have an unsettled legal status. 66186276B97229519707655.summary:
Oregon is among the more protective United States jurisdictions for a trans visitor at state level. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, places Oregon in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The same ranking records that the worst-law states carry up to five-year prison terms for gender-identity-based offences or arrest policies for bathroom use, a contrast that frames Oregon's position.

Statewide anti-discrimination protection has been in force since 1 January 2008 under the Oregon Equality Act, signed 9 May 2007, which prohibits unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations on the basis of gender identity. The statute defines sexual orientation to include gender identity regardless of whether identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from that traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. Senate Bill 2, signed by Governor Ted Kulongoski on 9 May 2007, extended the same prohibition across employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services, with exemptions for religious employers, organizations and institutions, creating uniform statewide protections that do not depend on locality. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option, X; June 2021 legislation updated the 2008 definition of gender identity, effective immediately.

State hate-crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity. Senate Bill 704, signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolished the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 2014 sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on an Oregon birth certificate solely by request. A 10 June 2016 circuit court ruling allowed a resident to legally change gender to non-binary, which the Transgender Law Center believed was the first such ruling in the United States. Since 1 July 2017 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered an X marker designating neutral or non-binary identity on licences and IDs, and X is also available on birth certificates. May 2017 legislation abolished the 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex.

Oregon operates a healthcare shield law. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists Oregon as a state with a shield law or executive order from 2023. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in Oregon has been banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. The law was signed by Governor Tina Kotek on 13 July 2023 after passing the House in May 2023 and, following a Republican boycott, passing the Senate with watered-down amendments. Nationally the same source records 16 states and the District of Columbia holding shields, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, while 32 states and 5 territories, 56%, hold none.

Public funding for gender-affirming care is established in Oregon. In January 2013, as part of a discrimination settlement, the state agreed to provide full medical insurance coverage for gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatments on public employee health plans. In August 2014 officials announced Medicaid would begin covering gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming healthcare.

Trans-inclusive school policy has survived litigation. A transgender-inclusive public schools policy withstood challenge after the District Court ruled against plaintiffs on 24 July 2018, the Ninth Circuit upheld it on 12 February 2020, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in December 2020 in Parents for Privacy v. Barr. April 2019 legislation, signed 6 May, amended a 1951 mental health law that had equated transvestites with pedophilia, passing 58-2 in the House and 29-0 in the Senate.

Two 2025 federal actions cut against this record. In July 2025 the Ninth Circuit ruled Oregon's adoption requirement to respect, accept and support a child's gender expression and sexual orientation unconstitutional, after the Department of Human Services prevented a woman from adopting. In June 2025 the United States Department of Education announced a Title IX investigation into the Oregon Department of Education for allowing transgender women to compete in women's sports.

Marriage and partnership recognition is settled state law. Same-sex marriage was legalized on 19 May 2014 when Judge Michael McShane struck down the 2004 Ballot Measure 36 constitutional amendment under the Equal Protection Clause; marriages from other jurisdictions have been recognized since 16 October 2013 per a Department of Justice opinion, and gender-neutral marriage was codified effective 1 January 2016. Domestic partnerships have been available since 4 February 2008 under the Family Fairness Act, and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1998. Oregon decriminalized same-sex sexual activity in 1972 following the 1971 repeal of the consensual sodomy law, with an age of consent of 18; a lewd solicitation provision was struck down on free speech grounds in a unanimous 1981 Oregon Supreme Court decision. Oregon became the third state to ban conversion therapy on minors, signed by Governor Kate Brown on 18 May 2015 and effective 1 July 2015. The state anti-bullying law covers bullying, cyberbullying and harassment in all public schools on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories. Same-sex couples, married or unmarried, may apply to adopt; lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction including in vitro fertilization, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent if married; surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted, though courts are generally favourable including for same-sex couples.

The country's state/province-level position for trans visitors is comparatively protective. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, places this state/province in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier. The same ranking records that the worst-law state/provinces carry up to five-year prison terms for gender-identity-based offences or arrest policies for bathroom use, a contrast that frames this position.

Statewide anti-discrimination protection has been in force since 1 January 2008 under a state/province Equality Act signed 9 May 2007, prohibiting unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations on the basis of gender identity. The statute defines sexual orientation to include gender identity regardless of whether identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from that traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. A companion bill signed the same date extended the prohibition across employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services, with exemptions for religious employers, organizations and institutions, creating uniform statewide protections that do not depend on locality. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option, X; June 2021 legislation updated the 2008 definition of gender identity, effective immediately.

state/province hate-crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity. A 2021 bill, signed in May and effective 1 January 2022, abolished the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 2014 sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on a state/province birth certificate solely by request. A 10 June 2016 circuit court ruling allowed a resident to legally change gender to non-binary, believed to be the first such ruling in the country. Since 1 July 2017 the state motor vehicles department has offered an X marker on licences and IDs, and X is also available on birth certificates. May 2017 legislation abolished a 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex.

The state operates a healthcare shield law. A national equality map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists this state/province as having a shield law or executive order from 2023. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal here has been banned in the patient's home state/province, directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. The law was signed by the governor on 13 July 2023 after passing the legislature with amendments following a boycott. Nationally the same source records 16 state/provinces and the national capital district holding shields, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, while 32 state/provinces and 5 state/provinces, 56%, hold none.

Public funding for gender-affirming care is established. In January 2013, as part of a discrimination settlement, the state agreed to provide full medical insurance coverage for gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatments on public employee health plans. In August 2014 officials announced Medicaid would begin covering gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming healthcare.

A transgender-inclusive public schools policy withstood challenge after the District Court ruled against plaintiffs on 24 July 2018, the appeals court upheld it on 12 February 2020, and the supreme court denied certiorari in December 2020. April 2019 legislation, signed 6 May, amended a 1951 mental health law that had equated transvestites with pedophilia, passing the legislature by large margins.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1972 following the 1971 repeal of the consensual sodomy law, with an age of consent of 18; a lewd solicitation provision was struck down on free speech grounds in a unanimous 1981 state/province supreme court decision. 66186276B98073251815399.name: Rhode Island
66186276B98073251815399.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to Rhode Island, because they are issued under national rules rather than state ones. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, new passport applications are processed only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry and screening follow the same national layer. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a separate exposure: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can reveal a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Against that background, Rhode Island is listed among the 'Most Protective' states in the anti-trans legal risk assessment published on 13 July 2026, in the gender-identity non-discrimination tier, and the assessment also places Rhode Island among jurisdictions whose shield protections are enforceable against out-of-state action. The same assessment reports erosion at the federal layer and concludes that the top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so a visitor's protection at the state level coexists with the document, visa and screening rules described above. No Rhode Island-specific restriction on identity documents, facility use or care appears in the source inventory.

Rhode Island is listed in mapresearch.org's transgender healthcare equality map among jurisdictions covered by shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches, which make protections enforceable against out-of-state action.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rhode Island (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression has been outlawed since 2001 in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations, with explicit bans in patient care, nursing and related healthcare added by a bill signed in June 2023, and repeal of the 1995 housing with 3 occupiers or less exemption effective January 1, 2023. Hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity or expression. The gay and trans panic defense was repealed by votes of 68-2 in the House and 27-0 in the Senate in June 2018, signed by Governor Gina Raimondo a month later and effective immediately. Since October 23, 2014, birth certificate gender change requires a Birth Certificate Request Form and affidavit from a physician, certified nurse practitioner or physician's assistant confirming transgender status, replacing the prior sex reassignment surgery requirement, while the Division of Motor Vehicles issues a corrected driver's license on a Gender Designation Form signed by the applicant. A third gender option X on driver's licenses and birth certificates was announced in August 2019 for availability from July 2020, and a June 2018 law ensures transgender people are correctly recorded on death certificates effective immediately. Single-occupancy toilets are legally allowed as gender-neutral bathrooms effective January 1, 2022 under a bill signed in July 2021. In March 2025 the Rhode Island Interscholastic League updated its transgender athletes policy so transgender athletes remain able to compete but member schools are responsible for ensuring compliance with all applicable state and federal law when determining gender-based eligibility, replacing the prior policy that allowed participation consistent with gender identity. Consensual same-sex sexual acts in private have been legal since anti-sodomy statutes were repealed in 1998 after House passage in May 1998 and Senate passage on June 2, 1998, signed by Governor Lincoln Almond, replacing prior penalties of 1 to 12 years and later 7 to 20 years imprisonment upheld as constitutional in State v. Lopes in 1995. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been outlawed since 1995 in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations, with explicit bans in patient care, nursing and related healthcare added in June 2023 and repeal of the housing with 3 occupiers or less exemption effective January 1, 2023. Hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation. The gay panic defense was repealed by 68-2 House and 27-0 Senate votes in June 2018, signed by Governor Gina Raimondo a month later and effective immediately. Conversion therapy on minors and state funding for such practices was prohibited by a law signed July 19, 2017 by Governor Raimondo effective immediately, after House votes of 69-0 and 62-0 and a Senate vote of 29-0. The anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of sexual orientation, explicitly includes cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all public schools.

66186276B17406925856308.name: Vermont
66186276B17406925856308.summary:
As of July 2026 Vermont is listed among the most protective US states on gender-identity nondiscrimination, though a national legal risk assessment notes that the federal layer is under attack through the DC House bathroom ban, so that tier on its own can no longer be considered fully protective.

State law bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices. The provision was added after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, signed May 22, 2007 by Governor Jim Douglas, and took effect July 1, 2007. The anti-bullying law also prohibits bullying, cyberbullying and harassment based on gender identity in all educational institutions.

Hate crime law provides additional penalties for a crime committed based on the victim's gender identity, added in 1999 to the 1990 law that originally covered sexual orientation. The gay and/or trans panic defence was abolished by legislation passed 144-1 in the House in March 2021 and 29-0 in the Senate in April 2021, signed May 5, 2021 by Governor Phil Scott and effective July 1.

Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors, which includes transgender minors, was banned by a bill approved unanimously in the Senate March 17, 2016, approved with amendments in the House April 26, accepted by the Senate April 29, signed May 25 by Governor Peter Shumlin and effective July 1, 2016. Vermont enacted S.132 (Act 138) signed May 25, 2016 prohibiting conversion therapy on minors and treating its performance on minors as unprofessional conduct under 18 V.S.A. §§ 8351-8353 and related 26 V.S.A. licensing statutes.

Vermont permits both preoperative and post-operative transgender individuals to change the gender marker on birth certificates and other state-issued documents upon court order supported by a letter from a licensed medical or mental health practitioner of surgical, hormonal, or other appropriate treatment for gender transition. Effective July 1, 2022, individuals born in Vermont can legally change sex marker to male, female or X based on self-determination without court order, mental health diagnosis, surgery, divorce or medical permission under a bill signed in April 2022 (H.628, Act 88, approved April 6, 2022, amending 18 V.S.A. § 5112 to allow issuance of a new birth certificate to reflect gender identity). Since July 1, 2019 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X on driver's licences and state IDs with no documentation needed.

Since July 1, 2018 all single-user public bathrooms must be marked as gender-neutral under a bill signed in May 2018. Since 2013 all health insurers underwriting in Vermont are required to cover transgender care including sex reassignment surgery. In May 2023 a law effective immediately by emergency clause legally protects, defends and shields transgender and non-binary people accessing gender-affirming healthcare across state lines coming into Vermont; Vermont has shield laws enacted in 2023 and 2024 that are enforceable against out-of-state action.

In October 2023 the Department of Education unanimously passed a policy to protect and defend transgender and non-binary students within schools and classrooms. In 2023 Mid Vermont Christian School's girls' basketball team forfeited a match against a team fielding a transgender girl citing fairness and safety and was as a result forbidden from competition by the Vermont Principals' Association.

Vermont has shield laws enacted in 2023 and 2024 that are enforceable against out-of-state action, placing it among the states with such protections.

The gay and/or trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation passed 144-1 in the House in March 2021 and 29-0 in the Senate in April 2021, signed May 5, 2021 by Governor Phil Scott and effective July 1. Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors, which includes transgender minors, was banned by a bill approved unanimously in the Senate March 17, 2016, approved with amendments in the House April 26, accepted by the Senate April 29, signed May 25 by Governor Peter Shumlin and effective July 1, 2016. Vermont permits both preoperative and post-operative transgender individuals to change the gender marker on birth certificates and other state-issued documents upon court order supported by a letter from a licensed medical or mental health practitioner of surgical, hormonal, or other appropriate treatment for gender transition, while effective July 1, 2022 individuals born in Vermont can legally change sex marker to male, female or X based on self-determination without court order, mental health diagnosis, surgery, divorce or medical permission under a bill signed in April 2022, and since July 1, 2019 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X on driver's licences and state IDs with no documentation needed. Since July 1, 2018 all single-user public bathrooms must be marked as gender-neutral under a bill signed in May 2018, since 2013 all health insurers underwriting in Vermont are required to cover transgender care including sex reassignment surgery, and in May 2023 a law effective immediately by emergency clause legally protects, defends and shields transgender and non-binary people accessing gender-affirming healthcare across state lines coming into Vermont. In October 2023 the Department of Education unanimously passed a policy to protect and defend transgender and non-binary students within schools and classrooms, while in 2023 Mid Vermont Christian School's girls' basketball team forfeited a match against a team fielding a transgender girl citing fairness and safety and was as a result forbidden from competition by the Vermont Principals' Association. Vermont reduced the penalty for sodomy from capital punishment to life imprisonment in 1861, enacted a 1937 law punishing oral sex participation with 1 to 5 years in state prison applicable to both heterosexual and homosexual activity, repealed that statute in April 1977, with adult private consensual noncommercial sodomy unenforceable under Lawrence v. Texas. Civil unions for same-sex couples were introduced in July 2000 as the first state status identical to marriage following a 1999 Vermont Supreme Court equal marriage benefits ruling, same-sex marriage has been legal since September 1, 2009 as the first state via legislature and governor rather than court decision, and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1994. Vermont law permits single LGBT individuals and same-sex couples to petition to adopt, provides lesbian couples access to in vitro fertilization with recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent to a child born via donor insemination irrespective of marital status, and in June 1993 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled in favor of a lesbian seeking to adopt her partner's two biological sons. Discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices was banned with protections added in 1992, with the anti-bullying law also prohibiting bullying including cyberbullying and harassment based on sexual orientation in all educational institutions. Hate crime legislation enacted in 1990 including sexual orientation provides additional penalties for a crime committed based on the victim's sexual orientation. Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors was banned by a bill approved unanimously in the Senate March 17, 2016, approved with amendments in the House April 26, accepted by the Senate April 29, signed May 25 by Governor Peter Shumlin and effective July 1, 2016, and the gay panic defence was abolished and repealed by the 2021 bill passed 144-1 and 29-0 and signed May 5, 2021 effective July 1.

The provision was added after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, signed May 22, 2007 by the governor, and took effect July 1, 2007. The anti-bullying law also prohibits bullying, cyberbullying and harassment based on gender identity in all educational institutions.

Hate crime law provides additional penalties for a crime committed based on the victim's gender identity, added in 1999 to the 1990 law that originally covered sexual orientation. The gay and/or trans panic defence was abolished by legislation passed 144-1 in the House in March 2021 and 29-0 in the Senate in April 2021, signed May 5, 2021 by the governor and effective July 1.

Since July 1, 2018 all single-user public bathrooms must be marked as gender-neutral under a bill signed in May 2018. 66186276B98555229882405.name: Washington
66186276B98555229882405.summary:
Washington stands under the national framework of the United States on travel documents, entry screening and facilities; that layer is carried by the parent record.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Washington among the most protective states in the country. The same assessment records that Washington's health-insurance laws cover facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, listing the state alongside Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland on that point, and it identifies refugee protections in Washington for people leaving states with hostile regimes.

That assessment also flags two November ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, as targeting transgender residents, so the protective ranking rests alongside an active challenge to it at the ballot.

Washington's shield laws and executive orders of the 2023 and 2024 batches are enforceable against out-of-state action, and the state is listed in a nationwide tracker of such measures. A trans person obtaining care in Washington is covered by state protections that reach conduct originating in other states.

Washington's prisons operate under court order and rulings that in October 2023 legally required the state prison system to provide gender-affirming healthcare and/or sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates.

Placement is nonetheless used as a sanction. In July 2024 a trans woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison. Birth-sex housing was applied as discipline, and the outcome is documented for 2024.

Washington's protective standing is a comparative position, not an absolute one: a July 2026 assessment ranks it among the most protective states while grouping it with Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland on insurance coverage for facial hair removal and gender-affirming procedures, which tells a visitor that the state's guarantees belong to a small cohort rather than a national norm.

64170238B96397749018979.name: Monaco
64170238B96397749018979.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has been legal in Monaco since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate-motivated conduct on the basis of sexual orientation is criminalised across several statutes. Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence on that ground.

Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 inserted sexual orientation into Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (five years).

A Monegasque court applied this framework in July 2010, sentencing a man to five days' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. It is the only documented prosecution in the sources.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned by law; Outright International reports such discrimination as rare but describes protections as very limited. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, a cohabitation agreement signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry.

Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in Monaco. LGBTIQ visibility is limited: roughly ten people are reported to dare to be openly out, no gay Pride is held anywhere in the principality, and there are no official gay bars, clubs or events. Visitors are directed to France or Italy for Pride.

Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it maintains close cultural and economic ties with France. France handles defence, and its armed forces allow openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve; Monaco itself maintains only a National Guard.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes that transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. The LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. The age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme every year of primary and secondary cycles to sensitise against racism and all article 1 discriminations (including sexual orientation), but the Council of Government did not approve the bill and its 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions. Same-sex couples' inability to adopt children directly affects family formation for youth, and most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

Same-sex partners have no access to equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax purposes rather than like married couples, and the cohabitation agreement is equally open to siblings and to parents and children.

The Council of Government did not approve the bill, and its replacement of 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

The 2023 US State Department Human Rights Report recorded no significant changes for Monaco and limited its significant issues to libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced; no torture, arbitrary detention or similar abuses were reported.

Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which treats homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. The gay travel guide Gay Voyageur pitches the roughly 200-hectare state as a luxury and relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene, and points visitors to Marseille, Nice and Lyon for gay nightlife and events.
64170238B96397749018979.localsOnly:

Residents have no statutory route to change legal gender, and no anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, education or services. Reported discrimination is described as rare, but there is no complaint mechanism to test that.

The 2012 replacement anti-discrimination bill left residents without the school sensitisation programme contemplated in 2011. Employment and public-accommodation protection on sexual-orientation grounds remains unenacted.

Monaco's only military formation is the National Guard; defence rests with France, whose forces accept openly LGBT service members.
64170238B96397749018979.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports a prosecution under Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 or under Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019, so enforcement of those provisions beyond the July 2010 case is unresolved.

No source addresses entry, visa or border-screening practice, customs questioning, or the treatment of gender markers on foreign passports at Monegasque borders. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether a visitor's documents are inspected for sex or gender inconsistencies.

Facilities, healthcare access, and any rule on restroom or single-sex-space use for transgender visitors are not sourced here. Neither are hate-crime statistics, police reporting practices, or the operation of the protection machinery for LGBTIQ visitors.

Outright International's characterisation of discrimination as rare is self-reported and carries no underlying data in the inventory; the absence of a statutory ban means official statistics on complaints cannot exist.

The July 2010 judgment is described only in secondary coverage; the court, the exact provision applied and any appeal outcome are not available from these sources.

Residents have no statutory route to change legal gender, and no anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, education or services. Reported discrimination is described as rare, but there is no complaint mechanism to test that.

The 2012 replacement anti-discrimination bill left residents without the school sensitisation programme contemplated in 2011. Employment and public-accommodation protection on sexual-orientation grounds remains unenacted.

The country's only military formation is the National Guard; defence rests with a neighbouring jurisdiction, whose forces accept openly LGBT service members.

SYN-ABW.name: Aruba
SYN-ABW.summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions that apply on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory ground of protection against discrimination in Aruba.

On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognise same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions, after a 2.5-year campaign sponsored by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes and an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered.

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

GlobalGayz describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and notes that same-sex adoption is legal. Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba; the last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

The Aruba Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including 'heterosexual or homosexual orientation'. On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

SYN-ABW.tangentialFactors:
Aruba is frequently described as one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands, and the Associated Press noted that at the time of the 2016 vote neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed same-sex unions. That comparison concerns sexual-orientation rights; it does not establish any differential treatment of trans visitors, and Aruba's anti-discrimination statute still omits gender identity.

The Kingdom-level endorsement of 22 April 2015 expressly named transgender persons among those due equal rights, but it is a statement of intent by Kingdom governments rather than an enforceable provision in Aruba's Criminal Code. The gap between that endorsement and the sexual-orientation-only wording of Articles 1:221, 2:61 and 2:62 is unresolved in the sources.

Public hostility documented on the island has been directed at visible same-sex couples rather than at trans people specifically. The Oduber-Lamer harassment of 2004 to 2007 and the Catholic Church's role in opposing the 2016 amendment indicate that visibility, not legal status alone, has driven risk.
SYN-ABW.localsOnly:
Aruba's own representation at the 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered. That statement is a local admission about resident conditions, not a visitor-facing finding.

Residents who are read as gender-nonconforming have no enumerated ground of protection under Articles 1:221, 2:61 and 2:62 of the Criminal Code, which name sexual orientation only. Local advocacy organisations, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, operate on the island, but the sources do not document any of them providing trans-specific legal representation.

Same-sex adoption is legal in Aruba, and registered unions open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples have been available since the 8 September 2016 vote. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, before the 12 July 2024 Supreme Court ruling made same-sex marriage legal.
SYN-ABW.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents airport or border screening practice in Aruba that treats binders, packers, breast forms or gender presentation differently from other travellers, and no source addresses gender markers on passports or identity documents as issued or read in Aruba. Whether Aruban authorities inspect or question documents whose gender marker does not match the holder's presentation is unresolved.

No source addresses access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone prescriptions or their customs treatment for visitors, and none addresses bathroom or facility access rules on the island. These remain not sourced rather than absent.

No source records any hate-crime or violence incident in Aruba against a trans person specifically. The documented harassment (the Oduber-Lamer case, 2004 to 2007) concerns a same-sex couple; whether comparable conduct against a trans resident or visitor would be prosecuted is unresolved.

The 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement naming transgender persons is a political statement by Kingdom governments. Whether it has been implemented in Aruban statute or practice is not sourced here.

Same-sex adoption is legal locally, and registered unions open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples have been available since the 8 September 2016 vote. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, before the 12 July 2024 supreme court ruling made same-sex marriage legal.

No source records any hate-crime or violence incident locally against a trans person specifically. The documented harassment (the court challenge of 2004 to 2007) concerns a same-sex couple; whether comparable conduct against a trans resident or visitor would be prosecuted is unresolved.

The 22 April 2015 state-framework endorsement naming transgender persons is a political statement by the governments in the framework. Whether it has been implemented in local statute or practice is not sourced here.

SYN-AIA.name: Anguilla
SYN-AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory and the law that governs a visitor is local law; United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only where an Order in Council extends it, so no United Kingdom-level anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by order of the Privy Council on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is among the British overseas territories that have not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place there.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.

SYN-BES.name: Bonaire Sint Eustatius and Saba
SYN-BES.summary:
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The civil-status and anti-discrimination law in force on the islands is Dutch national law, applied there in the same form as in the European Netherlands, with no separate island legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it.

No source in the inventory describes any provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

Travel coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023 places Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, citing its standing as part of the Netherlands, under whose strict anti-discrimination laws it says citizens and visitors are protected, and describing same-sex couples as warmly welcomed.

Registered unions for same-sex couples have been available in the islands since 2012. The first was recorded by the Census Office in Saba on 4 December 2012: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on Saba and both were visiting, which establishes that the island registry performs ceremonies for couples who are only passing through.

Saba Tourism's weddings page states that civil ceremonies run routinely through the island registry, that the Court Room in the Administrative Building is the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony, and that registrar Julieta Woods is flexible with couples' wishes. Caterers, florists and accommodation serving destination weddings operate on the island.

SYN-BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
SYN-BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered on an island of about 8 square miles with roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against Saint Barthélemy in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access; prescriptions and ongoing treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. French prison administration policy recognises only biological sex for placement, and trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex; a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. Detainees held in Saint Barthélemy fall under that same system. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

An aggregate index rates the collectivity 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.

Socially the territory is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors.

BLM detainees fall under this French system.

France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty draws on about 40 referrals since 2010. It finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

The French framework applies in Saint Barthélemy: legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Full equality under French law applies across about 8 square miles and about 10,000 residents. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, with no visible scene; discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10, with 9 positive rights and 1 red flag: legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access. No government LGBT+ travel advice exists; FCDO shows no warnings. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted.

Low crime, an open and accepting culture, no Pride-specific events, and staff trained for diverse guests. Visitors are high-end and discreet; there are no LGBTQ venues or scene, and no hostility is noted.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Saint Barthélemy (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: French law banned discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" in July 2012 and replaced that term with "gender identity" by the law of 18 November 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code; Chapter 2 of the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 after Constitutional Council approval on 17 November 2016, but they must go before a court to change the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. France legalised gender affirmative surgery domestically in 1979, removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 as the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location for gender affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first guidelines recommending puberty blockers plus calcium and vitamin D from at least Tanner stage 2. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Conversion therapy was legally banned by a bill passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine. A Senate-passed bill of May 2024 to ban medical transition under age 18, following a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report criticizing youth care, is opposed by the Macron government, unlikely to pass the National Assembly and had no update since 23 July 2024. All sodomy laws were repealed in 1791 during the French Revolution with no mention of private same-sex relations in the Penal Codes of 1791 and 1810, while a 1960 ordinance inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubling the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity, adopted via the Mirguet amendment, was repealed in 1980, and the discriminatory age of consent raised to 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual in 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still awaiting Senate vote. National legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services, and the law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and increased penalties when physical assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, enforced with the first conviction in January 2006 later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples, and same-sex marriage became legal nationwide including all overseas departments and territories after National Assembly approval 12 February 2013 by 329-229, Senate approval 12 April, Constitutional Council validation 17 May 2013, presidential signature 18 May 2013 and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. The historic MSM blood-donation ban dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence from 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, and fully removed 16 March 2022 so policy applies regardless of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in Saint Barthélemy but its joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies voting against, while Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Martin and Saint Barthélemy are noted for gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches, and Saint Barthélemy's reputation as an international celebrity tourist destination is stated to have produced a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than other French Caribbean territories. President Emmanuel Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as "unworthy of France" and announced future concrete measures after a rise in attacks.

SYN-BLM.tangentialFactors:
No government travel advice addressing LGBT+ visitors exists for Saint Barthélemy, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office records no warnings for the destination. Absence of official advice is an information gap rather than an assessment of safety.

No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the aggregate index, so the rating rests on legal and structural data instead of first-hand accounts from trans travellers.

The framework is national, so no local ordinance in Saint Barthélemy narrows or widens the protections a visitor encounters; there is no sub-national variation to account for on the ground.

The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for diverse guests. Discretion is the prevailing norm among a high-end, transient clientele, which keeps any visible scene absent rather than suppressed.

Crime is recorded as low and no hostility toward gay or trans visitors appears in the sources, a context that sits beside rather than offsets the documented detention risk under French prison policy.
SYN-BLM.localsOnly:
Residents of Saint Barthélemy change their legal gender marker under French law without surgery or sterilisation, and the anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity is in force for them as in France.

Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, but delivery takes place within a jurisdiction of about 8 square miles and roughly 10,000 residents, where the aggregate index records limited healthcare access as its only red flag. Ongoing prescriptions and continuity of treatment cannot be assumed to be filled locally.

SYN-BMU.name: Bermuda
SYN-BMU.summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory where local legislation governs. United Kingdom law, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code, does not extend automatically and could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not covered, leaving trans people without statutory protection against discrimination. The sources identify no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery.

Expression of gender identity is described as often difficult. In 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities.

Consensual sex between adult men is legal. The House of Assembly voted 22–16 on 14 May 1994 to decriminalise it, striking two sections of the Criminal Code; the debate divided the island, with religious leaders split and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change. Prior liability carried up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. Lesbian activity has never been illegal, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

The age of consent is unequal: 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019, against 16 for other sexual activity. A prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct had been found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Same-sex marriage is not legally available as of 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case under the Marriage Act 1944 and the Human Rights Act. The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act on 7 February 2018, effective 1 June 2018, replacing marriage with domestic partnerships open to same-sex and opposite-sex couples and making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Recognition of a partner therefore rests on the partnership register.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre', an instance of organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.
