The article states that, by omission, there is thus no protection from discrimination for transgender people. The article states that the ability of persons to express their gender identity is often difficult. As its example, the article states that in 2006 the Government attempted to ban Mark Anderson, also known as the drag queen "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The article provides no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, care, enforcement, penalties, or protection machinery beyond that omission and example. Homosexuality is legal in Bermuda; lesbian activity has never been illegal, while consensual private sexual conduct was legalised by the Stubbs Bill in 1994 after prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. As of 2022 the age of consent remains unequal at 18 years for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 versus 16 for other sexual activity, after a prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Criminal Code provision on gross indecency between men was repealed in 2019. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2013, following failed and dropped proposals in 2004-2006 and 2009. Same-sex marriage is not legally available since 2022, having been legalised by the Supreme Court in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche marriage-license case under the Marriage Act 1944 and Human Rights Act, replaced by domestic partnerships by law given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, restored by the Supreme Court on 6 June 2018 and Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, then banned again by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on 14 March 2022 with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Same-sex couples are allowed to adopt equally under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015. Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise for women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men. In November 2020 reporting, the government spent approximately £150,000 to legally appeal an unconstitutional case of a man charged and threatened with jail under the archaic "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into Bermuda.

SYN-COK.name: Cook Islands
SYN-COK.summary:
The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islanders, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the male-sex offences from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, with consent explicitly not a defence. Reported maximum terms differ across sources: the 2017 coverage gives seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while reporting on the repeal cites exposure of up to ten years for indecent acts between males. All sources agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited. The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage is not recognised locally and a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

SYN-COK.tangentialFactors:
The repeal followed a protracted legislative path. A 2017 select committee recommended removing sections 154 and 155, and the provisions were struck from the draft Crimes Bill, drafted with New Zealand assistance; MPs subsequently backtracked. In October 2020 members again pushed the bill's report back, this time by three months, before the 2023 passage.

Reporting on the 2020 deferral attributes the taboo underlying sections 154 and 155 to colonisation, describing the society as historically accepting of same-sex relations before that period.

Public submissions on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill opened in Parliament on 10 August 2017, the bill being intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act.

The 1969 offences were never enforced against residents in living memory, so there is no record of prosecutions of local men under sections 154 and 155.

The marriage bar applies to residents as well as visitors: Cook Islanders cannot contract a same-sex marriage locally, and no local mechanism recognises one contracted abroad.

The penalty figures for the 1969 provisions remain unresolved across the sources: the 2017 coverage gives seven years and five years, and the 2023 repeal coverage gives up to ten years. The inventory does not settle which figures were correct in the statute as it stood before 1 June 2023.

No source in the inventory addresses gender-marker change on birth certificates or passports, entry or security screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, or whether a New Zealand passport bearing a trans marker is accepted without question at Cook Islands entry.

Also unsourced: any anti-discrimination protection expressly covering gender identity, hate-crime provisions that would aggravate an attack on a trans person, facility or restroom access rules, and access to gender-affirming healthcare or to continued hormone treatment on the islands.

The inventory contains no reporting of violence against trans people in the Cook Islands, and no official statement from the Cook Islands government or the New Zealand government on trans-specific protection or risk.

SYN-CUW.name: Curaçao
SYN-CUW.summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, standing under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here, with autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

Same-sex sexual activity between men and between women is legal, with an age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse alike. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex therefore faces no conduct offence.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling, Curaçao recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, but offered no in-island marriage, civil union or other form of recognition. The August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, applicable to Curaçao, had required legal recognition.

The legislative route to that position ran through the Estates of Curaçao: a limited-rights proposal was put to the Estates in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute.

The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named in the source material do not include gender identity, and no region-specific authority on gender-identity coverage was identified.

Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice on the ground. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in the local press, while her party colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

No region-specific sourcing was found on gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry or border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, or the designation of facilities. Those areas are unassessed here rather than cleared.

Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

SYN-CYM.name: Cayman Islands
SYN-CYM.summary:
The Cayman Islands stands under the United Kingdom's framework. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

No local route to same-sex marriage exists. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban.

Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration. In December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. An overseas marriage therefore carries immigration effects in the Cayman Islands even though no domestic route to marriage exists.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation. Organisers asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection as a condition of the public-space route.

Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

The Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019; that ruling was overturned on appeal in Aug 2019, while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived.

SYN-CYM.tangentialFactors:

The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

Relationship recognition arrived through the courts and immigration administration rather than the statute book: the marriage ban was restored on appeal while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived. A visitor should not read the December 2020 ruling as a general marriage right.

The organisers' condition on displays of affection for the Pride route marks a public-space sensitivity that persists alongside the broad official participation recorded in 2021.

SYN-ESH.name: Western Sahara
SYN-ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory. Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate across the parts of it under Moroccan control, and a visitor there stands under Moroccan law wherever those institutions act. Human Rights Watch recorded that authority in a dispatch of 9 December 2005, covering the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; the organisation called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under that framework and carries six months to three years of imprisonment. The broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. Its own legal order is recorded by the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA as punishing same-sex sexual activity for both males and females with up to three years of imprisonment, and a global legality roundup published in July 2017 lists the state as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades. Both claimed frameworks therefore record criminalisation.

Protection machinery is absent on both sides of the dispute. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence, a conclusion it reaches in part from a 2010 statement by Ahmed Mulay Alli, the Sahrawi state's diplomatic representative in Mexico, that the constitution does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice and does not punish it. The statement resolves nothing for a visitor: the conduct is recorded as criminalised, while the protective text a traveller might rely on does not exist.

A visitor should expect screening, questioning and detention to be carried out by Moroccan officials in the controlled areas, under a morality provision whose wording leaves the decision to arrest largely with the officer on the street. No trans-specific entry rule, gender-marker rule or documented incident of trans-specific violence in the territory is recorded in the available sources.

SYN-FLK.name: Falkland Islands (Malvinas)
SYN-FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own Legislative Assembly, which legislates locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples. A public consultation ahead of the bill showed 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The provision covers sexual orientation only; the sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution.

United Kingdom frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, so protection and recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status, and holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under the CPE Ordinance 2014.

Three ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, the CPE Ordinance 2014 provides for sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and a Prisons Ordinance was enacted in 2017.

Stepchild and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since 2017.

The United Kingdom is responsible for the territory's defence.

Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

SYN-FRO.name: Faroe Islands
SYN-FRO.summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after friction between church and state.

In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics. The territory had neither at that date. Surveys of the period found violence and discrimination against openly gay people not uncommon and legally unaddressed.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. The refusal concerned the presence of an openly gay head of government at an official table.

Opposition to public visibility continued. In July 2015, when av Rana demanded that Pride be banned from its position two days before the national holiday, singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures and a Pride event, and the actions on record are a refusal to sit at a banquet and a call for a ban. Violence risk appears low on the sourced material.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was legalized across the Kingdom of Denmark; the age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the Faroe Islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988. The only criminal penalties touching LGBTQ people in the text are under the anti-discrimination law: anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Public petitioning also figures: a petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures, while an internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2006 openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out, and he and his family then received threatening telephone calls; police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn — nowhere else had the group been attacked. The 2007 law criminalises public threats, insults or degrading statements against LGBT people with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.

SYN-GGY.name: Guernsey
SYN-GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law permits only the issue of a new birth certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document. Visitors carrying both records, or documents issued at different times, should expect the earlier marker to remain on file.

On 10 December 2015 the States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were put and rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting; the States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Discrimination protections were built up in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, by 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a twelve-month deferral from around 7 November 2011, ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era. Other donation restrictions were unchanged.

Custodial safeguards are undocumented. Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded in the available sources, so a trans visitor has no sourced assurance about placement if detained.

SYN-GIB.name: Gibraltar
SYN-GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 took effect on 1 March 2007. The Act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is also a protected ground under the same Act.

Hate-crime coverage now extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy. The sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both.

Partner and family recognition is established locally: civil partnerships since March 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 after the Civil Marriage Amendment Act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December 2016, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender is 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

Reproductive and family formation routes are open to same-sex couples: in June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended its IVF policy to allow lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology, and in February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination.

The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.

sources.summary: The UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory; it also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014 granting most rights of marriage including adoption as mandated by the 2013 ruling, and same-sex marriage was legalised by the Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016 passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, receiving royal assent on 1 November and taking effect on 15 December 2016 with the first marriage the next day, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar where a deputy registrar opts out. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Constitution, in effect de jure legalising LGBT adoption, followed by civil partnership law amendments and effective 18 April 2024 the Adoption Act 2023 explicitly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended IVF policy to allow lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology, and in February 2021 surrogacy law allowed non-commercial altruistic surrogacy for individuals and married or civil-partnered couples unable to conceive with automatic recognition for children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation after 2002 proposals omitted it, but the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 effective 1 March 2007 prohibits discrimination in employment and goods and services on grounds including sexual orientation defined as orientation towards persons of the same sex, opposite sex, or both. Amendments to the Crimes Act 2011 approved 19 September 2013, assented 25 September and effective 10 October 2013 criminalised hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation, while in July 2021 the Justice Ministry was investigating proposals against lurking homophobia including a possible specific offence of denigrating a person as a result of sexual orientation.

SYN-GLP.name: Guadeloupe
SYN-GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework, which the parent record carries; this assessment covers only what is specific to the island.

Detention is the documented risk area. French prison rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, and a BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on their incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Practical support on the island is limited but real. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities, driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. The opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for overseas territories. Community organisations including Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025.

Community organising is described as advancing. An interview with Leïla of Secret's Out in September 2023 reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, with activism described as progressing after sister island Martinique; the interview also featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

SYN-GUF.name: French Guiana
SYN-GUF.summary:
French Guiana is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework. Identity documents, the criminal code, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate there exactly as in metropolitan France, and there is no separate local legislation on gender identity.

Legal gender recognition has been available on a simplified administrative basis since 2017, by declaration before a civil-status officer, with no requirement of surgery, sterilisation or psychiatric diagnosis. Anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity has been in force since 2012, and hate-crime sentence enhancement provisions were added in 2017. Nothing in French law criminalises trans status or gender expression.

Same-sex relations and same-sex marriage are legal under French law, and Pride events are held in the territory. The visible scene is small and anchored in Cayenne, with no venues listed by the GayOut travel guide, which rates French Guiana "Very Safe for LGBTQ+". That rating rests on formal legality rather than on the detention and healthcare conditions described below.

The most serious documented risk is custodial. A BuzzFeed News feature of January 2018 found that trans women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender occupy a legal gray area, with placement decided case by case and little consistent protection; that practice governs the prisons of French Guiana. The CGLPL, the national body responsible for places of deprivation of liberty, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations in the treatment of transgender detainees persist across French places of detention, a finding that extends to the territory.

Access to specialised transgender healthcare is limited by distance from mainland treatment centres, which adds travel cost and delay to any medical step in transition. Socially, transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility and make reporting of abuse less likely, including reporting to police.

Same-sex marriage following civil solidarity pacts in 1999 was legalised in 2013 with the law signed 18 May 2013 after the 17 May Constitutional Council ruling and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, and is legal in all overseas departments and territories, with French Guiana's two deputies recording one vote in favour and one abstention. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the Armed Forces, men who have sex with men blood-donation abstinence requirements of one year from 10 July 2016 and four months from 2 April 2020 were fully removed 16 March 2022 to an orientation-neutral policy, and the conversion therapy ban passed the Senate 7 December 2020, the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and was published 1 February 2022.

SYN-GUF.tangentialFactors:
The published traveller rating and the documentary record point in opposite directions. GayOut grades the territory "Very Safe for LGBTQ+" on the strength of formal legality, while the CGLPL opinion of May 2021 and the reporting of January 2018 describe conditions in custody that such a rating does not capture.

The healthcare constraint is geographic rather than statutory. Specialised and gender-affirming care sits mainly in mainland centres, so a person in French Guiana absorbs flights, accommodation and waiting time that a patient treated in a large mainland city does not.

Local visibility is limited. No venues are listed for the territory by the travel guides consulted, and the scene that exists is concentrated in Cayenne, which narrows the options for meeting others and for informal safety networks.
SYN-GUF.localsOnly:
Residents pursue legal gender recognition through the same prefectural and tribunal machinery used in Bordeaux: a declaration before a civil-status officer, with no medical evidence demanded. The procedure is administrative and does not depend on residency conditions specific to the territory.

Placement of a transgender prisoner is decided case by case, so a resident entering custody has no guaranteed assignment to a facility matching their legal gender and no consistent protection attached to that placement. The CGLPL found in May 2021 that serious violations in the treatment of transgender detainees persist across French places of detention.

For residents, every medical step in a transition depends on travel to mainland centres, and the resulting cost and delay fall on them directly. Transphobia and cultural taboos in the territory discourage visibility and weigh against reporting abuse to police, which limits reliance on the anti-discrimination and hate-crime provisions that are in force.

Locally enacted measures therefore remain an open question rather than a confirmed absence.

SYN-IMN.name: Isle of Man
SYN-IMN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach the island only by Order in Council.

The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills rather than through inherited Westminster statute, so the island's record must be read on its own terms.

Partner recognition is established. Same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act, reported on 28 July 2016, and the first conversion of a civil partnership into a marriage was completed within days of entry into force. Civil partnerships, legal since 2011, convert without a second ceremony, which indicates a routine registration process rather than discretionary approval.

The primary legislative record of that reform sits in Tynwald Hansard for 26 April 2016, which records the Legislative Council's Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016. The reform also had stated political sponsorship: on 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, a commitment that preceded the 2016 Act.

Non-discrimination protection on the island was first legislated in the employment sphere. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island with United Kingdom human-rights law.

Nothing in this inventory documents a gender-recognition procedure, identity-document marker rules, entry or visa screening that could disclose a trans visitor's status, hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, or facility access rules. Those questions are not evidenced here rather than shown to be absent from Manx law, and a visitor should treat them as open.

BBC (28 Jul 2016): same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act (2015-16 law reform); the first civil-partnership-to-marriage conversion was completed days after entry into force, with civil partnerships (legal since 2011) convertible without a second ceremony — confirming a smooth, routine registration process for couples.

BBC (30 Nov 2005): the House of Keys adopted an Employment Bill amendment protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds (tabling by Onchan MHK Peter Karran) — the island's employment non-discrimination milestone, aligned with UK human-rights law.

Separate units exist for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No birth-sex-vs-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit, and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice are documented: no usable finding on the prison-housing axis.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Isle of Man (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender persons to change their legal gender and to have their new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 with much of the law in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and ground of non-discrimination. A ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity conversion therapy was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the extensive sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and came into effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory and the first part of the British Isles to ban conversion therapy. In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. Private and consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with age of consent set at 21, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021 Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private, defined in Section 10 as more than two persons present or in a public-access place, and in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral. The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 passed with royal assent in July 2021 and took effect 1 July 2022 by proclamation, pardoning historical gay sex offences committed prior to 1992 explicitly based on the UK Alan Turing law of 2017. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022 on the 30th anniversary of decriminalisation the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992. Same-sex couples were granted civil partnerships by the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) effective 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage effective 22 July 2016 after royal assent 19 July 2016. By the Civil Partnership Act 2011 same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011, lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates from IVF and surrogacy and no laws acknowledge surrogacy. Under the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) effective 1 September 2006 dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation was made unlawful, and the Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation, defined to include attraction to same, opposite, either sex and lack of attraction to either sex, as a protected characteristic.

SYN-IMN.tangentialFactors:
The island's equality architecture has been built in stages, and the sequence matters for expectation-setting. Employment protection on sexual-orientation grounds came a decade before the marriage debate, in 2005; the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act and the Equality Bill 2016 followed in a single legislative session. Both were framed by Tynwald rather than imposed from Westminster.

The proximity of the Equality Bill 2016 to the marriage legislation indicates that discrimination protection and relationship recognition were handled as one reform programme, though the inventory does not record the substantive content of the Equality Bill.

Detention capacity on the island is limited to a single institution. Isle of Man Prison at Jurby, a GBP 41.7m facility on the former RAF Jurby site, has been fully operational since 14 August 2008 and is run by the Isle of Man Prison Service, with separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders, vulnerable prisoners and a segregation unit.

Existing civil partnerships convert to marriage without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force.

SYN-MSR.name: Montserrat
SYN-MSR.summary:
Montserrat stands under the United Kingdom's framework as a British Overseas Territory and must comply with international human rights instruments, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Domestically, Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. 'Discriminatory' is defined as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful in Montserrat since 2001. Lesbian conduct was never an offence. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for everyone, and the age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity, so a visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex faces an age of consent of 18 rather than 16.

Relationship recognition does not extend to same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal in Montserrat, and Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family.

Organised LGBT social infrastructure is close to absent. Montserrat has no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues. Several hotels on the island welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment. A 2012 account by GlobalGayz describes gay life as barely existing locally and the social scene as decimated.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north. Gay life barely exists locally: 'gays are everywhere but hardly here,' and the social scene is decimated.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

SYN-MTQ.name: Martinique
SYN-MTQ.summary:
Martinique is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework: Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so the substantive provisions a visitor would rely on — identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination and the marriage regime — are national law operating on the island.

Prison is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor detained here. Martinique's correctional establishments are French prisons and stand under the same placement rule as the mainland: under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, placement follows the gender marker on the detainee's identity documents rather than anatomy, which puts most trans women into all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them. Reporting from January 2018 records the threat in direct terms — 'we don't want any women here'.

The CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. sources.summary: French law governs Martinique, and the following national provisions apply in the department. Homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by a National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; the same law amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Christian Vanneste, an MP in Chirac's UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but must still go before a court to change the gender marker, while a first name change can be done at the registry office. The bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and dropping the original self-certification provision; before that, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, up from about 1,380 in 2018. Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. SYN-MYT.name: Mayotte
SYN-MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national framework. Identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France, and the French prison rules bind the island's places of deprivation of liberty as French establishments.

Nothing in that framework criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and it is one of the few jurisdictions in Africa and the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed. The National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people likewise extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not decide where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on site inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Because these are French establishments, the same standards and the same documented failures govern any facility holding a trans person on Mayotte.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023 only after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the law on paper is not the whole of what a couple faces.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, working in persons and family law, as available.

sources.summary: French law bans discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' since July 2012, with article 225-1 of the Penal Code amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, while transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery performed in-country was legalised in 1979 after previously only accessible abroad. Legal gender change without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or proof of medical interventions was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October after rejecting Senate amendments requiring medical treatment, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017, but still requires going before a court for the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and hate-crime provisions cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination, with a 16 May 2020 report recording a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared to around 1,380 in 2018. Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, with a recommendation for informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased demand as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'primarily social problem' advising extreme caution without changing actual practice. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euros fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity in private was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in nations and French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334 moved to article 331 on 8 February 1945 set 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974, and repealed 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand to equalise at 15. A 1960 Mirguet amendment inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity to repress pimping and other national scourges, was repealed in 1980 as part of an act redefining sexual offenses, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 with Senate vote still pending. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of services and goods, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal with maximum penalty of 45,000 euros fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 for injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Caledonia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people can change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 after a 17 November Constitutional Council ruling, effective 1 January 2017, but must still go before a court, while first-name change can be done at a registry office. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 as the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, though transgender organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale and in-country gender-affirming surgery legalised since 1979. Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" has been banned since July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" in Penal Code article 225-1 on 18 November 2016, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that ground. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and conversion therapy was banned by a law passed by the Senate 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022, following a 2019 proposal for two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine. For care, a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination, the National Academy of Medicine characterised increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and late-2024 pediatric guidelines recommend puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. A Senate bill passed in May 2024 to ban medical transition under age 18 after a March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report calling care a health scandal, but it has had no update since 23 July 2024, is opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly amid large protests, while in 2022 the DILCRAH scientific committee president was revealed as a member of the Observatory which called care "mutilation," leading to one committee resignation. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and that approach was retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied in adopting French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishment involving castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. A discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334, moved to article 331 in 1945, set 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974, then equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President Mitterrand. A 1960 Mirguet amendment inserting Penal Code article 330 alinea 2 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed compensation for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 with Senate vote still pending. National legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments with a maximum €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, amended the 29 July 1881 Press Law on injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, and increases penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage has been legal in all overseas departments and territories including New Caledonia under the law signed 18 May 2013 after a 17 May 2013 constitutional ruling, following registered PACS partnerships since 1999. Police recorded around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France.

SYN-PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
SYN-PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by Order in Council. Military service is likewise a United Kingdom responsibility rather than a local one.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a visitor faces no criminalisation exposure on that ground.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in force since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision and names sexual orientation, not gender identity.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. The Island Council approved the ordinance unanimously on 1 April 2015, Governor Jonathan Sinclair signed it on 5 May 2015, and it was published on 13 May 2015.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn, which supports recognition of a visitor's or resident's existing foreign partnership. Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Pitcairn's permanent population is roughly 50 residents, and none is known to be in a same-sex relationship. The territory has no reported record of trans-specific violence, and no sourced reporting documents hostility toward visitors on these grounds.

SYN-PYF.name: French Polynesia
SYN-PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs it in matters of justice and civil status. Trans visitors therefore enter a legal regime in which gender recognition, detention policy and the rights framework are set by Paris, while much of daily life is regulated by the territorial institutions in Papeete.

France's national treatment of trans detainees reaches French Polynesia. Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document, and Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments; a trans woman holding a male marker is consequently held with men. BuzzFeed News, reporting on the situation in France in January 2018, treated this as a legal grey area rather than a settled outcome.

The national preventive-mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that France's Law 2016-1547 removed the requirement for medical transition or surgery when changing the gender on civil status, but that no norms were ever added governing how detainees should be housed in line with that change. Serious violations were documented across French detention, and the CGLPL's framework applies to French Polynesia's prisons. A trans visitor who is detained in the territory is therefore exposed to housing arrangements that national regulators themselves have found incompatible with the country's own gender-recognition law.

Gender-diverse healthcare in French Polynesia is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Some trans residents, including rae-rae, face rejection from their families and leave for mainland France to obtain specialised services that the territory cannot provide. The gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint for a trans person staying any length of time.

A reform effort to narrow that gap failed. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France. After heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed.

The cultural setting is unusually documented. The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. The territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023, bringing territorial government and church representatives together with the University of French Polynesia. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

SYN-PYF.tangentialFactors:
The protection available to a trans visitor in French Polynesia rests on a national equality and anti-discrimination regime that France applies to the territory, while the everyday indicators a traveller can observe are cultural rather than institutional. The absence of visible protest or organised community signalling should not be read as absence of risk management; acceptance described by travellers is diffuse and social, and the underlying legal remedies run through French courts and national bodies rather than through territorial institutions.

Detention is where the mismatch between the national recognition framework and its application is sharpest. France has reformed who qualifies for a legal gender change without disturbing the rules that determine where a person is locked up, and the national preventive mechanism has recorded the resulting violations. A trans visitor whose documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation is the person most exposed to this, both at arrest and at any later stage of the process.

Healthcare capacity is a structural difference from mainland France, not a temporary shortage. Hormonal treatment available through reimbursement in Paris is not equally obtainable in Papeete, and the failed territorial bill confirms that the shortfall is recognised politically and left unresolved. Visitors who rely on continuity of treatment should plan around what is locally prescribed and compounded rather than around what the French social-security system covers on the continent.
SYN-PYF.localsOnly:
Residents are bound by the same French civil-status machinery that governs trans visitors: the gender on the civil registry determines identity documents, and the requirement for medical or surgical intervention was removed by Law 2016-1547. The CGLPL's finding that implementing norms for detention were never written applies to territorial prisons as much as to metropolitan facilities.

Reimbursement of progesterone and testosterone through the territorial social-security system was proposed and rejected after debate in the Territorial Assembly, so residents currently bear the cost of hormonal treatment that mainland France covers. Specialist services are concentrated abroad, and family rejection is recorded as a reason trans residents, including rae-rae, relocate to France.

The mahu role carries cultural standing within Polynesian society, and territorial institutions have engaged publicly with LGBTQIA+ questions through the 2023 colloquium involving the Vice-President, the territorial government, churches and the University of French Polynesia. That engagement concerns reflection and education rather than new territorial legislation.
SYN-PYF.outOfScopeNotes:
It is unresolved whether Article D248 and the gender-marker detention rule described in the 2018 BuzzFeed News report have been revised since that reporting; the inventory sources the position as it stood then and through the CGLPL's 2021 opinion, and does not document a later change.

The inventory does not state whether French Polynesia has any territory-specific anti-discrimination statute of its own, nor how the national protections are actually invoked in the territory. Travel-writer accounts of mainstream inclusivity are single-perspective and describe visitor experience rather than measured incidence; the absence of reported incidents in the sources is not evidence that none occur.

National law reformed who qualifies for a legal gender change without disturbing the rules that determine where a person is held, and the national preventive mechanism recorded the resulting violations. a trans visitor whose documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation is most exposed, at arrest and at every later stage.

Healthcare capacity is a structural difference from the parent nation, not a temporary shortage. Hormonal treatment reimbursed on the continent is not equally obtainable locally, and the failed jurisdictional bill confirms the shortfall is politically recognised and left unresolved. Visitors relying on continuity of treatment should plan around what is locally prescribed rather than around what national social-security covers at home.
