The preventive mechanism's finding that implementing norms for detention were never written applies to jurisdictional prisons as well.

Reimbursement of progesterone and testosterone through the jurisdictional social-security system was proposed and rejected after debate in the jurisdictional legislature, so residents currently bear the cost of treatment the parent nation covers. Specialist services are concentrated outside the state/province, and family rejection is recorded as a reason trans residents relocate to the parent nation.

The local third-gender role carries cultural standing in society, and jurisdictional institutions have engaged publicly with LGBTQIA+ questions through the 2023 colloquium involving the vice-president, the jurisdictional government, churches and the jurisdictional university. That engagement concerns reflection and education rather than new jurisdictional legislation.
SYN-PYF.blindOutOfScope:
It is unresolved whether the national criminal-procedure housing rule and the gender-marker detention rule reported in January 2018 have been revised since; the sources establish the position as it stood then and through the May 2021 opinion, and do not document a later change.

The sources do not state whether the state/province has its own anti-discrimination statute, nor how national protections are actually invoked locally. Travel-writer accounts of mainstream inclusivity are single-perspective and describe visitor experience rather than measured incidence, and the absence of reported incidents is not evidence that none occur.

SYN-REU.name: Réunion
SYN-REU.summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the statute adopted in France in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, making transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The term was replaced by 'gender identity' through amendment of article 225-1 on 18 November 2016, with parallel protection added in the Labour Code.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope. The regime took effect on 1 January 2017 after Senate approval on 6 November 2015, Assembly approvals on 24 May 2016, 12 July 2016 and 12 October 2016, a Constitutional Council ruling of constitutionality on 17 November 2016 and signature on 18 November 2016 with publication the following day. It requires an application before a court without psychiatrist certificates or proof of reassignment surgery; a first-name change can be handled at the registry office.

In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness by decree, though transgender rights organisations stated that nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 and treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale. Gender-affirming surgery within France was legalised in 1979.

In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded police identification of around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018; these are raw national counts without a per-capita denominator.

Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.

Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurred by the Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published on 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine.

In March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education announced that institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.

A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access to care by location, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterised increased treatment-seeking as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution without changing actual practice. A March 2024 Senate-commissioned report led to a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under 18, opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly, with no update since 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements.

This is the discrimination-protection basis in force in Réunion.

SYN-SHN.name: Saint Helena
SYN-SHN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can be applied only by Order in Council, so a visitor should expect the territory's own statutes and practices rather than the United Kingdom framework to determine how single-sex services, records and complaints are handled.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.

Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, and the applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is recorded on that basis.

sources.summary: As of 25 Apr 2026, same-sex sexual activity is legal in the territory, discrimination protections have been in force since 2009, and same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 2017 (Alchetron).

Consensual same-sex relations became lawful in 2001. The age of consent is equalised at 16 territory-wide. The territory is an Overseas Country or Territory of the EU, with EU Charter applicability (GayLawNet, accessed 23 Jun 2013, citing ILGA State-sponsored Homophobia).

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - discrimination banned territory-wide since 2009; same-sex marriage legal since 2017 (Ascension 1 Jan, Tristan da Cunha 4 Aug, Saint Helena 20 Dec); adoption since 2017; detailed vote records of the Ascension Island Council (5-0).
Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights on Ascension Island. The marriage ordinance was approved 31 May 2016 (5-0), signed and gazetted 20 June, and commenced 1 January 2017.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care, or violence provisions are documented. The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination. The Commission may conduct inquiries and investigations on persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or "gender reassignment". Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, "gender reassignment" means "an intended, current or past process (or part of such a process) for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent or not culturally associated with their assigned sex at birth". No extension of the Constitution Order 2009 sexual-orientation discrimination ban to gender reassignment, and no transgender-specific marriage, adoption, or penalty provisions, are documented. Homosexuality is legal in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining "discriminatory" as "affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status." The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes "understanding of the importance of equality" and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination, with power to conduct inquiries and investigations into suspected unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, sexual orientation means "a person's sexual orientation towards— (a) persons of the same sex; (b) persons of the opposite sex; or (c) persons of either sex". Same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 1 January 2017 under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance, 2016, on Tristan da Cunha since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance, 2017, and on Saint Helena since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017, with the first same-sex marriage in Saint Helena occurring on 31 December 2018. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010 for Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011 for Ascension Island, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, while a 2006 UK Government report recorded no adoptions in Saint Helena or Ascension Island for many years.

sources.title: Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance, 2017
sources.summary: Tristan da Cunha legalized same-sex marriage through the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017 effective 4 August 2017, defining marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extending eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples.

SYN-SHN.tangentialFactors:
Because the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex-services code does not apply of its own force, provisions elsewhere in the British Islands that shape how toilets, changing rooms and shelters admit people are not a reliable guide to what a visitor will encounter on Saint Helena, Ascension or Tristan da Cunha.

Ascension Island carried the territory's marriage reform first, and by the largest margin on record for the measure, with the Ascension Island Council voting 5 to 0 on 31 May 2016. Saint Helena, the most populous island, legislated last, on 20 December 2017.

GayLawNet's account of the territory's status as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union and the resulting Charter applicability was accessed in June 2013 and rests on the classification as recorded at that time; the current operational reach of the Charter in the territory is not addressed in the sources reviewed.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been available to residents since 2017. Residents' access to single-sex services and to remedies for discrimination remains a matter of local law, since the United Kingdom equality statute and its codes reach the islands only through an Order in Council.

SYN-TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
SYN-TCA.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not extend automatically to the Turks and Caicos Islands. Local ordinances and the territory's own constitution govern, and United Kingdom measures reach the territory only by Order in Council, so a visitor should expect the Turks and Caicos Islands' legislation rather than the United Kingdom's equality framework.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands since 2001, decriminalised through the United Kingdom-led Caribbean reform programme, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

The Court of Appeal ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar. Reading "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, the court held that a refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees of the constitution, while leaving the statutory definition of marriage untouched. The ruling secures residence recognition for the same-sex partners of residents and visitors; it does not create a right to marry locally.

Transgender status is handled operationally through United Kingdom document channels rather than through a published local statute. The United Kingdom HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the Turks and Caicos Islands, official 2025 operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor presenting a United Kingdom passport carrying a changed gender marker can therefore expect that document to be treated as valid here. The underlying local legal instrument, if one exists, is not documented in the available sources.

The social climate favours discretion over visibility. A resident account from May 2009 described virtually no public information about gay life in the territory, no visible social scene, and privacy as the everyday norm, attributing this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority. That account should be read as dated and impressionistic rather than as a finding on violence risk.

SYN-VAT.name: Holy See
SYN-VAT.summary:
Vatican City presents essentially no criminal-law exposure to a trans visitor. No documented criminal-law persecution of consensual homosexual conduct has occurred in the territory in modern times, and decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots. Nothing about being trans is criminalised.

No legal recognition of gender exists in Vatican City. No anti-discrimination protection, facilities rule, or document-amendment mechanism covers a visitor or a resident.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It holds only a few cells for pre-trial detention, and anyone sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. Because no domestic prison system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented trans-prisoner placement case for this jurisdiction.

The Holy See's institutional posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy even where the city-state's own law imposes nothing. The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document, Male and Female He Created Them, opposes what it calls gender theory, stating that it "denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman" and "eliminates the anthropological basis of the family." The legal baseline for a visitor is the city-state's own law, which is distinct from the Church's diplomatic and doctrinal positions.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Vatican City (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 2021, Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher delivered a letter to the Italian ambassador to the Holy See expressing concerns over an Italian parliamentary bill meant to legally protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination. The objection specifically targeted the section prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. The letter claimed that prohibition constituted a violation of freedom of speech and of religion. It asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated. Since 1890 the territory of what is now Vatican City has had no criminal laws against non-commercial, private, adult and consensual same-sex sexual activity under a legal code based on the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 in force since the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. The age of consent is set at 18 years for all persons regardless of gender, except for sexual relations within marriage recognized as valid by the Catholic Church and Vatican City laws where the legal age is 14. Foreign diplomats must not be part of a same-sex family and must not be divorced to be accredited, with openly gay French nominee Jean-Loup Kuhn-Delforge in a civil pact rejected in 2008 and openly gay practising Catholic single nominee Laurent Stefanini rejected in 2015, leading France to leave the post vacant from March 2015 to May 2016 before nominating another diplomat in May 2016. Vatican City has always expressed disagreement with any civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples, and while Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church he remained firm that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God. The Vatican reserves the right to remove, suspend and dismiss immediately any official and employee who publicly admits to being gay or questions the general policy of the Vatican towards homosexuals. In 2021 Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher delivered a letter to the Italian ambassador expressing concerns over an Italian bill meant to legally protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination, claiming the prohibition of incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation violated freedom of speech and religion and asking for reformulation. On 13 January 1998 LGBTQ activist Alfredo Ormando set himself on fire on St. Peter's Square under Vatican jurisdiction in protest against deep-rooted refusal expressed by the Catholic religion towards homosexuality and died days later in hospital from severe burns.

SYN-VAT.tangentialFactors:
In 2008 Catholic officials rejected France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to name a different envoy. It is a documented instance of the Vatican government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations, and it indicates the institutional climate a visibly LGBT person may encounter around the Holy See's own organs rather than any rule applied to visitors.

The current Holy See posture on blessing same-sex couples is set by the DDF declaration Fiducia Supplicans, issued under Pope Francis on 20 March 2023, which permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 DDF press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Both items concern sexual orientation and institutional diplomacy more directly than they concern trans visitors, but they establish the direction of official policy in a territory where doctrine and government are held by the same institution.
SYN-VAT.localsOnly:
Residents of Vatican City have no mechanism to amend gender markers on identity documents, no route to legal recognition of gender, and no anti-discrimination remedy on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. The territory's small resident population stands under a civil code that contains no such provisions.

The 2019 Congregation for Catholic Education document is the reference point for education policy across the institutions the Holy See directs, framing gender identity as a question of anthropology to be corrected through dialogue rather than a matter of individual status.

Residents sentenced by Vatican City courts serve their sentences in Italian prisons, with the costs covered by Vatican City, because the territory has no prison of its own. Any resident serving a custodial sentence therefore leaves the jurisdiction's custody entirely, and no Vatican authority operates a placement policy inside the receiving facilities.

No documented trans-specific prisoner placement case was found for this jurisdiction. The absence of documentation is not evidence that a policy exists or that none does; it is unresolved.

SYN-VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
SYN-VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded the position publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do." The decriminalisation arrived by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly.

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. The territory stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Family status remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under British Virgin Islands law was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not itself a ruling on whether such a marriage is recognised in the territory.

sources.summary: Britain scrapped the homosexuality laws in its five remaining Caribbean territories, including the British Virgin Islands, by Privy Council order after local legislatures refused to act, according to an AP report of January 2001 republished by GLAPN. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded, 'there is nothing we can do.'
GlobalGayz (Aug 2012/2017) rates the BVI among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia as 'silent and invisible' and gay life there as lived in secret.

BVI News (29 Jul 2022): the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack in the case testing whether the UK same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under BVI law.

SYN-VGB.tangentialFactors:
GlobalGayz (August 2012, updated 2017) rates the British Virgin Islands among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia there as "silent and invisible" and gay life as lived in secret. That account describes social climate rather than law, and it suggests a gap between formal legality and everyday discretion that a trans visitor may also experience.

The decriminalisation of same-sex intimacy was imposed by the United Kingdom's Privy Council after the local House of Assembly declined to legislate, which indicates a local legislature less receptive than the imposed outcome might suggest. The Forbes-Lettsome marriage litigation, in which the BVI Christian Council intervened and sought to appeal, shows organised religious opposition actively contesting family recognition in the courts.
SYN-VGB.localsOnly:
Residents gained decriminalisation through an external judicial order rather than through their own representatives, and the public response of legislator Orlando Smith framed the change as having no local remedy. The BVI Christian Council's pursuit of appeals in the Forbes-Lettsome case indicates that local religious bodies continue to litigate against recognition of foreign same-sex marriages, with implications for residents' family formation.

Protection against discrimination for residents rests on British Virgin Islands legislation, not on the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, unless a specific Order in Council extends it. Residents seeking to rely on United Kingdom equality protections must first establish whether such an extension order exists for the territory.
SYN-VGB.outOfScopeNotes:
The Forbes-Lettsome proceedings are recorded here only up to 29 July 2022, when the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders. The subsequent course and outcome of the case, and whether any ruling on recognition of the United Kingdom same-sex marriage has since issued, are unresolved in the available sources.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, marker changes on documents, screening or identification procedures at entry, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and bathroom rules in the British Virgin Islands. Whether British Virgin Islands legislation provides any statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity is likewise not sourced here and should be verified against local statute.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 has ever been extended to the British Virgin Islands by Order in Council, in whole or in part, is not established by the available sources; the inventory states only that it does not apply automatically.

SYN-WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
SYN-WLF.summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic and stands under the French national framework: the civil and criminal codes of France apply locally unless a local measure overrides them. No law in force criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 statutory extension covering employment, housing and access to services.

Legal gender-marker change is available on the basis of the 2016-17 French reforms, which removed the requirement for surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis. A trans visitor whose documents already reflect their lived gender can present them without entering a separate local procedure. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained.

Nothing in the sources indicates trans-specific screening at entry or in local administrative processing. Practical exposure to harm is concentrated in two areas: detention and everyday social conditions. Under the French prison framework that applies here, trans women whose legal gender is marked male, largely those without reassignment surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a situation described in reporting as a documented legal grey area; one such transfer to a men's facility in Lille took place in 2014.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014. Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wallis and Futuna (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' has been banned since 2012, with the term replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Effective 1 January 2017 after a Constitutional Council ruling on 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, transgender people can legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical proof, but must go before a court, while first-name change can be done by registry office after the self-certification provision was dropped. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access to gender-affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized the rise as an epidemic-like and primarily social phenomenon urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government and stalled since 23 July 2024, while late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 retained in the Penal Code of 1810 for colonies, while the 1960 Mirguet amendment doubling the penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980 and the discriminatory age of consent of 21 then 18 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still pending Senate vote. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services has been banned since 1985 with Labour Code protection, and same-sex marriage signed 18 May 2013 after Constitutional Council approval 17 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier following PACS partnerships from 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013 is stated as legal in all overseas departments and territories. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, creating the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality. Police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019 versus around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France. Conversion therapy was banned by law published 1 February 2022 after Senate passage 7 December 2020 and Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 carrying two years imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and the MSM blood-donation ban from 20 June 1983 recalled in 2009 moved from one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016 to four months from 2 April 2020 to removal on 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation, with lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces.

SYN-WLF.tangentialFactors:
France's national preventive mechanism against ill-treatment issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on transgender persons held in places of deprivation of liberty, finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention. The finding rests on referrals concerning approximately 40 transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts, and it extends the mechanism's earlier opinion of 30 June 2010 on trans prisoners. As a French collectivity, Wallis and Futuna stands under that detention framework.

The statutory protections that apply here are national in origin rather than locally drafted, and the sources do not document how local authorities apply them. Social conditions differ sharply from the formal legal position: acceptance and healthcare access are constrained by the territory's small population of about 11,000, its isolation and the dominance of Catholic and Polynesian norms.
SYN-WLF.localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal recognition of their gender do so through the French procedure established by the 2016-17 reforms, which requires neither surgery nor a psychiatric diagnosis. Residents who need ongoing gender-affirming care face practical barriers: the small population and geographic isolation limit local medical provision, and care beyond basic services generally means travel abroad.

Local society combines established gender-diverse roles, of the fakafafine type, with strong pressure toward concealment. Catholic teaching and prevailing Polynesian norms shape how gender non-conformity is received in family and community settings, and stigma persists alongside the visibility of those roles.

72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
Visitors in Centro stand under Italy's national framework, and the region contributes its own documented record on several points.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence covering 2012 to 2025 names six regions with the highest victim counts. Lazio and Toscana, both in Centro, are two of the six, alongside Lombardia and Piemonte in Nord-Ovest and Campania and Puglia in Sud. The study supplies the per-region distribution of violence; the ranking is by raw victim counts, which track population, and the source provides no per-capita denominator.

On 24 January 2025 a Bologna first-instance court recognised a transphobic motive in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the trans-movement association that helps sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans as civil party. This is the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in Italy.

On 30 August 2025 Rome's municipal administration announced that the Consiglio di Stato had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking 'gender' ideology in schools. The court found the images discriminatory, one showing a boy being given a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not be used for messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly concerning minors. The anti-trans campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The ruling confirms that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted in Rome.

On 5 March 2026 the Court of Cassation confirmed the appeal-court acquittal of trans woman Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson, known as Patrizia, over the 27 April 2021 death of Samuele De Paoli in Perugia. The court found that the death was caused by cardiac arrhythmia from accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the charge of homicide final. The case, in the region's main university city, was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant.

72843720B99597932318450.name: Nord-Ovest
72843720B99597932318450.summary:
Visitors in Nord-Ovest stand under the national framework of Italy, which the parent record carries in full. The findings below are specific to this region: its own municipal measures, its own documented pattern of hate-motivated violence, and the custodial practice that would apply to a trans person detained here.

Milan inaugurated Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, allowing transgender people to use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents. LifeGate presents the measure as a milestone for transgender rights in the country, and ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Turin runs a parallel practice, Identita Alias, at municipality level and in its libraries.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of aggressions by region and city covering 2012 to 2025 shows that two of the constituent regions making up Nord-Ovest rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence. That ranking is by raw counts of incidents and victims only; the source provides no per-capita or population denominator, so it establishes that violence is documented at scale here rather than that these regions are more dangerous per resident than smaller ones.

Custodial placement tracks legal sex. La Repubblica's 2013 investigation recorded a prison administration count of 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities: trans women were held in men's sections, prisoners who had undergone sex-change surgery were sent to the women's sections, and female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who, according to their identity card, count as men. Where cells were lacking, trans prisoners were put in isolation, described in the report as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety. Protected sections, including the G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples, imposed limitations that extended to partner visits.

The 2010 baseline for that practice was different in form and similar in effect: transgender prisoners were located in women's prisons, where they were often segregated for their own safety. In the 2011 Terni case, the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of aggressions by region and city, 2012-2025, shows that the region's two constituent regions rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence.

The report states that until then transgender prisoners had been located in women's prisons 'where they are often segregated for their own safety' - the documented 2010 baseline for placement practice in Italy. Repubblica (2013) later reported the Pozzale project was abandoned.

Segregation practice: in some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking - described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety - and protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia (Rome) and the protected section at Poggioreale (Naples) imposed limitations, including on partner visits. 82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta stands under the Canadian national framework for human rights, criminal law, entry and federal custody. The province's own trans-specific lawmaking is a 2024 package of three statutes that passed final legislative stage on 4 December 2024. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alberta (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, with all jurisdictions explicitly including gender identity as a prohibited ground as of 2017. Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Charter to include transsexuality and HIV/STDs, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while private-sector complaints proceed under applicable federal or provincial human rights statutes. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, which requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity and has prompted calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, the Education Amendment Act, 2024 and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, and in 2025 Alberta passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to block those Charter challenges. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Communities, acknowledged contribution to institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights and personal suffering, shame, trauma and distrust, stated “We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization, shaming, disrespect or hate,” and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and makes it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families in addition to or in place of the birth parent. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150), and the remaining anal-intercourse offence in section 159 was repealed June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75 after courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta each declared it unconstitutional under Charter equality provisions, leaving a general age of consent of 16 since June 2019 and 18 where there is trust, authority, dependency or exploitation. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly including sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations as of 2017. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country worldwide and first in the Americas to do so with no residency requirement, following court rulings in several provinces and one territory between 2002-2005, while Alberta’s 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005. Same-sex adoption was legalized province by province from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011 as the last jurisdiction, with Alberta legalizing stepchild adoption in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007. In 2022 Canada became the third country worldwide and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as statutorily defined. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister issued a formal parliamentary apology for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, and on June 21, 2018 the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent allowing RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions, requiring notification to involved provincial or municipal police and courts, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from pardon or record suspension as recognition the act should never have been a crime. In December 2020 Canada’s police chiefs apologized for decades of oppression and opposition from the 1960s to the present, acknowledging institutional bias, intolerance and human rights violations. In a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, a sexuality-tolerance finding distinct from transgender tolerance. In that same 2020 Privy Council Office poll, 87.6% said they would be “comfortable” if a neighbour was a transgender person, the article’s documented transgender-specific tolerance statement. 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18-29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013, and June 2013 polls showed majority support for same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have same adoption rights and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children, all sexuality-specific findings. The article notes Canada was ranked first indicating least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024, general LGBTQ rankings not disaggregated for transgender people.

82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
Saskatchewan stands under the national framework of Canada. Provincial human rights law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, and transgender people are able to change their legal gender in the province under its own rules.

The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 requires schools to obtain parental consent before students under 16 may use a gender-related preferred name or have their gender identity recognised at school. The province passed the Act while invoking the notwithstanding clause of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which shields the provision for five years from being struck down on Charter grounds.

On 22 August 2023 the Saskatchewan education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies requiring schools to seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, requiring parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and pausing third-party school programs. Human rights groups called for repeal of the law, and litigation followed.

UR Pride Centre challenged the policy. The Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan ruled on 11 August 2025 in Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74, setting aside the 2023 chambers decision and holding that courts lack jurisdiction to test section 1 and section 15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where section 33 has been invoked, so the policy stands. The same judgment granted the government's appeal in part and held that a judge does have jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, allowing UR Pride's litigation to continue in the Court of King's Bench.

On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it would hear the appeals brought by both the province and UR Pride against that Court of Appeal decision. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

The consent requirement governs school settings and binds school-age residents of Saskatchewan. It imposes no document, entry or screening condition on visitors, but it is the clearest expression in the province of official hostility toward trans recognition.

No Saskatchewan-specific rule or case governing the placement of transgender prisoners in provincial correctional institutions appears in the sources; provincial correctional policies vary and only national policy for federal custody is documented.

82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
Visitors in New Brunswick stand under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Provincial education policy is the layer where New Brunswick differs from the rest of Canada. Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development took effect on 17 August 2020, was revised on 1 July and 23 August 2023, and was revised again effective 1 January 2025. Under the current text, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them informally in school, with parental consent encouraged but not required; formal use of a chosen name in official records for a student under 16 still requires parental consent. The revision was made by the Holt government and goes beyond the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

The application clause of Policy 713 covers the school environment as a whole and names the people it binds: all students, school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. A non-resident present in a New Brunswick classroom, whether as a visiting professional, student teacher or volunteer, is therefore subject to the same name, pronoun and privacy rules as a pupil.

The 2023 revisions remain the reference point for what the province is capable of imposing. Changes taking effect on 1 July 2023 barred teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, in accordance with their gender identity. The Progressive Conservative government of Premier Blaine Higgs made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two others were removed, eight party members including six cabinet ministers boycotted question period over the handling of the file, and dissidents called for a leadership review. The Holt government's 1 January 2025 revision undoes the 2023 consent rule, which had drawn protests outside the legislature and a constitutional challenge by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

Facilities are addressed by Policy 713 as originally written: the 2020 policy requires schools to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Whether that requirement survives verbatim in the text revised on 1 January 2025 is not established by the sources.

In federal custody, the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution matching their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on their identification documents. Requests are assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved overriding health or safety concern exists under the service's 2022 gender-diversity policy. As of 2025 the service recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's; between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 requests from people assigned male at birth for placement in women's institutions, with 35 approved, 72 denied and 22 withdrawn. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the unclear health-or-safety override and the absence of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism. This federal policy is the framework a trans person in federal custody in New Brunswick stands under.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in New Brunswick (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, explicitly listed as a prohibited ground in human rights acts as of 2017. The concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, with section 15 applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities but requiring private complaints to be brought under federal or provincial human rights statutes. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting legal action by human rights groups. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts but were shielded by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights against Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Transgender, and Queer communities, stating police must stand against transphobia and creating the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force upon royal assent. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause in section 15 of the Charter as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16, rising to 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency or exploitation, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. Former Criminal Code section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was held unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta and was repealed on June 21, 2019 through Bill C-75. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize it. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act granted royal assent June 21, 2018 allows the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from pardon or record suspension. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults and make it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code. 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessed same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt and 76% agreeing same-sex couples are just as likely to successfully raise children. A poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020 found 91.8% would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. That same Privy Council Office poll found that 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person.

82249235B4167839012994.tangentialFactors:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights inside a single election cycle, and reversing it back. The 2020 policy protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion, the 2023 amendments restricted it, and the December 2024 decision restored it effective 1 January 2025. A visitor encountering school-facing rules in the province is reading a policy with a documented history of being rewritten by order of the executive rather than by statute.

The 2023 episode drew sustained public and political contestation. About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the review, at which Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, said the policy saves lives and warned that removing it would cost children. Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 consent rule.

Two provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans residents, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. Those rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they place New Brunswick's 2023 episode inside a wider provincial direction running alongside the human-rights statutes.

The national hate-crime climate cuts against the statutory protections. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the previous year; over the longer arc police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement. No New Brunswick-specific hate-crime figures are in the sources.

14339913B23556801435424.summary:
Scotland forms part of the United Kingdom and its visitor-facing position rests on United Kingdom law; the material below is Scotland's own layer. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported 7,115 hate-crime charges for 2025-26, up 17% on the previous year and the highest annual total since 2003-04. Charges carrying a transgender-identity aggravation reached 104, a rise of 21% from 86 and the highest level since the 2021 Act took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category.

Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25 in the first annual report under the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021. Rates per 10,000 residents were highest in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each; 62% of recorded offences carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator. That publication gives no transgender-identity figure per head.

Scottish law attaches penalty enhancement to crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity under legislation enacted in 2009, and the hate-crime statute passed in March 2021 by 82-32, received royal assent a month later and took effect on 1 April 2024 with gender identity written in explicitly. A trans visitor therefore stands in a jurisdiction where identity-motivated hostility is an aggravating factor at charge and sentence.

Legal gender change in Scotland remains governed by the national Gender Recognition Act 2004. Scotland's own reform route did not reach the statute book: the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was introduced in March 2022 and passed by 86-39 that December, applying only to Scotland, then blocked by the United Kingdom government under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 while awaiting royal assent, the first use of that power against Scottish legislation. In 2018 the Scottish Government announced plans for an "X" sex descriptor on identity documents and a lower minimum transition age of 16.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, which passed on 4 February 2014 by 108-15 and received royal assent on 12 March 2014, with the first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to perform them. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under their current sex-marker status can marry in Scotland, and civil partnerships have been available since 2005.

31927357B79016588373767.name: Distrito Federal
31927357B79016588373767.summary:
The Distrito Federal stands under the national framework of Mexican equality law, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that the states without such procedures should adopt them. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Lethal violence against trans people is documented at national scale. The annual report published in May 2025 by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective recorded 115 violent incidents against LGBT+ people across Mexico in 2024, of which 59 were killings. Transgender Europe's monitoring counts 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months, and AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

Within that national pattern the Distrito Federal is a single data point, and in 2024 it was the largest one. For the first time Mexico City topped the national count with 17 LGBT+ homicides, 11 of them trans women, ahead of Nuevo León's 5. Part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger, but the raw figures remain a negative signal for a visitor.

The institutional response is the strongest of any Mexican state. Mexico City's congress approved transfeminicidio as a distinct crime in the local penal code on 19 July 2024, making the capital the second state to create the offence. The reform is known as the Ley Paola Buenrostro, after a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety. Article 148-Ter, added to the local code on 23 August 2024, typifies the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of her gender identity or expression.

Investigation practice has been reorganised around that offence. A dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit was created in December 2024 to cover all violent deaths of trans women, and its investigators may no longer demand legal name or gender change or medical documentation from trans people, removing a documented route to outing and delay when a crime is reported. The prosecutor's instrument FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for transfeminicide alongside feminicide investigations, and on 25 August 2025 the mayor of Mexico City launched a new Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the capital.

Enforcement remains the open question. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the analysis must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B79016588373767.tangentialFactors:
Document barriers elsewhere in Mexico indicate what obstructed recognition looks like in practice. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police; the same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023. A visitor whose papers do not match presentation can expect the same friction at checkpoints and counters.

The state-by-state comparison is uneven in both directions. Nuevo León's 5 LGBT+ homicides in 2024 against the capital's 17 shows how concentrated the recorded toll was, and the capital's reporting infrastructure inflates its relative position without negating the underlying level of violence. On the legislative side the Distrito Federal was the second state to typify transfeminicide, which means other states still lack the offence entirely and cases there are prosecuted, if at all, under ordinary homicide provisions.

Impunity is the recurring regional condition rather than a local exception. The Inter-American Commission's 2024 warning that impunity may have reached alarming levels, together with the unpunished 2016 murder that gave the Ley Paola Buenrostro its name, frames the practical value of the new offence as untested. Beer's LSE USAPP analysis makes the same point nationally: formal rights that are rarely enforced fairly or uniformly.

31927357B30741484985331.name: Nuevo Leon
31927357B30741484985331.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities at the camp). A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke. The gap between nominal coverage and protection is documented in the observatory review 'transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.'

Context for comparison: Mexico City pairs a similar lethality record with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit (Dec 2024), mandatory-response protocols and a gender police force (Aug 2025); Nayarit was first in the country to typify the crime (March 2024). Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.

31927357B49073316106075.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
31927357B49073316106075.summary:
Michoacán has not typified the killing of LGBT people as a hate crime under state law, an absence acknowledged by the state's own welfare officials and by civil-society monitors. Attacks against the community concentrate geographically in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence, so risk inside the state is uneven rather than uniform: Morelia, the state capital, records the largest absolute number of LGBT homicides, but enforcement of any protective framework is weak throughout.

Homicide against LGBT people in Michoacán is sustained and documented. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT, presented by Raúl Martínez of Colectivo Michoacán es Diversidad, counted 46 LGBT homicides in the state between 2015 and 2024, distributed across Morelia (11), Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5 each) and Zamora (4). The deadliest year was 2015, with 10 victims. Trans women accounted for 27 of the 46 homicides, and the 25 to 39 age bracket was the most affected. Thirteen disappearances of LGBT people were reported between 2022 and 2024, a figure whose investigation status the civil-society data does not resolve.

The pattern continued into 2026. Six homicide cases against LGBT people were identified in the state in the first four and a half months of that year, three in Morelia and one each in Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío. One of them was 'Daniela', a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026; a suspect was arrested, an outcome that stands out against the surrounding pattern of inaction. At least 56 aggressions against the community have been registered in Michoacán since 2014.

Impunity is the decisive variable for a visitor assessing protection. Of the 46 hate-crime cases recorded by civil society in the state since 2015, only one was moving toward judicial proceedings: the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro. The state prosecutor's office keeps no disaggregated data on these cases, and the victims commission, the state human rights commission and the state council against discrimination lack the capacity or budget to act. No public prevention policy for LGBT violence exists in the state.

sources.summary: El Sol de Morelia reports that the majority of attacks on the LGBT community in Michoacán concentrate in Tierra Caliente, and that the state has not typified the murder of sexual-diversity people as a hate crime.

La Jornada (15 Apr 2026) reports the arrest of a suspect in the killing of 'Daniela', a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia (2 Apr 2026), and counts six LGBT+ homicides in the state in the first four and a half months of 2026.

31927357B5337219705256.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
31927357B5337219705256.summary:
Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many Mexican states now operate administrative recognition procedures while others lack them entirely, and that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

Veracruz was among the last states to legislate. The Human Rights Watch state-by-state map shows that only in 2025 did the state's Congress reform the Civil Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. The same page documents no prison-placement rule for Veracruz and no information on where trans prisoners are housed; its Veracruz content concerns civil registry and identity documents only.

The state's record on lethal violence is the worst in the national monitoring data. Letra S's report "Muertes violentas de personas LGBT+ en México — Informe 2021" (May 2022) found that Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases in 2021, against Guanajuato with 9, Estado de México with 7 and Chihuahua with 6; 19 of the 32 states recorded victims.

The 2025 figures show the same concentration. Letra S's annual impunity report of 7 May 2026 records 60 LGBT+ people murdered nationwide in 2025, of whom 35 (58.3 percent) were trans women, a national trans-women homicide rate of 23.7 per 100,000. The state ranking places Puebla first with 7 killings and Veracruz and Guanajuato second with 6 each; a Veracruz case in that count is the November 2025 killing in a motel in Oluta.

Diario de Xalapa reports that Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 recorded hate crimes against the LGBT community. Jornada Veracruz reports that the state prosecutor's office holds several open LGBT-murder files, according to activist Leonardo Ruiz of Orgullo Xalapa, among them Edhibaldo Presa Parra, a Universidad Veracruzana professor found dead on 7 January. Activists say suspicion of a hate crime rests on motive patterns, including prior harassment, aggravating factors and the victim's orientation, and attribute unresolved cases to impunity in the state prosecutor's office; data cited from 'Soy Humano' put Veracruz below the national average in 2024.

Recorded totals understate the harm. The Letra S 2021 report notes under-reporting: in a third of 2021 cases no victim name was published, and in 43 percent the recorded sex was male without attention to gender identity.

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
Oaxaca created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2019 reform to its civil code. The procedure was extended to people aged 12 and over by decree in 2021, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopened access for children under 12, fully opening the route. Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity legislation governs identity documents; it does not address where trans inmates are held.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people and against muxes is documented at state level. Oaxaca's human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022. Muxe teacher Marimar "Estrellita" Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

An April 2025 profile by Trendencias described Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and simultaneously its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community. It reported violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate, and named among the murdered muxe Cristian Hernandez Cutino, 31, and stylist Zulma Hernandez Mendoza, 43. The state response described in the same profile is stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer Goola "Lado Sur" festival in Juchitan circulated an invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted". Muxe activists, including defender Felina Santiago, who has carried out three decades of advocacy, filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body over the transphobic exclusion. Three velas went ahead on 26 May 2024, with muxes affirming that they are part of local society and culture.
