1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
Tripura stands under India's national framework, and the national assessment of legal recognition, identity documents, entry, facilities and healthcare applies to visitors here without regional modification. The Tripura-specific record contains no statute, court order or state policy of its own on any of those questions.

What the region's own sources document is checkpoint enforcement. Tripura police detained transgender people in three separate border operations during 2024. On 2 August 2024, officers at the Panisagar check post in North Tripura district stopped a bus bound for Mumbai and held seven Bangladeshi nationals, two of them transgender individuals and five described in the reporting as disguised as third-gender. A joint 24-hour operation on 9 November 2024 detained twelve Bangladeshi nationals including minors and transgender people: six in the first group, three of them transgender, were held after midnight while travelling to Mumbai, and a second group of six, including three children from Khulna, was held at Udaipur Railway Station, with a local helper arrested for facilitating the movement. A further operation reported by Sentinel Assam apprehended fifteen Bangladeshi nationals including seven transgender individuals within 24 hours, after a bus search at the Panisagar checkpoint on the Assam-Agartala highway found detainees carrying fraudulent Aadhaar and PAN cards en route to Mumbai via Guwahati.

The police framing in the August 2024 incident matters for how a visitor is read. Describing five passengers as disguised as third-gender treats third-gender presentation as a cover for irregular travel rather than as an identity. A trans or gender-nonconforming traveller passing through Tripura's highway and rail checkpoints should expect gender presentation to be read by officers as a possible concealment tactic, alongside the document checks that define these operations.

Tripura shares an 856-km porous border with Bangladesh, and the sources show sustained bus and rail screening along the Assam-Agartala corridor. The inventory records no instance of a person being searched, detained or questioned on account of gender identity alone; every detention described rests on nationality and document offences.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal stands under India's national framework. Parliament's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill of March 2026 replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, so trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result. Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities; in November 2024 openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In West Bengal itself, a group of trans women heading to RG Kar Medical College filed an FIR on 18 August 2024 alleging an RPF constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them to check her gender and made inappropriate remarks; Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegations and counter-filed an FIR against the group, while footage showed the trans woman in tears. Transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities; bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

West Bengal registered 3 of the 7 Transgender Persons Act cases filed nationally in 2021, the highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala, though national totals remain very small at 20 cases from 2019 to 2023, a figure the report attributes to police-registration bias rather than low incidence. A 2025 survey recorded prevalence of 27.2% physical violence and 22.3% sexual violence against trans people. South Dinajpur police arrested Bangladeshi transgender person Ali Mondal, also known as Bijli Mondal, from Sirajganj district, along with the e-rickshaw driver who brought her across the border, for allegedly infiltrating India, illustrating exposure to immigration enforcement for trans border-crossers.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. West Bengal is one of the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board, but its constituted board operates without a functioning policy framework; nationally, most boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since creation, and the 17 existing boards are mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism or any power, with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

1811400B91946361694107.name: Punjab
1811400B91946361694107.summary:
Punjab has no statute of its own targeting transgender people. A trans visitor to Punjab stands under India's national framework, which the parent record carries.

The national layer binding Punjab includes the Supreme Court's 6 September 2018 judgment in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, which struck down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, held that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserved the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender identity, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing.

The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019) is the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab. It was passed by the Lok Sabha on 5 August 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 November 2019, received presidential assent on 5 December 2019, and has been in force since 10 January 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. On 27 January 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

Punjab's own signal is social rather than statutory. Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 Rose Garden parade after mounting resistance from Sikh religious organisations including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition; the Washington Blade reported this on 23 April 2025. Public visibility of LGBT+ life in Amritsar therefore carries a documented risk of organised religiously-framed obstruction, which a visitor planning to attend or appear at Pride events should weigh.

1811400B21167269026319.name: Tamil Nādu
1811400B21167269026319.summary:
Tamil Nadu operates within a national framework that narrowed in March 2026, when India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill and replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

Tamil Nadu is the most protective sub-national layer a trans visitor will encounter in India. It was the first state to introduce a transgender welfare policy, in 1995, maintains a dedicated Transgender Welfare Board, and adopted a comprehensive State Policy for Transgender Persons in 2025. On 4 August 2025 the Madras High Court, in WP 7284 of 2021, recorded that the state had brought that policy into effect and called it "a victory for transgender and intersex persons after their long struggle", expressly commending the government. Active judicial confirmation of executive protection of this kind is rare and gives a visitor a concrete institutional recourse in this state.

The state's official transgender-welfare portal publishes the gender-change application kit, comprising an affidavit form, a certificate of identity for change of gender, membership ID relaxation and user manuals, and documents the wider regime: free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, access to housing and citizenship schemes, and the thirunangai and thirunambi administrative categories embedded in governance.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery nationally. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Tamil Nadu's courts are also demonstrably being used. Crime-data analysis published on 30 January 2026 records the state as the only one with a Transgender Persons Act case in 2020, one of one nationally, and again in 2022, with 7 of the 11 national cases in 2023. The same analysis cautions that registration figures understate actual incidence.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people and a state government with an unusually deep welfare and recognition apparatus.

1811400B45534780755480.name: Kerala
1811400B45534780755480.summary:
Kerala stands under India's national transgender-rights framework while operating a substantial state layer of its own. In November 2015 it adopted the country's first government transgender policy, addressing the right to identify as "male", "female" or "TG" (third gender) and providing for equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, life, liberty and justice, and non-discrimination on grounds of sex.

Kerala is among the states and union territories reported to Parliament in December 2021 as having constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules, the body that coordinates state benefits for transgender residents.

Surgical care has been a state project with persistent delivery gaps. In March 2016 the Social Justice Department proposed free sex reassignment surgery in government hospitals, at least in medical colleges, from the next financial year. Before that proposal there was no in-state SRS facility, and patients travelled to Chennai or Bengaluru at costs of Rs 2–5 lakh for male-to-female and Rs 4–8 lakh for female-to-male procedures, on top of six months to two years of counselling, a year or more of hormone therapy and post-surgery observation. Implementation depended on health ministry approval and on training multidisciplinary teams in urology, endocrinology, sexology and psychology. Many government hospitals still cannot offer surgery for want of trained staff, so patients fall back on costlier private institutions where care standards are uneven and where reimbursement schemes require patients to raise the full fee before any refund.

Two facilities mark the state's provision. The Government Medical College Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram completed its first sex reassignment surgery in January 2017 through staged procedures over three years. The Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam opened in February 2017 what is described as the country's first government clinic exclusively for the transgender community, running twice a month with a specialised panel and also serving sex workers, after a District Legal Services Authority proposal prompted by transgender patients' reported apprehension about approaching hospitals and consequent reliance on self-medication. Health cards denoting transgender status were distributed through the clinic, and the same authority proposed separate public toilets for transgender persons to the district collector.

Deaths have driven policy. The suicide of Anannyah Kumari Alex, who alleged botched gender affirmation surgery, triggered protests over irregularities and the absence of a specific protocol in private hospitals; the state appointed an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and initiated steps for free surgeries in government hospitals. The suicide of Praveen Nath, Kerala's first transgender bodybuilder, drew attention to transphobic groups described by Social Justice Minister R. Bindu as rooted in religious fundamentalism, with cyberbullying and transphobic media coverage identified as causes.

A recent spate of killings of transgender people, with lack of responsible police investigation, has raised security concerns, alongside a rise in police harassment when transgender people attend stations to file complaints. The Director General of Police issued a direction that such grievances be addressed without delay.

Recorded case numbers are very small and reflect police registration rather than incidence. Kerala accounted for 2 of the 7 nationwide Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023, a joint-highest state total with Tamil Nadu in 2023. The reporting organisation cautions that national counts are tiny because of registration bias, so these figures understate violence.

Conversion therapy is widely practised by licensed psychiatrists and psychologists as well as by unqualified practitioners, despite position statements from multiple professional bodies condemning the practice as unscientific and illegal.

Public hostility is documented and has reached the courts. In December 2023 the High Court of Kerala described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a "serious issue" and asked authorities to take necessary action. The October 2023 annual pride march in Malappuram was attacked by a homophobic mob, followed by a police lathicharge. At least two LGBTQ people have died by suicide amid what sources describe as all-time-high cyberbullying, and hate-speech allegations have been made against mainstream politicians. Opposition is attributed to meninist groups, conservative political groups, religious organisations and social conservatism.

Discrimination in employment and housing persists despite the state's early policy lead. Community resources include Queerythm's 24/7 helpline for members in distress, Queerala's campaigning on healthcare, curriculum and workplace policies, and Sahayathrika for LGBTIQA+ members assigned female at birth. The Kerala Queer Pride march in Thrissur has run since July 2010 and Queerythm walks since 2017, both focused on sensitising police and media to prevent violence and discrimination.

PIB federal reply (Dec 2021): Kerala is among the 12 states/UTs reported to parliament as having constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kerala (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) the Supreme Court recognized a "third gender," affirming freedom from discrimination and right to equality, and Kerala became the first state to follow up with a government transgender policy in 2015 addressing the right to identify as "male", "female" or "TG" (Third Gender) with provisions for equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, life, liberty and justice, and non-discrimination based on sex. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 bans unfair discrimination against transgender people in educational establishments and services, employment, healthcare, use of goods, accommodation, services, facilities, benefits, privileges or opportunities available to the public, right to movement, right to reside, purchase, rent or occupy property, opportunity to stand for or hold public or private office, and in government or private establishments. In 2016 the State Government proposed free sex reassignment surgeries in government hospitals, Kannur district allocated budget for employment and skill training, and the government later provided reimbursement for gender affirming surgeries plus scholarships for transgender students in classes 7 to 10, but lack of training means many government hospitals cannot offer surgery forcing reliance on costlier private institutions with stigma, lack of care standards and fund-disbursement problems because patients must raise funds before refund. The Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam opened in 2017 a clinic exclusively attending to the transgender community with a specialized panel, described as the first government clinic of its kind and also open to sex workers after a DLSA proposal following health-concerns campaigning, while a February 2016 Gender Park in Kozhikode opened by President Pranab Mukherjee was dedicated to gender equality and LGBT issues. A 2017 Social Justice Department workshop in Kozhikode with around 30 transgender representatives discussed identity cards, pension for those over 60, skill development training, scholarships and educational loans, and driving lessons for employment as Uber drivers, and Kochi's 2016 first transgender school for 10th and 12th board exams and vocational training for 10 students aged 25-50 ceased functioning as a school after three months and became a hostel for transgender Kochi Metro staff. A recent spate of killings of transgender people with lack of responsible police investigation raised security concerns, alongside a rise in police harassment when transgender people approach stations to file complaints that resulted in a DGP direction to address grievances without delay. The suicide of Anannyah Kumari Alex alleging botched gender affirmation surgery triggered protests and discussion of irregularities and absence of specific protocol in private hospitals, leading the state to appoint an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and initiate steps for free surgeries in government hospitals, while the suicide of Praveen Nath drew attention to mushrooming transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism. Homosexual intercourse was criminalized under Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code in 1861 as voluntarily having "carnal intercourse against the order of nature." In 2009 the Delhi High Court in Naz Foundation v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi found Section 377 prohibitions on private, adult, consensual, non-commercial same-sex conduct violated fundamental rights, but on 11 December 2013 the Supreme Court overturned that order while noting Parliament should debate the matter, followed by protests, and on 28 January 2014 dismissed review petitions by the Central Government, Naz Foundation and others. On 2 February 2016 the Supreme Court agreed to review criminalisation and on 6 September 2018 unanimously struck down Section 377 as unconstitutional for infringing autonomy, intimacy and identity, legalising same-sex sexual activity in India including Kerala. Same-sex marriages are not recognised or performed in India, though movements for recognition have emerged in Kerala and nationally. In line with Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is prohibited via Article 15 of the Constitution, but this extends only to discrimination by state or government bodies. Gay conversion therapy is widely practised by both licensed psychiatrists/psychologists and quacks despite position statements by multiple psychiatrist/psychologist organisations condemning the practice as unscientific and illegal. For transgender-specific conditions, the article reports "societal discrimination, particularly in employment and housing, and various implementation issues remain major problems" despite Kerala's early policy lead. Transgender activist Vijayarajamallika, head of Kochi's transgender school, stated "the school aims at making transgender people eligible for taking decent jobs and living a dignified life," reflecting employment barriers, while Minister R. Bindu blamed cyber bullying and transphobia in the media for the suicide of Praveen Nath, Kerala's first transgender bodybuilder, describing him as a martyr amid mushrooming transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism. More broadly for LGBT visitors, the article notes historical and contemporary opposition especially due to meninist groups, conservative political groups, religious organizations and social conservatism, with increasing recent opposition including hate-speech allegations against mainstream politicians and all-time-high cyberbullying linked to suicides of at least two LGBTQ persons. In December 2023 the High Court of Kerala described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a 'serious issue' and asked authorities to take necessary action. The October 2023 annual pride march in Malappuram was attacked by a homophobic mob leading to lathicharge by police, while Kerala Queer Pride since July 2010 in Thrissur and annual walks by Queerythm since 2017 focus on sensitisation of police and media to prevent violence and discrimination. Community protection resources noted are Queerala campaigning for sensitisation of healthcare, curriculum and workplace policies, Queerythm running a 24X7 helpline for members in distress, and Sahayathrika for female-born LGBTIQA+ members, amid an easing climate from prior invisibility where few opted to come out for fear family would "take them to a psychiatrist or file a police complaint against friends."

sources.title: National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014)
sources.summary: On 15 April 2014 the Supreme Court recognized hijras/transgenders as a third gender who could no longer be forced to identify as male or female and required their treatment as socially and economically backward with OBC reservation in educational admission and employment, Centre and state social welfare schemes, public awareness to erase stigma, construction of special public toilets and provision for special medical needs, legal entitlement to affirmed sex after surgical change without discrimination, and protection from harassment and discrimination including misuse of IPC section 377, with the ruling limited to eunuchs/hijras/transgenders and not to gay, lesbian and bisexual persons.

1811400B45534780755480.tangentialFactors:
Kerala's record is one of early policy leadership followed by incomplete implementation: it was the first state to adopt a transgender policy in 2015 and opened what is described as the country's first government transgender clinic in 2017, yet the same sources document absent surgical capacity, uneven private care standards, refund arrangements that require patients to pre-fund treatment, and discrimination in employment and housing as continuing major problems.

The state's high ranking on recorded Transgender Persons Act cases is a raw-count ranking with a national denominator of only 7 cases in 2021 and 11 in 2023, and the source itself attributes the small totals to police-registration bias. A joint-highest sub-national total on such a small base cannot be read as a measure of comparative danger, and no per-capita figure is provided.

Assessments of the social climate diverge in tone rather than in fact: sources describe an easing from prior invisibility, when few people came out for fear their family would "take them to a psychiatrist or file a police complaint against friends", alongside documented increases in cyberbullying, transphobic groups and organised opposition. Both trends are sourced to the same period.

The state's own institutions carry much of the protection machinery: a Transgender Welfare Board, a Social Justice Department that has convened workshops on identity cards, pensions and training, a state police direction on complaint handling, and a High Court that has intervened on cyber attacks against the community.

1811400B78322693766699.summary:
Assam stands under India's national framework, and no Assam-specific statute on gender recognition, criminal law or facilities was identified in the sources reviewed; the national assessment applies.

Assam's complaint machinery under the Transgender Persons Act has been reachable. Of the seven cases registered nationally under the Act in 2021, two were in Assam; the 2023 national tally recorded none in the state. A Queerbeat crime-data report of 30 January 2026 cautions that national counts are tiny (20 cases across 2019 to 2023) because of police-registration bias, so low counts do not indicate low incidence. The same report's 2025 survey puts prevalence of physical violence against trans people at 27.2% and sexual violence at 22.3%.

As of December 2021, Assam had not constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under the 2019 Rules; a Parliamentary reply from the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment listed 12 states and union territories that had done so, and Assam was not among them. No state welfare machinery coordinating housing, surgery or pensions therefore existed in Assam at that date.

Transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody, a state-specific instance of the police-conduct concerns documented elsewhere in India.

1811400B11231190780494.name: Uttar Pradesh
1811400B11231190780494.summary:
Uttar Pradesh stands under India's national framework for transgender persons. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity under Article 15; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents remain a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities, indicating that intrusive document screening has been applied to trans travellers in Uttar Pradesh and that the state's high court has intervened against it.

The most trans-visible public space in Uttar Pradesh is the Maha Kumbh gathering in Prayagraj. On 12 February 2025, at the fourth ceremonial bath of the 45-day fair, Pavitra Nandagiri, a Mahamandaleshwar of the Kinnar Akhada and one of the gathering's highest-ranking monks, led 15 transgender spiritual leaders in the ritual bathing, marching alongside Naga Sadhus and Aghori. The episode documents an institutionalised trans religious hierarchy operating openly in the state.

Trans-specific violence is documented. Kajal, a 25-year-old transgender woman in Kanpur, was killed in a home-invasion robbery; the record dates to 10 August 2025, a suspect was later arrested, and her 12-year-old adopted brother also died. The killing was logged in the 2025 international transgender day of remembrance list through local press reporting.

Protection machinery at state level is mandated but its Uttar Pradesh implementation is not established in the sources. The Ministry of Social Justice stated on 8 December 2021 that state governments must constitute Transgender Welfare Boards under section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules, 2020, and all state governments were reminded on 9 October 2020 to act.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.

Checkpoint friction against trans people is recorded elsewhere in India and shapes what a visitor may face in transit. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. Judicial protection elsewhere in India is stronger than the national picture suggests. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Intersex minors remain at risk nationally: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants. 1811400B70654311394581.name: Chhattīsgarh
1811400B70654311394581.summary:
Chhattisgarh stands under India's national framework. The national record carries the layers that matter most to a trans visitor here: recognition rules for identity documents, entry and stay, screening practice, criminal-law protection and access to transition-related care. No Chhattisgarh-specific statute, document rule, screening practice or facilities rule was identified in the sources, so the national assessment applies unchanged within the state.

Trans-specific violence is documented at the state level. On 22 November 2024 the transgender woman Kajal, known as "Coca Cola", was lured out, stabbed and dumped in an abandoned quarry at village Dhabadih in Baloda Bazar district. The killing was a contract murder ordered for Rs 12 lakh by a rival, Tapasya, to block Kajal's ascent to the Jora Math community head seat, the "guru gaddi". Five suspects were arrested and Rs 10.5 lakh seized. The motive was succession within the state's trans community leadership rather than anything a visitor does, but it establishes that disputes over community standing in Chhattisgarh have been settled by paid killing.

14911670B7632012573600.name: Ceara
14911670B7632012573600.summary:
Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, and adds its own layer of measures. Law No. 17,480, sanctioned by Governor Camilo Santana and published on 19 May 2021, requires every public and private establishment in the state, effective 90 days after publication, to display a visible notice of at least 50 cm by 50 cm on the exterior or at an entrance stating that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is expressly prohibited and listing the phone number of the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies for complaints, clarifications and reports.

On 16 November 2006 Governor Lúcio Alcântara signed a law mandating inclusion of educational material on sexual orientation in the training of the state's Civil and Military Police, published in the Official Gazette on the 26th of that month. On 7 March 2013 State General Attorney Francisco Sales Neto issued decision 02/2013 obligating all notaries statewide to accept same-sex marriages, effective 15 March 2013; same-sex marriage has been legal in Ceará since 2013.

On 22 May 2024 the Court of Justice of Ceará authorized Brune Bonassi to rectify documents to reflect a neutral gender, making Bonassi the first non-binary person in the state to obtain such rectification. Ceará was set to issue its first birth certificate recognizing a person as non-binary. The Supreme Federal Court's 1 March 2018 ruling that a transgender person may change official name and sex without surgery or professional evaluation, by self-declaration of psychosocial identity alone, applies in the state, as does the 13 June 2019 ruling treating discrimination on grounds of gender identity and of sexual orientation as crimes akin to racism.

Violence against trans people in Ceará is documented at a high level. Per the ANTRA dossier reported by G1/Globo on 28 January 2025, Ceará was the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024, with 11 killings, the third highest raw count nationally, in a state of some 9.2 million people, about 0.12 killings per 100,000 residents. Per the 9th ANTRA dossier reported on 26 January 2026, Ceará was among the states with the most trans killings in 2025 with 8 cases, about 0.09 per 100,000 residents, tied with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking; Brazil totalled 80 killings, down 34% against 2024 and still the highest worldwide, with 1,261 killings recorded 2017-2025. These rankings are by raw count only and track population, so they say little about per-capita risk relative to smaller states. Among the 57 victims with race data nationally, 70% were Black, an average of 77% over 2017-2025.

On 12 December 2017 the Sobral Municipal Chamber approved Bill No. 2154/17, authored by Councillor Adauto Izidoro Arruda, prohibiting pedagogical activities reproducing the concept of "gender ideology" or any discussion of gender diversity in all municipal and private schools in Sobral, by majority vote with the sole opposing vote of Councillor Maria Socorro Brasileiro Magalhães, and forwarded the bill to Mayor Ivo Gomes to sanction or veto.

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison
sources.summary: Wikipedia's general overview article (28 Sep 2026) reports no codified Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy. Its Brazil paragraph states only that traumatic social vulnerability and stigma facing travestis and transgender people shape rehabilitation. For comparison, the article sets out international placement norms: Scotland's 2022 inspection standards admit trans and intersex prisoners to facilities matching their lived or experienced gender, and Canada places prisoners by gender identity.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Brazil
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' article (28 Sep 2026), in its Politics section, states that LGBTQ people have a special place in Brazilian prisons, separate from other prisoners; that transgender people ('transsexuals') have the right to be called by their social name and not their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons; and that LGBTQ prisoners may choose male or female clothing. The statement is footnoted (ref. 253) to a Mix Brasil (UOL) article, 'Vivemos uma inercia no congresso...', archived 18 Jan 2012.

14911670B91095571793858.name: Rio Granda do Norte
14911670B91095571793858.summary:
Rio Grande do Norte stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage recognition, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate across the country, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled like anyone else's at entry and in family matters. No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies in Rio Grande do Norte.

The dominant visitor-facing signal is lethal violence against trans people. ANTRA's dossier for 2024 recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally, 16 per cent below the 145 recorded in 2023 and close to the 125-per-year average for 2008 to 2024; five of the victims were human-rights defenders and 95.9 per cent were travestis or trans women. The same dossier documents systematic under-counting because official bodies do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, which is the basis on which Rio Grande do Norte appeared with zero recorded killings in 2024.

The ninth ANTRA dossier, covering 2025, records 80 trans killings nationwide, Brazil's eighteenth consecutive year at the top of the global tally. In the state ranking Ceará and Minas Gerais lead with eight each, while Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte appear with four each. Against a population of roughly 3.5 million, four cases yield about 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and around three times the national figure of roughly 0.38 per million. The jump from zero in 2024 makes Rio Grande do Norte the sharpest deterioration in the dataset, and the dataset itself cautions against reading a single-year zero as evidence of safety.

Lethal violence against trans women in the state continued after both counted years. In the early hours of 4 May 2026, Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was shot dead inside her rented home in the Dom Jaime Câmara neighbourhood of Mossoró after five men broke in and killed her while she slept; military police found the body on a routine patrol and one suspect was arrested with a pistol and booked for illegal firearms discharge and armed criminal association. In late February 2026 a transgender woman known as Naomi was found dead in her own home in Praia da Pipa, in the Tibau do Sul municipality, killed by stab wounds, with the Civil Police opening an investigation.

Detention, if it arises, is governed by national rather than state rules. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires that a person held as LGBTI be recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and that placement be fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference. Trans, travesti and intersex people must be asked whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell; LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. No Rio Grande do Norte placement policy is documented in the sources held, and practice elsewhere in the country has been found to diverge sharply from this framework.

14911670B91095571793858.tangentialFactors:
The violence picture is regional as well as national. Of the 80 trans killings recorded in Brazil in 2025, 38 fell in the Northeast, the region containing Rio Grande do Norte, and the two states topping the ranking, Ceará and Minas Gerais, recorded eight each. Small absolute numbers mean a single incident moves a state's rate sharply, and the volatility between 2024 and 2025 indicates an environment that can turn quickly rather than one that has stabilised.

Official recording is unreliable in the victim's favour. ANTRA's 2024 dossier attributes the low national count partly to systematic under-counting by official bodies that do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, so a recorded figure of zero is a data artefact of the counting method as much as an assessment of risk.

Beyond the state, national conditions supply the background against which a trans visitor moves. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle. A May 2024 investigation documented drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. Courts have also applied the hate-crime provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

The gap between protective text and practice is documented in detention. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the Rio de Janeiro state prison system, finding trans women housed in units operated as masculine or in so-called neutral or security units, and describing placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study records a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, clothing, accessories and cosmetics.

Protection machinery has widened nationally: an analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.

Paraíba stands under Brazil's national framework, and the state's own signal is concentrated in documented violence against trans people. Prison placement rules apply in Paraíba's state system through a federal portaria issued by the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República and reported by G1 on 17 April 2014. Transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units. Gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces. LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, and may choose male or female clothing. Non-compliance carries no sanction. No Paraíba-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or case is documented.

14911670B44044837234259.name: Minas Gerais
14911670B44044837234259.summary:
Minas Gerais is a state within Brazil and stands under the national framework set out for that country: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, an equal age of consent regardless of sexual orientation, and, since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions under which discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punished and transphobia is treated on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family-law status are handled the same as anyone else's at entry.

The dominant visitor-facing risk in Minas Gerais is lethal violence against trans people, and the state sits at the severe end of the national picture. The ANTRA dossier for 2024, published 27 January 2025, ranks Minas Gerais second nationally with 12 trans killings during the year, behind São Paulo with 16 and ahead of Ceará with 11. The cumulative count for the state across 2017 to 2024 is 100.

The following year's figures put the state at the head of the national ranking. The ANTRA dossier for 2025, reported on 26 January 2026, records Minas Gerais tied with Ceará in first place with 8 trans killings during 2025, within a national total of 80.

Detention in the state operates under a defined federal rule-set. A portaria issued on 17 April 2014 by the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República sets housing rules for LGBT prisoners across Brazil's prison system and applies within the Minas Gerais state prison system. Transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, together with the choice of male or female clothing.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Minas Gerais (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 15 December 2017 Decree No. 47,306 created the Social Name Card authorizing trans and travesti individuals to use social names for identification purposes. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration without surgery or professional evaluation, while since 2023 the Minas Gerais Public Defender's Office has held free Pride Month initiatives to assist non-binary people with name and gender marker changes, with Tai Barreto changing documents on 29 May 2025 through a Defender lawsuit though non-binary individuals still face challenges. In 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled discrimination based on gender identity illegal nationwide, supplemented by municipal bans on gender-identity discrimination in Juiz de Fora (Law 9791, 12 May 2000), Alfenas (Law 3,277, 11 September 2001) and São João del-Rei (Law 4,172, 12 December 2007). On facilities, Uberaba's ban on unisex restrooms enacted 7 October 2022 after 12 September 2022 approval was struck down in 2024 after a 2023 Defender lawsuit, and Belo Horizonte's law signed 20 November 2023 authorizing religious institutions to prohibit transgender people from using restrooms corresponding to gender identity was struck down by preliminary injunction in August 2025. In August 2026 the Court of Justice ordered a Contagem shopping mall to pay 2,000 reais compensation to a trans woman denied women's restroom access in a 2019 incident where a guard demanded proof of "sex change," reversing a Contagem court denial for insufficient evidence. On violence and protection, a 1 July 2024 Federal University of Minas Gerais and Public Prosecutor study found 60% of deaths involving trans people and travestis resulted from violence with 74% of victims Black or Pardo, in 2025 Minas Gerais tied Ceará for highest murders of trans people and travestis, and on 15 July 2026 the Court of Justice with the National Council of Justice launched an incident reporting mechanism for LGBTQ violence in Belo Horizonte. Homosexuality has been legal since 1830 when Emperor Dom Pedro I sanctioned the Imperial Penal Code removing sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Minas Gerais since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision in compliance with the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. On 24 May 2011 the Court of Justice authorized adoption by a lesbian couple in Patos de Minas, and since 2015 same-sex adoption has been legal nationwide through a Supreme Federal Court decision. At state level, on 15 January 2002 Law No. 14,170 prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation and on 3 January 2007 Law No. 16,636 established May 17 as State Day Against Homophobia, while in 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal nationwide. Municipal protection includes Belo Horizonte Law 8176 of 29 January 2001 and Law 8719 of 11 December 2003, Contagem Law 3506 of 10 January 2002, Juiz de Fora Law 9791 of 12 May 2000, Alfenas Law 3,277 of 11 September 2001 and São João del-Rei Law 4,172 of 12 December 2007 prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination, plus Alfenas Law 4,120 of 18 May 2009 on Municipal Day of Struggle against Homophobia. Despite measures, violence is frequent with Minas Gerais ranked second-highest for violence against LGBTQ people in 2017.

14911670B2612452665424.name: Pernambuco
14911670B2612452665424.summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest raw count of any Brazilian state in the ANTRA dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind only Ceará and Minas Gerais at 8 each, against a national total of 80. In a state of some 9.1 million people this equals roughly 0.08 per 100,000 residents. Valor Internacional reported the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, and Diario de Pernambuco carried the state ranking on the same date. The ranking is by raw count only; the sources provide no per-capita comparison between states.

The annual figure has fallen from 13 in 2022 to 9 in 2023, 8 in 2024 and 7 in 2025, so 2025 is the lowest count since 2022 while remaining among the highest in the country. Over six years Pernambuco recorded 83 violent deaths of trans people, the sixth-highest raw count in the national ranking for that period; the dossier counts 349 such killings across the Northeast from 2017 to 2025.

Killings are concentrated outside the Recife capital region. On 2 October 2025 a trans woman was shot dead inside her home in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste interior; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive, and no arrests were reported at publication. On 7 July 2021 Fabiana da Silva Lucas, a 30-year-old Black trans woman, was found dead along highway PE-160 in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe, killed by several knife strikes, the state's third recorded killing of a trans or travesti person that month; police told press that a 22-year-old suspect known as 'Gaúcho' was lynched by locals at the scene.

Pernambuco operates its own anti-violence machinery. Law No. 18,634, signed by the president of the Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco on 13 July 2024 and instituted on 4 July 2024, establishes the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, covering discrimination and violence based on gender identity, sexual orientation and sex characteristics. It recognises such violence as structural and incompatible with democratic rule, requires attention to intersecting race, territory, class, gender, age, religion and disability vulnerabilities, and mandates violence-data monitoring with a compiled methodology, protection and reception services, an emergency-support network for civil-society services, mapping and training of reception facilities, and data collection with research bodies.

In June 2026 state deputy João Paulo (PT) presented Bill No. 4.092/2026 to create a State Policy for Integral Health Promotion of the LGBTQIAPN+ population within the Unified Health System. The bill would reinforce the right to a social name in registrations and care, address travestis and transexuais who delay or avoid care for fear of mistreatment, direct health services to combat LGBTphobia and institutional discrimination, require continuous training of public health professionals, and mandate production and publication of LGBT health indicators.

The judiciary of Pernambuco has recognised gender identity directly. In 2023, following a 2022 lawsuit by the Public Defender's Office of Pernambuco, the Court of Justice of Pernambuco authorised Tarlazza Messina to change documents to reflect their gender identity, the first non-binary legal recognition in the state, registering gender as 'não binárie' on the birth certificate.

Municipal hostility has been checked. On 13 December 2017 Garanhuns enacted Municipal Law No. 4432/2017 banning discussion of gender theory in municipal schools, passed 11-to-1 despite a state prosecution recommendation to reject it. On 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck the law down, lifting the ban on gender-related instruction in the city's schools.

Prison placement for trans detainees in Pernambuco stands under the national framework of National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 2021: placement is decided by a judge after consulting the person, who must be told about male, female and LGBTI-specific units and whose declared preference is recorded, with LGBTI-specific spaces barred from use as disciplinary isolation. No Pernambuco-specific placement rule, special unit or documented case was identified in the sources; the state's prison administration (Secretaria de Administração Penitenciária e Ressocialização de Pernambuco) issues no trans-specific guidance in the material reviewed. Conjugal visitation for same-sex partners has been available in all Brazilian jails since February 2015 under the National Criminal and Penitentiary Council.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Pernambuco (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2019, discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court, a broad provision covering gender identity alongside sexual orientation. On 13 July 2024, the president of the Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco signed Law No. 18,634, which establishes the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, a broad LGBTQIA+ protection measure not transgender-specific alone. In June 2026, state representative João Paulo (PT) presented a bill to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in the Unified Health System, covering gender identity alongside sexual orientation in care. On 1 March 2018, the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex without surgery or professional evaluation, by self-declaration of psychosocial identity. In 2023, following a lawsuit filed in 2022 by the Public Defender's Office of Pernambuco, the Court of Justice of Pernambuco authorized Tarlazza Messina to change documents to reflect gender identity, making them the first non-binary person to do so in the state. On 15 October 2025, the Supreme Federal Court struck down a 13 December 2017 Garanhuns municipal law signed by Mayor Izaías Régis prohibiting "gender ideology" in city schools, following lawsuits by the Prosecutor General of the Republic and the Socialism and Liberty Party. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830, and homosexuality is legal in Pernambuco. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Pernambuco since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision implementing a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. Since 2010, same-sex adoption has been officially permitted in the state through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 9 October 2008, Judge Élio Braz of the 2nd Court of Childhood and Adolescence in Recife permitted a male homosexual couple to adopt two sisters from a shelter with new birth certificates listing two parents, with the Public Prosecutor agreeing and declining further action. On 2 March 2012, a Recife court authorized adoption of a baby by a gay couple, the first in the country to register a child with both fathers' names. Since 2019, discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 13 July 2024, the president of the Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco signed Law No. 18,634 establishing the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, a broad measure covering sexual orientation alongside gender identity. In June 2026, state representative João Paulo (PT) presented a bill to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in the Unified Health System.

sources.title: Law No. 18,634 - State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco
sources.summary: On 4 July 2024 Pernambuco instituted the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People to confront discrimination and violence based on gender identity, sexual orientation and sex characteristics and promote full citizenship, with objectives to monitor violence data with compiled methodology, strengthen and implement protection, promotion and defense services and reception for those in vulnerability and social risk, build a governmental and non-governmental response network, and expand protection statewide, recognizing such identity-based violence as structural, historical and incompatible with democratic rule and human rights and requiring consideration of intersecting race, territory, class, gender, age, religion and disability vulnerabilities, to be implemented transversally through reception-service guidelines, emergency support to civil-society services respecting individual liberty and citizenship, and government reception policies focused on assistance, health, citizenship, culture, public security and justice including mapping and training of public and civil-society reception facilities, data collection and knowledge production with research bodies and universities, partnerships with municipalities and public-private entities, and support for aligned civil-society initiatives, prioritizing victims of identity-based violence/discrimination, those with actual or imminent rupture of family/community ties, and those with compounded vulnerabilities, with regulation by the Executive and entry into force on publication.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil ruling of 1 March 2018 on gender identity
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court, applicable in Pernambuco, held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression and authorized alteration of name and gender in the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization, on the basis that gender identity is a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize.

sources.title: Court of Justice of Pernambuco 2023 ruling authorizing Tarlazza Messina document change
sources.summary: In 2023 in Pernambuco the judiciary for the first time recognized non-binary gender and authorized rectification of Tarlazza Messina's birth certificate to register gender as 'não binárie'.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court decision of 2019 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity
sources.summary: On 24 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (6 of 11 justices) voted to treat transphobia and homophobia as crimes equivalent to racism, punishable under Brazil's racism law until Congress adopts specific LGBT-protection legislation.

sources.title: Municipal law of Garanhuns signed 13 December 2017 by mayor Izaías Régis prohibiting 'gender ideology' in schools
sources.summary: On 13 December 2017 Garanhuns, Pernambuco enacted Municipal Law No. 4432/2017 prohibiting direct or indirect discussion and pedagogical including extracurricular activities on gender theory, questions, identity or ideology in municipal schools effective upon publication after 11-to-1 council approval despite a late-November 2017 state prosecution recommendation to reject it as reinforcing stereotypes and prejudice against those not conforming to dominant standards.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court decision of 15 October 2025 striking down Garanhuns 'gender ideology' law
sources.summary: On 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck down Garanhuns, Pernambuco's municipal law prohibiting teaching about gender, thereby lifting the ban on gender-related instruction in local schools.

sources.title: Bill presented June 2026 by state representative João Paulo (PT) on non-discrimination in Unified Health System
sources.summary: In June 2026 Pernambuco state deputy João Paulo (PT) presented Bill No. 4.092/2026 to create the State Policy for Integral Health Promotion of the LGBTQIAPN+ population in the SUS, reinforcing the right to use the social name in registrations and care and respect for gender identities, setting as objectives expanded SUS access with special attention to travestis and transexuais who avoid or delay seeking care for fear of mistreatment plus mental health, violence prevention and vulnerability reduction, and setting as directives combating LGBTphobia and institutional discrimination in health services, continuous training of public health professionals for humanized respectful care, and production, segmentation and publication of LGBT health data and indicators subject to data-protection laws.

14911670B2612452665424.blindSummary:
The state/province recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest raw count among the state/provinces of the country in an ANTRA dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind only two state/provinces at 8 each, against a national total of 80. In a state/province of some 9.1 million people this equals roughly 0.08 per a small population. A national newspaper reported the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, and a regional daily carried the ranking on the same date. The ranking is by raw count only; the sources provide no per-capita comparison between state/provinces.

The annual figure has fallen from 13 in 2022 to 9 in 2023, 8 in 2024 and 7 in 2025, so 2025 is the lowest count since 2022 while remaining among the highest in the country. Over six years the state/province recorded 83 violent deaths of trans people, the sixth-highest raw count in the national ranking for that period; the dossier counts 349 such killings across one subregion from 2017 to 2025.

Killings are concentrated outside the capital region. On 2 October 2025 a trans woman was shot dead inside her home in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste interior; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive, and no arrests were reported at publication. On 7 July 2021 Fabiana da Silva Lucas, a 30-year-old Black trans woman, was found dead along highway PE-160 in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe, killed by several knife strikes, the state/province's third recorded killing of a trans or travesti person that month; police told press that a 22-year-old suspect known as 'Gaúcho' was lynched by locals at the scene.

The state/province operates its own anti-violence machinery. Law No. 18,634, signed by the president of the Legislative Assembly on 13 July 2024 and instituted on 4 July 2024, establishes the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, covering discrimination and violence based on gender identity, sexual orientation and sex characteristics. It recognises such violence as structural and incompatible with democratic rule, requires attention to intersecting race, state/province, class, gender, age, religion and disability vulnerabilities, and mandates violence-data monitoring with a compiled methodology, protection and reception services, an emergency-support network for civil-society services, mapping and training of reception facilities, and data collection with research bodies.

In June 2026 a state/province deputy presented Bill No. 4.092/2026 to create a State Policy for Integral Health Promotion of the LGBTQIAPN+ population within the national health system. The bill would reinforce the right to a social name in registrations and care, address travestis and transexuais who delay or avoid care for fear of mistreatment, direct health services to combat LGBTphobia and institutional discrimination, require continuous training of public health professionals, and mandate production and publication of LGBT health indicators.

The state/province's judiciary has recognised gender identity directly. In 2023, following a 2022 lawsuit by the state Public Defender's Office, the Court of Justice of the state/province authorised Tarlazza Messina to change documents to reflect their gender identity, the first non-binary legal recognition in the state/province, registering gender as 'não binárie' on the birth certificate.

Municipal hostility has been checked. On 13 December 2017 Garanhuns enacted Municipal Law No. 4432/2017 banning discussion of gender theory in municipal schools, passed 11-to-1 despite a state/province prosecution recommendation to reject it. On 15 October 2025 the national supreme court struck the law down, lifting the ban on gender-related instruction in the city's schools.

Prison placement for trans detainees stands under the national framework of National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 2021: placement is decided by a judge after consulting the person, who must be told about male, female and LGBTI-specific units and whose declared preference is recorded, with LGBTI-specific spaces barred from use as disciplinary isolation. No state/province-specific placement rule, special unit or documented case was identified in the sources; the state/province prison administration issues no trans-specific guidance in the material reviewed. Conjugal visitation for same-sex partners has been available in all jails nationally since February 2015 under the National Criminal and Penitentiary Council.

14911670B2612452665424.tangentialFactors:
The 2025 count of 7 is a raw figure; the sources give no per-capita comparison between Pernambuco and the states ranked above or below it, and Pernambuco's population of some 9.1 million makes it one of Brazil's larger states. A high raw count therefore does not by itself establish a higher per-capita rate than smaller states.

The national framework applies in Pernambuco alongside the state layer: legal gender recognition without surgery or judicial authorisation (STF, ADI 4275, 1 March 2018), transphobia treated as equivalent to racism since the Supreme Federal Court's 24 May 2019 vote of 6 of 11 justices, and nationwide prohibition of discrimination on gender-identity grounds since 2019.

Interior municipalities carry disproportionate risk relative to the capital. Both the October 2025 Belo Jardim killing and the July 2021 Santa Cruz do Capibaribe killing occurred in the Agreste, consistent with the dossier finding that most such killings in the state take place outside Recife.

The ANTRA methodology counts all media-reported killings of trans people irrespective of documented motive, and international comparisons are distorted by differences in documentation capacity; the 2025 figures should be read as reported counts rather than verified motive-specific tallies.

Residents of Pernambuco are covered by Law No. 18,634 of 13 July 2024, the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, which obliges the state executive to regulate and implement protection, reception and data-monitoring services statewide, prioritising victims of identity-based violence, those facing rupture of family or community ties, and those with compounded vulnerabilities.

Residents may seek gender-marker and name rectification through the civil registry under ADI 4275 without surgery or judicial authorisation; the Court of Justice of Pernambuco applied this in 2023 to recognise non-binary gender for the first time in the state, following a suit by the state Public Defender's Office.

Bill No. 4.092/2026, tabled in June 2026, would entrench social-name use and anti-discrimination duties inside Pernambuco's public health network; until enacted, SUS users in the state rely on existing national social-name rules and the bill's provisions are not binding.

Trans detainees held in Pernambuco's prison system are placed under national Council of Justice rules requiring a judge's reasoned decision after consultation, with recorded preference, transfer rights where violence or serious threat exists, and a prohibition on using LGBTI-specific units as disciplinary isolation. The state prison administration has issued no separate trans-placement instrument in the material reviewed.

14911670B19428866735507.name: Bahia
14911670B19428866735507.summary:
Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil and stands under Brazil's national framework: the constitutional and criminal prohibitions on discrimination and hate crimes on gender-identity grounds, legal gender recognition without surgery, same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality, and National Council of Justice Resolution 348 and 366 governing the placement of LGBTI detainees all extend to Bahia and to its prison system.

Bahia carries a high trans homicide burden by raw count. The ANTRA 2025 dossier records 7 trans killings in the state during 2025, behind the leading states at 8, and across the 1,261 killings documented nationally between 2017 and 2025 Bahia ranks third by raw count with 97, after São Paulo with 151 and Ceará with 107; Valor Internacional's state-level breakdown for 2025 places Bahia behind the Ceará and Minas Gerais pair. A 2022 ANTRA dossier ranked Bahia seventh in the country that year, with 7 killings of travestis in the state.

Police in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in western Bahia, are investigating the killing of Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, as a feminicide. She was choked to death over the weekend of 6-7 December 2025; the suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove her body to the police station himself and was released after confessing and asserting self-defence, and the Civil Police confirmed the feminicide line of inquiry.

State-level protection exists in Bahia's own law. The Legislative Assembly passed the Millena Passos Law on 1 June 2022, banning discrimination on the ground of gender identity, signed on 30 June 2022 by Assembly President Adolfo Menezes and named for the trans activist Millena Passos; a parallel bill banning discrimination on sexual orientation was passed and signed on the same dates. Bahia was the first Brazilian state to enact an anti-discrimination ordinance, in 1997.

Documents and public administration follow state rules of their own. Transgender people in Bahia have been able to change their name and legal gender since 2008, with gender self-determination permitted since 2018. On 23 May 2017 Governor Rui Costa decreed that travesti and transsexual persons may use their social name and have their gender identity recognised across all organs of the state's direct and indirect public administration, with the social name required to appear alongside the legal name on official documents and guardian authorisation needed for minors. On 11 May 2022 the Court of Justice of the State of Bahia allowed a third gender option on documents.

Salvador, the state capital, moved in the opposite direction on schools: the City Council approved a bill banning the teaching of gender identity in schools on 17 December 2025, signed into law by Mayor Bruno Soares Reis on 26 March 2026, and the municipal law now prohibits gender-identity material in Salvador's schools.

Partner and family recognition is documented locally. Notaries in Bahia have recognised same-sex marriages since 26 November 2012, the stable-union book is recognised by the National Institute of Social Security for inheritance and pension purposes with 30 reported legal cases in the state including a surviving same-sex spouse's pension, and on 9 March 2010 a Salvador court authorised adoption by a lesbian couple.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Brazil (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Fetched (HTTP 200, cached). Documents the national framework governing trans prisoners that applies uniformly across Brazilian states including Bahia: LGBTQ people have a special, separate place in Brazilian prisons; transsexuals have the right to be addressed by their social name rather than birth name; to be forwarded to women's prisons (i.e. placement by gender identity); and to choose male or female clothing. No state-level/state-DOC (Secretaria de Administração Penitenciária da Bahia) placement detail is given.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Bahia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people have been able to change their name and legal gender since 2008, with gender self-determination permitted since 2018, and the Bahia Public Defender's Office in partnership with other agencies carries out joint efforts to facilitate document rectification. On May 23, 2017, Governor Rui Costa signed a decree granting transgender people the right to use their social name instead of their legal name, requiring the social name be accompanied by the legal name on official documents and guardian authorization for minors. On May 11, 2022, the Court of Justice of the State of Bahia allowed a third gender option on documents, and on December 26, 2024, Governor Jerônimo Rodrigues sanctioned Law 14,806 exempting costs for protest certificates to make document rectification free of charge for transgender people. On June 1, 2022, the Legislative Assembly passed the Millena Passos Law banning discrimination based on gender identity, signed on June 30, 2022 by Assembly President Adolfo Menezes and named in honor of transgender activist Millena Passos. On December 17, 2025, the Salvador City Council approved a bill banning the teaching of gender identity in schools, signed into law on March 26, 2026 by Mayor Bruno Soares Reis. A preventative STD/AIDS program for transvestite sex workers in Bahia produced a booklet, folder and poster with realistic language and images, providing weekly safe-sex workshops and interventions that recorded 900 interventions and distribution of 14,400 condoms in six months. In 2008, Léo Kret, a travesti club dancer, won a Salvador city council seat with 12,861 votes and upon taking office defied dress-code norms by insisting on a strictly feminine wardrobe and on using the women's restroom. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Bahia and throughout Brazil since 1830. Same-sex marriages have been recognized by notaries in Bahia since November 26, 2012, while the homosexual stable union book is recognized by the National Institute of Social Security for inheritance sharing and pension receipt, with 30 reported legal cases in Bahia including a surviving same-sex spouse receiving a pension after the companion's death. On March 9, 2010, a court in Salvador authorized adoption of a child by a lesbian couple. Bahia was the first Brazilian state to enact an anti-discrimination ordinance in 1997, and on June 1, 2022 the Legislative Assembly passed a bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, signed into law on June 30, 2022 by Assembly President Adolfo Menezes. Documented violence includes Grupo Gay da Bahia's 2004 list naming 159 murdered LGBTQ community members that year plus a list of alleged human rights abuses, with some deaths caused directly by homophobia, and a 2022 homophobic attack on a teenager in Camaçari that generated national repercussions and mobilized state authorities.
