Rio de Janeiro state stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Courts have applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Lethal violence against trans people in Rio de Janeiro state is low relative to the country as a whole. Three trans and travesti people were killed in the state in 2025, roughly 0.18 per million residents, below the national rate. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, records 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34 per cent year on year, with the country still first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence.

Violence against trans people also reaches the state's courts as an enforcement matter. The Rio de Janeiro state court (TJ-RJ) decreed preventive detention of a man accused of exploiting trans women in Niterói, a former city-hall employee there until January 2026, with pre-trial custody confirmed in the extortion case.

Detention is governed nationally by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; on arrest a judge fixes the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person about their preference among male, female and LGBTI-specific units, and within a unit whether the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, later changes of placement are possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

14911670B85657526756793.localsOnly:
Placement in Rio de Janeiro state prisons does not reliably follow the national framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in the state's prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights.

The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, alongside national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

14911670B6484683145874.name: Goias
14911670B6484683145874.summary:
Goiás stands under Brazil's national framework; the provisions recorded here are specific to the state. Goiás Decree No. 9,755/2020 is the state's own instrument. It sets out guidelines on LGBTphobic violence and defines that violence to include discrimination, bullying and cyberbullying.

ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, records 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, with the victims overwhelmingly travestis and trans women killed with extreme violence, and it places Brazil first in world rankings for such killings. Five of those 80 victims were killed in Goiás. That five is a raw count and the dossier gives no population-adjusted figure for the state; it sits within a national total that was 122 killings in 2024.

Restroom access is contested at municipal level in the state. Novo Gama enacted a 2015 law prohibiting transgender people from using public restrooms in accordance with their gender identity. The Associação Nacional de Travestis e Transexuais challenged the ordinance, and Justice Cármen Lúcia ordered the municipal government to explain and justify it, fixing a deadline of 11 June 2024.

The Court of Justice of Goiás has ordered recognition of non-binary identity on official documents. On 28 August 2023 it granted document rectification for a non-binary person after registry offices had refused a request made by the Public Defender's Office in February 2020.

In a second case, a court in Goianira authorised a name change but refused the gender marker change, reasoning that no specific law provides for non-binary recognition; on 12 December 2025 the Court of Justice of Goiás allowed the marker change on appeal by the Public Defender's Office.

sources.summary: SBT News (26 Jan 2026) reports ANTRA's ninth annual dossier: 80 trans and travesti people were killed in Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, and Brazil is first in world rankings. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Goiás accounts for 5 of the 80 national victims.
Sergipe Em Debate (27 Jan 2025) reports ANTRA's dossier for 2024, which recorded 122 trans and travesti killings in Brazil, 16% below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Brazil (Wikipedia) - LGBTQ people in Brazilian prisons
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' states in its Politics section that LGBTQ prisoners have a special place in Brazilian prisons, separate from other prisoners; that transsexuals have the right to be called by their social name rather than their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons; and that LGBTQ prisoners may choose male or female clothing. The passage is footnoted to G1's 17 Apr 2014 report 'Governo publica portaria com direitos para presos gays e travestis', archived 12 Jul 2018, so the legal grounding is a 2014 federal portaria granting rights to gay and travesti prisoners. No instrument more recent than that portaria is cited for these rules.

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia) - Brazil section
sources.summary: Wikipedia overview article (fetched and read in full, 4 Oct 2026). Its Transgender issues > Brazil section contains no trans-prisoner placement rule - only discussion of social vulnerability, stigma and fragmented identity of travestis and transgender people during rehabilitation; international sections show placement norms elsewhere (e.g., Canada placing by gender identity, Italy's admission discretion). Negative evidence: this general overview documents no Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, special unit or segregation-for-placement practice.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Goias (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination based on gender identity was banned in 2019 through a Supreme Federal Court decision. Goiás Decree No. 9,755/2020 establishes guidelines and defines LGBTphobic violence, including discrimination, bullying, and cyberbullying. Since 1 March 2018 under a Supreme Federal Court ruling, a transgender person may change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. Since 3 July 2014 under a Goiás State Board of Education rule, transgender and travesti students may use their social names in schools. A 2015 Novo Gama municipal law prohibits transgender people from using public restrooms in accordance with their gender identity; after challenge by the Associação Nacional de Travestis e Transexuais, Justice Cármen Lúcia set a deadline of 11 June 2024 for the municipal government to explain the law. On 28 August 2023 the Court of Justice of Goiás granted document rectification for non-binary person Mar Dias after registry offices initially denied the Public Defender's Office request made in February 2020. In the case of Kali Julie Dias initiated 29 January 2025, a court in Goianira authorized name change but denied gender marker change citing absence of a specific law for non-binary recognition, but the Court of Justice authorized the gender marker change on 12 December 2025 on appeal by the Public Defender's Office. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1830. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Goiás since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision in compliance with the Supreme Federal Court's 2011 decision. Same-sex adoption has been officially permitted since 2015 through a Supreme Federal Court decision. Discrimination based on sexual orientation was banned in 2019 through a Supreme Federal Court decision. Goiás Decree No. 9,755/2020 establishes guidelines and defines LGBTphobic violence, including discrimination, bullying, and cyberbullying.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court challenge to Novo Gama bathroom law - Justice Cármen Lúcia order
sources.summary: Novo Gama, Goiás enacted a municipal law prohibiting trans people from using bathrooms and STF Minister Cármen Lúcia ordered the city to explain and justify the law under constitutional challenge.

sources.title: Goianira court and Court of Justice of Goiás decisions - Kali Julie Dias case
sources.summary: In Goianira, Goiás, non-binary person Kali Julie Dias won the right to alter the gender marker on official identity documents to reflect non-binary identity.

sources.title: Supreme Court injunction 20 February 2020 and STF plenary vote 25 April - Novo Gama 'gender ideology' teaching ban
sources.summary: On 25 April 2020 the STF plenary unanimously struck down Novo Gama (GO) Law 1.516/2015 that banned gender-diversity content and references to gender ideology in municipal schools and required prior vetting of all teaching materials, holding it usurped the Union's exclusive competence over national education bases and violated gender equality, plural and democratic education, and state secularism, following the May 2017 MPF challenge and a prior suspending injunction by Minister Alexandre de Moraes.

sources.title: Legislative Assembly of Goiás bill - 24 August 2022
sources.summary: On 24 August 2022 the Legislative Assembly of Goiás approved a bill prohibiting 'gender ideology' in schools in Goiás.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling - 1 March 2018 on name and sex change
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Plenary of the Supreme Federal Court held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity/expression as a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize and therefore permitted alteration of name and gender in the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization.

14911670B48776179681147.name: Para
14911670B48776179681147.summary:
Pará stands under Brazil's national framework. Within that framework the state has its own layer of protection and its own documented gaps: since 2007 a constitutional amendment of the State of Pará has prohibited discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds, and the state's own observances and bodies — Law No. 7261 of 21 April 2009 establishing the State Day to Combat Homophobia, Law No. 10570 of 11 June 2024 establishing the State Day of Bisexual Visibility, and Decree No. 3831 of 8 April 2024 creating the State Council for Sexual Diversity within the State Secretariat for Racial Equality and Human Rights — are framed around sexual orientation rather than gender identity. Gender-identity claims in Pará have therefore been pursued through individual litigation and through the national layer rather than through state statute.

State schools are the clearest area of settled trans-specific provision. Portaria No. 016/2008 of the Pará State Secretariat of Education, issued on 10 April 2008, guarantees travesti and transsexual students in the state public school system the right to use their social name in enrolment, class records, attendance lists and other internal school documents.

Documentation has been contested case by case. On 21 June 2025 Ember Alves Oliveira became the first person in Pará to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker, after the registry office in Ananindeua refused rectification. The registry relied on Provision No. 73 of the National Council of Justice, which does not provide for a third gender option, and refused the first-name change without stating any legal justification, prompting a lawsuit by the Public Defender's Office of the State of Pará. The office argued that documentation failing to reflect a person's gender identity is a source of suffering and anguish and a violation of human dignity.

Access to facilities is the sharpest current exposure. On 14 July 2026 Governor Hana Ghassan signed a law authorising religious temples and schools to restrict bathroom use on the basis of biological sex. Before enactment the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended a veto, arguing that the law would violate the rights of transgender people and the principle of secularism, and on 15 July 2026 the Socialism and Liberty Party announced that it had filed a lawsuit against the measure. A trans visitor entering a temple or a school in Pará now faces a state-authorised restriction that national equality provisions do not automatically displace.

Violence remains documented. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier records 5 trans and travesti people killed in Pará in 2025, out of 80 recorded across Brazil that year. The figure is a raw count from a national tally; no per-capita or population denominator is supplied for Pará, so the number indicates documented killings rather than a comparative risk rate against other states.

sources.summary: SBT News (26 Jan 2026) reports ANTRA's 9th annual dossier: 80 trans and travesti people were killed in Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, and Brazil ranks first in world rankings. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. This national dossier supplies this record's 2025 count of 5 of 80.

Sergipe Em Debate (27 Jan 2025) reports ANTRA's dossier recording 122 trans and travesti killings in Brazil in 2024, 16% below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders. The dossier is the source for this record's 2024 comparison year, and Pará's 2024 position cannot be fixed from the audited sources.

14911670B9724590061217.name: Alagoas
14911670B9724590061217.summary:
The state's own statutory protection dates to Constitutional Amendment No. 23, enacted by the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas on 22 March 2001, which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Alagoas moved ahead of the rest of the country on relationship recognition. On 7 December 2011 the Court of Alagoas opened marriage to same-sex couples throughout the state, the first Brazilian state to do so, and couples do not need a judge's approval to obtain a marriage licence. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status, a marriage contracted in Alagoas is therefore available without a judicial step.

On 3 March 2026 the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas enacted a law prohibiting the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades in the state. LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the Supreme Federal Court; no ruling is recorded in the sources.

Violence data for the state come from the annual dossiers of ANTRA. The ninth dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, counted 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil during 2025, of whom 2 were in Alagoas. The 2024 dossier, reported by CNN Brasil on 27 January 2025, counted 122 killings nationally, of whom 6 were in Alagoas. Both are raw counts. The sources give no population denominator for Alagoas and no general homicide rate for the state, so its share cannot be converted into a per-capita comparison and the figures are not a measure of relative risk. The national dossier recorded that victims were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, the region that includes Alagoas.

The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Alagoas accounted for 2 of those 80 killings.

CNN Brasil (27 Jan 2025) reports ANTRA's 2024 dossier. Brazil ranked first in the world for the killing of trans people for a 16th consecutive year, with 122 people killed in 2024, a figure 16% below 2023. The victims were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, and the crimes were marked by extreme violence. Alagoas accounted for 6 of those 122 killings.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alagoas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In March 2018 the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled that transgender people may change their legal gender without undergoing surgery or hormonal therapy, which were previously requirements. A transgender individual seeking to change gender to reflect gender identity can now simply apply to do so at a registry post in the country. No judicial document is required for the change. No medical report is required for the change. Since 2019 discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court. On October 15, 2021 Fênix da Silva Leite became the first non-binary person to change their documents in the state, through a court decision. On December 7, 2011 the Court of Alagoas legalized same-sex marriage throughout the state of Alagoas, being the first Brazilian state to do so. Same-sex couples do not need to have judge's approval to have a marriage license. On March 22, 2001 the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas enacted Constitutional Amendment No. 23 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation. On May 5, 2016 Alagoas enacted a law establishing the Escola Livre program prohibiting "ideological and political indoctrination" in the state's schools. On March 21, 2017 Supreme Court Justice Luís Roberto Barroso suspended that law through a preliminary injunction. On March 3, 2026 the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas enacted a law prohibiting the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades in the state. That law was challenged in the Supreme Federal Court by LGBTQ rights organizations.

14911670B2082355341666.name: Mato Grosso
14911670B2082355341666.summary:
Mato Grosso stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and the 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism under constitutional and federal criminal provisions. The age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. Entry, visa and gender-marker rules operate on the same footing for trans visitors as for anyone else, a position confirmed by an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 covering same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules nationwide.

Detention carries a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where arrested or imprisoned LGBTI people are housed. Recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. The place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Violence against trans and travesti people remains documented at national scale. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, released on 26 January 2026, records 80 murders of trans and travesti people across Brazil in 2025, 34 per cent below 2024, alongside at least 75 attempted homicides marked by excessive violence. Mato Grosso accounted for 3 of those killings in 2025, placing the state 12th among Brazilian states, and has recorded 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017.

Within Mato Grosso, a jury has explicitly recognised the gender dimension of a trans woman's killing. On 16 April 2026, businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison for the feminicide of trans woman Mayla, found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside the MT-485 highway in Sorriso, together with procedural fraud and corpse concealment. The jury held that the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.

sources.summary: ANTRA's 9th annual dossier (released 26 Jan 2026, reported by SBT News): Brazil recorded 80 murders of trans and travesti people in 2025, 34% down on 2024 but with at least 75 attempted homicides and crimes marked by excessive violence; per-state 2025 counts - Ceara and Minas Gerais 8 each, Bahia and Pernambuco 7 each, Goias, Maranhao and Para 5 each, Alagoas 2, Mato Grosso 3; 1,261 murders over 2017-2025 (avg 140/year); 97% of victims travestis/trans women, over half aged 18-29, 70% Black among racially-identified cases; 67.5% of killings happened in interior cities rather than capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policies are harder; Brazil has led the global ranking since 2008. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mato Grosso (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. In 2019 discrimination based on gender identity was banned through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 4 February 2025 Cuiabá Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill to establish biological sex as the sole criterion for athlete participation in city competitions, stating that trans women should compete in men's sports. On 19 August 2025 the Cuiabá City Council passed a law banning trans athletes from competing in women's sports, signed by Mayor Abilio Brunini and published in the Official Gazette on 15 September 2025. The Mato Grosso LGBTQIA+ Pride Parade Association and the state Public Defender's Office filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn the law and obtain 600,000 reais in damages for moral harm, which was dismissed by the Court for Collective Actions on 30 October 2025, with the Association stating it would appeal to the Court of Justice of Mato Grosso. On 1 November 2025 a trans woman was expelled from a pizzeria in Feliz Natal after using the women's restroom, the owner was taken to the police station for gender identity discrimination and released on 2 November following a custody hearing, with the case under investigation by the Civil Police as of 16 September 2026. On 30 July 2025 Professor Maria Inês da Silva left the Municipal Conference of the Unified Health System in Cuiabá after being interrupted by Mayor Abilio Brunini for using gender-neutral language, an action condemned by health organizations, women's rights groups, and Black rights organizations. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830 and homosexuality is legal in Mato Grosso. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Mato Grosso since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision in compliance with a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. Same-sex adoption has been officially permitted in the state since 2015 through a Supreme Federal Court decision. The 1989 Constitution of Mato Grosso Article 10, item III prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and requires implementation of measures to ensure no one will be harmed or privileged on account of birth, race, color, sex, marital status, nature of work, age, religion, sexual orientation, political or philosophical beliefs, physical or mental disability, and any other particularity or condition. On 4 February 2025 Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill to ban participation of minors in Cuiabá's Pride events.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the STF held that equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression and that trans persons may change name and gender on the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization because gender identity is a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize.

sources.title: Civil Police investigation - Feliz Natal pizzeria incident 1 November 2025
sources.summary: On 1 November 2025 in Feliz Natal, Mato Grosso, a 39-year-old trans woman was expelled by a pizzeria owner after using the women's bathroom following complaints from staff and customers; the owner was detained for gender-identity discrimination and released on 2 November 2025 after a custody hearing subject to precautionary measures, with the case under judicial secrecy under investigation by the Civil Police and monitored by the Mato Grosso Public Prosecutor's Office.

sources.title: Court of Justice of Mato Grosso - Sinop 'gender ideology' law struck down
sources.summary: On 10 November 2022 the Mato Grosso Court of Justice granted preliminary relief holding unconstitutional Sinop's March 2022 municipal law prohibiting distribution, exhibition and dissemination of didactic material containing "gender ideology" in the city's public and private schools, on grounds of violation of the Federal Constitution and Mato Grosso Constitution and excess of municipal legislative competence, in an action brought by the Procuradoria-Geral de Justiça against the Sinop City Council with participation of OAB-MT.

sources.title: Court of Justice of Mato Grosso - state 'gender ideology' teaching ban struck down
sources.summary: On 21 August 2026 the Órgão Especial of the Mato Grosso Court of Justice unanimously declared unconstitutional the state law sanctioned in April 2026 that prohibited teaching and dissemination in state public schools of content on so-called "gender ideology," gender identity and sexual orientation, including films, music, paintings and other artistic materials, thereby voiding the ban and restoring schools' pedagogical autonomy to address gender identity and sexual orientation on grounds of formal usurpation of the Union's exclusive competence over education guidelines under Article 22 of the Federal Constitution and violation of academic freedom, pluralism of ideas, and protection against bullying and discrimination.

14911670B84195346134564.name: Distrito Federal
14911670B84195346134564.summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Protection machinery has also widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

Killings remain the sharpest measure of the gap. The ninth annual dossier of the National Association of Travestis and Trans People, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil during 2025, a fall of about 34 per cent year-on-year, and places the country first in world rankings for such killings. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, and were killed with extreme violence. The dossier is national in scope; its table records 2 killings in the Distrito Federal in 2025, out of the national total of 80.

10402087B89016843004490.name: Sachsen
10402087B89016843004490.summary:
Sachsen is a state within Germany and stands under the German national framework: legal gender recognition, identity documents, marriage and equality protections are governed at national level and cannot be disapplied by the state. The findings below are those specific to Sachsen itself.

Sachsen carries an elevated risk rating on the strength of a documented far-right attempt to disrupt Pride in Dresden. On 31 May 2025 thousands marched through Dresden for CSD while neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest aimed at stopping the march; TAG24 reported that the demonstration went ahead despite the disruption attempt. Public visibility as a gender-diverse or LGBTI person at organised events in the state therefore carries a confrontation risk that is not present in the same form in states where Pride passes without organised far-right counter-mobilisation.

Sachsen is also a co-sponsor of an organised multi-state effort to narrow trans self-determination law. Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thuringia jointly launched a Länder initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, framed around preventing misuse of the self-declaration route after the Liebich case. The initiative is a legislative threat directed at residents of these three states: it seeks to add checks to a process that the national law made available by three months' notice, and Sachsen's government is a named sponsor rather than an incidental participant.

Antenne Bayern/dpa: Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thuringia jointly launched a Länder initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) after the Fall Liebich abuse case, aiming to block misuse of self-ID. Sachsen co-sponsors the organised multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law, a documented legislative threat to trans people in Sachsen.

25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
Comunitat Valenciana stands under two layers of law. The national layer is Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights: under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Other operative provisions of the same national statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force across Spain since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. Within the Comunitat Valenciana, the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, sentenced a group over a June 2022 incident in a park in the Patraix district of Valencia, where an 18-year-old and several minors insulted, chased, filmed and mocked a trans woman because of her gender identity; the adult defendant accepted six months' prison, suspended on condition of committing no offence for two years, plus a EUR 720 fine and a EUR 1,000 moral-damages payment to the victim, and two minors were sentenced separately to supervision measures. The case was handled by the hate-crime prosecutor.

The regional layer adds two statutes of its own. Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género, published as BOE-A-2017-5118, makes its purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from the one assigned at birth; it obliges public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana to treat people according to their felt gender identity, and its Title III provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI, published as BOE-A-2019-281, is the community's general equality statute: it covers non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, sets access and admission rights under Article 56, reverses the burden of proof under Article 57, and establishes a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions under Articles 58 to 66 for discrimination against LGTBI people.

With administrative self-declaration at national level, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Other communities in the same inventory carry a single statute, among them Cataluña (Ley 11/2014) and Aragón (Ley 4/2018).

LGTBI federation's 2025 radiography of public educational policies across Spain's autonomous communities, covering gender-identity protocols and education legislation in each, places the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage, and records that the Valencian parliament completed its gender legislation.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passage by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 and by the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains in force in the province.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than repeal. A national DNU of December 2024 added consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care and is under litigation. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors; legal experts called it illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts, with the outcome not recorded in the sources available here.

The provincial Ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, documented in a submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for its June and July 2016 review that provincial police, or third parties acting under police cover, committed violence, persecution and harassment against trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province.

Trans and travesti women in the province face indirect criminalisation through drug-offence and street-offence prosecutions. After Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences in 2005, microtrafficking enforcement in La Plata's Zona Roja became the operative instrument of this practice, even though the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence.

In February 2025 the national government banned housing trans women convicted of sexual crimes, human trafficking, or any violent crime against a woman in women's prisons. This policy is national; Buenos Aires province has no trans-specific placement rule of its own, and no separate trans housing unit is recorded.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina reached a documented high in 2025, with at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity recorded during the year, averaging one every 38 hours. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence for Gabriel Marino's 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
Subcarpathian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, where detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The local-authority hostility of the past decade has formally ended. The county of Łańcut in Subcarpathian Voivodeship repealed its anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session on 27 April 2025, the last such measure in Poland; at the wave's peak about one third of the country's territory was covered by these documents. The voivodeship's own council had already repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on 20 September 2021, so a visitor arriving now encounters no standing regional declaration of that kind, although the resolutions were political statements rather than entry restrictions.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The wider legal environment remains in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms it, and death by stoning is the penalty provided under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001.

On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men to death by stoning for homosexuality, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested at Gwada village, Ningi LGA, on 14 June 2022. Presiding judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi held that they had violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001 and granted a 30-day appeal window. Relatives of the convicted men said the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. Reuters described the sentence as the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria.

The UK Home Office note records that the 2022 Bauchi sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and that a further report placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in Bauchi in May 2024.

Earlier convictions in the state were reversed on appeal. Jubrin Babaji was convicted on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and sentenced to death by stoning; the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed the sentence for denial of counsel and a defective confession. Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction was quashed on 14 November 2003. Amnesty International recorded a number of cases in which convictions and sentences to death were quashed on appeal.

In 2007 Bauchi state police arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Shari'a penal code. The charges were later reduced to vagrancy, and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial; the pre-trial detention dissolved by the end of 2011.

Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held in custody under Shari'a charges for years.

27671186B50148357657004.name: Kano
27671186B50148357657004.summary:
Kano State stands under Nigeria's national framework and operates its own religious penal code, the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, which took effect on 26 November 2000. Consensual same-sex activity under that code draws 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the person is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the person is or has been married.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 covers the twelve northern states operating Sharia codes. Its comparative table lists the Kano Sharia Penal Code (2000) as prescribing death by stoning for married or previously married men, and 100 lashes with imprisonment for up to one year for unmarried men. The note records the codes as remaining in force, and Kano's capital maximum as applying to same-sex acts between women as well as men.

Kano sits in the harshest tier of that northern group for conduct between women: the Home Office table gives Kano and Katsina a maximum penalty of death for 'lesbianism', while the other ten states punish it by flogging and up to six months' imprisonment.

Kano's separate Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men, an offence that bites on clothing and presentation rather than on sexual conduct.

Enforcement against gender-nonconforming presentation is documented within the state. Eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on hisbah premises in Kano state in 2023.

The USCIRF 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation draws on 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara, and records hisbah (religious police) activity in each state, with Kano the most active command. That case count spans three states and is not a Kano-only figure.

27671186B99510750195830.name: Sokoto
27671186B99510750195830.summary:
Sokoto State operates its own penal regime in addition to Nigeria's national framework: the Sharia Penal Code Laws took effect across the state on 31 January 2001. Under that code, male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes otherwise. Sexual acts between women, recorded in the code as wsafa, draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment.

The code is not a dead letter on paper. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa in Sokoto State convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while her co-accused was discharged and acquitted. 27671186B69054806776702.name: Yobe
27671186B69054806776702.summary:
Yobe State stands under Nigeria's national framework and is one of the twelve northern states that adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the twelve states that had done so by 2002, the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law. Sharia was established in Yobe in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim, within the 1999-2002 wave that created the state's parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims; the state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims.

Under the UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on SOGIESC in Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025), the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment (3 years for attempts) and is silent on women. Sharia penal codes in the twelve northern states apply to Muslims, with death the maximum penalty for men in all twelve, and penalties for acts between women ranging from death in a minority of states to flogging and imprisonment. The note's enforcement-and-Hisbah section records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023 and observes that few secular cases reach court.

27671186B21163522287660.name: Zamfara
27671186B21163522287660.summary:
Zamfara State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework and, in addition, under its own Sharia criminal-law layer, which Zamfara itself introduced. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on the extension of Sharia to criminal law records that Zamfara's governor was the first to move, promulgating the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. By 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and those twelve remain the only states in Nigeria where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

The Zamfara State Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice at the time, Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, set out the state's own account of the adoption at a seminar sponsored by the Jama'atu Nasril Islam on 6 July 2000. His account describes the enabling statute, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution, which created Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and made possible the codification of a Sharia Penal Code. Court administration passed to the Grand Kadi on 29 June 2000, alongside policy measures directed at prostitution and gambling.

The adoption process began with a committee appointed by Zamfara's governor in June 1999, mandated to study implementation of Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law. By the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had followed. The codification of offences and punishments produced a penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of all twelve states apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc.

27671186B753479316714.name: Borno
27671186B753479316714.summary:
Borno stands under the national framework of Nigeria, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests on Borno's own legislation as well as that framework. The state's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000) was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act and pimping offences in the state. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender' shall upon conviction be punished with death. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. The death penalty for same-sex intercourse is enacted in Borno's own statute, so the state's criminalisation does not depend on the federal framework for its severity.

Borno is among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, according to Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. Borno enacted a separate Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003. The parallel Shari'a layer in Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

The Shari'a provisions that apply to Muslims in Borno, as one of the twelve northern states, criminalise same-sex sexual acts between men and between women. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria (June 2025) records the maximum penalty for sodomy for men as death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note devotes a section to enforcement of the Shari'a provisions and the posture of the hisbah morality police.

Exposure differs by religion and by court. 27671186B90305463766462.name: Gombe
27671186B90305463766462.summary:
Gombe State operates two overlapping criminal regimes against same-sex conduct. The Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed on 23 November 2001, is Gombe's own enacted statute; Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Gombe among the twelve northern states that had adopted Sharia into criminal legislation by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law.

The penalties under Gombe's statute are severe and gendered. Gombe, Jigawa, Kano and Zamfara share a sodomy offence punishing unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); the lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe defines gross indecency in its own formulation as 'any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour.' The enacted statutory text criminalises same-sex conduct by men and women beyond the federal code.

The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states, including Gombe, and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah (morality police).

Gombe has enforced these provisions in a mass arrest. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State PRO Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, with 17 females present, and that they would be charged in court for 'social vice; a crime in Gombe State.' The Guardian of 23 October 2023 independently confirmed the arrests, with Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirming them and spokesperson Buhari Saad stating that 21 of the 59 detained males were involved in gay activities while the remaining males and 17 females were invited guests and onlookers; officers also voiced concern over the participants' ages.

Jigawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework and its own Sharia Penal Code Law 2000 (Law No. 12 of 2000), signed 18 December 2000 and in operation from 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). Jigawa is one of twelve northern states that had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002, and, with those states, remains among the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) lists Jigawa in a twelve-state Sharia penalties table under a Sharia Penal Code (2000). Married men face death by stoning; unmarried men face 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year; same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes with imprisonment of up to six months. The June 2025 note confirms the Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa.

Jigawa's code sits among four states, with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara, whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajam); lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment. Jigawa's code includes an 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence and criminalises conduct the federal code does not reach, including women's same-sex conduct.

27671186B54051914323789.name: Kaduna

27671186B99661334382691.name: Katsina
27671186B99661334382691.summary:
Katsina State stands under the national framework of Nigeria and additionally operates its own Shari'a criminal layer. Human Rights Watch (2004) records the spread of Shari'a adoption across northern Nigeria, listing twelve states concerned: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. The process traces from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000, and the provisions cited remain in force.

Katsina's own statute is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, which came into operation on 20 June 2001 and was gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23 of 27 August 2001, as annotated in Ostien's volume on Shari'a implementation in northern Nigeria.

The penalty exposure for a trans visitor in Katsina is the most severe tier documented anywhere in Nigeria. Ostien's annotation records Katsina among the three states, with Kaduna and Kebbi, whose sodomy text reads that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm). The same annotation's footnote 183 shows that only Kano and Katsina reach stoning to death as the maximum for the lesbianism offence, against the harmonised code's base of 50 lashes and up to six months. Katsina is therefore one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as between men.

Wikipedia's coverage of LGBTQ rights in Nigeria describes the punishment structure across the Shari'a-governed northern states as ranging from lashing or caning to capital punishment, and records lesbianism, meaning carnal acts or stimulation between women, as punishable by imprisonment or caning in most states with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria, version 4.0 of June 2025, records that Nigeria operates a hybrid legal system in which a Shari'a criminal layer applies in twelve northern states, that this layer's provisions extend to women, and that arrest data for the offences is limited.

27671186B53868438251790.name: Kebbi
27671186B53868438251790.summary:
Kebbi is one of twelve northern Nigerian states that adopted criminal Shari'a in the wave that began with Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law (enacted 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000). By 2002 Kebbi had Shari'a criminal legislation and Shari'a courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, a jurisdiction no other Nigerian state outside this bloc holds.

Kebbi's own statute is the Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21 of 2000), signed and brought into operation on 1 December 2000 and published in Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1 (Supplement, 31 December 2000). Its enacted text provides that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm). Kebbi is one of only three states, with Kaduna and Katsina, whose written law carries that capital wording for men's acts.

The same Kebbi statute criminalises same-sex acts between women with up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The UK Home Office country note of June 2025 carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Shari'a penalties table (section 8.4.3) recording these penalties, confirming that Kebbi's Shari'a layer extends criminalisation to conduct between women and leaves the state's code broader in scope and harsher than the federal SSMPA for Muslim defendants.

Wikipedia's coverage places Kebbi inside the northern Shari'a block where same-sex acts carry penalties ranging up to capital punishment, and notes that death penalties for lesbianism are applied only in Kano and Katsina, placing Kebbi in the lashing-and-imprisonment tier for women's conduct, consistent with Kebbi's own statute. The same coverage records a cross-dressing layer in the north: prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women, with a Kano court imposing one year's imprisonment in 2025 under Kano's provision allowing up to one year or a fine.

The cross-dressing provision is a Kano rule, not a Kebbi one; no equivalent Kebbi cross-dressing statute is documented in these sources. No housing, segregation or placement rule for trans prisoners in Kebbi or elsewhere in Nigeria is recorded in the sources reviewed.

27671186B79778155682183.name: Niger
27671186B79778155682183.summary:
Niger State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and additionally carries its own state-level Sharia criminal layer. Human Rights Watch (2004) lists Niger among the twelve northern states that adopted Sharia criminal provisions, a wave traced from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law of 27 October 1999; these provisions remain in force.

Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, signed 22 February 2000, in operation 4 May 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000, amends the 1960 Penal Code so that certain offences applied to Muslims carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims. It defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68. A Muslim visitor outed in Niger State therefore stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) sets out the hybrid legal system, the twelve-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women, and notes the limits of available arrest data.

Separately, Niger's own national law has hardened sharply. Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted March 2025, criminalises all LGBTQIA+ acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts with 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs, expressly covering changing or attempting to change one's birth sex, and punishing creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues with 10 to 20 years and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties.

Since March 2025, Article 24 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman; since June 2026, marrying a person of the same sex or officiating, organising or witnessing such a wedding carries 10 to 20 years. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. After the 2026 code took effect, dozens were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding.

Enforcement incidents include two young women in Maradi prosecuted in 2022 for lesbianism, acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act; and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025, prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. Two men caught naked in a parked car were arrested for public indecency and fined.

As of December 2022 Niger had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, when Maradi lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise them, with no scheduled debate.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Niger (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalizes all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs (€152,448.94; US$176,604.56). The punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs (€762,244.71; US$882,829). Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity. After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalized in 2026, and before that change the age of consent was 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts. Article 25 of the March 2025 Refoundation Charter criminalizes same-sex sexual relations and LGBTQIA+ acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes same-sex sexual relations with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of one's romantic relationship with a person of the same sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs, with no mitigating circumstances or suspended sentences allowed. Since March 2025 under Article 24 marriage is defined as a union between a man and a woman, and since June 2026 getting married to a person of the same sex and officiating, organizing or bearing official witness to same-sex weddings is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison. There are no broad protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation, but Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs, while Law 2015-36 which had prohibited discrimination including sexual orientation was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged. Enforcement included two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined a small fee, two young women in Maradi in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act, and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. After the 2026 code, dozens were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, LGBTQ people went into hiding, and organizations providing HIV prevention services to MSM stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP. Gay men and lesbians experienced societal discrimination with strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness based on sexual orientation were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organizations operated in secret partly because they were not formally registered. Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition hindering relocation and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. Niger's attitude toward LGBTQ issues is described as usually discreet, even though male prostitution was prevalent in Niamey and effeminate men were known for having always been part of Niger's culture by organizing traditional wedding ceremonies and supporting themselves that way. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The article documents no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the only official cultural-values statement concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values".

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
Imo State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The state's own record shows two distinct exposures for a trans visitor: community vigilantism carried out in the name of anti-gay enforcement, and active police operations against same-sex gatherings as recently as February 2025.

On 26 April 2018, two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets on accusation of gay sex. An inquiry by NoStringsNG found that the victims were themselves arrested by police and may need legal support. The episode documents community violence followed by police processing of those it targeted, so accusation alone can expose a person to both mob action and detention.

Police enforcement in Imo is current, not historical. On 19 February 2025 the Imo Police Command reported foiling a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels, Orogwe, in Owerri West, arresting a number of gay and lesbian suspects and placing attendees who fled on a police search list. Attendance at a social venue therefore carries a documented risk of arrest, and departure from the scene does not close the matter.

27671186B63712480376187.name: Edo
27671186B63712480376187.summary:
Edo State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and the state's own record adds a distinct pattern: lethal mob violence against people accused of same-sex conduct, with no documented law-enforcement protection for the victims.

The Nigerian Observer reported on 10 June 2010 from Benin City, Edo State's capital, that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped a mob after being caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm, Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the mob then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. The report records no police intervention, arrest or prosecution, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing.

In May 2018, in Ekpoma, a mob lynched one of two men caught together; the other escaped. The killing was framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage, and the report documents fatal community violence in Edo State.

Edo's police machinery has also pursued same-sex couples directly. The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote Edo community in February 2008. A mob beat both men; Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and police arrested Jerry for interrogation. A community lynching attempt was answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.

Nationally, The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) recorded 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived SOGIESC across Nigeria during its 2024 reporting period, published January 2025. TIERs provides no Edo-specific breakdown and states the figures represent only a fraction of the true scale.
