65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh operates a provincial sharia criminal code alongside the national criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat has been enforced since 23 October 2015. The code's provisions are applied to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, so a trans traveller's exposure does not depend on religion or residency.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by birth sex. Both offences carry up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than current presentation or documents, a trans visitor whose identity papers, appearance or partner are read as same-sex conduct falls inside the offence.

The provisions were first applied on 23 May 2017, when an Islamic court in Banda Aceh had two men publicly caned with 82 lashes each for gay sex before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque. Two men aged 20 and 23 were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations the same year, and several further cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings followed.

On 11 August 2025 a sharia court sentenced two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing, following an April arrest in which police broke into a toilet. The caning was reported on 26 August 2025. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences.

Enforcement against transgender women in Aceh has taken a different form. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. Accounts of a January 2018 parlour raid in the province describe officers shaving the heads of transgender women, stripping their shirts and bras and parading them in the street while forcing them to shout that they would become men.

Legal scholarship from Aceh's Islamic university analyses a rising number of waria cases in Banda Aceh through the lens of sharia law enforcement, indicating that enforcement against transgender women in the province is an ongoing subject of local legal study rather than an isolated episode.

sources.summary: QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405): 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement' by UIN Ar-Raniry scholars (keywords: Law Enforcement, Waria, Aceh, Islamic Law, Qanun). Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens.

CBS News/AP (26 Aug 2025): two men were publicly caned in conservative Aceh province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences.

iNews Aceh (undated local report, Feb-2025 round-up context): Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah Banda Aceh secured an alleged gay couple in a boarding house; a local advocate urged police to investigate and boarding-house owners to monitor tenants. The report concerns a gay couple, and no trans person is identified in it.

UNSW Human Rights Research Centre reports that transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility. The report covers the January 2018 detention of twelve transwomen. Its scope is Indonesia-wide rather than Aceh-specific.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Aceh (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Cross-dressing is not per se illegal in Indonesia, and transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry a person of the opposite legal gender, exemplified by Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female and by Aprilio Manganang in 2021 as the first service member to legally change gender from female to male although his case was intersex assigned female at birth. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers including Kartu Tanda Penduduk for residents of Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua, recognizing only male and female descriptors with no third gender/X option and printing gender at birth unless court recognition was already obtained, on the stated reasoning that many were undocumented where families did not approve. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive. In Aceh transgender people have faced targeted enforcement: in January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing, and closed their beauty salons, and in a January 2018 parlour raid in Aceh police tortured LGBTQ citizens, shaved the heads of transgender women, stripped their shirts and bras, and paraded them in the street forcing them to shout "to become men". In Jakarta the Social Agency declared waria to be socially dysfunctional and regularly conducts raids against transgender women, taking detained individuals to city-owned rehabilitation centres where they are incarcerated with homeless people, beggars and street buskers and only released upon documentation of lack of homelessness and a signed promise not to repeat the offence, with officials stating this is to create a deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously they must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, while the judicial system takes the contrary position recognizing actual genders and authorities have in some cases arrested and prosecuted perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community. Aceh has special autonomous status implementing Islamic Sharia-based criminal law (Qanun Jinayat), with authority granted in 2005 to introduce Sharia law for Muslim residents and the 2014 Qanun Jinayat providing that consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are punishable by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, set for enforcement by the end of 2015. Enforcement outcomes in Aceh include the 2017 sentencing of two young gay men aged 20 and 23 to public caning, several high-profile cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings for same-sex relations, and the 11 August 2025 sentencing of two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing after April arrest when police broke into a toilet. Nationally Indonesia has allowed private consensual same-sex activity since 1993 at age 18, has no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and the Penal Code does not prohibit non-commercial private consensual activity between consenting same-sex adults. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year imprisonment for unmarried partners, with the spokesperson stating the draft will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD stating it did not criminalize an LGBTQ person and only targets adults committing sexual violence or rape of underage same-sex children and immoral acts in public, while Article 421(1) punishes obscene acts against a same-sex person in public with maximum 1 year and six months imprisonment or maximum fine category III. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, households headed by same-sex couples lack the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples are ineligible to adopt as only married husband-wife couples can adopt. As of 2019 no specific law protects from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity nor prohibits hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, though a 2015 police circular states processing of hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity and Head of National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation. Police have conducted repeated raids and detentions for gay parties and saunas under pornography-related offences, including the November 2016 Jakarta raid after an Islamic Defenders Front tip-off, May 2017 arrest of 141 men for a gay sex party with ten charged and detention of 144 in the Atlantis Gym raid, October 2017 arrest of 51 in a Central Jakarta sauna with six charged including the owner, and 2025 raids detaining 56 on 1 February, nine on 24 May, and arresting 75 on 22 June near Jakarta. The article states: "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." The article states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama." The article states transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. The article states discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon, though violence is quite rare, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often face employment exclusion forcing reliance on prostitution and other illegal activities. The article reports officials justify rehabilitation detention as creating a deterrent against being transgender and cites the Ulama Council position that those unwilling to cure themselves medically and religiously must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, evidencing institutional rejection despite noted cultural presence.

65028918B88589358118692.name: Lampung
65028918B88589358118692.summary:
Lampung province stands under Indonesia's national framework. The province's own record of official conduct toward transgender people includes a November 2018 operation in which the Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three trans women, detained them at its Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the incident.

OutRight International's study of discriminatory regional regulations names Lampung among eight Indonesian provinces where such rules operate, examined at both province and district level. A trans visitor in Lampung is therefore subject to two layers of provincial regulation in addition to the national framework.

sources.summary: UNSW human-rights review of anti-trans violence in Indonesia: documents that in November 2018 three transwomen were raided by Satpol PP (the regional morals-and-order force) in Lampung province — detained at the Satpol PP office and hosed down at the firefighter building, with an officer recording it — alongside a national pattern of transwomen murdered in 2017 (Bone, Semarang, South Sulawesi) and election-cycle anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying from 2016 onward; an SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians (Nov 2016) found LGBT people hated by 16.6%.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study analyses discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta — at both province and district level. Lampung is named among them.

65028918B84835514626455.name: West Papua
65028918B84835514626455.summary:
West Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, add their own criminalisation, but West Papua is not among them.

The dominant risk in this province is the conduct of the security forces rather than any trans-specific provision. A report of 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network records 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands areas of West Papua, covering the period through early 2025. Most victims were male and under 24; seven were female, seven were minors aged 15 to 17. The report's finding is near-total impunity, summarised as impunity, secrecy and silence. Any visitor held or questioned by officers in the province faces an accountability environment in which abuse is unlikely to be answered for.

Military activity in the province has intensified. The Papua human-rights monitor's quarterly report for the third quarter of 2025 records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. Police in Sorong arrested more than a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans.

No trans-specific finding is recorded for West Papua in these sources. The general security-force pattern nonetheless amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor, since stops, document checks and detention in the province are handled by units already documented committing ill-treatment with impunity.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in West Papua (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Cross-dressing is not, per se, illegal in Indonesia, and transgender people are allowed to change legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry people of the opposite legal gender. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if they are "not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously" they must be willing "to accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed." The judicial system takes the contrary position, with Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female, and there have been cases where perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community were arrested and prosecuted. Targeted enforcement includes January 2018 North Aceh police arrest of twelve transgender women with forcibly cut hair, compelled men's clothing and closed beauty salons, and Jakarta Social Agency declaration of waria as socially dysfunctional with regular raids and incarceration in city-owned "rehabilitation" centres with homeless people, beggars and buskers until documentation and signed pledge, with officials stating this creates deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with Kartu Tanda Penduduk including residents of Papua, but recognizes only "male" and "female" with no third gender/X designator and prints gender at birth unless court recognition obtained, citing undocumentation where families disapprove blocking work or social services. Transgender people who do not hide gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive, with discrimination and harassments not uncommon though violence quite rare. In the military, Aprilio Manganang in 2021 became the first service member to legally change gender from female to male, although his case was intersex assigned female at birth and raised as a girl. Private, non-commercial consensual sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex has been allowed nationally since 1993 at 18 years of age, with no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and a 2003 national bill to criminalize same-sex activity with cohabitation, adultery and witchcraft failed with no subsequent reintroduction. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year in prison for unmarried partners, while the draft spokesperson stated it will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD said it only targets adults who commit "sexual violence" or rape of underage same-sex children and public immoral acts, though same-sex marriage is not legally recognized effectively placing all same-sex sexual activity outside legal recognition. Aceh, allowed special autonomous Sharia law under 2014 Qanun Jinayat, punishes consensual adult same-sex acts by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, with public caning imposed including two young gay men aged 20 and 23 in 2017 and two men aged 20 and 21 sentenced 11 August 2025 for kissing after April arrest when police broke into toilet. Police have repeatedly raided private "gay parties" and gay saunas under national pornography law in the 2010s-2020s, including November 2016 Jakarta raid, May 2017 arrest of 141 men with ten charged and detention of 144 at Atlantis Gym Jakarta, October 2017 arrest of 51 with six charged, February/May/June 2025 South Jakarta hotel/villa raids detaining 56, nine and 75, August 2025 arrest of three for creating LGBTQ Facebook page facing up to 12 years and 6 billion rupiah fines, and 22 May 2026 sentencing of 25 to prison for violating anti-pornography law. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships or adoption by same-sex couples, limiting adoption to husband-wife married couples, and as of 2019 provides no specific anti-discrimination protection nor hate-crime prohibition based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Limited protection machinery cited is a 2015 police circular to process hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity, Regulation of Head of National Police No. 8 of 2009 duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation, and theoretical constitutional and Human Rights Law No. 39/1999 guarantee against employment discrimination on any ground. The article states "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." It further states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama," noting transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. For trans visitors, the article reports discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon though violence is quite rare, but those not hiding gender identity often cannot maintain legitimate employment and are forced into prostitution and other illegal activities, while gays in jails are often sexually abused due to orientation and do not report due to trauma and fear of return. Documented violence includes the January 2018 Aceh parlour ransacking where police tortured all LGBTQ citizens, shaved transgender women's heads, stripped shirts and bras and paraded them forcing them to shout "to become men," criticised by human rights organisations. Care context notes the 2012 Health Ministry estimate of around 31 thousand transgender women and Yayasan Srikandi Sejati founded 1998 focusing on transgender health providing HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, amid lack of school sex education and early movement focus leading public to believe AIDS was a "gay disease." Control environment includes the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction prohibiting presentations suggesting same-sex relations punishable by fine or up to seven years, March 2016 broadcasting commission policy banning programs making LGBTQ behaviour appear "normal" discouraging effeminate, transgender or cross-dressing figures, bans on sites/apps with "gay" or LGBTQ terms including Grindr, and widely practiced openly advertised conversion therapy including rehabilitation centre treatment with de facto legalization by some city governments after the "RUU Ketahanan Keluarga" Family Resilience draft was rejected by 5 of 9 factions.

65028918B28198720309323.name: Central Kalimantan
65028918B28198720309323.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and Central Kalimantan stands under that national framework. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Central Kalimantan has no equivalent provincial criminalisation.

Physical risk is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue; on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor and arrested 75 people, and Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

65028918B37605681672150.name: North Sumatra
65028918B37605681672150.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and North Sumatra stands under that national framework. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

North Sumatra is one of eight focus provinces examined in OutRight Action International's mapping of national laws and discriminatory regional regulations affecting women and LGBTIQ people, alongside Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. The study finds substantial overlap across the country but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its conclusions hold for provinces outside the focus set. A visitor to North Sumatra therefore faces both the national morality provisions and locally varying administrative restrictions on presentation and movement.

The only documented legal-recognition case for North Sumatra is favourable in outcome. Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan, became the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally to match his identity; after a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application. The judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but otherwise stayed out of LGBTI issues entirely, and the court process produced no enforcement action against him or his partner. Reporting frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and records that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case was filed.

It finds much overlap but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

North Sulawesi stands under the national framework applicable across Indonesia. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with reporting indicating that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, and in Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; North Sulawesi is not among the provinces with that regime.

Provincial divergence for a visitor in North Sulawesi is not documented. OutRight Action International's 2022 study of national laws and regional regulations examined eight focus provinces, Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta, finding significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear; North Sulawesi is not among the eight, and the Sulawesi entry in that set is South Sulawesi, a different province. No sourced record of an enforcement incident, raid, arrest, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people in North Sulawesi was located. The visitor-facing risk profile therefore follows the national picture: the new KUHP in force since January 2026, with police extortion and arbitrary detention the main documented mechanism of pressure. 65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is hostile to transgender visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Yogyakarta is not among the two provinces where provincial criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity is recorded under regional religious law, so the provincial Sharia penalties imposed in Aceh and South Sumatra do not extend to this special region.

OutRight Action International's mapping of Indonesian national laws and discriminatory regional regulations (Katjasungkana and Wieringa, 2022 file copy) examined regional regulations across eight focus provinces, Yogyakarta among them, and found substantial overlap alongside significant regional variation in the content of those regulations, including dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The study states that its findings hold for regions beyond the focus set, so a visitor should expect some form of locally enacted restriction on trans visibility here even where no provincial anti-trans statute exists.

The clearest enforcement-adjacent event on record in Yogyakarta concerned a trans institution rather than a visitor. On the night of 24 February 2016 the Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women (waria) study Islam, was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal it. BBC reporting described rising hate speech against LGBT people, especially in Yogyakarta. The Banguntapan district head, Jati Bayubroto, justified the closure on the grounds that the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; the founder, Shinta Ratri, said about 20 waria attended the weekly weekend classes, which taught ordinary Islamic instruction.

The closure meeting itself ran about two hours at the Jagalan ward office from around 20:00 on 24 February 2016, attended by ward and residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander, and, in an earlier session on 19 February, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief. A waria witness said a Front Jihad Islam leader delivered fiery anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds, with no provincial anti-trans statute cited. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, described LGBT people as 'fellow children of the nation' and said the regional government would study the issue.

The Al-Fatah pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community are operating again years after the 2016 closure. Reporting from June 2021 recorded an aromatherapy-candle making class held at the pesantren on 12 June 2021 with the local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and noted that waria continued performing even when donors refused even masked performances. Economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.

65028918B6070530336190.tangentialFactors:
Indonesia's physical risk picture is worsening nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Compared with Aceh, where two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025 under provincial religious law applying to anyone present including foreign visitors, Yogyakarta carries no recorded provincial sexual-conduct penalty. The difference is one of legal layer, not of safety: the national code, the national expression offences and the vigilante environment apply here as everywhere in Indonesia.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the constitutional equality guarantees, the Equality Court under PEPUDA, legal gender recognition and the national hate-crime statute apply here as they do across the country.

A 2024 criminology thesis from the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban reports significant victimisation of self-identifying queer people in KwaMashu Township. Based on in-depth interviews with 15 participants recruited through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, the study documents queerphobic violence in township settings, assesses how adequate support and interventions are, and records the safety strategies residents adopt for themselves.

The province's top traditional authority has an openly hostile record toward gay people. Remarks made by Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini at a harvest festival in January 2012 prompted demands for an apology; police opened an investigation, and both the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighed in on the royal family's account. Traditional leadership, not only the state, shapes the local climate around gender and sexuality.

sources.title: Transgender prisoners challenge prison authorities (GroundUp)
sources.summary: GroundUp news feature (6 Aug 2025, Elna Schutz) documenting where transgender prisoners are held in South Africa: Jade September, a transgender woman, was imprisoned in the male section of Pollsmoor and won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which ruled that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. Reports that the resulting Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure (SOP) for LGBT+ prisoners requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. Also notes Lawyers for Human Rights representation of 'NM', a transgender woman serving a long-term sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, in litigation against DCS over gender-affirming healthcare, and rights organisations' concern about implementation of the SOP.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre - Lawyers for Human Rights
sources.summary: Lawyers for Human Rights case page (14 Nov 2025): the South African High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), finding unfair discrimination and harassment because DCS refused to allow her to express her gender identity (feminizing attire, she/her pronouns) and failed to provide appropriate accommodation. The court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, rejected DCS's contrary argument, and ordered DCS to immediately implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs relating to transgender inmates, and provide the prescribed medical care. Subject-verified: documents that trans inmates are accommodated inside the standard national corrections system (here Johannesburg Correctional Centre) and that placement/accommodation obligations rest on DCS SOPs enforced through litigation.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities (SAHRC)
sources.summary: South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT (designated 4 Dec 2024), media statement (14 Nov 2025) welcoming the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, judgment (delivered 10 Nov 2025) in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). Describes Mokoena, assigned male at birth and identifying as female from early childhood, being restricted from wearing feminine clothing and makeup and misgendered while in a correctional facility. Subject-verified: an official state human-rights body confirming that transgender persons are held in the ordinary correctional system and that the 2025 ruling affirms their rights in correctional facilities, including accommodation.

76434192B51294388644125.name: Nothern Cape
76434192B51294388644125.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. The Northern Cape province stands under that national framework, and no provincial statute narrowing it is documented.

The province recorded at least three LGBTIQ+ community members killed during 2024. On 14 May 2024 in Paballelo, Upington, Jo-Ann Isaks, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was found dead in her burning room with multiple stab wounds to the upper body; a family member noticed the flames at about 23:00. On 1 June 2024 in Kimberley, Karabelo Pudumo, an 18-year-old transgender Grade 10 learner at Pescodia High School, was stabbed more than 20 times, allegedly by a man she had been drinking with after he realised she was transgender. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. 76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga
76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the Constitution of 1996 and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act of 2000 prohibit unfair discrimination on grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation through the Equality Court, consensual conduct carries no offence based on gender identity or sexual orientation, legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, and the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 names gender identity and sexual orientation as protected grounds.

Traditional leadership structures in the province have publicly opposed these protections. In June 2010, after meeting at Hazyview, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its Provincial Houses issued a letter stating they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, describing the practice as immoral, warning of ostracism and violence, and vowing a five-year campaign against it. In 2016 the National House of Traditional Leaders asked Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. These positions do not change the law but signal hostility from locally influential institutions.

Deadly anti-LGBTIQ violence has occurred inside Mpumalanga. Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, half naked with stab wounds. On 2 January 2020 about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others; the local mayor called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence.

Public LGBTIQ+ visibility is also documented. Mpumalanga's first Pride march was held on 9 August 2014 in Nelspruit (Mbombela) with around 1,000 participants, police supplying about 20 officers in a visible and supportive role, and the event launching the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement as an umbrella group for the province's LGBTI organisations.

Police treatment of LGBTIQ+ people in the province remains contested. At a Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August 2026, community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about alleged discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations, saying they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance. One participant alleged that after a sexual assault in eMbalenhle, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she 'didn't fight back'; attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation. A visitor needing police assistance in Mpumalanga should expect uneven reception.

76434192B37104984973577.name: Limpopo
76434192B37104984973577.summary:
Limpopo stands under the national framework of the Republic of South Africa: the Constitution's guarantees against unfair discrimination on grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, the Equality Court machinery under PEPUDA, decriminalisation of consensual conduct, the Civil Union Act, and the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 all apply in the province.

The province's distinctive exposure arises from its former-Bantustan rural districts, where customary jurisdiction operates alongside the ordinary courts. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustan areas, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction for those subject to it.

HRW further reported that rural LGBT people in these areas already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. Mamba Online, writing on 18 April 2012, reported that the Traditional Courts Bill, then under provincial public hearings, would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system, with lesbians punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices and no opt-out available; those who could do so were expected to leave rural areas. Traditional leaders were also reported as opposed to the 2006 Civil Union Act.

A trans visitor to Limpopo's rural former-Bantustan districts should therefore expect a materially different practical environment from the urban national picture: local customary forums may apply hostile norms, police cooperation is documented as poor, and the ordinary equality and hate-crime protections may be difficult to access in practice.

76434192B85643022077130.name: North West
76434192B85643022077130.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge brought against the Department of Correctional Services with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Within North West province, the principal sub-national legal divergence is the reach of traditional and customary courts. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the former-Bantustan geography, which includes North West, as standing under a separate legal system; HRW's earlier reporting on the Traditional Courts Bill (29 May 2012) described a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction, and recorded that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, with chiefs' courts punishing lesbians in rural areas. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended, and the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law, and no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

Healthcare access is the sharpest practical constraint on the ground. The trans community in North West cannot access hormone replacement therapy at any public health facility in the province; the North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people in response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the South African Human Rights Commission, and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to obtain it. A visitor dependent on prescribed HRT should expect no provincial public provider and should carry a sufficient supply.

Hate-crime evidence for the province is thin but exists. The Love Not Hate campaign research conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being (2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. North West is therefore one of only three provinces ever to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and this national campaign study, which measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

76434192B98113213215773.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006, legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. The Eastern Cape has no separate provincial trans statute, ban or enforcement regime; visitors to the province are covered by these national instruments.

Detention in the province runs under a placement rule fixed nationally rather than locally. In Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), delivered by the Gauteng High Court sitting as an Equality Court on 14 November 2025, the Department of Correctional Services conceded that the regulations to the Correctional Services Act on vulnerable inmates and its own Standard Operating Procedures require inmates to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where feasible and safe, and that those Standard Operating Procedures prescribe single-cell accommodation for transgender inmates. The court ordered single-cell placement or placement with inmates of the same gender identity. That is the operative rule for transgender prisoners in Eastern Cape correctional centres, including St Albans, Mthatha and East London; no province-specific trans placement case is on record. The same judgment held that refusing prescribed gender-affirming health care and refusing feminising clothing and accessories are unlawful, with hormone treatment to be provided at state expense. Reporting in August 2025 recorded rights organisations' doubt that the Department's standard operating procedure is implemented in practice, so detention remains an elevated-risk setting.

Legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that excludes non-binary people through its binary sex classification; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force, and the cost of affirming one's gender through the process is described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people in the province face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care in the Eastern Cape is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year, a concrete service bottleneck for a visitor needing continuity of hormone therapy or other prescribed care.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month nationally, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships, a pattern that holds in the Eastern Cape's township and rural areas. Within the province, Eastern Cape police arrested four suspects over the killings of two women in Gqeberha on 2 May 2025, in a case that drew public outrage and renewed calls to confront rising gender-based violence.

A further exposure is jurisdictional rather than statutory. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction; it reported that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. For a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor outside the metro civil-society belt, the practical forum is therefore as likely to be a chief's court as a magistrate's court.

76434192B98113213215773.tangentialFactors:
The Eastern Cape's exposure profile is set less by provincial law than by the interaction of national protection machinery with rural customary jurisdiction and a thin service base. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable at malls, hotels, gyms and workplaces throughout the province.

Gender-based violence provides the ambient crime backdrop. The Gqeberha arrests of four suspects over two women's killings in May 2025 illustrate a provincial pattern of lethal violence against women that is not trans-specific but shapes the risk environment for any visibly gender-nonconforming traveller, particularly after dark and in informal settings such as taverns. The December 2024 assault on Aobakwe Mahlobo in Tshwane is the clearest documented trans-specific hate crime in the recent record and establishes that targeted violence against trans women continues in social venues, with arrest following in that instance.

Comparison with the rest of the country is unhelpful in one respect and instructive in another: the binding remedies created by the Mokoena judgment bind the Department of Correctional Services nationwide, so trans prisoners in Eastern Cape centres hold the same orders as those in Gauteng, but the province has no litigation of its own pressing implementation, which may slow uptake.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng stands under the national framework of South Africa. The province's own contribution to the evidence base is substantial: the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa, 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors', was conducted in 2003/04 by OUT LGBT Well-being with the University of South Africa Centre for Applied Psychology (Wells and Polders) under the Joint Working Group research initiative, with partner organisations including Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, the Gay and Lesbian Archive and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

The Love Not Hate campaign research of 2016, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being and hosted by the Gay and Lesbian Archive, records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have ever been done in South Africa: the 2003 study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. Gauteng therefore carries one of the country's few provincial-level hate-crime measurements, though the data is now two decades old.

On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman from Soshanguve living in Winterveld, was attacked at a tavern in Tshwane at about 1:30 am. A man stated that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live', smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, and said 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', cutting her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead; the wounds were stitched at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, and as of 6 January 2025 MambaOnline reported the case had shown no progress. This is the province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court in Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). The court found that the Department of Correctional Services committed unfair discrimination and harassment against a transgender inmate by refusing to let her express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, and ordered the Department to implement the required accommodations and to enforce its own standard operating procedures. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. The judgment demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

The same judgment is the only documented determination of where trans prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: initially housed in the Medium A section where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing; later transferred to Medium C; and at the time of the judgment housed in C Single Section, a segregated or solitary-confinement unit of Medium C. Despite requesting a single cell she was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates, first two cisgender gay men and then one cisgender male, which the Department justified by overcrowding. The court found that the Department's standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, and ordered the Department to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate standard operating procedures.

76434192B56312278962278.name: Western Cape
76434192B56312278962278.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

The Western Cape stands under that national framework. Nothing in the sourced material identifies a provincial statute, prohibition, enforcement action or official directive restricting trans people in the province, and no provincial rule conditions bathroom or changing-room use on sex assigned at birth or on legal gender status.

What the province supplies is an enforcement-and-response gap. On 19 February 2025 Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River in Cape Town, was threatened with removal from Green Point Athletic Stadium after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her "Look at you, you're a man", ordered her to use the men's bathroom and asserted that he had the final say. 19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: France's rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors.

Paris and its suburbs carry a disproportionate share of France's recorded anti-LGBT+ offending. The Interior Ministry's statistics service recorded 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences nationwide in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délicts rising 14% per year since 2016; only about 4% of victims file complaints. Acts concentrate in urban units above 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris, whose recorded rate of 22 per 100,000 residents stands against a national rate of 7. The ministry note attributes part of that gap to non-resident victims and commuters, and records that more than 70% of recorded victims are men.

Large LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now draw far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response. Paris Pride on 28 June 2025 was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry, with CRS police reinforcements deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march; police were framed as separating the opposing groups.

Paris holds France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure. As of 2004 the city counted 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, hosts France's only officially organised gaybourneys, and stages the annual Paris Pride parade. The city also carries a documented targeted-violence history: Bertrand Delanoë, France's first openly gay mayor of Paris, elected in 2002, was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals.

19338628B95725112529620.name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
19338628B95725112529620.summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur stands under this national framework, and the region's own record adds one episode of appearance policing on public beaches. On 1 August 2023 the mayor of Fréjus issued an order prohibiting swimming while wearing 'covering and baggy clothing' on the commune's sea beaches, in force until 17 September 2023 and carrying a €135 fine.

The administrative tribunal of Toulon suspended that order on 5 August 2023, in freedom-of-relief order n° 2302537 brought by the Ligue des droits de l'homme, finding a grave and manifestly unlawful attack on fundamental freedoms: manifestation of religious conviction, freedom of movement, and freedom of dress in public space. It condemned the commune to pay €3,000.

Toulon's order followed the Conseil d'État's ruling of 17 July 2023 on an identical arrêté at Mandelieu-la-Napoule, where the Ligue des droits de l'homme had already contested the ban; observers noted that the Fréjus communiqué justified the prohibition on laïcité grounds while safety was cited publicly, framing religiously marked swimwear as the target. The order no longer operates, so the residual visitor-facing effect on this region's beaches is a signal that visible non-conformity in public dress can attract mayoral prohibition until a court stops it.

28173009B98838729156012.name: Chechnya
28173009B98838729156012.summary:
Chechnya is a republic of Russia and stands under the Russian national framework, but the practical exposure a visitor faces here is materially harsher than the national baseline. Human Rights Watch documented a February 2017 police purge in which men believed to be gay were rounded up, held in unofficial facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared and others were returned to their families barely alive, with captors outing them and urging honour killings. The same report establishes that top regional officials knew of the operation despite Ramzan Kadyrov's denial.

The purge was not a single event. Novaya Gazeta reported on 11 January 2019 that persecution of gay men had reactivated, with warnings circulated through VKontakte LGBT-group administrators telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov's press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. The paper's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men produced no criminal case. A renewed purge beginning December 2018 detained around 40 people including gay men and women, with two killed, and by May 2019 police had resumed unlawful detentions, beatings and humiliation of men presumed gay or bisexual.

The scale of the 2017 operation was large: authorities detained more than 100 men across Grozny and other settlements for actual or suspected non-traditional sexual orientation, holding them in a secret prison in Argun and multiple detention centres where they were beaten and tortured with electric shocks. At least three detainees were killed and further killings were alleged; some reports put the death toll as high as 20. Those released fled the republic, and users abandoned LGBT messenger groups and closed social-media accounts, because non-traditional orientation carries lethal honour-based retaliation risk under close social monitoring.

Detention in Chechnya has since become a route to the battlefield in Ukraine. The Insider reported on 4 September 2024 that the SK SOS crisis group documented Chechen security forces coercing detained gay men into military service, with at least seven sent to the frontlines and one already killed; the methods began before the 21 September 2022 mobilisation order. In early September 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they would be sent to the front.

The conscription machinery operates as a generalised coercive tool beyond the gay-specific cases. A Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation recorded a mass wave of unlawful detentions in which people were held over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, and forced to sign contracts; families have had to recruit two 'volunteers' to free a detained relative.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 involving abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. It assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note also records the 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, which exposes support or activity to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising to 6 to 10 years, with violence spreading beyond the region.

There is no safe complaint or judicial recourse for an LGBT person in Chechnya: retaliation is treated as practically inevitable, and authorities are alleged to encourage families to kill those suspected of homosexuality. De facto there are no protections for LGBT citizens despite Russia's laws formally applying. The republic's current imposition of Islamic law contradicts Russian federal law and the Chechen constitution's own provision that Chechnya is secular and no religion may be made official or mandatory; in 1999 Chechen president Aslan Maskhadov introduced sharia law under which sharia courts imposed the death penalty for homosexuality and adultery.

European Union sanctions were imposed in March 2021 on two Chechen government officials for government-sponsored violence against LGBTQIA+ individuals. The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims, and the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Dagestan (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, and transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. In April-May 2023 proposals sought to rule out the possibility of changing a person's gender purely by changing the documents and to ban gender reassignment without surgery, with the Duma Speaker claiming 2,700 such document changes had been made in recent times amid claims men sought changes to avoid conscription for the special operation. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living in a foreign country may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provides that people who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences can only be drafted during war times, while officials stated different sexual orientation should not be considered a deviation and non-standard orientation does not forbid service but should not be revealed to avoid beating. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated teaching children that instead of men and women there are supposedly some other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 removal of Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed and July 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage with no legal recognition offered. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 including 365 fatalities and annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar and club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings. Between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist with founders convicted for leading an extremist organisation, including Centre T, Coming Out, LGBT Resource Centre, Irida, Kallisto movement, Moscow Community Center for LGBT+ Initiatives, Parni Plus, Russian LGBT Network, and T9 NSK. In Chechnya since February 2017 authorities conducted forced disappearances including secret abductions, imprisonment and torture targeting persons based on perceived sexual orientation with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead in extrajudicial killing, followed by a December 2018 purge with around 40 detained and two killed, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report as ignored by authorities and leading to EU economic sanctions in March 2021 on two officials. In 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by systemically refusing permits for pride parades, and in August 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld blocking Moscow Pride permits yearly through 2012 citing possibility of public disorder.
