sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Ingushetia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations and persons, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, addition of activist Karèn Shainyan to the terrorist and extremist list with a 5-year prison sentence in absentia, and March-May 2026 court outlawing of nine LGBTQ organisations including Centre T with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 re-legalisation removing Article 121, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment and a maximum five years under the 1961 revision, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and in the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia case the European Court of Human Rights ruled failure to offer any legal recognition violated rights, though Russia left the court in 2022. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, does not officially record hate crimes against the community, and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation. Adoption is allowed for single persons regardless of sexual orientation but for couples jointly only if a married heterosexual couple, and foreign single adopters are barred if their country recognises same-sex marriage. Authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations and to authorize pride parades, with a 2010 European Court of Human Rights fine for discrimination over pride bans and an August 2012 Moscow City Court ruling upholding a yearly ban through 2012 citing public disorder, while pro-LGBTQ groups have been declared extremist and prohibited. Documented violence includes an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010-2020 with 365 fatalities, tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with premeditated group hunts via dating apps, and Chechnya purges involving forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment and torture with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three extrajudicial killings from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed in the December 2018-January 2019 purge, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two Chechen officials.

Karachay-Cherkessia stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition has been prohibited outright since the law signed in July 2023 banning gender-affirming surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents. A visitor presenting documents whose marker does not match their presentation has no lawful route to resolve the discrepancy inside the republic.

The republic sits within the North Caucasus, which the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) singles out as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. Trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the North Caucasus, Karachay-Cherkessia included, are assessed as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented across 2017 to 2024. Under the national extremist-designation regime the note records sentences of two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He reports year-on-year deterioration, covering the North Caucasus republics including Karachay-Cherkessia.

The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of material that makes minors interested in gender transition and applies to all age groups. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transition, and single-person foreign adoption is permitted only if that country recognises neither same-sex marriage nor gender transition.

Russian law provides no anti-discrimination protections on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity and no hate-crime designation on those grounds. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent has stood at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but same-sex couples are ineligible for protections available to opposite-sex couples, with neither marriage nor civil unions permitted.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 European LGBTI legal and policy ranking scores Russia at 2%, citing explicit bans and legal limitations that make legal gender recognition practically impossible.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Karachay-Cherkessia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Russian law prohibits transgender people from changing their legal gender and bans gender-affirming care. The ban was enacted in July 2023 and prohibits both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents without surgery. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transition and applies to all age groups. A 2024 adoption law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transition, and single-person foreign adoption is permitted only if that country recognises neither same-sex marriage nor gender transition. Military-related discussion in 2023 linked legal gender change to draft avoidance, with proposals aimed at preventing trans women from changing legal status from male to female without surgery and the Duma Speaker claiming about 2,700 such decisions had been made. President Putin stated on 30 September 2022 that teaching children about other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, following 1993 re-legalisation that removed Article 121 of the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with up to five years imprisonment under the 1961 code and three to five years under Article 154-a added in March 1934. The age of consent has stood at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Russian law provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and same-sex couples are ineligible for protections available to opposite-sex couples, with neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions allowed and a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage. A 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added to the unified terrorist and extremist list on 22 March 2024, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement since the ruling has included arrests of gay bar owners, fines or imprisonment for displaying the rainbow flag, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Documented enforcement and violence linked to sexual orientation includes the reported detention and torture of over 100 men since February 2017 in Chechnya with at least three extrajudicial killings reported 1 April 2017, a further purge reported in January 2019 with around 40 detained and two killed, and an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities.

28173009B7235812138525.name: North Ossetia–Alania
28173009B7235812138525.summary:
North Ossetia–Alania stands under the legal framework of the Russian Federation, and that framework carries the heaviest anti-trans penalties in Europe. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition on official documents; the federal 'propaganda' statute of 2013 was expanded in December 2022 to apply to people of all ages and to material that makes minors interested in gender transition; and in November 2023 the Russian Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' an extremist organisation, which makes participation in LGBT activism a criminal offence. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with explicit warnings addressed to LGBT travellers.

The North Caucasus region, including this republic, is treated as a distinct and more dangerous category in the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025). The note singles the region out as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It records systematic regional campaigns against LGBT people running from 2017 to 2024, and notes that the 2023 extremist designation carries two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, an on-the-ground defender speaking in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he describes year-on-year deterioration. His account covers the region including North Ossetia–Alania.

The federal laws apply to this republic without modification, which means visible LGBT activity a visitor brings into North Ossetia–Alania sits entirely outside federal legal protection. New laws effective 1 July 2023 further reclassify homosexuality as a mental illness. Enforcement nationally has escalated in both volume and severity: Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, and within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, searching and photographing about 100 patrons at one venue.

28173009B89423349656391.name: Stavropol Krai
28173009B89423349656391.summary:
Stavropol Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023. The expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition, and the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation. Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation. The US State Department carries a Level 4, Do Not Travel advisory for Russia with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and Global Affairs Canada advises avoiding all travel to the country.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. Within this zone, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are assessed as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns recorded across 2017 to 2024. Charges following the 2023 extremist designation carry two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

Movement into the neighbouring North Caucasus entities is restricted for visitors: Global Affairs Canada reports that Ministry of Interior special permission is required to enter Kabardino-Balkaria, including the Elbrus area, Karachai-Cherkessia and North Ossetia. The same advisory records that 2SLGBTQI+ persons and the families of their allies have been attacked, harassed and abused, that advocacy organisations have been treated as extremist since January 2024, and that foreign visitors are subject to surveillance.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, speaking to the Human Rights House Foundation as a North Caucasus defender in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He reports a year-on-year deterioration in conditions.

28173009B19676032168465.name: Moscow
28173009B19676032168465.summary:
Visitors in Moscow stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation, in which the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist was formally entered on the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024. The designation has produced arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols on extremism charges.

The federal law of July 2023 banning gender transition outright, both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition, applies in Moscow as it does nationwide.

Enforcement in Moscow has been direct. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution records that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life in Russia that year, and that Kotov, the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024.

Public assembly is not available. Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally.

28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Visitors in Orenburg Oblast stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025; The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian, on 27 July 2024, followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction in which that extremism designation first produced a criminal prosecution against a commercial leisure venue. The Central District Court of Orenburg registered materials in Russia's first criminal case under the "international LGBT movement" ban on 10 July 2025; the investigation into staff of the Pose club had been opened in March 2024 and the case was sent to court on 9 July 2025.

The proceedings concluded with Russia's first known "LGBT extremism" convictions. On 29 June 2026 Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that Pose club owner Vyacheslav Khasanov was sentenced to 7 years' imprisonment plus forfeiture of 1 million rubles, manager Diana Kamilyanova to 6 years and 3 months, and art director Alexander Klimov to 2 years and 3 months. A visitor present at a comparable venue in Orenburg Oblast therefore faces exposure to an extremism charge carrying a multi-year term, on top of the national propaganda, detention and deportation provisions.

36201628B69282955287113.summary:

36201628B88329767373181.name: Central Visayas
36201628B88329767373181.summary:
Central Visayas stands under the national framework of the Republic of the Philippines. National law does not criminalise same-sex relations or transgender identity, and no provision of national law penalises a person for being transgender. There is no administrative legal gender recognition process: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress since 2000 without passage. The protections that exist form a patchwork of sectoral statutes and sub-national ordinances: the Safe Spaces Act, the Magna Carta of Women and Republic Act 11166 penalise slurs, ridicule and discrimination tied to sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, while SOGIE ordinances cover eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities nationwide.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. Detention carries acute risk, as transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories with no gender-matched placement. Some local ordinances outside this region restrict presentation in public, including Marawi City's December 2004 ban on men appearing in female attire and Kabacan's November 2019 prohibition of cross-dressing for Muslims.

Within Central Visayas, the operative layer of protection is municipal. 36201628B47630810559445.name: Central Luzon
36201628B47630810559445.summary:
Central Luzon stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision criminalising a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised in the country. No administrative legal gender recognition process exists: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route. No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force, the SOGIE Equality Bill having been pending in Congress since 2000.

The clearest documented threat to a trans traveller in Central Luzon is trafficking and sexual exploitation in commercial sex venues, not any rule against being transgender. The United States government's Trafficking in Persons Report 2024 states that traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas across the Philippines. Within the region the operations on record cluster in one Pampanga city's bar district, where trans women are also concentrated in sex work.

On 17 June 2025 the National Bureau of Investigation announced that its Bataan District Office had arrested five people for human trafficking in Barangay Balibago, Angeles City: Alvin Baguio, registered owner of Field Sensation's Bar, together with Reden Roa, John Parro, Shirly Calilong and Marilyn Ferrer. The case began with a 19 May 2025 referral from Destiny Rescue Pilipinas Incorporated. Agents ran an entrapment and rescue operation on 1 June 2025 in which 'barfine' transactions ranged from P5,000 to P10,000, and 45 victims including 13 minors were rescued and turned over to the social welfare agency.

On 10 March 2025 the same NBI district office arrested foreign national Shin Ki Jung and accomplices in Angeles City for violations of R.A. No. 11862, the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2022, and R.A. No. 7610. A complaint from the husband of a trafficked victim alleged that women were recruited as Korea-bound performers as cover for work at a club in Angeles City; a subsequent rescue operation freed 12 victims including 5 minors. The arrested subjects were presented for inquest before the Office of the City Prosecutor of Angeles City.

Reporting by the Preda Foundation published on 21 November 2019, originally from The Fuller Project, found that hundreds of girls are supplied each year in Angeles City to meet demand from foreign men paying for sex, many of them American, in the city that hosted a former US military base. More than 150 women and girls interviewed by The Fuller Project said they wanted to leave prostitution but did not know how. City-regulated 'entertainers' must take weekly STD tests, a requirement activists criticised as marketing the sex industry as clean, and advocates warned that a new airport terminal on the city's outskirts could triple visitor numbers and expand sex trafficking.

On 13 August 2025 a Philippine daily reported the murder of an LGBTQ pageant winner in Batangas. The victim was crowned in Lipa City days before the killing and sustained 13 stab wounds; police work the case as a homicide. 36201628B63748016552864.name: Cagayan Valley
36201628B63748016552864.summary:
Cagayan Valley stands under the national framework of the Philippines: the country does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, which allies planned to endorse to the 20th Congress on 28 July.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, since 2000, without passage. The protections that do exist form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, and in 32 cities and municipalities, alongside sectoral statutes. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment; the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Violence against trans people in Cagayan Valley is documented and recent. On 31 July 2024, Cabansag was stabbed to death in Ilagan City, Isabela, following an alleged kidnapping and rape; three suspects were identified. On 23 June 2025, 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, formerly Gian Molina, an incoming first-year Business Management student at Cagayan State University-Caritan Campus and a hair-and-make-up artist active in local gay pageants, resident in Zone 7, Centro, Peñablanca, Cagayan, was found floating in the river between Amulung and Iguig in Cagayan two days after being reported missing; her mother cited visible marks of physical assault. A criminology student of the University of Cagayan Valley, named online as 'Menco de Guzman'/'Sherwin Kyqle', voluntarily surrendered to the Peñablanca police station, admitting he picked Kierra up on Saturday night but denying involvement. This is the second trans-woman killing documented in Cagayan province within the 2024-2025 national series. LGBTQIA+ groups including CSU Crystal, LGBT Pilipinas Taguig City Inc. and Bahaghari chair Reyna Valmores Salinas demanded a full investigation, justice and immediate passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill (House Bill No. 5551; Senate Bill No. 1600), noting no national anti-discrimination law has passed in 25 years.

Nationally, violence continues: in June 2025 two killings occurred within days, including Kierra Apostol and a trans woman former journalist and activist shot inside a clinic in General Santos. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; there is no gender-matched placement. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao instead transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Local ordinances restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.

Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.

36201628B91065962446027.summary:
Western Visayas stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex relations and trans identity are not criminalised and no provision of national law punishes a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress since 2000 without passage, and the protections available to a visitor rest on sub-national and sectoral law: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities, the Magna Carta of Women, the Safe Spaces Act, and Republic Act 11166, which prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression. Of the five provinces in this region, only Iloilo appears in the national inventory of provinces with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance.

Institutional exclusion on gender-presentation grounds has occurred inside the region. In October 2022 Capiz State University issued a hair-and-uniform directive that excluded students perceived as trans women, and an advocacy campaign followed. A legal-NGO case study dated December 2025 examines that exclusion and its aftermath; the university's binary haircut rules shaped students' everyday conduct, and one graduate reported that cutting her hair in earlier years felt like a loss of self-confidence.

The exclusion did not end in institutional exclusion. At its 21st commencement exercises on 7 August 2025, Capiz State University produced its first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude, Khaz-JP Padilla, batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honor; reporting attributes the outcome to the advocacy campaign that followed the October 2022 directive. Padilla has described carrying out her transition once pandemic-era online classes freed her from the haircut rule.

For a trans visitor the practical position is legality without a general remedy. Nothing in national law criminalises trans presence or presentation, and a 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 62 for trans travellers, within the 'Exercise Caution' band, with 81 for HIV-positive travellers. Refusal of entry or service by establishments, and exclusion from private and public spaces, remains possible with little or no legal consequence where no local ordinance applies.

36201628B64564033926366.name: Ilocos Region
36201628B64564033926366.summary:
The Ilocos Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision of national law criminalising a person for being transgender. It also has no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity: the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, a blockage campaigners cite as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy. Protections are sub-national or sectoral, so what a visitor can invoke depends on the specific locality they are in.

Local instruments of that kind exist within the region. Ilocos Sur is one of eight provinces nationwide with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance, and Bayambang in Pangasinan is among the 32 cities and municipalities carrying such an ordinance. Bayambang Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023, dated 16 October 2023 and authored by Coun. Benjamin Francisco S. De Vera, protects lesbians, gays, bisexuals, transgenders, queers and intersex persons in the municipality against any and all forms of discrimination solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics, and provides penalties for violation.

The ordinance sets an escalating penalty ladder. A first offence carries a fine of at least PHP 1,000 or one month's imprisonment; a second, at least PHP 2,000 or one month and a day to six months; a third, at least PHP 2,500 or six months and a day to eight months; and later violations carry one year's imprisonment plus at least PHP 2,500. Violators must also complete mandatory human rights education. Complaints are filed through the barangay mechanism under the Katarungang Pambarangay provisions of R.A. 7160, the Local Government Code of 1991, giving a person discriminated against in the Pangasinan corridor a defined local complaint route.

The ordinance carries provincial endorsement. Pangasinan Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution No. 799-2024, adopted at the session of 19 August 2024 in Lingayen, declared Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 to conform with the Bill of Rights and with Section 16 of R.A. No. 7160, affirming the municipal instrument at provincial level.

Recourse is not uniform across the region. In the rural parts of two of its provinces, a customary-justice system maintained by Itneg elders, adopted and modified as the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group, operates as an alternative dispute-resolution body alongside Philippine courts and police, so the institution handling a dispute may not be a national court.

Trans-specific exposure remains national in character. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (R.A. 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and allow markers beyond male and female. Transgender women are detained according to birth sex, and violence is documented and recent: in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

36201628B49646111072560.name: ARMM
36201628B49646111072560.summary:
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, begun 29 March 2019, sets out the region's structures and rules of governance and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause directs that justice be dispensed "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws". Nothing in the regional code addresses gender identity or gender non-conformity.

A Shari'ah Justice Code proposed in the Bangsamoro Parliament on 14 July 2026 would widen Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status field it has occupied since the Code of Muslim Personal Laws (Presidential Decree 1083, 1977), reaching into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution. The proposal rests on the region's organic-law authority and on the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. For a visitor, the practical consequence is that a dispute can be routed to a Shari'ah forum rather than a civil court, and the applicable law follows the forum.

Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums, with written opt-in clauses allowing civil entities to take on matters otherwise within that jurisdiction. A visitor married to a Muslim spouse therefore enters a legal-pluralist marriage regime in which the forum that hears a matter determines which body of personal law applies.

Bangsamoro Parliament (2026-07-14) proposed a Shari'ah Justice Code of 10 books extending Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status law confined since PD 1083 (1977) into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and ADR, resting on BOL authority and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums with written-opt-in clauses for civil entities, the legal-pluralist marriage regime that applies to a visitor married to a Muslim spouse.

In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, Davao-region provinces, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; parliament passed it unanimously. Christianity Today reported it in 2024-11 with local Christian-leader reaction. The measure carries Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing.

It states that the 24 April 1980 murder of tribal leader Macli-ing Dulag turned public opinion and made the dam dispute a landmark ancestral-domain case in the country, and records the September 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord that created the Cordillera Autonomous Region, with later plebiscites failing to ratify autonomy. It identifies the region as the least populated in the country according to the 2020 Census of Population and Housing, with fewer residents than the national capital. It records numerous ethnic groups including a majority-Igorot province, a continuing Cordillera autonomy movement, and the earlier Cordillera People's Liberation Army ceasefire secured by the Aquino government.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in CAR (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: There is no legal gender recognition. There are no laws protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in health, employment, education, and access to goods and services. Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military. There are no laws against psychology or medical practices being used as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data protects sexual orientation as sensitive data, with Article 17 stating "Any processing of sensitive data is prohibited due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms"; the article describes this protection only for sexual orientation and does not state coverage for gender identity. The Central African Republic signed a joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity at the United Nations condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people. Male and female same-sex sexual activity are legal. The penal code criminalizes public expression of love between persons of the same sex with imprisonment for six months to two years or a fine of between 150,000 and 600,000 CFA francs ($300 and $1,200). When one participant is a child, the adult may be sentenced to two to five years imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs ($200 and $1,600). In 2012 there were no reports that police arrested or detained persons under these provisions. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples, and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned under Article 7 which defines marriage as the union between one man and one woman with family and marriage under protection of the State. Alternatives Centrafrique has documented cases of people being arrested due to false accusations of same-sex intercourse. "societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons was entrenched, and many citizens attributed the existence of homosexuality to undue Western influence." Cultural stigma continues to persist, and due to criminalization of public same-sex affection along with cultural stigma the LGBTQ community has to conceal itself. LGBTQ people face discrimination in education, healthcare, and employment. Religious preach conversion, but this is rarely enacted since people keep their LGBTQ identities hidden. While there were no reports of violence against LGBTQ people, it is unclear if this is due to lack of incidents or victims not reporting it. Alternatives Centrafrique states that LGBTQ people have experienced mistreatment and torture by law enforcement. Being diagnosed with HIV is used as a source of stigmatization in the workplace leading to harassment, blackmail, and firings.

68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu stands under the national framework of South Korea. The city-specific signal concerns the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, held every year since June 2009 without interruption and regarded as the country's second-largest LGBT event, typically running a week or two in late June with a pride parade and film festival.

Organised opposition recurs annually and is substantial. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups formed a 'gay issue countermeasure committee' in Daegu to block LGBT events, and this opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street. In September 2025 a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee has filed injunction bids against the festival in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025; the court dismissed each. In 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. Police have restricted the march to a single bus-only lane, and organizers framed the event as resistance to 'hate and discriminatory politics'.

Venue restriction litigation continued into the 2026 edition. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, comprising the Daegu-Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of venue, claiming roughly 34,000 signatures, which it calls unusually large for a single Commission petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Daegu's Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It responds to the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act.

68945753B59172752195743.name: North Chungcheong
68945753B59172752195743.summary:
North Chungcheong Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between adults is legal. The surviving criminal provision is Military Criminal Act article 92-6, which punishes consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted. In 2017 the military ran what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

This province is the location of the gravest documented harm to a transgender service member in South Korea. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, the country's first openly transgender soldier, was found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021, aged 23. She had been compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap, and her challenge to that discharge was rejected in July 2020. Her death triggered national debate on the treatment of transgender troops. The Daejeon District Court later ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Ministry of National Defence recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgical precondition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a South Korean court held that requiring sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity, ruling for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had undergone years of hormone therapy, and held that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals who are unmarried may have their gender legally recognised even when they have minor children, overturning an 11-year-old precedent; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

National law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot adopt children jointly. The 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity: an anti-discrimination bill has been introduced eight times since 2007, the June 2020 draft included gender-identity provisions, and prosecutors and activists called for its passage after Byun Hee-soo's death. LGBTI organisations can register, though an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a documented problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal available, that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows transgender teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers called for legal and institutional reform of school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state itself. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when roughly 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Following Byun Hee-soo's death, the National Human Rights Commission honoured her and national pressure for protection grew, but no new law at provincial level followed; the protection gap is national, not local.

On 2 July 2024 a metropolitan district court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from a youth LGBTQ+ centre presented on 20 March 2024 shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state: in November 2023 the national human rights commission flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the national health ministry rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. At a Pride event in a port city, about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at a 2018 Pride in another large city some 2,000 police protected 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ young people in the country were harassed by classmates and that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During a May 2020 COVID-19 cluster traced to a nightlife district, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told an international news outlet he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in a public-health journal, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. An international human-rights organisation's 2025 world report describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

The province has its own student human-rights ordinance, enacted on 10 July 2020, whose Article 15 covers gender identity and sexual orientation. The provincial council passed a repeal bill on 24 April 2024; the provincial education office challenged it before the highest court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in effect, and it argues that repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties. 68945753B43731078897969.name: Gyeonggi
68945753B43731078897969.summary:
Gyeonggi Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, and the national assessment applies alongside the province-specific findings below. The sources yield no Gyeonggi-specific rule on criminal exposure, entry, identity documents, screening, facilities or healthcare access; what they document is a provincial protection instrument covering students.

Gyeonggi-do enacted South Korea's first student human rights ordinance in 2010. The ordinance provides non-discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which are the provisions most contested in the 2024-26 repeal wave against student-rights ordinances elsewhere in the country. Gyeonggi-do and Seoul are the only two jurisdictions whose ordinances also include a right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy.

The ordinance is administered rather than dormant. The Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights, and the province marks a Student Human Rights Day.

Its durability is the live question. On 28 April 2024 the Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it, following an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to the ordinance's sexual-orientation clause and pushed through by the ruling People Power Party council. At that date six regional education offices, Gyeonggi among them, still enforced comparable ordinances, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher quoted in the reporting defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition. The Seoul model was itself first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province, so the repeal movement has targeted the province's own template.

A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.

47653553B66835736668351.summary:
Región del Bío-Bío stands under Chile's national framework for trans people. Legal gender recognition has operated under Gender Identity Law 21,120 since 27 December 2019: adults change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry with no therapy or surgery required, applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and people under 14 cannot use the law although the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Within Chile, Región del Bío-Bío accounted for 5.89% of the national case total in 2024, the third-highest share of any region, and Concepción was among the cities recording the most documented incidents, with five. Care facilities in the region have been the subject of a formal discrimination complaint: on 14 October 2016 Movilh Chile reported that Movilh-Biobío had filed a complaint with the Seremi de Salud, Mauricio Careaga Lemus, concerning the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where patient Hanna Jiménez Carrasco, interned from 28 September to 3 October 2016, was placed and treated as male despite public policy and the legal duty to use her chosen name and social sex. The complaint alleged brutal and illegal discriminatory acts by hospital staff.

47653553B97418467345315.summary:
RegiÃ³n de Tarapacá stands under Chile's national legal framework. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, people aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and those under 14 cannot use the law although the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance in the criminal code. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. Chile's Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, while the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Transphobic violence remains documented under this framework. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, with the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

The controlling risk for a transgender visitor to Tarapacá is judicial rather than statutory. In early October 2023 the Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled in whole the trial of Jhonatan Cañon for the 2022 murder of trans woman Yuri Pizarro in Tarapacá, holding that Chile's femicidio offence covers only 'a person biologically female' and so the conviction could not stand as framed. The annulment voided the strongest gendered-violence conviction available and took effect in Tarapacá, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction.

Regional incident data point the same direction. Movilh's XXIII annual report, published in March 2025 on 2024 figures, records that Tarapacá held about 2% of nationally documented homo/transphobic cases and ranked among the fastest-rising regions, at +18.18% year-on-year, with growth also recorded at +19.51% in the period tables.

47653553B86325292267162.name: RegiÃ³n de Magallanes y AntÃ¡rtica Chilena
47653553B86325292267162.summary:
Magallanes y Antártica Chilena falls under Chile's national framework, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute does not permit the procedure for those under 14 although it recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence is documented nationally and in this region. The XXIII annual report of Movilh, published in March 2025 on 2024 data, places Magallanes at 0.96% of the national case total while recording it among the regions with the largest percentage increases, at +100% year-on-year. In Punta Arenas, trans woman Kenia Chacón was attacked in 2024 in a case prosecuted as attempted femicide; on 15 April 2026 SernamEG announced it would appeal the sentence, which imposed four years of partial internment against the five years of total internment the prosecution had sought, and the victim's mother publicly denounced that the attack was devalued because of her daughter's gender identity.

Nationally, a young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific protections that reach this region. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and rules on entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Protection for trans women under Chile's strongest gendered-violence offence is contested in the north. The Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman, holding that the femicide offence protects only "a person biologically female" and that the conviction could not stand as framed. Increases occurred in 11 of Chile's 16 regions. In regions with shares this small, a single case can dominate the rate, so the regional figure is a weak indicator of underlying incidence.

The region's earlier trajectory ran against the national trend. Movilh's report covering 2021, published April 2022, showed homophobia and transphobia complaints and cases falling 12 per cent across Chile, the first drop in eight years, which the report tied to the visibility won by the sexual-diversity movement in the year equal marriage was approved. In five regions the figures rose, and Arica y Parinacota was one of them, with reports climbing by around 300 per cent against 2020.

47653553B78904739401519.name: RegiÃ³n Metropolitana de Santiago
47653553B78904739401519.summary:
Chile's Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019, applies in full to the Región Metropolitana de Santiago. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry, with no therapy or surgery required. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute's under-14 exclusion cannot stand as written: on 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, a ruling that applies only to that case.

Non-discrimination and hate-crime rules also apply nationwide. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence is documented in Santiago and elsewhere. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Local authority practice across the capital's comunas diverges sharply, and a visitor's experience of municipal protection depends on which comuna they are in. On 15 April 2026 the Ñuñoa municipal council approved Chile's first anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one; it bans hate speech, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal good-practice seal and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings, and it was drafted by the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department head María Fernanda Ulloa and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel.

sources.summary: Movilh Chile (15 Apr 2026): Ñuñoa's municipal council approved Chile's first anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one — banning hate speech, obliging non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creating a communal good-practice seal, and requiring anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings; drafted by the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department head María Fernanda Ulloa and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel.

The Clinic (30 May 2025): after committing to Movilh to raise the LGBT flag for the 17 May anti-homophobia date, the Vitacura municipality reversed under pressure from its republican councilors and refused to fly it, while neighbouring Santiago and Ñuñoa comunas participated. The refusal marks a municipal-level retreat in the capital's affluent comunas.

10402087B60477050509260.name: Bayern
10402087B60477050509260.summary:
Bayern stands under Germany's national framework on legal gender recognition, identity documents, relationship recognition and anti-discrimination, and that layer is carried by the national record. What follows is specific to the Free State.

A prohibition on gender-inclusive German took effect in Bavaria on 1 April 2024. It bars gender-neutral word forms in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing a government declaration of December 2023 together with a cabinet decision amending the language rules that govern public authorities. Critics dismiss the measure as symbol politics while pointing out that it reaches every public counter, registry office and classroom in the state. A trans visitor dealing with a Bavarian registry office, town hall or university therefore deals with offices operating under an official register from which gender-neutral wording has been excluded.

Bavaria has co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, an organised Land-level attempt to make the nationwide self-declaration route stricter. The contested ground behind the initiative was the Act's treatment of children's gender entry: the Bundesrat's criticism of 20 October 2023 held that the draft allowed parents to decide changes for under-14s "without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare". The Free State government's posture toward self-declaration is therefore openly restrictive, even though the procedure itself remains the national one.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Germany
sources.summary: National framework applying to Bavaria. Adults have been able to change legal gender since 1980. The Self-Determination Act was approved by the cabinet in August 2023 and passed the Bundestag 374-251 on 12 April 2024; it lets adults over 18 change first name and gender by self-determination with three months' notice, in force since 1 November 2024. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and goods and services, with some protections varying by region. This is the federal baseline within which Bavaria's gender-language ban and the Länder push to tighten the SBGG operate.

sources.title: Selbstbestimmungsgesetz
sources.summary: The Self-Determination Act (SBGG), the federal law the Bavarian Bundesrat initiative sought to tighten, passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 by 374-251 with 11 abstentions and the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024, was gazetted 21 June 2024, and allowed changes to be registered from 1 August 2024, taking effect 1 November 2024. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Berlin (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Hirschfeld's Institute for Sexual Science held studies of the first gender-affirming surgeries among decades of research, destroyed when the institute at In den Zelten was sacked on May 6, 1933 and burned. The article states there were no explicit laws against exhibiting non-gender-conforming behavior, so enforcers criminalized queer women through other provisions with incarceration for so-called anti-social behavior under an extremely vague definition and no reliable numbers. Contemporary Berlin is described as having a rise of queer spaces catering to marginalized groups within the LGBTQ community such as transgender individuals. FLINTA spaces are defined as "Frauen, Lesben, Intergeschlechtliche, Nichtbinäre, Trans und Agender Personen," meaning those who do not fit into a cis male gender identity, motivated by discomfort around cis men and male-domination of many queer spaces. Male-exclusive venues Lab.Oratory and Boiler historically catered exclusively to male patrons with cases of feminine men and gender queer individuals rejected, with entry policy evolving since the 2000s to include more types of non-female gender expressions though instances of exclusion still occur, while a concept of queer masculinities including gay, bi, trans and queer men reshapes selection. Cited studies indicate gay, lesbian, and trans individuals especially may engage in drug use as a means of coping with societal marginalization and discrimination, exacerbated by multiple minority stress including gender identity. Several thousand men were sentenced under Section 175 of the Reich Criminal Code between 1933 and 1945, with about 6,000 actually interned to camps with a presumed high death rate, and upon liberation inmates feared re-incarceration with fears justified. In 1950 East Germany returned to the pre-Nazi version of Section 175 while Section 175a continued to be applied, from the late 1950s homosexual acts among adults were no longer punishable, and in 1968 a new penal code made same-sex sexual acts with minors punishable for both women and men in §151, deleted with effect from July 1, 1989. West Germany retained the Nazi-era versions of Sections 175 and 175a for two decades, convicting 50,000 men from 1945 to 1969, roughly the same amount as during the Nazi era. Reforms in 1969 and 1973 effectively made only sexual acts with males under age 18 punishable, while the age of consent for lesbian and heterosexual acts was 14 years. Section 175 was completely repealed in 1994, four years after unification, for the territory of the old Federal Republic. Those punished under the broader version in effect until 1969, many suffering imprisonment and entry in the national criminal record with life-long employment and housing consequences, were not rehabilitated until 2017. Compensation, only for actually convicted men still alive and eligible, was 3,000 euros and an additional 1,500 euros for each year of detention suffered, described as negligible.
