10402087B85226028911536.name: Hessen
10402087B85226028911536.summary:
Hessen stands under Germany's national framework: identity documents, legal gender recognition and equality protection are set nationally and apply in this state without local variation. What follows covers only Hessen's own policing, courts, incidents and facilities.

Police-registered queer-hostile offences in Hessen rose from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023, to 135 in 2024 and to 141 in 2025, a more than fourfold increase within four years. Interior Minister Roman Poseck (CDU) described the development as alarming, and in a May 2026 answer to a Grüne Landtag inquiry called the recorded figure only the tip of the iceberg, given the high dark figure from victims who do not report. The 2024 total comprised 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult.

Enforcement outcomes are thin relative to the volume of reports. Suspects were identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings and six convictions followed. Poseck attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces. Hessen police maintain dedicated contact officers for this hate crime, and LSBTIQ* liaison officers have been established in all police headquarters since 2010 under a governing framework concept; the state government states it will pursue prosecutions consistently.

The figures are raw counts with no per-capita denominator, so they show the direction and scale of reporting in Hessen rather than a measure of relative danger against other German states. The Federal Criminal Police Office's situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people notes that a new federal reporting category now makes state-by-state comparison possible but that classification changes can inflate individual state counts, so cross-state numbers need caution.

A January 2026 incident in Kassel, cited by Poseck, saw a male couple homophobically insulted, threatened and spat on aboard a tram.

At Frankfurt Airport, trans woman artist BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act after a male security officer refused her a search by a female officer during screening on 23 November 2024 and told her she was not a woman. Frankfurt Airport apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and promised training for security staff on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers.

10402087B23625801106445.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
10402087B23625801106445.summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt stands under the German national framework: identity documents, equality protections and marriage law are set nationally, and the Land government cannot lower that floor. What is specific to this Land is a political and custodial record in which the placement of a trans prisoner has been contested by the state's own authorities.

A dpa report updated on 2 June 2026 records that Sachsen-Anhalt, Sachsen and Thüringen jointly brought an initiative to the Bundesrat to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The proposal would create an "abuse review" mechanism allowing registry offices to intervene on objective, documentable grounds. The initiative was triggered by the Liebich case, is backed by Union MPs and resisted by the SPD, and runs alongside a scheduled evaluation of the Act by the federal family ministry.

The case behind the initiative began in this Land. BBC News reported on 20 August 2025 that Marla-Svenja Liebich, then Sven Liebich, was sentenced in July 2023 by the Halle District Court in Sachsen-Anhalt to one year and six months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult, and changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office under the Self-Determination Act at the end of 2024. The chief public prosecutor in Halle told MDR Sachsen-Anhalt that Liebich would begin the term at Chemnitz women's prison.

That placement did not hold. DW reported on 16 July 2026 that Liebich, legally registered as a woman since 2025, was transferred after extradition from the Czech Republic to the men's prison at Zeithain in the Meissen district. Prison management said the decision prioritised the safety of women at the Chemnitz facility. She had been arrested in the Czech Republic in April 2026, and a court has yet to decide whether the legal gender changes can be reversed.

For a trans visitor, the practical reading is that custody placement in Sachsen-Anhalt is decided case by case and can be revisited after intake. The Halle prosecutor's stated plan to begin the sentence at a women's prison was overridden by a safety rationale for women prisoners, while the Land government is simultaneously arguing in the Bundesrat that gender declarations should be open to registry-office review on abuse grounds. A trans person detained here should expect placement to be contested rather than settled by the gender marker alone.

10402087B67217417145666.name: Thüringen
10402087B67217417145666.summary:
Thüringen stands under Germany's national framework. The national floor of constitutional and equality protection, identity documents and marriage law applies in the state and is not within the state government's power to remove; what follows is the Thüringen-specific layer.

In the state election of 1 September 2024, AfD Thüringen, classified by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution as right-wing extremist, took 32.8% of the vote, ahead of the CDU at 23.4%, the BSW at 15.8% in its first state election, Die Linke at 13.1% and the SPD at 6.1%. The CDU, BSW and SPD formed the first so-called Brombeerkoalition under minister-president Mario Voigt, a minority cabinet without its own Landtag majority. That parliamentary configuration is the one in which the AfD fraction has pressed its gender-policy agenda.

The AfD fraction moved that the Landtag's existing ban on gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools be consistently implemented, in a motion titled "Keine Gendersprache an Thüringer Schulen" asserting that schools must not be a socio-political experimental field. The same parliamentary grouping has proposed dismantling the state's equality machinery. Formal, multi-layered institutional hostility to gender policy in Thüringen rests on this configuration.

On 2 June 2026 Thüringen co-signed an initiative from Sachsen and Sachsen-Anhalt to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act following the Liebich case. The initiative frames anti-abuse amendments alongside stronger recognition of trans and intersex status, so the state is a party to a move to restrict the self-declaration route rather than acting alone.

No trans-specific safety finding was documented for Thüringen. The sources record no prosecution, assault or enforcement action against a trans visitor in the state, so the risk picture there rests on political posture and on the exposures that apply across Germany.

14339913B89763821047858.name: Wales
14339913B89763821047858.summary:
Wales stands under the United Kingdom framework on legal gender recognition, single-sex spaces and sex-based segregation, with devolved powers over education, health and equality policy shaping how that framework reaches residents and visitors.

14339913B6930312138089.name: Northern Ireland
14339913B6930312138089.summary:
Northern Ireland stands within the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 framework, in which the Supreme Court's ruling now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery. In August 2026 the UK equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. Trans visitors to Northern Ireland therefore use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement and searching follow the parent framework. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the same argument had been aired in that court on 5 February 2026, where government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy to treat trans women as strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth, and on 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance placing custody searches and stop-and-search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear on biological sex, while endeavouring to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request.

Northern Ireland's own education authorities have moved against trans-inclusive practice. On 8 September 2025 BBC News reported that guidance supporting transgender pupils was withdrawn from the Northern Ireland Education Authority's website after Education Minister Paul Givan requested its removal, arguing that it conflicted with departmental policy and with the law in Northern Ireland. The withdrawn guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity, and teachers' representatives warned that its removal ignores the practical realities faced in schools.

Protection machinery in Northern Ireland remains incomplete. On 14 December 2025 BBC News reported that other Northern Ireland Executive parties blocked Justice Minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in the region's new hate-crime legislation. Long had sought executive approval in early November 2025 with a response deadline in mid-November, against a bill that had held executive agreement since December 2024, and she cited Police Service of Northern Ireland statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.

Northern Ireland sits on equality legislation different from the Great Britain statute and is still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling, so the precise reach of the single-sex provisions in local equality law is not yet settled by any Northern Ireland court.

Gender recognition documents carry entry and administrative consequences across the United Kingdom. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. Within the United Kingdom a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents, and if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors is restricted under the parent framework. NHS England stopped prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people in March 2024, renewed that suspension indefinitely in December 2024 with reconsideration due in 2027, and by April 2025 had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year following the Cass Review of April 2024, which also led to the closure of the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024. Schools and sport carry parallel exclusions: the Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams, while transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010.

Long cited PSNI statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Northern Ireland (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Gender Recognition Act 2004 applies to Northern Ireland and provides for a person's change of gender to be officially recognised, introduced after the 2002 case of Goodwin v United Kingdom in which the European Court of Human Rights ruled the United Kingdom's failure violated articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights. To change gender, a person must demonstrate gender dysphoria and have lived in the relevant gender for two years before applying for a gender recognition certificate. Before the 2020 introduction of same-sex marriage, a person had to be unmarried before changing legal gender. In May 2021 a Northern Ireland court judgment on a challenge to the UK gender recognition law made a binding ruling that gender dysphoria based on an individual's mental dynamic is no longer legally required, due to the WHO decision in 2019 no longer treating gender identity disorder under DMD-IV as a mental illness or mental disorder. That ruling applies only to Northern Ireland so far and not the rest of the UK, but sets up a legal precedent for the rest of the UK in the future. The Sex Discrimination (Gender Reassignment) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1999 provides a degree of protection for transgender people who are undergoing gender reassignment in employment and vocational training. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1982 under the Homosexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 1982 which came into force on 8 December 1982, following the 22 October 1981 European Court of Human Rights 15-4 ruling in Dudgeon v United Kingdom that criminalisation of male homosexual acts under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 violated Article 8. Anti-LGBT criminal provisions were removed throughout Northern Ireland by section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 abolishing buggery and gross indecency, with private gay sex between more than two people legalised but cottaging remaining illegal, and the age of consent equalised at 17 by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000 effective in 2001 then reduced to 16 by the Sexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 2008. Civil partnerships have been available to same-sex couples since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, and same-sex marriage took effect on 13 January 2020 under regulations signed 19 December 2019 after UK Parliament legislation receiving royal assent on 24 July 2019 required extension if the Assembly did not reconvene by 21 October 2019, with the first wedding on 11 February 2020 after a 28-day notice period and religious and church same-sex weddings permitted since 1 September 2020. Same-sex couples were granted full adoption rights in 2013 after High Court 2012 and Court of Appeal 2013 rulings that the ban was discriminatory and a breach of human rights and rejection of a further Supreme Court appeal. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 requires public authorities to have due regard to promoting equality of opportunity between persons of different sexual orientation through Equality Schemes monitored by the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland. The Employment Equality (Sexual Orientation) Regulations (NI) 2003 effective 2 December 2003 prohibit discrimination and harassment in employment, higher education and vocational training, and the Equality Act (Sexual Orientation) Regulations (NI) 2006 effective 1 January 2007 prohibit discrimination in goods and services, premises, education and public functions. The permanent blood donation ban on men who had sex with men moved to a one-year deferral effective 1 September 2016, to a 3-month deferral effective 1 June 2020, and from August 2021 monogamous gay and bi men may donate without a waiting period while non-monogamous gay and bi men must wait 3 months, and historic convictions became eligible for pardon under the Policing and Crime Act 2017 Alan Turing Law extended by a November 2016 Legislative Consent Motion, though by June 2019 only two men had sought pardons and both failed.

14339913B6930312138089.tangentialFactors:
On 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people. The warning addresses the parent framework rather than Northern Ireland's own statute, but the two regimes are being revised in parallel, so a visitor may encounter the same political argument twice, once at United Kingdom level and once in Belfast.

The litigation record in Scotland shows how far the prison and custody question has already been argued. The Court of Session heard on 5 February 2026 that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland pressed its challenge to the policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate; Lady Ross's June 2026 judgment resolved that dispute against the prison service's guidance. Trans visitors to Northern Ireland who face custody should expect the biological-sex placement rule rather than identity-based placement.

The December 2023 refusal to recognise foreign gender recognition certificates drew domestic political criticism on grounds unrelated to trans welfare: Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand, while Women and Equalities Minister Kemi Badenoch called the changes long overdue.

The judicial history around puberty blockers runs in both directions. Bell v Tavistock of December 2020 found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers, and that judgment was overturned on appeal in September 2021, before the Cass Review reversed the clinical direction again in April 2024. Families reported in April 2025 that some had turned to black-market or overseas hormones in response to the prescribing freeze.

Northern Ireland's hate-crime bill and its education guidance are both products of a devolved administration whose parties disagree along the same lines seen elsewhere in the United Kingdom, which means the practical outcome for a visitor depends on which department or body they are dealing with rather than on a single regional rule.

Existing protections therefore rest on other provisions of local law rather than on the new statute's identity-based aggravation.

Trans pupils in Northern Ireland schools lost the departmental guidance that had recommended gender-identity-matched changing rooms when Education Minister Paul Givan ordered its removal from the Education Authority's website in September 2025. Teachers' representatives stated that removal ignores the practical realities, so day-to-day arrangements in individual schools are now unsettled rather than governed by a published regional document.

Gender recognition for Northern Ireland residents runs through the United Kingdom process, including the December 2023 restriction on certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states such as Sweden, New York State and Belgium, and the requirement that a spouse consent to issuance or the marriage be terminated.

Northern Ireland's equality framework is not the Great Britain Equality Act 2010, and the regional administration has stated it is still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling; residents challenging exclusion from single-sex services would litigate under that separate local framework.

82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
The Northern Territory stands under the Australian national framework. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, in force immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.

Vilification coverage across Australia is uneven, and the Northern Territory sits at the unprotected end. New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation; South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also cover gender identity; the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither. The territory's own hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among its motives, so federal coverage of those motives dates only from 2025.

Within that frame, protection has been withdrawn rather than extended. The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 commencing 27 July 2026) removes the civil provision that made it unlawful to offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, gender identity included, and to have a complaint heard by the NT Anti-Discrimination Commission. The Country Liberal Party government confirmed the repeal on 2 March 2025, three years after adding the provision; a bill followed in July 2025 and passed parliament on 17 October 2025, the government having earlier backtracked from scrapping the section outright. Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby framed the change as restoring freedom of speech and religion, including letting religious schools again hire only co-religionists. NT Anti-Discrimination Commissioner Jeswynn Yogaratnam publicly rebuked the move, warning the government may be 'opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech'.

Official hostility has reached beyond statute. The NT government banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals in February 2025 and issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors.

Entry, documents and facilities carry no trans-specific friction. No Australian jurisdiction confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, federal identity documents are issued uniformly across the country, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering Australia. Birth-certificate sex-marker change in the Northern Territory has required clinical treatment since 2018. Marriage equality has applied nationwide since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result nationally; the territory's own postal-survey Yes vote was 60.6%. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009 and recognises overseas same-sex marriages automatically.

82085004B60194602145168.name: Victoria
82085004B60194602145168.summary:
Victoria's anti-vilification regime is set by the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025 and assented to on 8 April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958, repealing the existing racial and religious tolerance statute, and is directed at equal participation and public safety. Vilification on the grounds of gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation carries up to five years' imprisonment, with political, religious and academic exemptions; the criminal provisions take effect on 30 June 2026.

Gender identity has been a prohibited ground of discrimination in Victoria since 2000, under the Equal Opportunity (Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation) Act 2000 amending the Equal Opportunity Act 1995, and was retained in the replacement Equal Opportunity Act 2010. Sex characteristics were added as a protected attribute effective 2021, and the Justice Legislation Amendment (Police and Other Matters) Act passed in September 2022 extended protection to on-duty Victoria Police officers on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds.

Religious exemptions have been narrowed but not eliminated. The Equal Opportunity (Religious Exceptions) Amendment Act 2021, effective 15 June 2022, bars religious schools and organisations from discriminating against employees because of sexual orientation, gender identity or marital status, and bars government-funded bodies from refusing services on those grounds, except where conformity with doctrine is an inherent requirement of the job, such as hiring a religious studies teacher. Exemptions remain under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 for religious organisations including adoption and fostering agencies and charities that receive no government funding, allowing them to discriminate against LGBT employees and clients.

Victoria prohibits conversion practices. The Change or Suppression (Conversion) Practices Prohibition Act passed the lower house 55-0 in December 2020 and the Legislative Council 27-9 on 5 February 2021, with penalties of up to approximately $200,000 AUD or ten years' imprisonment, taking effect in February 2022, one year after royal assent. It followed the Health Complaints Act, effective 1 February 2017, which empowered the Health Complaints Commissioner to issue warnings and temporary or permanent practice bans after a May 2018 investigation.

Gender transition is legally recognised by Victoria. Birth certificates are issued by the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and since November 2025 updated regulations removed all fees and costs for an application to change sex on a birth certificate. Victorian driver licences carry no recorded gender marker. Earlier law required a person to be unmarried and to undergo sexual reassignment surgery before changing recorded sex; the unmarried requirement, which had been due to lapse in December 2018, was removed early by Parliament in May 2018, while an August 2016 bill to remove the surgery requirement and allow parents to alter a child's gender descriptor with the child's informed consent failed. Passports and marriage remain Commonwealth matters.

Victoria is the only Australian state to maintain an LGBTIQA+ Commissioner. The office dates from the appointment of an inaugural Gender and Sexuality Commissioner in July 2015, charged with aligning Commonwealth and state records on passports and birth certificates and strengthening workplace protections for transgender workers; it was later renamed Commissioner for LGBTIQ+ Communities. Joe Ball, a transgender man, was appointed on 23 September 2024 for a three-year term to advise government on safe and inclusive policies, services and programs and to lead implementation of Pride in our Future, Victoria's ten-year LGBTIQA+ equality plan.

A Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people; ABC News reported the findings on 29 August 2024. The state government says it is reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups will press for their implementation.

On care for trans young people, the Supreme Court of Victoria upheld in August 2024 the availability of puberty blockers for transgender children experiencing stress and anxiety.

Vilification based on gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation was criminalised by the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-vilification and Social Cohesion) Bill passed March/April 2025, assented 8 April 2025 and effective 30 June 2026, with maximum 5 years imprisonment and political, religious and academic exemptions plus a Sam Kerr clause, amid reported funding cuts risking backlog at the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission established in 1975. Buggery was a crime in Victoria from 1958 until December 1980 when the Hamer Liberal government repeal passed 72-7 effective March 1981, with the death penalty on the books for sodomy until 1949, an equal age of consent set at 18 then lowered to 16 by the Crimes (Sexual Offences) Act 1991, and a loosely worded soliciting for immoral purposes clause enabling continued police harassment of homosexual men until the late 1980s including entrapment mass arrests at Black Rock Beach reported in 1976. Any remaining legislation banning sex between consenting adults in private was removed by royal assent effective 1 March 2022 and in effect by May 2022. Intentional HIV transmission singled out under Crimes Act Section 19A with up to 25 years imprisonment compared to 20 years maximum for manslaughter was repealed by the Crimes Amendment (Repeal of Section 19A) Act 2015 passed 28 May 2015, assented 2 June 2015 and effective immediately with conduct now dealt with as causing serious injury, while an April 2022 Act repealed all HIV legislation on mandatory public health notifications, blood donations and human tissue services effective 15 February 2023. Victoria was the first state to create an expungement scheme for historical homosexual offences no longer criminal, passed 15 October 2014 and effective 1 September 2015 allowing the individual or representative of a deceased person to apply to the Secretary of the Department of Justice and Regulation, after which the person may lawfully claim not to have been convicted and the conviction does not appear on a police records check avoiding travel and employment restrictions, followed by a formal parliamentary apology on 24 May 2016. Sexual orientation has been a protected attribute since 2000 retained in the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 alongside federal protection under the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013, with the December 2021 religious-exceptions reform effective 15 June 2022 prohibiting religious schools and government-funded bodies from discriminating against employees or refusing services because of sexual orientation. Vilification based on sexual orientation alongside gender identity, sex and sex characteristics carries up to 5 years imprisonment under the 2025 anti-vilification law effective 30 June 2026, and same-sex conduct-related conversion practices carry up to approximately $200,000 AUD or 10 years jail effective February 2022, while same-sex marriage has been legal since December 2017 federally and domestic relationships have been registrable since 1 December 2008 under the Relationships Act passed 10 April 2008.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
New South Wales stands under the Australian national framework. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.

State-level vilification coverage is narrower than in several other Australian jurisdictions. New South Wales, the Australian Capital Territory and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, while South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also name gender identity and the Northern Territory and Western Australia name neither. A trans visitor in New South Wales therefore retains federal discrimination remedies, including the Tickle v Giggle precedent, but has no state vilification ground specific to gender identity.

The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 took effect on 4 April 2025. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm are punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years, and Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025 with civil referral pathways available. The state's other principal recent instrument is the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024.

Trans visitors have been killed in the state. In July 2021 ABC Background Briefing reported the investigation into the killing of Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines who was visiting Australia, in Wagga Wagga; the perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month term, a custodial outcome far below a murder sentence.

The restrictive machinery reported elsewhere in Australia does not apply here: no law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering New South Wales or Australia, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access for young people rests on state-commissioned evidence: a New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research. That review stands in contrast to the restrictions operating in Queensland public health services.

82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Visitors in every state, Western Australia included, stand under that national framework, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

State protection in Western Australia runs through a narrower formulation. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex, and the official WA Government guidance states that a person has gender history where they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such. Direct discrimination, including treating a person as their former sex, and indirect discrimination are both unlawful under the Act. The binary, medically-inflected wording means a non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may fall outside the state-law definition and would rely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint. Western Australia has no state anti-vilification offence, civil or criminal, and no statutory charter binding public authorities.

Complaint eligibility under the state attribute has historically been tied to recognition certificates or a registry change through the Births, Deaths and Marriages framework. On 16 April 2024 Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024, which repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, described by the ministers as the only remaining board of its kind in Australia. The Board's functions move to a streamlined administrative process within the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and applicants are no longer required to undergo medical or surgical reassignment. A statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, now suffices, and a 'non-binary' sex descriptor becomes available. Stricter rules apply to under-18s through parental consent or Family Court of WA permission, and the Act contains a statutory review clause after three years. The reform implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations.

The registration reform reshapes the state discrimination attribute itself. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 amends section 4(1) of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. The Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001, does not operate retrospectively, and commences by proclamation; once it is in force, gender history complaints must comply with the new registration requirements.

Two complaint routes exist and only one may be used. A complaint may be lodged with the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 within 12 months, with acknowledgment of receipt within a week and a free conciliation conference to follow, or with the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 within 24 months, reduced to 12 months for employment matters. Choosing one route forecloses the other.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere in the world: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity in Western Australia, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held nationally since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and records, and pressure to roll back existing rights, alongside systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Western Australia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Western Australian law recognises a transgender person's change of sex, with sterilisation required before 2012 until the High Court in AB v Western Australia (2012) held two transgender men who had undergone mastectomies and hormone treatment did not need sterilisation to obtain a gender recognition certificate. Legislation introduced in August 2018 repealed the requirement to be unmarried for a change of sex on a birth certificate, passing the lower house on 20 November 2018 and the upper house on 12 February 2019, receiving royal assent on 19 February 2019 and commencing on 19 March 2019. The Births, Deaths, Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 passed both chambers in September 2024 to formally abolish and repeal the WA Gender Reassignment Board, receiving assent on 26 September 2024 and taking effect on 30 May 2025. That Act permits male, female, indeterminate/intersex and nonbinary options and allows change of sex on a birth certificate once a year on appropriate clinical treatment signed off by a doctor, nurse or psychologist with no sexual reassignment surgery required, subject to a $195 non-refundable fee and up to 4 weeks waiting. Reported November 2020 policy allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their own gender identity for strict health and safety reasons so long as they have no sexual offences on their criminal record. In October 2021 a Western Australia Supreme Court order in an Australian legal first removed custody entirely from a family for continuing abuse of their transgender child, following the April 2021 suicide of a 15-year-old transgender teenager in Perth that prompted calls to immediately reform archaic birth-certificate sex or gender legislation. For protection, transgender Western Australians are currently classified as Gender History under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 and Gender Reassignment Act 2000 only if reassigned gender as certified, providing technically less protection than sexual orientation, with announced reforms to add gender identity and sex characteristics, repeal the exemption allowing discrimination by religious schools, and a 2026 Public Order Bill to criminally ban harassment based on gender identity still passed only in the lower house, while no law currently bans conversion therapy. Private same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Law Reform (Decriminalisation of Sodomy) Act 1989 effective 23 March 1990, but the Act set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual male acts versus 16 for heterosexual acts and created offences of promoting or encouraging homosexual behaviour in primary or secondary teaching or public policy. Equal age of consent at 16 and repeal of the promotion offences came via the Acts Amendment (Gay and Lesbian Law Reform) Act 2002. Historical homosexual convictions became expungeable under the Historical Homosexual Convictions Expungement Bill 2017, passed by the Assembly on 22 February 2018 and the Council with amendments on 23 August 2018, approved on 11 September 2018, assented on 18 September 2018 and effective 15 October 2018, requiring a mandatory test of historical homosexual offence considering consent and ages and allowing family members of deceased persons to apply, accompanied by the Premier's formal parliamentary apology to the LGBTIQ community. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2002 to prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, education, accommodation and provision of goods, services and facilities, supplemented federally by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013. No law in Western Australia currently bans conversion therapy, with the government stating a bill would only be introduced after the March 2025 state election, leaving WA as the only mainland state to legally allow the practices and, as of September 2026 with Tasmania, the only Australian places without explicit criminal prohibition. A 2026 Public Order Bill to explicitly criminally ban harassment based on sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house but had yet to pass the upper house.

On 16 April 2024 the state Premier and Attorney-General announced the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024, which repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, described by the ministers as the only remaining board of its kind nationally. The Board's functions move to a streamlined administrative process within the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and applicants are no longer required to undergo medical or surgical reassignment. a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, now suffices, and a 'non-binary' sex descriptor becomes available. Stricter rules apply to under-18s through parental consent or permission from the state's Family Court, and the Act contains a statutory review clause after three years. The reform implements the state law reform commission's 2018 recommendations.

The registration reform reshapes the state discrimination attribute itself. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 amends section 4(1) of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. The Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001, does not operate retrospectively, and commences by proclamation; once it is in force, gender history complaints must comply with the new registration requirements.

Two complaint routes exist and only one may be used. a complaint may be lodged with the state Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 within 12 months, with acknowledgment of receipt within a week and a free conciliation conference to follow, or with the national human rights commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 within 24 months, reduced to 12 months for employment matters. Choosing one route forecloses the other.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held nationally since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights nationally, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and records, and pressure to roll back existing rights, alongside systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

82085004B93533858076668.tangentialFactors:
Western Australia's reform sits inside a wider state-level movement. Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. The WA announcement also linked the registration reform to a planned new Equal Opportunity Act and a ban on conversion practices slated for 2025.

Detention is the sharpest residual risk across the country, and the practice Western Australian visitors would meet if detained is set by interstate precedent rather than by any WA instrument in this inventory. Queensland's inspection standards issued in August 2023 direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, a placement rule with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery; oversight there passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, after a 2009 corrective services procedure was assessed as largely ineffective. Equivalent Western Australian detention placement standards are not covered by the sources assembled here.

The exclusionary activism behind Tickle v Giggle indicates that private and platform-level exclusion can arise even where the statute protects gender identity, and the outcome was a compensation award rather than an injunction preventing exclusion in the first place.

82085004B40257551482390.name: Australian Capital Territory
82085004B40257551482390.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

The territory's Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, giving a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or public facility a legal review mechanism that common-law states without a charter lack. The territory is also one of four jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for this territory; the absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and the self-identification custody rule, places it modestly above the national average.

A conversion-practices ban has been in force since early 2021, with offending practices attracting up to a 12-month custodial term or a fine, alongside civil penalties giving a tribunal power to issue orders and order redress; practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this territory is recorded in the dossier.

sources.summary: ABC News, 3 Jul 2020: national survey of trans prisoners — experts estimate up to 400 trans and gender-diverse people in Australian cells, often inappropriately housed and at elevated risk of physical and sexual violence; NSW, Victoria, the ACT and Tasmania run explicit self-identification policies while QLD/NT/SA are unclear. ACT-relevant: names the ACT's explicit self-ID prison policy.

The Human Rights Law Centre report 'Ending Strip Searching in Australian prisons' (2026), produced with the trans-community groups Flat Out and FIGJAM, documents strip-searching practice in Australian prisons, including those in the ACT, and its disproportionate harms for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners.

sources.title: Human Rights Act 2004 | Acts | ACT Legislation Register
sources.summary: The official ACT Legislation Register lists the Human Rights Act 2004 (A2004-5) as In Force, with the current republished version and a full republication history back to 1 July 2004. Section 31 provides that interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. The register also records uncommenced amendments by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025. The Act is the statutory rights framework that ACT public authorities must operate within.

sources.title: Serious barriers in accessing health care for Canberra's transgender community highlighted in new study - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 16 April 2022 that the ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals, including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, resulting in 'excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel'. The article records 20 young transgender people on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, some patients waiting a year for an appointment, GP demand rising 20-40 per cent a year, and the study calling the ACT 'the only jurisdiction not to have a comprehensive gender-focused health service' in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic. The study documents a shortfall of institutional capacity for transgender health care in the ACT.

sources.title: LGBTQ conversion therapy banned in Canberra as Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passes - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 27 August 2020 that the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill, so that from early 2021 conversion practices used on protected persons attract up to a 12-month jail term or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties giving the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. The statute is an ACT criminal and civil protection measure.

25490228B8471183517505.name: Castilla y León
25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Castilla y León stands under Spain's national framework. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition of the acquired gender is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Other operative provisions of the same statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Castilla y León, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Regional legislation is being built on top of the national floor. The PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León on 20 December 2024, framed as an end to the "sexilio", the out-migration of LGBTI people from the region, with group leader Tudanca urging the fastest possible processing. On 11 June 2025 the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the bill, which runs to 76 articles, into consideration after the PP abstained and Vox opposed; the bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands, and advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

25490228B48808997991554.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
25490228B48808997991554.summary:
Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain with no LGTBI or gender-identity statute of its own. The legislative index at planlgtbi.es states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no regional LGTBI statutes and must instead apply the national equality framework together with central-government policies, so a trans visitor to Ceuta is dealing directly with Spanish law and Spanish institutions rather than with any local ordinance.

The statutory gap is documented rather than incidental. FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ public policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, identifies Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law promoting LGTBI+ rights. The same report records legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla. A 2020 precedent study had already placed Ceuta and Melilla at the bottom of the rankings for trans-student recognition and protection.

Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Other operative provisions of the same statute reach the day-to-day conditions of a stay: a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Ceuta's border position shapes protection needs for trans people held there. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli called transfer the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those still in Ceuta.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
Kelantan stands under the national framework of Malaysia, and its own Sharia legislature has moved to re-criminalise conduct struck down at federal level. On 13 August 2026 the Kelantan state assembly passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026, which replaces the 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 that the Federal Court struck down in February 2024 on federalism grounds. 15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
Terengganu is one of the 13 states of Malaysia and stands under the national framework: sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, and the state's own Sharia enactments add offences of cross-dressing, liwat and musahaqah that reach Muslims only. A foreign visitor in Terengganu is exposed to the federal provisions on the same terms as a resident; a Muslim visitor is additionally exposed to the state enactments.

Terengganu's own official posture is openly hostile. In May 2025 a state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices, installed at strategic locations across the state, are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, and that the state wants people to regard the acts as "dirty, wrong, and to be avoided". This is state-level endorsement of anti-gay messaging, publicly stated by a serving member of the executive council.

Thirteen civil-society organisations, including Justice for Sisters, wrote to the Kuala Terengganu City Council in May 2025 demanding removal of the signboards. Their letter condemned the boards as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law, and criticised the executive councillor's defence of them as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. The signboards remained in place as of the date of that reporting, and no record of the council's response is sourced here.

For a transgender visitor, the practical signal is the combination of a documented hostile official stance, public messaging installed at state level, and the discretionary ground-level enforcement of the state Sharia enactments, under which presentation is judged by officers rather than by any statutory definition.

15666254B71428205180864.name: Kedah
15666254B71428205180864.summary:
Kedah stands under Malaysia's national framework: the federal Penal Code's sections 377A and 377B criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, and these provisions apply to foreign visitors as well as citizens. Section 377D's undefined offence of "gross indecency" adds up to two years as a discretionary charge. Non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone.

Kedah additionally maintains its own state criminal law through the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Sections 23 and 24 criminalise liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex), punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment, or up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination. Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, with a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment; female cross-dressing is not criminalised under this section. These state offences apply only to Muslim persons, and enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, whose officers determine on the ground where compliant presentation ends and the offence begins.

Enforcement in Kedah has targeted transgender people directly. In October 2020 a private birthday party in Kedah was raided and 30 trans women were singled out and arrested, and a coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups expressed concern that the event organiser was then probed for "encouraging vice" — a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of transgender persons alongside trans people themselves.

Women convicted of musahaqah under Kedah's enactment may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to six months under section 52, a custodial alternative to prison prescribed by the same law.

Malaysia provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and no form of partner recognition or same-sex marriage is available. Identity-document marker changes are routinely rejected by the Registration Department, and the 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict that sex is determined at birth, though never gazetted and not legally binding, is applied in practice. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors.

65028918B28366581005022.name: West Java
65028918B28366581005022.summary:
West Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Sub-national variation sits inside that framework. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions, and in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Those provincial provisions apply to foreign visitors present in those provinces, not to West Java; West Java's own exposure comes from national law, national police action and street violence.

Police in West Java investigate and break up LGBT gatherings even where no offence is alleged. On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police confirmed the detention of 75 people, 74 men and one woman, at a privately rented villa in Puncak in Bogor Regency, following a tip from local residents; police described the event as an LGBT family gathering held to avoid detection. Amnesty International, which said the gathering violated no law, called the operation a discriminatory raid and a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and demanded release and accountability.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
West Sumatra stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

West Sumatra carries no equivalent provincial religious criminal regime. The operative restrictions here are regional public-order bylaws made by city and regency authorities under Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism, and they bind anyone within the locality. Bukittinggi City adopted Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order, which targets LGBT people and is framed in the text as a response to local religious values and Minangkabau customs. In Limapuluh Kota regency, the regional legislature (DPRD) finalised on 13 May 2026 a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation folded into a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, carrying administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people.

Physical risk in Indonesia is rising. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Document and status rules offer no cover. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option, legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali

Same-sex marriage remains unrecognised for visitors and residents alike.

Bali's own social environment differs from the national legal picture. Peer-reviewed ethnographic fieldwork published in 2025, drawing on four case studies in Bali, documents a visible transpuan (trans feminine) community living with precarity, discrimination and informal resistance, challenging narratives of pure victimhood while confirming real material insecurity.

Traveller-facing guidance rates Bali 6.3 out of 10 overall but gives it a legal score of 2.0, warning that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risk under Indonesian law and advising visitors to keep affection quiet despite the island's tolerant reputation. A March 2026 guide describes Bali as broadly welcoming on a 'live and let live' basis, while noting that the new Criminal Code in effect from January 2026 adds complexity to the legal backdrop. Same-sex relationships are not separately criminalised under a Bali-specific provision; the exposure runs through the national code.

Same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia. Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, and public displays of affection warrant discretion across the island.

65028918B17554737605304.name: South Sulawesi
65028918B17554737605304.summary:
South Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, with Amnesty International stating the gathering violated no law and calling the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Within that framework South Sulawesi carries its own layer of proposed restriction. In April 2025 the Mayor of Makassar reaffirmed a commitment to pushing an anti-LGBT regional regulation (Perda) after a same-sex act at a night-entertainment venue went viral, and the deputy chair of the DPRD Makassar law-drafting body (Bapemperda) voiced support, arguing such a regulation is needed to preserve moral and religious norms. The episode marks a formal municipal push in Makassar toward an anti-LGBT regulation in 2025.

The push is not isolated. The OutRight Action International report 'Creeping Criminalisation' by Katjasungkana and Wieringa covers eight Indonesian provinces, South Sulawesi among them, and records how provincial and city bylaws criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under regional autonomy. Sub-national instruments of this kind therefore already operate in the province alongside the national code.

As of April 2026 the Makassar rule remains proposed (Ranperda) rather than enacted. The Makassar city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) is intensifying LGBT 'prevention' through socialisation and education aimed at school-age children, plus case handling with counselling and a safe house for reported individuals, in response to community reports; DP3A head Ita Isdiana Anwar says most reports come from worried families. DPRD Kota Makassar member Muchlis Misbah, citing a Komisi D monitoring meeting that showed rising LGBT numbers alongside HIV/AIDS cases, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement.

The proposal has been in the legislative pipeline since at least January 2023, when Makassar's anti-LGBT raperda entered the 2023 local legislative programme (prolegda) as a 'priority for discussion'. Two DPRD Makassar members, including PKS-faction member Azwar ST, said the proposal models itself on Perda already passed elsewhere such as Bogor. Constitutional-law expert Bivitri Susanti called such raperdas a 'trend ahead of the political year' that risks worsening discrimination and persecution of LGBT people, and noted that the central government does little to stop discriminatory local regulations.

31927357B17004778023462.name: Aguascalientes
31927357B17004778023462.summary:
Aguascalientes stands under Mexico's national framework, and legal gender recognition in Mexico is settled state by state. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records that Aguascalientes 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people'; its reporting of 31 March 2025 places the state among those that have not legislated such a procedure. The state therefore operates no administrative mechanism of its own for changing name or gender markers on official records.

The March 2024 Human Rights Watch report on the cost of absent recognition names Aguascalientes among the non-reforming states whose trans residents have no lawful marker procedure. Its documented consequence is that trans people carry documents contradicting their lived identity, which amplifies discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

A court-ordered route now exists. Infobae reported on 9 April 2026 that the Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 on a draft by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, held that the state Civil Code's requirements for changing the gender on a birth certificate, namely judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations, are discriminatory and violate privacy. The Court ordered the Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal note revealing a prior gender. The immediate effect is confined to the persons represented by the civil association that brought the case, so the ruling establishes a recognition route in the absence of legislative reform without yet establishing one for the state's trans population generally.

No trans-specific homicide offence covers the state. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide; Aguascalientes is among the states that have adopted no comparable reform.

Violence and coercive practice persist according to local accounts. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem of Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente say conversion-therapy operations continue in the state under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one such space reached the group the previous year. The same activists state that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression.
