31927357B35339934753022.name: Baja California
31927357B35339934753022.summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that patchwork, but the gap between statute and practice documented across Mexico applies here as elsewhere: Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly.

Lethal violence against women in the state is under-classified. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 March 2025 that under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila 1,179 women have been killed in Baja California while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide. The same reporting places female economic participation in the state at roughly 46-47%, 14th of 32 states.

Extradition machinery has been used in feminicide cases. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 July 2023 that Brayan Rivera was presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson in provisional detention for extradition, accused by Mexico of the feminicide of Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed on 24 January 2022 in room 404 of Hotel Cascadas beside Bar Hong Kong in Tijuana's tolerance zone. A US federal court determined probable cause on 29 June 2023; he was arrested at his parents' Downey, California home, where officers found the Hotel Cascadas rent receipt and rope and gloves. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the Baja California attorney general called the 30-year-old a serial perpetrator, said extradition could take from 15 days to two years, and that nearly a decade of open case files were being reviewed; the investigation had linked him to at least three feminicides: Ángela (January 2022), Elizabeth (14 February), and Karen, 28 (30 August 2021, Motel Hacienda Soler).

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on Tabasco: no legal gender recognition procedure there exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment - the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Comparative context for Baja California: the Guardian (24 July 2024) reports that Mexico City criminalized transfemicide on 18 July 2024 under the Paola Buenrostro law, with sentences of up to 70 years, in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people. Nationally, over 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022.

31927357B33389180120223.name: Baja California Sur
31927357B33389180120223.summary:
Baja California Sur does not criminalise the presence of trans people. The state's elected congress created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2021 reform to the state Civil Code, and after the Supreme Court of Mexico ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents from that procedure was unconstitutional, the congress passed a further Civil Code reform in 2024 extending recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people.

El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform approved by the Baja California Sur congress allows minors to change their gender marker and chosen name on birth certificates, with the administrative process described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children. The XVI Legislature worked the bill to the terms of the June 2023 Supreme Court ruling that had struck down the adult-only limit.

Human Rights Watch's state-by-state tracker of legal gender recognition in Mexico (March 2025) records Baja California Sur among the states that have legislated an administrative procedure, and documents how the Supreme Court rulings drove the expansion of recognition to minors.

Recognition procedures are not uniform across Mexico. Human Rights Watch's report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that Tabasco has no legal gender recognition procedure, exposing trans residents to institutional mistreatment: healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling their legal names, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez remained unsolved.

31927357B65177449444732.name: Chiapas
31927357B65177449444732.summary:
Chiapas has not reformed its state legislation to create a procedure for legal gender recognition. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state assessment of 31 March 2025 places Chiapas among the Mexican states with no administrative route to change the name or gender marker on identity documents.

Recognition is available only case by case through the courts. A trans resident of Chiapas who wants documents matching their identity must petition a judge, with no administrative application, no published timeline and no standard outcome; until a ruling issues, the documents remain as issued.

The gap has a direct bearing on document checks during a visit. With no state procedure through which a name or marker can be aligned, any mismatch between a trans visitor's identity documents and their presentation stands unresolved for the length of a stay, and Chiapas authorities have no state-level mechanism for correcting it on the spot.

31927357B32124965101143.name: Coahuila de Zaragoza
31927357B32124965101143.summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza stands under the national framework of Mexico, where Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that most states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition while warning that implementation differs sharply between them, and where same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

Coahuila is one of the states that has legislated. The 2018 Law on the Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila, articles 124 to 128, established an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity; the Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker of March 2025 records it among the 32 states with such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform. The bill reached the plenary of the Congress of Coahuila through proposals from several parliamentary groups and an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira, and the dictamen was approved unanimously. It reformed article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and created the Civil Registry law, whose article 2, fraction XI, defines gender identity as the personal and internal conviction.

The procedure is in working use. Ricardo Malacara, director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, stated in March 2023 that roughly 1,500 people had completed the legal gender-identity change before the Civil Registry from early 2019 to March 2023, in both directions, male to female and female to male.

Recognition on paper does not settle the wider risk environment. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, second only to Brazil's 100; a Guardian report of 24 July 2024 states that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. On 18 July 2024 the legislature of Mexico City made transfemicide a crime carrying sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, to investigate LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. No Coahuila-specific incident or enforcement pattern appears in the sources assembled here, so visitor-facing risk in the state tracks the national baseline rather than a documented local pattern.

31927357B75771156097737.name: Colima
31927357B75771156097737.summary:
Colima is a state of Mexico, and a trans visitor's exposure there is set by the national framework rather than by any Colima statute identified in the sources reviewed. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised anywhere in the country, and nothing in the inventory indicates that Colima has enacted a law targeting trans presence.

Legal gender recognition in Mexico is decided state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that, as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operate one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. The sources reviewed do not state which of these categories Colima falls into, so a visitor should not assume a recognition procedure exists there.

Where no state procedure exists, the consequences are documented. Human Rights Watch records identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. A joint Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, written from Tabasco, found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and excludes trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. That report also records the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and notes that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

Transfemicide has been made a specific crime in two of Mexico's 32 states. Mexico City passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, punishable by up to 70 years, following Nayarit, which set a maximum of 60 years. Impunity for transfemicide is thought to run higher than the already high general homicide impunity rate. Colima has not been identified in the sources as having enacted such a statute.

31927357B41082348713023.name: Mexico
31927357B41082348713023.summary:
Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none at all. Only seven states extend recognition to children.

In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people face identity-document mismatch that drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Recognition in Mexico depends on the state a person is in.

Tabasco has no legal gender-recognition procedure, according to Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion (6 March 2024). Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Context includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and the fact that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. Trans people in Tabasco live without documents that match their gender.

Mexico City has operated the longest-standing sub-national recognition regime. Amendments to the Mexico City Civil Code took effect on 13 March 2004 allowing transgender people to change gender and name on their birth certificates. In September 2008 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a law making it easier to change gender on birth certificates; the legislature approved that measure 37-17 in late August 2008, formalising the procedure and replacing a prior process lacking specific rules that could take years in court. On 13 November 2014 the Legislative Assembly of Mexico City approved a gender identity law making the process much quicker and simpler.

Other states have legislated recognition procedures on their own timelines: the Michoacan Congress approved a gender identity law on 13 July 2017, Nayarit's on 20 July 2017, Coahuila passed a gender identity bill on 13 November 2018, the Hidalgo Congress approved a law on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosi began authorizing legal gender changes on 17 May 2019.

On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Court held that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity.

Private same-sex sexual conduct between adults ceased to be a criminal matter in 1871 through adoption of the Napoleonic Code. A federal anti-discrimination law took effect on 11 June 2003 creating a national council to enforce it, and Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended in 2001 to prohibit discrimination, with the term sexual orientation inserted in June 2011. Mexico City passed an anti-discrimination ordinance covering sexual orientation on 2 September 1999, the first of its kind in the country.

Marriage recognition has been extended nationwide: Mexico City passed same-sex marriage on 21 December 2009 with effect on 4 March 2010, upheld 9-2 by the Supreme Court on 5 August 2010; on 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court issued a jurisprudential thesis deeming marriage restrictions to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring judges to validate such unions through amparo, with nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalised on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling, though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz.

Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatan Mayas, with Zapotecs recognizing a traditional third gender known as muxe, intermediate between male and female. Muxes are assigned male at birth but typically act and behave like women and do both women's and men's work, and having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck. Although perceived as different from the general heterosexual male population, muxes are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities, though mestizo police occasionally harass muxe boys, prompting Zapotec parents to defend their right to be themselves.

Visible and well-attended LGBTQ marches and pride parades have occurred in Mexico City since 1979, in Guadalajara since 1996, and in Monterrey since 2001.

31927357B15886886594254.name: Nayarit
31927357B15886886594254.summary:
Nayarit stands within Mexico's federal legal framework. A 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match their gender identity. The Human Rights Watch roundup of 31 March 2025 counts Nayarit among the 22 of Mexico's 32 states that have legislated such procedures, alongside eight states with none and two more that recognise it in practice without legislation; the same document records 2019 national Supreme Court guidelines and notes that only seven states extend recognition to children.

Nayarit is the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in 2024. Mexico City followed in July 2024 as the second jurisdiction to do so, with up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law. The Nayarit measure also lets friends, not just relatives, identify and claim bodies and drive investigations, a provision relevant where families disown trans relatives. In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, a figure believed to be higher for transfemicides.

31927357B98648037880103.name: Queretaro de Arteaga
31927357B98648037880103.summary:
Querétaro de Arteaga stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and its state-by-state table lists Querétaro among the six states that have never legislated any such procedure. A trans visitor to Querétaro therefore has no local administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity; the papers carried on arrival are the only identification available, and they cannot be corrected there.

Where recognition is absent, mismatched documents are the documented exposure. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and it presents Tabasco as the clearest case among the six states whose legislatures still refuse any procedure. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Querétaro's Penal Code cuts the other way on one specific point. The reform prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies, was published and is in force as of reporting on 20 September 2023, and it sets two to six years' imprisonment, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture.

sources.summary: Tribuna de Querétaro reports (20 September 2023, with Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación spokesman Walter López) that the reform to Querétaro's Penal Code prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called 'conversion therapies', was published and is in force. It sets a penalty of two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture. The group calls it a milestone compared with states where the ban remains unpublished, while saying a first generation of LGBTIQ+ reforms is still pending. Querétaro's congress banned conversion practices with two to six year penalties.

31927357B98648037880103.blindSummary:
The province stands under the parent nation's national framework, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. a national human-rights organization reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the parent nation's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and its state/province-by-state/province table lists the province among the six states that have never legislated any such procedure. a trans visitor to the province therefore has no local administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity; the papers carried on arrival are the only identification available, and they cannot be corrected there.

Where recognition is absent, mismatched documents are the documented exposure. The organization's report of 6 March 2024 found that delays and refusals in one sister state/province leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and it presents that state/province as the clearest case among the six whose legislatures still refuse any procedure. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in a river in August 2023.

The province's Penal Code cuts the other way on one specific point. The reform prohibiting efforts to correct sexual orientation and gender identity, commonly called conversion therapies, was published and is in force as of reporting on 20 September 2023, and it sets two to six years' imprisonment, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the statutory reference unit and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the regional convention to prevent and punish torture.
31927357B98648037880103.localsOnly:
Residents of Querétaro who need a name or gender marker change have no state procedure to apply to, since the state has never legislated one; the practical consequence documented elsewhere in Mexico is carrying identity documents that contradict lived identity. Human Rights Watch's Tabasco research was co-authored with a local trans community organisation, and the organization frames Tabasco as the clearest instance of a legislature refusing any procedure.

The conversion-practice ban is resident-facing protection with real penalties attached. Walter López, spokesman for the Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación, described the published reform as a milestone compared with states where a comparable ban remains unpublished, while stating that a first generation of LGBTIQ+ reforms is still pending in the state congress.

Same-sex marriage has been available nationwide since 2009, so partnership recognition does not depend on Querétaro's own legislation.

31927357B98648037880103.tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people across Mexico intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, with the killings drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety. Querétaro has not adopted comparable legislation.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture. Human Rights Watch's 31 March 2025 backgrounder likewise calls on the states that lack recognition procedures to adopt them and warns that implementation differs sharply from one state to another.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B22618747134228.name: San Luis Potosi
31927357B22618747134228.summary:
San Luis Potosí stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains unevenly implemented. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and set out a per-state compliance picture showing that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

San Luis Potosí is among the states that have acted. The state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, following a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law that created an administrative recognition procedure with implementing regulations issued by gubernatorial decree. The state is listed among the states that enacted a gender-identity law in 2019.

Partnership recognition is settled here as well. Same-sex marriage took effect in San Luis Potosí on 21 May 2019, after the state Congress voted 14-12 in favour on 16 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal in the state from the same month. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

The state's hate-crime statutes recognise motivation by gender and sexual preference, which gives trans victims a route to aggravated treatment of an attack. Its local anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender but does not name gender identity, leaving a gap in the statutory protection a trans visitor would be able to invoke.

The distance between statute and practice is the recurring national finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many states operate administrative recognition procedures while calling on those that lack them to adopt them. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Two official responses frame what a trans visitor can expect from authorities. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, a statute named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished and which activists describe as critical to their sense of safety. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found for San Luis Potosí, and no border-screening or document-procedure information specific to the state is recorded.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch backgrounder dated 31 March 2025 on trans rights in Mexico reports that 22 of 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by March 2025, and sets out the per-state compliance picture.

31927357B30231562725156.name: Sinaloa
31927357B30231562725156.summary:
Sinaloa stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, a national benchmark against which Sinaloa's own status is measured.

Sinaloa's legislative record on gender identity is contested across sources. Wikipedia's Mexico-wide LGBT rights article lists Sinaloa among the states that enacted a gender-identity recognition law, dated there to 2022. That dating conflicts with the March 2025 Human Rights Watch count, which records Sinaloa as having legislated no legal gender-recognition procedure. The state's actual local-law status therefore requires verification against the state code before either account is relied upon.

On relationship recognition, the Mexican Supreme Court ordered Sinaloa to legalize same-sex marriage within 90 days on 15 May 2018, and the Sinaloa Congress passed a same-sex marriage law on 15 June 2021. Civil unions are available in the state to both same-sex and opposite-sex couples.

Sinaloa's local law bans discrimination on grounds of both sexual orientation and gender identity, and the state's hate-crime statutes cover gender and sexual preference. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has both marriage recognition and statutory discrimination and hate-crime coverage in the state, subject to the enforcement gap documented nationally, where progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely applied uniformly.

31927357B37261891092938.name: Sonora
31927357B37261891092938.summary:
Sonora is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework of Mexico. Within that framework, Sonora has legislated its own gender-recognition procedure: the state's Congress approved the Ley de Identidad de Género on 1 October 2020, allowing people who identify with the opposite gender to modify their official documentation, according to Hermosillo-based daily El Sol de Hermosillo. Wikipedia's LGBT rights in Mexico page lists Sonora among 25 Mexican states with a gender identity law, dated to 2020.

Human Rights Watch's country overview of Mexico, dated 31 March 2025, reports that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and names six whose legislatures had enacted none. Sonora is not among the states lacking such a procedure.

Sonora's Congress banned conversion therapies (ECOSIG) on 6 December 2022. The state's hate-crime laws recognize motivation by gender and sexual preference, and Sonora ratified the 2011 constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

By 31 December 2022 every Mexican state, including Sonora, had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling.

31927357B81008000569871.name: Tabasco
31927357B81008000569871.summary:
Tabasco stands under Mexico's national framework, and within it the state has not reformed its legislation: Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that Tabasco has no legal gender recognition procedure, placing it among eight Mexican states with none, while two further states handle recognition in practice only.

Where no procedure exists, identity documents never match a trans person's gender. Human Rights Watch's Tabasco-dedicated report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024), produced with a local community centre for inclusion, found that this documentary mismatch curtails trans residents' rights across four socio-economic areas of daily life.

The same report documented the enforcement consequence directly: mismatched identity documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 March 2024 that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Violence against trans people in Tabasco has been documented with a named case. The Human Rights Watch report of 6 March 2024 records the murder of Karina Gómez, a trans woman, in Tabasco in August 2023; the same report sets these findings against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
Legal gender recognition is unavailable in Tamaulipas. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table of 31 March 2025 records that the state legislature has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people. The table places Tamaulipas among the eight Mexican states with no procedure at all, against 22 of 32 states that have legislated an administrative procedure, with two further states offering recognition in practice only. A trans person whose identity documents are issued in Tamaulipas therefore has no administrative route to change those documents to match their gender identity.

Criminal law in Tamaulipas moves in the opposite direction. On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas state Congress unanimously approved reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. The reforms explicitly ban conversion therapies, carrying prison terms of two to six years and fines of up to 2,000 UMA, with penalties rising by half where victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or where the conduct occurs in a subordinate setting such as a family, medical or workplace relationship.

The gap between criminal protection and administrative recognition remains open as of early 2026. On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups, including Tamaulipas Diversidad, Vihda Trans A.C., Tendremos Alas A.C. and La Resistencia Trans, agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law alongside anti-discrimination and health reforms. The participating groups noted that these initiatives have been pending since June 2025, and that the absent Gender Identity Law continues to limit trans people's access to health care, education and employment in the state.

31927357B22008724034476.name: Tlaxcala
31927357B22008724034476.summary:
Tlaxcala stands under Mexico's national framework and adds its own statute on top of it. The state congress's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and the decree text is published on the state congress's own site. The procedure requires no court proceeding, which is the legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update identity documents in Tlaxcala.

Tlaxcala's civil-union law took effect on 12 January 2017, giving a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship a state-level recognition instrument.

31927357B35199150741361.name: Yucatan
31927357B35199150741361.summary:
Yucatán operates an administrative route to legal gender recognition. A 2024 reform to the state's Civil Registry Law, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024, created a procedure through which transgender people can update the legal gender recorded on their identity documents without obtaining a court order. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of 11 March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis. This is the fact a trans visitor's document situation turns on when entering or being stopped in the state: the gender marker on a Mexican identity document issued here can be corrected through an administrative filing rather than litigation.

Yucatán stands under Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition, which remains unfinished and uneven across the country; the administrative procedure described above is the layer specific to this state.

Relationship recognition for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship arrived first through the courts and then through statute. The Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled on 1 July 2013 that two petitioners were able to marry, and the first same-sex couple legally married in the state on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015, and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán then passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended the secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022, so marriage in the state now rests on statute as well as court order.

Yucatán is listed as enacting a ban on conversion therapy on 25 August 2021, placing a protective statute on the books alongside the state-level bans elsewhere in Mexico.

31927357B22408340646138.name: Zacatecas
31927357B22408340646138.summary:
Zacatecas operates a legislated administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated such a procedure, and Zacatecas is not among the six states named as lacking one.

Deputies of the 64th Legislature of Zacatecas approved a reform of the Family Code on gender identity on 23 December 2022 by 14 votes in favour to 7 against, following a positive opinion from the Justice Committee. The reform provides for issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature records that in 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines implementing the law, with both entries linked to the official state gazette.

On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved a ban on conversion therapies, defined in the Penal Code as ECOSIG (efforts to correct sexual orientation or gender identity), by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis. Inciting hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or promoting such practices, carries one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code. A gender-identity law initiative debated alongside the constitutional and family-code reform at that time failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending; the Family Code reform passed in December 2022.

82249235B96958463903898.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
82249235B96958463903898.summary:
Newfoundland and Labrador stands under the Canadian federal framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial healthcare coverage is universal.

Legal gender recognition in the province operates without a surgery requirement. An amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009, given Royal Assent 13 April 2016, removed the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with a December 2015 ruling of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission on complaints brought by two trans women.

A second amendment, given Royal Assent 23 June 2021, extended the route to residents who were not born in the province but have lived there at least three months. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and can be used to update records in other jurisdictions; it serves as the identification document for people born outside Canada. The same amendment aligned with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates.

Current requirements on the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador's official page: applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s, with consent of the other parent or guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15. Applicants must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months. There is no fee for the change application itself; charges apply only to official copies of updated documents ($35 for a new birth certificate, $30 online).

One documented cross-border caveat applies. The province states it cannot guarantee that a birth certificate carrying an X gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations, so a provincial record with that marker may not travel cleanly.

Police-reported hate-crime data is favourable for the province but rests on small numbers. Statistics Canada (30 March 2026 release, 2024 data) recorded 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% jump the previous year, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador had the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000, tied with Manitoba, against Ontario's highest at 16.0. The province's recorded rise of 51% reflects 19 incidents in 2023 against 29 in 2024, so the percentage change is statistically fragile. Police figures capture only reported incidents. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report examines national police-reported data including offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity; Egale Canada is an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Newfoundland and Labrador (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gender identity is explicitly included as a prohibited ground of discrimination in human rights acts in all provinces and territories and by the federal government as of 2017, prohibiting discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. The concepts of sex under section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, providing equality protection applicable to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities. In Saskatchewan, The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoked the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. In Alberta, the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were met with legal challenges, after which Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 invoked the notwithstanding clause. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69, with the general age of consent for all sexual activities 16 since June 2019, or 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency. Section 159 of the Criminal Code on anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta, with repeal pursued through Bill C-32 incorporated into Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent on June 21, 2018, allowing the RCMP and federal departments or agencies to destroy or remove any judicial record of conviction for homosexual acts prior to being lawful in 1969 or anal intercourse under section 159. Sexual orientation was held constitutionally protected under section 15 in Egan v Canada in 1995, and failure to include it in human rights law was held a violation in Vriend v Alberta in 1998. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide on July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so. Same-sex adoption was legalized in Newfoundland and Labrador in 2002, with joint adoption legalized in all provinces and territories by 2011, and conversion therapy was statutorily banned nationwide for minors and adults in 2022 and made a crime under the Criminal Code. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found that 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. The same poll separately measured sexuality tolerance, finding 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, preserving a distinct result for transgender acceptance. Historical record states many transgender people in traditional Indigenous roles were in positions of reverence, where they acted as caretakers of children who had lost their families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle, with terms including Cree napêw iskwêwisêhot, Ktunaxa titqattek, Blackfoot aakíí'skassi, and Ojibwe ikwekaazo and ininiikaazo. Following colonisation and spread of Christianity by missionaries many traditions died out and transgender individuals were forced and assimilated, with Indigenous groups in the early 1990s reclaiming customs and proposing "two-spirit" to refer to a traditional and cultural "third gender," with LGBT2S or LGBTQ2S increasingly used. Formal state apologies acknowledged past harm, with the Prime Minister on November 28, 2017 apologizing "For the oppression of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and two-spirit communities," and the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police in December 2020 apologizing for harm to Two-spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Communities and stating "We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization."

Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the national human rights statute and under the hate-motivation provisions of the national criminal code, both added by national legislation the upper chamber passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in the country restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: national authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, and nationally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial healthcare coverage is universal.

Legal gender recognition in the state/province operates without a surgery requirement. An amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009, given Royal Assent 13 April 2016, removed the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with a December 2015 ruling of a board of inquiry under the provincial human rights commission on complaints brought by two trans women.

A second amendment, given Royal Assent 23 June 2021, extended the route to residents who were not born in the state/province but have lived there at least three months. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and can be used to update records in other jurisdictions; it serves as the identification document for people born outside the country. The same amendment aligned with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates.

Current requirements on the provincial government's official page: applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s, with consent of the other parent or guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15. Police-reported hate-crime data is favourable for the state/province but rests on small numbers. The national statistics agency (release dated 30 March 2026, 2024 data) recorded 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% jump the previous year, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. The state/province had the joint-lowest rate among provinces at 5.3 per 100,000, tied with another province, against the highest province's 16.0. The province's recorded rise of 51% reflects 19 incidents in 2023 against 29 in 2024, so the percentage change is statistically fragile. Police figures capture only reported incidents. 82249235B3191732862561.name: Prince Edward Island
82249235B3191732862561.summary:
Prince Edward Island stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply in Prince Edward Island as they do across the country.

Legal gender recognition in Prince Edward Island carries no surgery requirement. A 2016 amendment to the Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration of the gender the applicant identifies with, supported by a letter from a doctor. The regime has operated on that basis ever since. An adult born in the province may apply if resident there for at least three months; the application requires completed forms including a physician statement and a written statement by the applicant, signed before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics.

Provincial photo ID can carry a non-binary or undisclosed marker. Since 4 December 2018 Islanders completing a driver's licence at Access PEI locations may select 'gender not listed', shown on the licence as X, or 'prefer not to say', shown as a blank, alongside male and female. The Government of Prince Edward Island stated that the province was the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say' blank option.

National police-reported hate-crime data gives no Prince Edward Island figure. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000 population, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. The release reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province.

sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, with explicit inclusion as prohibited grounds in human rights acts as of 2017. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, enacted while invoking the section 33 notwithstanding clause. Alberta in 2024 passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, followed by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 which used the notwithstanding clause to prevent those challenges. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Trans and Queer communities, stated police must stand against transphobia and marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) took effect upon royal assent, after an era when sex between men was a capital crime and gross indecency was enforced. Section 159 of the Criminal Code criminalizing anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta, and was repealed on June 21, 2019 through Bill C-75, setting the age of consent for anal intercourse at 16, matching the general age of consent of 16 since June 2019 and 18 where a relationship of trust, authority or dependency exists. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the section 15 equality clause as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15. Parliament enacted the Civil Marriage Act on July 20, 2005 making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide without a residency requirement, following court rulings from 2002 to 2005 and a Supreme Court reference in December 2004, while same-sex adoption was legalized province by province culminating with Nunavut in 2011 after Prince Edward Island allowed joint adoption in 2009. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited by all provinces and territories and the federal government, with explicit inclusion in human rights acts as of 2017. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and make subjecting anyone to it a crime as defined in the Criminal Code. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau issued a formal apology on November 28, 2017 for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, and the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent on June 21, 2018 allowing the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for homosexual acts prior to 1969 and anal intercourse under former section 159 for living and deceased persons. 82249235B52639524229375.name: Quebec
82249235B52639524229375.summary:
Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under the national framework set out in the country's own record. Provincially, gender identity and gender expression have been prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms since 2016, reaching employment, housing and public and private accommodation.

Provincial enforcement is documented. On 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring on the ground of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

Quebec's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial heard with 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people (2021 QCCS 191). The Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code.

Correctional placement is the sharpest adverse finding in the provincial record. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province would be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety. The directive was issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. The directive reverses the province's previous practice of considering gender identity in placement, and it bears on a visitor only if detained in Quebec.

On relationship recognition, Quebec created civil unions in 2002 by amending the Civil Code, giving couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation the same effects as marriage in matters of family, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance. That status is valid only in Quebec.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Ontario (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: All federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, including in employment, housing and public and private accommodations as of 2017. Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been interpreted so that the concepts of sex and physical disability include transsexuality, providing equal protection guidance for courts interpreting human rights laws. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, which drew calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, and in 2025 the government passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to prevent the challenges. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister issued a formal parliamentary apology for the oppression of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm from not fully supporting Two-spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Communities, acknowledged institutional bias, intolerance and human rights violations causing suffering, shame, trauma and distrust, pledged to stand against homophobia, transphobia and other marginalization, and created the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150) received royal assent. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities is 16, rising to 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency or exploitation, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. Former Criminal Code section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta as violating Charter equality, and was repealed through Bill C-75 which received royal assent on June 21, 2019 setting the age at 16. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is protected under section 15 of the Charter as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) it held failure to include sexual orientation in Alberta human rights law violated section 15. Parliament enacted the federal Civil Marriage Act on July 20, 2005 making Canada the fourth country worldwide and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide, after court rulings required it in most provinces and territories by July 2005. Same-sex adoption was legalized province by province from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011, with stepchild adoption in Alberta from 1999 and joint adoption from 2007. In 2022 Canada became the third country worldwide and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and make subjecting anyone to it a crime as defined in the Criminal Code. On June 21, 2018 the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent allowing RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons as recognition of historical injustice distinct from pardon or record suspension. In a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. In the same poll, 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, preserving a distinction between sexuality tolerance and transgender tolerance. The article documents that different Indigenous groups had traditions referring to transgender, gender variance or sexual identity in which many transgender people in traditional roles were in positions of reverence as caretakers of children who had lost families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle. It states that following colonisation and the spread of Christianity by missionaries many of these traditions began to die out, transgender individuals were forced and assimilated into Europe-centric culture and perceptions changed even among Indigenous peoples, before Indigenous groups in the early 1990s sought to reclaim customs including proposing the term "two-spirit" for a traditional and cultural "third gender."

82249235B50381585000441.summary:
Manitoba stands under the framework of Canada. Federal protections for gender identity and gender expression apply in Manitoba as they do across the country, and the province's own Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public and private accommodations.

As of March 2025 the Manitoba NDP government had a bill before the Legislative Assembly to extend the Human Rights Code to cover gender expression as well. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe stated the change would bring Manitoba in line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing; the bill was scheduled for debate later in 2025, and Trans Manitoba's executive director Charlie Eau welcomed it. Until the amendment is passed, gender expression is not a named prohibited ground in Manitoba's provincial code, though federal protections and Charter interpretation still apply.

Manitoba has enacted trans-specific recognition at provincial level. In May 2024 the legislature passed a bill recognizing March 31 as the Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a transgender backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park. The province has raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, most recently in November 2023, an observance first marked eight years earlier; that year's flag was raised by Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara issued a statement that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans.

Manitoba recorded the joint-lowest provincial police-reported hate-crime rate in Canada for 2024, at 5.3 per 100,000, alongside Newfoundland and Labrador, against a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba was among the eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining, recording no increase in 2024 while the national total rose 1% to 4,882 incidents. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and Statistics Canada's release breaks out motivations by category rather than establishing trans-specific hate-crime volume.

Legal gender recognition in Manitoba follows the provincial rules that apply across Canada, with vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson, speaking at the 2023 Remembrance observance, said the day memorializes people murdered as a result of transphobia and that this violence shows no sign of slowing.

The concepts of sex under section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement, with courts required to interpret human rights statutes consistently with the Charter.

82249235B9619254975586.name: Yukon
82249235B9619254975586.summary:
Yukon stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-motivation provisions, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodation is prohibited in Yukon as in all provinces and territories, with gender identity and expression explicitly listed as prohibited grounds in all Canadian human rights statutes as of 2017. Section 15(1) Charter equality concepts of sex and physical disability have been interpreted to include transsexuality, applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement; claims against private businesses proceed under the applicable human rights statutes interpreted consistently with Charter values.

Legal gender recognition is available in Yukon. Vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates fall under territorial jurisdiction, and transgender people can change their legal gender under varying territorial rules.

National hate-crime data shows a rising pattern for trans-motivated incidents. Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024' (30 March 2026) reports 4,882 police-reported hate crimes in 2024, up 1% on 2023 and 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive yearly increase and up 184% since 2020. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average near 50. Police-reported hate-crime rates run about 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), a gap that bears on sparsely populated territories where reporting infrastructure is thinner. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis examines the same national data and does not report Yukon-level victimisation.

Yukon's own legislature has placed trans residents on cross-party record. On 30 March 2026 the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility, with Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praising the courage, resilience and contributions of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, acknowledging that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and citing a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of a suicide attempt.

Official hostility toward trans-inclusive school policy has been met with ministerial defence. In June 2024 a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood; a replacement was promptly put up, and on 12 June 2024 Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy (SOGI 123).

Canada in 2022 became the third country and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults, making it a Criminal Code offence. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for institutional bias and pledged to stand against transphobia through an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee.

Sub-national policy turbulence in schools and sport is concentrated in other provinces, not Yukon: Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 using a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and Alberta's 2024 Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were shielded from legal challenge by Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause.

Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on 27 June 1969. Since June 2019 the general age of consent is 16, rising to 18 where a relationship of trust, authority or dependency exists, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. Criminal Code section 159 on anal intercourse was repealed by Bill C-75, which received royal assent 21 June 2019; assented 21 June 2019, S.C. 2019, c. 25, the repeal applies in Yukon and bars conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid.

In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 Charter equality as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide on 20 July 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, the first country to do so without a residency requirement. Adoption by same-sex couples was legalized in Yukon in 2003, part of nationwide legalization completed by Nunavut in 2011. On 21 June 2018 royal assent to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allows persons convicted of certain homosexual acts before 1969 or anal intercourse under repealed section 159 to have records destroyed, following the 28 November 2017 prime ministerial apology.

In a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office, 87.6% said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual next-door neighbour.

Many transgender people in traditional Indigenous roles held positions of reverence as caretakers of children who had lost families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle, with distinct terms such as Cree napew iskwewisêhot and iskwew ka napewayat, Ktunaxa titqattek, Blackfoot aakii'skassi, Inuit sipiniq, and Ojibwe ikwekaazo and ininiikaazo. Those traditions declined after colonisation and the spread of Christianity with forced assimilation; in the early 1990s Indigenous LGBTQ groups proposed "two-spirit" to reclaim a traditional cultural third gender, now frequently used in LGBT2S and LGBTQ2S designations.

sources.title: Yukon Government hears feedback on 2SLGBTQ plan - Yukon News
sources.summary: Yukon News (29 April 2025) reports the Yukon government published community feedback on its LGBTQ2S+ Action Plan, the first of two check-ins the government committed to when the plan was released in 2021. 82249235B82395866892480.name: Northwest Territories
82249235B82395866892480.summary:
The Northwest Territories stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. The territory has no criminalising law of its own, and national criminal law, the self-declaration gender framework and the entry rules apply here directly.

Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act replaced the surgery requirement with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Healthcare coverage is universal.

The territory's first legislation specifically addressing transgender and non-binary people was open to feedback as of June 2026. The Northwest Territories Legislative Assembly sought comment from police and the Northern Mosaic Network on proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and the Change of Name Act to make the legislation more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people, including an option for an applicant to request that a name change not be published in the NWT Gazette. RCMP Chief Superintendent Dyson Smith asked MLAs to remove or amend the registrar general's option not to notify authorities, on the grounds that criminal records are tied to a person's legal name and that officers may put themselves in danger if records are not transferred to a new name. Yellowknife North MLA Shauna Morgan pressed the RCMP on how officers could verify a legal name without identification.

The national hate-crime picture is worsening for gender-diverse people. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% on the year and 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity and gender expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and 184% above the 2020 level. Sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, yet June 2024 alone recorded 113 of them against a monthly average near 50. Because rates run roughly 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, and metropolitan reporting infrastructure in the territories is thin, the national figures are an imprecise guide to what is recorded in the Northwest Territories.

Communities in the territory have publicly backed trans and Two-Spirit people. Inuvik, the northernmost community, hosted a regional Pride celebration in June 2023 at which youth from across the Western Arctic and Beaufort Delta took part in workshops, a film screening and a parade, and observed a moment of silence at the Inuvik Community Greenhouse for Frank Gruben, an LGBTQ2S community member from Aklavik missing since 2023. In the Sahtu region, the hamlet of Tulita held its first Pride celebration on 28 June 2025 as a joint effort of Chief Albert Wright School, the hamlet administration and the local RCMP detachment, with more than 50 attendees, a barbecue and the painting of an RCMP cruiser; Const. Matt Ryan described the day as creating a safe and welcoming space for the 2SLGBTQI+ community, with RCMP covering the food and paint.

RCMP covered the food and paint while the hamlet and school provided volunteers, firewood and the venue, and organizers planned monthly inclusive school events from September. This is small-community NWT evidence of police-community partnership explicitly welcoming transgender residents.

82249235B23927232378620.summary:
Nunavut stands under Canada's national framework, and layers its own statutory protection on top of it. In March 2017 the Legislative Assembly voted unanimously on third reading of Bill 31, amending the territory's Human Rights Act to add gender identity and gender expression alongside sexual orientation as prohibited grounds of discrimination. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited; at the time Nunavut was the first Canadian territory to list these grounds, with nine provinces and one territory already doing so.

Nunavut's birth certificates carry a non-binary option. On 18 September 2025, Members of the Legislative Assembly voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore a third non-binary sex-designation on Nunavut birth certificates through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck the provision from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill. The bill then passed third reading, and sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone stated that the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals.

The territorial government funds gender-affirming care. Reporting from 22 March 2022 states that Nunavut's Health Department began funding transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty named among covered procedures, under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside Iqaluit.

Nationally, police-reported hate crime targeting gender identity and expression rose 8% to 139 incidents in 2024, a fourth consecutive annual increase and a 184% rise since 2020, according to a Statistics Canada release published 30 March 2026. Sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658. Hate-crime rates run roughly 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a gap relevant to Nunavut, which has no metropolitan reporting hub of that scale. Egale Canada's analysis of the same police-reported data supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures.
