sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nunavut (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: As of 2017, all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground of discrimination in their human rights acts, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15(1) of the Charter to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions in Canada including law enforcement authorities. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, with controversy over its requirement that schools obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request the use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, but the government shielded them by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm, institutional bias and rights violations toward Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia and other marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force upon royal assent. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16, with age 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency and close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15, after former section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause of the Charter as an analogous ground under section 15, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide on July 20, 2005 with the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize it, following court rulings between 2002 and 2005, while same-sex adoption was legalized in all provinces and territories with Nunavut last in 2011. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and made it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code, the third country in the world and first in North America to do so. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records of pre-1969 homosexual convictions and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from a pardon or record suspension, following the Prime Minister’s formal apology on November 28, 2017. On sexuality-specific tolerance, 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessing same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing that “same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt children as heterosexual couples do” and 76% agreeing that “same-sex couples are just as likely as other parents to successfully raise children”. Canada was referred to as the most gay-friendly country when ranked first for least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The largest cities feature gay areas including Toronto’s Church and Wellesley, Montreal’s Gay Village, Vancouver’s Davie Village and Ottawa’s Bank Street Gay Village, with Pride celebrated every summer in major cities with federal, provincial and municipal political figures. 14339913B95766344400054.name: England
14339913B95766344400054.summary:
Equality enforcement in England runs through the Equality and Human Rights Commission, the body that enforces the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales. The United Kingdom Supreme Court's unanimous judgment of 16 April 2025 in the For Women Scotland challenge held that "woman" and "sex" in the Act mean biological woman and biological sex, so a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. Those definitions fix what a trans visitor can expect from services, searches and detention allocation in England.

The operative enforcement guidance a visitor meets at venues, transport and services is the Commission's code of practice, updated on 20 May 2025 after the Supreme Court ruling. It advises that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety.

Custody decisions in England stand under the same Supreme Court holding that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex. A judicial review reported on 5 February 2026 was testing how far that ruling reaches into prison accommodation across the whole state, with government lawyers arguing that a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while the challengers called an identity-based policy "Orwellian".

The Home Office's England-and-Wales bulletin published on 9 October 2025 records 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025, with the transgender strand down 11% and the sexual-orientation strand down 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence: the Crime Survey estimate is about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year. These are the official baseline for trans-hostile incidents in the jurisdiction where the national framework applies directly.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in England (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 1970 Corbett v Corbett barred transgender people from changing the sex marker on their birth certificate, which also prevented legal marriage to a person of the other gender as it would have been treated as an unrecognised same-sex marriage. In 1996 P v S and Cornwall County Council held that European anti-gender discrimination law applied to trans people, and in 2002 Goodwin v United Kingdom found the UK in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights for maintaining that status quo, leading to the Gender Recognition Act 2004. A December 2002 Lord Chancellor's policy document categorically stated that transsexualism "is not a mental illness." Since 4 April 2005 the Gender Recognition Act 2004 has allowed transgender people to change legal gender and obtain a new birth certificate giving full recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. Applicants must present evidence to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate, must have transitioned for two years before issuance, and are not required to have undergone sex reassignment surgery though such surgery counts as supporting evidence, with formal approval for medical gender reassignment available on the NHS or privately. Under the Act as originally framed, a married transgender applicant was required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance of a certificate, and a married couple including a transgender partner could not directly re-register but had to dissolve the marriage, obtain gender recognition, then register for civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs. ILGA-Europe's executive in 2020 expressed concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" as the UK fell to ninth place with 66%, dropping further to 22nd place with 45% by 2025. The 1533 Buggery Act made male anal sex a civil offence punishable by death in England and Wales, later removed as capital by section 61 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 while male homosexual acts remained imprisonable, and lesbian acts were never criminalised as civilian offences. The Sexual Offences Act 1967, receiving royal assent 27 July 1967, provided limited decriminalisation in England and Wales only where the act was consensual, in private limited to two persons, and both were aged 21, a higher threshold than 16 for heterosexual acts and strictly interpreted to exclude hotel rooms or homes with a third person present. Equalisation came through the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000, in force 8 January 2001, lowering the age of consent to 16 throughout the UK and for the first time creating an age of consent for lesbian acts, followed by the Sexual Offences Act 2003 in force 1 May 2004 which removed privacy conditions and created sex-neutral offences. Section 28, introduced in the 1980s to prohibit "promotion of homosexuality" by schools and local authorities, was repealed in 2003, while discrimination protections in place since 1999 were extended to all areas by the Equality Act 2010 and the ban on open service by LGBT personnel was officially lifted in 2016 after non-enforcement since 2000. The Merchant Shipping (Homosexual Conduct) Act 2017 repealed sections 146(4) and 147(3) of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, and the Policing and Crime Act 2017 in effect 31 January 2017 provided posthumous pardons and a disregard application process for historic convictions, with "disregards" available since 2012 under the Protection of Freedoms Act. Civil partnerships with most rights of marriage were legalised by the Civil Partnership Act 2004 effective 5 December 2005, adoption by same-sex couples in England and Wales took effect 30 December 2005 under the Adoption and Children Act 2002, and same-sex marriage in England and Wales was allowed by the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 in force 13 March 2014 with first marriages 29 March 2014. ILGA-Europe gave the UK the highest score in Europe in 2015 with 86% progress toward "respect of human rights and full equality" for LGBT people, but the score fell to 66% and ninth place by 2020.

82085004B13995298844162.name: Queensland
82085004B13995298844162.summary:
Queensland is a state within Australia and stands under the national framework, while carrying its own layer of gender-identity law. Amendments to the Anti-Discrimination Act commenced on 29 April 2024, moving serious vilification out of that Act and into the Criminal Code with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment, raised from six months. The amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity, as stated by the Queensland Human Rights Commission. The Queensland Human Rights Commission separately announced stronger discrimination protections for gender-diverse people as part of an Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 rewrite, describing a modernised 'gender identity' attribute and revised vilification provisions.

Queensland was the first Australian state to enact a criminal ban on conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the Queensland parliament on 13 August 2020, criminalising practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity, with fines and jail time for practitioners; the maximum penalty is 18 months' imprisonment plus fines. Survivors told SBS the law does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Gender identity is a protected attribute under Queensland's anti-discrimination law, with state protections for sexuality and gender identity introduced in 2002. Transgender and intersex Queenslanders can update government records and birth certificates: the formal divorce requirements for such updates were repealed in 2018, and the surgery requirements were repealed in 2024. Since 1 September 2021 Queensland formally includes the 'X' non-binary option on marriage certificates, forms and documents alongside male and female.

Healthcare access for trans minors is the sharpest adverse measure in force. Queensland's Health Minister Tim Nicholls halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria in January 2025, formalised by a 28 January 2025 Queensland Health directive that exempts existing Queensland Children's Gender Service patients. Equality Australia called Queensland an 'outlier state'. The ban remains legally contested, and affected families report private treatment costs of hundreds of dollars per injection, nearly $2,000 in one case.

Queensland's criminal and relationship law is comparatively permissive. Private consensual sex between men has been legal since 1991 and lesbian sexual acts were never criminalised; the age of consent was equalised to 16 for all sexual acts in 2016, Queensland being the last Australian jurisdiction to do so, replacing section 208's penalty of up to 14 years for anal sex involving a person under 18. A 2017 law expunging criminal records of men convicted of consensual homosexual acts took effect on 30 June 2018, and the gay panic defence was abolished in 2017. Same-sex couples may enter a civil partnership under state law or live in an unregistered de facto relationship recognised since 2002, and may become parents through adoption, foster care, altruistic surrogacy and, for lesbian couples, IVF, with adoption eligibility open since 11 November 2016.

82085004B14973555098025.name: South Australia
82085004B14973555098025.summary:
South Australia stands under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. The precedent binds service providers nationally, including in South Australia.

State law supplies a parallel remedy. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to protect gender identity and sexual orientation, so discrimination on that ground is actionable under South Australian statute as well as federal statute.

Identity documents are the clearest visitor-facing advantage. Since 23 May 2017, under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016 (royal assent 15 December 2016), a South Australian can change the sex descriptor on a birth certificate with appropriate clinical treatment, with no sex-reassignment surgery required and no forced divorce if married. Non-binary and 'indeterminate' sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates. With the ACT, South Australia was one of the first two Australian jurisdictions to allow the sex recorded on a birth certificate to be changed without sex-reassignment surgery.

Hate-crime sentencing laws explicitly covering sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021, giving trans visitors protection at sentencing that some other Australian states lack.

Relationship recognition is settled: registered domestic relationships date from 1 August 2017, same-sex couples could adopt from 17 February 2017, and same-sex marriage has been legal since December 2017 under the federal Act, with the 2017 postal survey returning a 62.5% 'Yes' result in South Australia.

Criminal-law history runs in a protective direction. South Australia was the first Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexual activity, the law commencing 2 October 1975, and it was the last to abolish the gay-panic defence, doing so on 1 December 2020 with effect from 1 April 2021. The Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 passed in October 2024 and is in legal effect from 1 April 2025.

Historical convictions are handled by a distinctive scheme: South Australia is the only Australian jurisdiction whose approach to historical gay convictions is 'spent' rather than expunged, under the Spent Convictions (Decriminalised Offences) Amendment Act 2013, in force 22 December 2013.

82085004B70793016411369.name: Tasmania
82085004B70793016411369.summary:
Tasmania stands under the Australian national framework, and its own layer adds protections beyond the federal floor. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 (Tas) prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics, and was amended in September 2013 to extend protections to transgender and intersex people and to prohibit offending, humiliating, intimidating, insulting or ridiculing a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. Tasmania is one of the Australian jurisdictions whose vilification law names gender identity as a protected ground.

Legal gender recognition in Tasmania is among the most permissive in Australia. The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment Act 2019 received royal assent on 8 May 2019 and took effect on 5 September 2019, permitting self-declared gender registration on Tasmanian-registered births with no medical certificate or other medical document required. A person aged 16 or over may register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or another self-described neither-entirely-male-nor-female gender by statutory declaration of identity and lived or seeking-to-live gender, subject to the Registrar's power to refuse terms outside the prescribed set. Parents or guardians may register a gender for children under 16, supported by the child's own gender declaration where able, or by statements of consistency with the child's will and preference with optional counselling evidence for those under 18. Birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and cannot be changed except to correct an initial error, but it ceases upon gender registration. The same reforms allow individuals to remove a gender descriptor entirely, allow parents to change the legal gender of their children, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. The 2019 legislation passed the House of Assembly on 10 April 2019 after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, having already cleared the Legislative Council; the Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal.

Historical offences carry an expungement and compensation regime. Cross-dressing was an offence under the Police Offences Act 1935 until its repeal in 2001, with Tasmania the only Australian state to have criminalised cross-dressing. Under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017 (royal assent 21 November 2017), charges and convictions for cross-dressing offences under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting, instigating, aiding or abetting, are eligible for expungement on application to the Secretary, or by specified representatives where the person is deceased or lacks capacity. Eligibility for expungement took effect 9 April 2018, with compensation payments of up to $75,000 effective 2 August 2026, following a parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

Tasmania decriminalised consensual homosexual activity through the Criminal Code Amendment Act 1997, passed 1 May 1997, royal assent 13 May 1997, in force the following day, after penalties of up to 21 years that were the harshest in the Western world and after the United Nations Human Rights Committee decision in Toonen on 31 March 1994 and the federal Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994. Tasmania was the final Australian jurisdiction to do so, refusing to repeal after that federal act commenced on 19 December 1994 and acting only when faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania. The age of consent in Tasmania is 17 years, equal for all forms of sexual activity and shared only with South Australia.

A hate crimes bill that explicitly includes gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act passed the lower house in September 2025, with the upper house yet to vote. As of September 2026, conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted in Tasmania. No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern of violence against trans people is documented in the sources held here.

82085004B12086860067424.name: Other Territories
82085004B12086860067424.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act 1984, which was amended by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status is prohibited alongside sex, marital or relationship status, pregnancy and breastfeeding across areas of public life including work, accommodation, education and the provision of goods and services. As a Commonwealth statute applying throughout Australia, including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, this is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor on Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Jervis Bay territory stands under.

In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Gigble that this protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Reuters reported the outcome on 23 August 2024 as a landmark case in gender-identity discrimination.

None of the territories in this group has its own territory-specific statute covering sexual orientation, gender identity or intersex status, and no divergence from the national framework is documented in the sources. Each instead sits inside a state legislative scheme: Norfolk Island has been incorporated into New South Wales legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016, while Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, the Australian Indian Ocean Territories, are jurisdictions where Western Australian laws apply. Jervis Bay territory stands under the national and New South Wales framework on the same basis.

The federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Vilification coverage beneath that layer remains uneven across Australia: New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also cover gender identity, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither.

No law in the parent framework confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering Australia or its territories. An 'X' sex descriptor on identity documents is available across the states and territories with concurrent federal protection, and same-sex adult private sexual conduct has been legal nationally since the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994.

Marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result in the national postal survey. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access is where official policy has tightened, and the tightest measures are in the state layer that governs these territories' neighbouring jurisdictions. Since November 2017 a transgender child could access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and doctors agree, with surgery generally unavailable until 18. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, exempting existing patients; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, and a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research.

Detention carries a stated rule with discretion attached in the jurisdictions whose law reaches these territories. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission, and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process. The 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.

Roraima stands under Brazil's national framework rather than a state statute of its own: the provisions on same-sex marriage, adoption, gender-marker recognition, anti-discrimination and custody placement described in the national record apply in Boa Vista and across the state without local modification, and the full national layer is carried by the parent record.

The measure is municipal and confined to athletics; it does not alter criminal law, document rules or entry conditions for a visitor.

Roraima State Ordinance No. 1,797/2023 is a state-level instrument directed at combating homophobia, placing the state government on the record in favour of protection rather than restriction.

sources.summary: Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, though civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International reports that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections.

An OAB/SP guide for expatriates states that Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Major cities including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

14911670B26412867168762.name: Amapa
14911670B26412867168762.summary:
Amapá's own legal layer sits on top of the national framework. Law No. 1,417/2009 provides administrative sanctions for discrimination motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation within the state public service. State Law No. 2,790/2022 makes discrimination on those grounds a crime, and Ordinary Law No. 2,710/2022 typifies anti-LGBTQ discrimination at state sports venues, football stadiums included, as an administrative offence. State Law No. 1,680/2012 established the State Day to Combat Homophobia, observed each 27 May.

Two state bodies carry the protection machinery: the State Council for Combating Discrimination and CELGBT, which run awareness campaigns and issue public repudiations of discriminatory acts against the LGBTQIAPN+ population. The source inventory contains no state-level enforcement statistics or case outcomes for these laws, so how they operate in practice cannot be assessed from the material available.

Civil-registry rectification is handled locally. On 19 February 2022 the Public Defender's Office of Amapá filed the state's first request for name and gender rectification on behalf of a non-binary person, treating the request as legally viable on the same self-determination basis as for transgender people and arguing that the registry should reflect social presentation. The procedure follows the ordinary civil-registry alteration process, and the Defender's Office assists applicants. Since 2022 the office has made legal gender change accessible to non-binary people in the state.

Gender-affirming care is available through the public system. On 13 February 2025 the Macapá municipal government opened the state's first Municipal Trans Outpatient Clinic, at the Papaléo Paes Specialties Center, running Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 17:00. It offers free multidisciplinary transition care to trans, travesti and non-binary people with no age restriction: general medicine, nursing, endocrinology, gynecology, dermatology, psychiatry, urology, cardiology, psychology, nutrition, social work, physiotherapy, speech therapy, dentistry, laboratory tests, ultrasound, mammography, densitometry, vaccination, rapid tests, Pap smear collection and dressings, with testosterone cypionate and estradiol supplied under clinical protocol. Entry is by referral from a basic health unit or by walking in; the first appointment is a general-practitioner evaluation with onward referral, and clinical demands unrelated to gender transition are excluded. Statewide gender-affirming services also run through the University Hospital of the Federal University of Amapá and the AMA-LBTI Center, which serves lesbian, bisexual, travesti, transsexual and intersex women.

Family formation has drawn judicial attention. In mid-2025 the Court of Justice of Amapá ran the campaign "Every form of love can also be family" under CNJ Resolution No. 532/2023, aimed at ensuring transgender people face no discrimination during the adoption qualification process. Adoption by same-sex couples has been recognised in the state since the national 2010 ruling; a couple from Santana obtained an adoption in 2016 after six years of proceedings, and in 2017 the Legislative Assembly considered a bill extending maternity or paternity leave to same-sex adoptive couples on the same terms as heterosexual families.

14911670B46798344041190.name: Amazonas
14911670B46798344041190.summary:
Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework, and adds its own layer of protection. State Ordinary Law No. 3079 of 12 September 2006 prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity across employment, housing and other areas, and a provision in force since 2 August 2006 prohibits the manufacture, sale and distribution of symbols inciting discrimination, prejudice, hatred or violence on gender-identity grounds.

Non-binary recognition is not available in practice through Amazonas registries. In 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person in the state to obtain recognition, doing so only after a rectification in Rio de Janeiro and an intervention by the Amazonas Public Defenders Office in Manaus, where no gender-neutral marker existed. Non-binary recognition in the state remains decided case by case.

Facilities are a live exposure in the state capital. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a municipal law prohibiting unisex or multigender restrooms, and Equaldex records that bathroom access in Amazonas carries no explicit legal protection.

Access to gender-affirming care is contested on two fronts. On 10 June 2025 the governor of Amazonas signed Law 7552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. In the opposite direction, in November 2023 the State Public Defenders Office opened a collective procedure to monitor public health services for trans and travesti people, covering hormone treatment, outpatient services and the refusal of authorisation for transsexualising surgeries including sexual reassignment surgery; after an October 2023 meeting, Manaus municipal health officials committed to dispensing standardised medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions for hormone therapy and to designating reference primary-care units in each zone of the city, and the state health secretariat was required to report on gaps in equitable care and hormone therapy. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutors Office recommended that Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualisation services, including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and for presentation to the Ministry of Health.

Recorded violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas is thin and structurally undercounted. Research published in the Brazilian Journal of Public Security finds that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are underreported, and the Brazilian Public Security Forum has registered 43 cases. For 2021-2022, crimes reported in Manaus and the interior involving homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual persons accounted for 0.36% of all reports, with homophobia and transphobia motives and the categories of gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality absent from the records; LGBT victim data were few and poorly structured, victims were not infrequently recorded as perpetrators because of failures in police occurrence reports, and public agents were unprepared to handle these demands. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with residents reporting that he had been bullied by other young people in the region.

State and municipal law also restricts LGBTQ expression and public presence. Amazonas Ordinary Law No. 6463, enacted 10 October 2023, expressly prohibits the use of neutral language, non-binary dialect or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public agencies across the state. State Law 6469 of 2023 prohibits the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades, with fines of up to 10,000 reais for non-compliance. On 17 October 2024 the Legislative Assembly enacted a law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality; it was amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and instead prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media.

Protection machinery exists at state level alongside those restrictions. In 2021 the State Public Defenders Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group, focused on human rights violations and on training security agents. In August 2024 the Amazonas State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right, aimed at LGBTQ youth expelled from their homes, which states that conversion therapies are prohibited and ineffective and points readers to the Specialized Human Rights Public Defender's Office. In November 2012 a judge of the Amazonas Court of Justice authorised the state's first adoption by a same-sex couple.

14911670B46798344041190.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the country's national framework, and adds its own layer of protection. state/province Ordinary Law No. 3079 of 12 September 2006 prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity across employment, housing and other areas, and a provision in force since 2 August 2006 prohibits the manufacture, sale and distribution of symbols inciting discrimination, prejudice, hatred or violence on gender-identity grounds.

Non-binary recognition is not available in practice through the state/province's registries. In 2022 a resident became the first non-binary person in the state/province to obtain recognition, doing so only after a rectification in another state/province and an intervention by the state/province Public Defenders Office in the capital, where no gender-neutral marker existed. Non-binary recognition in the state/province remains decided case by case.

Facilities are a live exposure in the state/province capital. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of the capital signed a municipal law prohibiting unisex or multigender restrooms, and a global equality index records that bathroom access in the state/province carries no explicit legal protection.

Access to gender-affirming care is contested on two fronts. On 10 June 2025 the governor of the state/province signed Law 7552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. In the opposite direction, in November 2023 the State Public Defenders Office opened a collective procedure to monitor public health services for trans and travesti people, covering hormone treatment, outpatient services and the refusal of authorisation for transsexualising surgeries including sexual reassignment surgery; after an October 2023 meeting, municipal health officials committed to dispensing standardised medications on a public ambulatory prescription for hormone therapy and to designating reference primary-care units in each zone of the capital, and the state health secretariat was required to report on gaps in equitable care and hormone therapy. In August 2024 a national prosecutors' office recommended that the state/province formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualisation services, including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and for presentation to the national health ministry.

Recorded violence against LGBTQ people in the state/province is thin and structurally undercounted. Research published in a national public security journal finds that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state/province are underreported, and a national public security forum has registered 43 cases. For 2021-2022, crimes reported in the capital and the interior involving homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual persons accounted for 0.36% of all reports, with homophobia and transphobia motives and the categories of gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality absent from the records; LGBT victim data were few and poorly structured, victims were not infrequently recorded as perpetrators because of failures in police occurrence reports, and public agents were unprepared to handle these demands. On 5 July 2025 a man was beaten and killed in the capital after reacting to homophobic insults, with residents reporting that he had been bullied by other young people in the region.

state/province and municipal law also restricts LGBTQ expression and public presence. state/province Ordinary Law No. 6463, enacted 10 October 2023, expressly prohibits the use of neutral language, non-binary dialect or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public agencies throughout the state/province. State Law 6469 of 2023 prohibits the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades, with fines of up to 10,000 reais for non-compliance. On 17 October 2024 the state/province legislature enacted a law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality; it was amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and instead prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media.

Protection machinery exists at state level alongside those restrictions. In 2021 the State Public Defenders Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group, focused on human rights violations and on training security agents. In August 2024 the state/province Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right, aimed at LGBTQ youth expelled from their homes, which states that conversion therapies are prohibited and ineffective and points readers to the Specialized Human Rights Public Defender's Office. In November 2012 a judge of the state/province Court of Justice authorised the state/province's first adoption by a same-sex couple.

14911670B32365136910534.name: Piaui
14911670B32365136910534.summary:
Piauí stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, and the sources record no state-level departure from it beyond the measures set out below. Homosexuality is legal in the state. Piauí has carried its own statutory ban on discrimination based on sexual orientation since Ordinary Law No. 5,431 was signed by the Governor on 29 December 2004.

Ordinary Law No. 5,916, enacted on 10 November 2009 and published on 12 November 2009, guarantees travestis and transexuais the right to be identified by their social name on registrations, forms, medical records and related documents when using the services of any direct or indirect body of the state public administration. The law defines the social name as the name by which these people recognise themselves and are recognised socially, requires it to appear first and prominently with the civil identification below, directs the Executive to designate, within 60 days, the body responsible for registering and issuing social-name identification, and retains use of the civil name where public interest or the rights of third parties require it.

Family recognition in Piauí runs through the notaries rather than the courts. From 14 December 2012 the Court of Justice of Piauí authorised every notary in the state to issue marriage licences to same-sex couples, with no judge's approval needed; the change was published in the Diário de Justiça on 17 December 2012. In 2012 Judge Maria Luiza de Moura de Melo e Freitas of the 1st Children and Youth Court granted adoption rights to a lesbian couple who had lived together in a stable union since 2007.

On 20 July 2021 the Court of Justice of Piauí authorised a non-binary person to rectify their documents to reflect their gender identity, the first recognition of a non-binary gender marker in the state. The sources do not establish whether that route is now available routinely at registries across Piauí.

In Teresina, the state capital, the City Council approved a bill on 17 June 2026 by 12 votes in favour, 5 against and one abstention prohibiting transgender women and travestis from using women's public restrooms. Mayor Sílvio Mendes signed it into law on 30 July 2026, after LGBTQ rights activists protested that the bill is unconstitutional. The measure is municipal rather than statewide, and the sources record no court ruling on its validity.

A 2015 Grupo Gay da Bahia report listed Piauí as the second Brazilian state with the highest risk of LGBTQ people being murdered. That ordering is by raw count with no per-capita or population denominator supplied, and the underlying methodology counts all media-reported murders of LGBTQ people irrespective of motive, a method critics call unscientific. The figure is LGBTQ-wide and is not specific to transgender people.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

OutRight International's report states that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

14911670B96632893955983.name: Acre
14911670B96632893955983.summary:
Acre is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried in the Brazil record: nationwide marriage, gender-marker self-declaration and the 2019 criminalisation of transphobia on the same footing as racism apply here as elsewhere in the country. What Acre adds is a state and municipal layer of anti-discrimination, social-name and document-rectification instruments, and a documented pattern of social friction outside the capital.

Assessments of Brazil describe enforcement as uneven in practice. Smaller cities and rural areas, including those in Acre, may present more social friction than the major cities despite identical legal rights.

Violence data for the state is thin. The Associação de Homossexuais do Acre recorded 18 murders of homosexual people in the state between 2007 and 2018, 14 of them in Rio Branco. That is a raw count over eleven years with no per-capita denominator published, so it does not by itself establish Acre as more dangerous than a larger or smaller state. State government and Public Prosecutor's Office material issued in January 2025 states that no trans deaths were recorded in Acre in 2024.

Rio Branco Law 2389, enacted 30 December 2020 and in force from 5 January 2021, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in the municipality and reaches conduct a visitor is likely to meet: refusing entry or stay in any public or private establishment open to the public, selective service not required by law, denying or surcharging hotel, motel or pension lodging, denying or surcharging the rental, purchase or lending of property, restricting access to buses and taxis, refusing school enrolment, and inciting discrimination or violence through any medium. Individuals and legal entities are liable. Penalties run from a warning and a fine set by municipal regulation to suspension of activities or operating licence for up to 30 days and interdiction or loss of licence, graded by gravity, recidivism and economic capacity. Any resident may complain, with confidentiality on request.

State Law 3,355 of 18 December 2017 guarantees the nome social in all acts, registrations, records and forms of the state's direct and indirect public administration. Rondônia stands under the national framework of Brazil. 14911670B86532577506919.name: Sergipe
14911670B86532577506919.summary:
Sergipe stands under Brazil's national framework and adds a layer of its own. Homosexuality is legal in the state, and Sergipe was among the first states in Brazil, with Mato Grosso do Sul, to write a ban on sexual-orientation discrimination into its state constitution in 1989. On 5 July 2012 the State Judiciary Power issued Provimento nº 06/2012, which regulated same-sex marriage throughout the state.

On 17 December 2025 Sergipe became the first Brazilian state to prohibit discrimination based on gender identity in its own constitution. Constitutional Amendment No. 59, proposed by state representative Linda Brasil (PSOL), amended article 3(II) of the State Constitution to guarantee state-level protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, with violators subject to punishment by law effective upon promulgation.

Since 2025 Sergipe has allowed individuals to change the gender marker on their documents to non-binary.

On 28 August 2025 the Court of Justice of Sergipe announced gender-neutral restrooms at the Palácio da Justiça in Aracaju, operating on the ground, 1st and 8th floors and usable by any person regardless of gender identity. The same announcement mandates that in all Sergipe judiciary units male and female bathrooms be used in a way that respects each person's gender identity, and requires gender-equity demands to be built into all new constructions and renovations.

Restrictive initiatives sit alongside these protections. On 1 December 2020 state representative Rodrigo Valadares (UNIÃO) tabled a bill to prohibit the use and teaching of gender-neutral language in Sergipe's public and private schools and in state public offices, requiring traditional Portuguese in schools, official notices and public offices.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), with joint adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015) and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option exists nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. Salabert and Hilton, the first transgender federal legislators, were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report, 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, updated April 2026): Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper - same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia/transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice: major cities (Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Florianopolis) are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

14911670B72497658138655.name: Tocantins
14911670B72497658138655.summary:
Tocantins has no state statute of its own prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; the absence of such a law is recorded by the state's own Public Defender's Office. Protection in Palmas and across the interior therefore rests on Brazil's national framework, which applies here without any state-level variation. Same-sex marriage has applied in Tocantins since 2013 and joint adoption since 2010, under that national framework rather than any Tocantins enactment.

Name and gender-marker rectification in Tocantins is administrative. Trans men, trans women, non-binary, queer and travesti persons may request rectification of first name and/or gender marker at the civil registry where their birth was registered, on gender self-determination alone, with no medical or psychological report, no proof of surgery and no proof of hormonal treatment, following the Supreme Federal Court's understanding since 2018 and National Council of Justice norms. The change takes full legal effect in the birth certificate and in all official documents. The procedure is free on proof of inability to pay, and judicial recourse arises only if the request is denied. Rectification to a non-binary or unspecified gender is the exception: it requires a judicial decision.

Tocantins's own institutions have built the machinery for this. In August 2022 the Public Defender's Office of Tocantins asked the state General Inspectorate of Justice to authorise inclusion of the term "non-binary" in documents, and in 2023 the General Inspectorate published a resolution authorising non-binary people to change their documents to carry a third gender option. On 31 January 2023 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Tocantins issued Provimento No. 3, consolidating extrajudicial service norms and providing civil-registry procedures for registering a birth with a transgender parent and for the averbação of an altered first name and sex for transgender and non-binary persons. On 29 January 2026 the state Public Defender's Office published guidance explaining the name and gender-marker change process for trans people.

In Palmas, on 27 August 2018, Supreme Federal Court Justice Luís Roberto Barroso suspended the article of a municipal law that prohibited teaching about gender and sexuality in schools, allowing such teaching to proceed.

14911670B28216513632935.name: Espirito Santo
14911670B28216513632935.summary:
Espirito Santo stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, which applies uniformly in every state of the country. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, binding on all civil registries after a 14-1 vote, and on 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled, in the ADO 26 case, that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines.

A trans visitor entering Espirito Santo is handled on the same footing as anyone else in matters of entry, status and family law. Name and gender-marker changes require no surgery, spousal-visa equality applies, joint adoption has been available since 2015, and LGB people serve openly in the armed forces. Explicit national discrimination protections have been in force since 2019.

The protective framework is thinner in places than it appears. Outright International's 2026 country status records that the 2019 ruling makes discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity federally criminal, but that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists, and that repeal efforts are active in Congress. The Superior Court of Justice ruled in 2023 that nonbinary people may amend their civil records, while intersex people still lack specific legal protections.

Within Espirito Santo the practical picture splits by settlement size. Larger cities carry established legal infrastructure for name changes, marriage registration and counsel, whereas smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction for visibly trans people. The state's capital region and its interior municipalities are therefore not equivalent settings for a trans traveller.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Espirito Santo (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person may change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 22 January 2025 the Public Defender's Office of Espirito Santo filed suit to secure name and gender rectification for a non-binary person from Vitoria, and the court granted the request and authorized rectification. On 27 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly with the Public Defender's Office held a free event to facilitate name and gender changes on official documents for trans, non-binary and travesti individuals. On 6 June 2022 the Vitoria City Council approved a bill to ban installation of unisex restrooms in the city, which had not yet been vetoed or signed by the mayor. On 14 April 2024 the Legislative Assembly approved a bill to restrict athletes' participation in competitions based on biological sex, which Governor Renato Casagrande vetoed on 28 April. On 3 August 2012 a judge in Colatina authorized registration of the marriage of lesbian couple Ediana Calixto and Kamila Roccon as the first same-sex marriage recognized in the state. The State Public Prosecutor's Office appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August, then on 20 September the state Court of Justice reversed and authorized recognition. On 15 August 2012 the General Inspectorate of Justice issued a Circular Letter requiring all Civil Registries to treat same-sex marriage the same as opposite-sex couples, making Espirito Santo the third Brazilian state to address the subject statewide. In 2015 the city of Cachoeiro de Itapemirim passed a law prohibiting "ideological indoctrination" in city schools. On 21 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. LGBTQ rights organizations sued in the Supreme Federal Court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck down the law in May 2026 by an 8-2 vote with Justice Carmen Lucia stating it violated the Brazilian Constitution.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mato Grosso do Sul (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In March 2026 the Campo Grande City Council approved by a vote of 13-11 a bill prohibiting transgender women from using women's public restrooms. On April 29 the Public Defender's Office of Mato Grosso do Sul opened an investigation to examine the city's law. On May 5th Congresswoman Erika Hilton denounced the law to the Brazilian Federal Prosecution Office. On 18 July 2026 the Public Defender's Office of Mato Grosso do Sul announced that non-binary people could change their documents to reflect their gender identity through court decisions. Homosexuality is legal in Mato Grosso do Sul. In 1989 Mato Grosso do Sul enacted a state constitutional provision banning discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. It was among the first states in Brazil to do so, alongside Sergipe. On 2 April 2013 the Court of Mato Grosso do Sul authorized marriage between same-sex couples in the state.

14911670B46470234103867.name: Sao Paulo
14911670B46470234103867.summary:
São Paulo state stands under Brazil's national framework, which is applied uniformly across all 27 states. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, binding on every civil registry after a 14-1 vote, and joint adoption has been available since 2015. Name and gender-marker changes require no surgery, spousal-visa equality operates on the same footing as for any other traveller, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people serve openly in the armed forces. A trans visitor's documents and status are therefore handled on the ordinary terms at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Transphobia is prosecuted on that footing, and the provision has been applied to commercial conduct inside the state: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. A visitor who faces discriminatory conduct in São Paulo can invoke the same provision.

No specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists; the protection rests on the 2019 ruling and constitutional provisions, and repeal efforts have been tabled in Congress. In 2023 the Superior Court of Justice allowed non-binary people to amend their civil records, while intersex people have no specific legal protections.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city that hosts Pride events drawing thousands of tourists.

Arrest carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, ask trans, travesti and intersex people their preference, and record it in a reasoned decision. Placement can be changed later, transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine, and documents that travestis and trans women are held in masculine-operated units, with some placed in so-called neutral or security units; it treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Comparable national norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

14911670B30315977547221.name: Parana
14911670B30315977547221.summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record.

Access to sex-separated facilities is contested in Paraná's own legislature and councils. In 2021 state representative Mara Lima introduced a bill banning unisex bathrooms statewide and requiring separate male and female facilities; on 16 November 2021 the Curitiba City Council approved a municipal bill of the same kind introduced by councilman Ezequias Barros. On 4 October 2023 the Curitiba City Council passed a protest motion against Resolution 2/2023 of the federal Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, which told educational institutions to guarantee bathroom and changing-room use according to each student's gender identity. The Ministry had stated that the resolution was not binding and obliged no school to adopt it, and the Curitiba vote was symbolic, to be converted into an official letter to the federal government.

Civil registry markers in Paraná have moved in both directions within a two-year span. In 2023 the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of 'non-binary' in the civil registry gender marker, then revoked it in November 2023, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to 'male' and 'female' only. In 2025 the same court authorized a third gender option on documents.

Municipal sport rules in Londrina are the most litigated local restriction. On 26 April 2024 Londrina enacted a law banning transgender people from competing according to gender identity, with a R$10,000 fine for non-compliance. On 26 February 2026 the City Council approved a motion to bar transgender athlete Tiffanny Abreu from the Brazilian Women's Volleyball Cup; the Brazilian Volleyball Confederation filed suit in the Supreme Federal Court and Justice Cármen Lúcia issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing her to compete. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organizations filed suit against the Londrina law in the Supreme Federal Court, and on 7 August 2026 rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin voted to strike the law down.

Same-sex civil marriage has been available across Paraná since 26 March 2013, when the state authorized it in all cartórios under the same procedure and documentation as heterosexual marriage and allowed conversion of a stable union into marriage without judicial authorization. The General Inspector of Justice of Paraná ruled the same day that same-sex marriage and the conversion of stable unions to marriage must use normal marriage procedures.

Curitiba registered what the source describes as the first recognition of a same-sex union in Brazil, in 2004, granting common-law marriage status to an English-Brazilian couple who had cohabited fourteen years, a status previously limited to opposite-sex couples.

Family formation has been tested repeatedly in Paraná's courts. On 14 May 2009 the 2nd Court of Childhood, Youth and Adoption granted the first gay-couple adoption in the state to a Curitiba couple, finding a stable and affectionate union able to raise a child in a healthy environment. On 27 October 2010 Judge Sergio Luiz Kreuz in Cascavel authorized irreversible adoption of an eight-year-old child with cerebral palsy by a gay couple together twelve years, under Superior Court of Justice precedent. On 16 September 2011 Maringá justice authorized adoption of two children by a lesbian couple.

14911670B68448774564157.name: Rio Grande do Sul
14911670B68448774564157.summary:
Rio Grande do Sul stands under Brazil's national legal framework for LGBTI people. The sources covering this state record no deviation from that framework material enough to distinguish it, so a trans visitor in Rio Grande do Sul is governed by the same rules that apply in every other Brazilian state.

Same-sex marriage has been available nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds all civil registries and was adopted in a 14-1 vote. Spousal-visa equality and joint adoption follow from the same regime, with adoption rights in place since 2015. An expat legal guide updated on 5 April 2026 confirms that name and gender-marker changes require no surgery, so a visitor's documents are assessed on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Explicit national discrimination protections on those grounds have been in force since 2019, and courts have applied them to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

The text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. The same overview reports that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists, that repeal efforts are before Congress, and that intersex people lack specific protections.

Conditions vary with the size of place. Larger cities have legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction. Rio Grande do Sul has a substantial rural interior beyond the capital region, where that friction falls thickest and formal support is thinnest.

Arrest and imprisonment carry a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are detained are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, ask trans, travesti and intersex people which they prefer, and record the declared preference. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

The 13 Jun 2019 ADO 26 ruling makes homophobia and transphobia crimes equivalent to racism. Larger cities have legal infrastructure, and smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rio Grande do Sul (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2019, discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 1 March 2018, the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person may change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 27 January 2020, the Rio Grande do Sul government installed signs in women's restrooms of state government offices stating use in accordance with gender identity and installed unisex restrooms. In August 2021, Special Secretary of Culture Mário Frias criticized those restroom measures as posing risks to children. On 22 April 2022, Rio Grande do Sul Justice allowed non-binary people to change first name and sex in the birth record to include 'non-binary' upon request to a notary without judicial authorization, but in December 2023 the Court of Justice revoked that provision. On 28 September 2025, a Porto Alegre court ordered a bar to pay 10,000 reais compensation for denying a trans man access to the men's restroom, and on 28 May 2026 an appellate court overturned that decision. Homosexuality is legal in Rio Grande do Sul. On 19 December 2002, the Legislative Assembly enacted State Law No. 14,896 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation. On 29 May 2012, four of six notaries in Porto Alegre agreed to convert civil unions into marriages. On 11 November 2005, a Bagé judge permitted adoption of two brothers by a lesbian couple in a seven-year stable union, described as Brazil's first LGBTQ adoption. On 6 April 2006, same-sex couples in committed relationships were allowed to register at any notary office with rights to jointly own property, establish custody of children, and claim pensions and property on a partner's death. On 27 April 2010, the Superior Court of Justice recognized shared adoption of two sons by Bagé lesbian couple Lídia Brignol Guterres and Luciana Reis Maidana to secure pension, separation and inheritance rights. On 3 June 2011, Pelotas justice authorized adoption of a four-year-old by a gay couple with the biological mother's consent.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court - 2019 nationwide gender identity discrimination ban
sources.summary: On 24 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia and homophobia as equivalent to racism, punishable under Brazil's racism law until Congress enacts specific LGBT-protection legislation.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 on name and sex change
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Federal Supreme Court held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression as a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize, and therefore authorized change of name and gender on the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization.

sources.title: Statement by Special Secretary of Culture Mario Frias - August 2021
sources.summary: In August 2021, Rio Grande do Sul's Secretariat of Culture maintained a women's bathroom designated as inclusive of trans women and travestis, which federal Special Secretary of Culture Mario Frias publicly criticized.

sources.title: Rio Grande do Sul Justice provision of 22 April 2022 on non-binary rectification
sources.summary: On 22 April 2022 the Rio Grande do Sul judiciary authorized non-binary people to change first name and gender directly in civil registry offices in RS.

sources.title: Porto Alegre court order of 28 September 2025 - bar restroom denial case
sources.summary: In Porto Alegre on 28 September 2025 a court condemned a bar for preventing a trans man from using the men's restroom.

sources.title: Appellate court decision of 28 May 2026 overturning restroom case
sources.summary: On 28 May 2026 in Rio Grande do Sul, the judiciary acquitted a nightclub of a transfobia allegation.

1811400B75807316846587.name: Madhya Pradesh
1811400B75807316846587.summary:
Madhya Pradesh has no state-specific transgender statute and no documented state-level enforcement series. Legal uniformity across the country sets the deviation at ±0.02, so a visitor to Madhya Pradesh is assessed against the national framework rather than any provincial rule.

That framework was altered on 25 March 2026, when India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. The amendment replaces the self-identification route affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014 with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Recognition now rests on medical certification. The amendment makes medical-board and district-authority certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery and conditions identity recognition on medical certification, a direct documents consequence for a trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. The bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
