1811400B6111924962807.name: Goa
1811400B6111924962807.summary:
Goa stands under India's national framework: the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 and the amendment passed by Parliament on 25 March 2026 operate in this state as in every other state and union territory, and no Goan statute or enforcement pattern diverging from the national position is on file.

Goa has taken one region-specific step under that framework. On 7 May 2025 the state constituted a 14-member Model Transgender Welfare Board, headed by the Chief Secretary, under the 2019 Act and its 2020 Rules, to oversee implementation of welfare schemes and safeguard transgender persons' rights in healthcare, education, employment and housing.

Registration and visibility of trans Goans remain very low. The 2011 Census recorded 398 transgender persons in Goa out of 487,803 nationally. As of 2024 only 12 transgender people were listed on Goan electoral rolls, the first registrations having occurred in 2022.

A 2018 Goa Livelihoods Forum study found that 87% of transgender respondents had dropped out of school because of harassment, an indicator of the social environment a trans visitor may observe.

Same-sex activity was decriminalised nationally in 2018 by Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, and federal law has recognised transgender identity since NALSA v. Union of India in 2014. The 2019 Act prohibits discrimination based on gender identity.

Goa applies the Goa Civil Code, which defines marriage as between a man and a woman; there is no legal recognition for same-sex marriages or civil unions in the state. After the Supreme Court's 2023 decision not to legalise same-sex marriage, activists in Goa urged legislative steps but no bills have been introduced. The Supreme Court noted in 2023 that same-sex couples have the right to cohabit and enjoy some protections under law.

There are currently no state-level anti-discrimination laws protecting sexual orientation in Goa.

sources.summary: Federal law has recognized transgender identity since NALSA v. Union of India in 2014. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. In 2025 Goa formed the Model Transgender Welfare Board under the provisions of that Act to facilitate welfare schemes for transgender people. In 16th century Goa, the Goa Inquisition criminalized same-sex activity with death penalty by burning to ashes and confiscation of property to the Crown, as applied in 1528 to a Muslim man and later to 16-year-old Portuguese army soldier Alberto Homem. Under the 1568 Constitutions of the Archbishopric of Goa, same-sex activity was classified as a serious sin punishable by deposition from office and lifelong penance in a religious institution for a clergyman and excommunication until repentance and required penance for a layman. In 1644 the Tribunal of Goa sought clarification on female same-sex acts and the majority concluded such acts generally did not constitute sodomy but sexual immorality rather than the crime of sodomy. Goa applies the Goa Civil Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman with no legal recognition for same-sex marriages or civil unions, though in 2023 the Supreme Court noted same-sex couples have the right to cohabit and enjoy some protections under law. Following the Supreme Court's 2023 decision not to legalize same-sex marriage, activists in Goa urged legislative steps but no bills have been introduced. There are currently no state-level anti-discrimination laws protecting sexual orientation in Goa.

1811400B21086746745937.name: Himāchal Pradesh
1811400B21086746745937.summary:
Himāchal Pradesh has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern of its own in the available sources; a visitor to the state therefore operates under India's national framework, which Parliament altered on 25 March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of reporting, with protests held in Mumbai on the day of passage. The amendment replaces the self-identification route established by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling and narrows legal recognition to the male and female categories together with historically accepted socio-cultural identities such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex people. Trans men, trans women and non-binary or gender-fluid people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

The amended scheme conditions recognition and surgery on official process. Certification from a medical board and a district authority is required for gender-affirming surgery, and identity recognition rests on medical certification rather than self-declaration. The amendment also adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender, amending the 2019 law. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay remains mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor to Himāchal Pradesh, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

Certification by a medical board and a district authority becomes mandatory, including for gender-affirming surgery. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

10402087B60055985875400.name: Baden-Württemberg
10402087B60055985875400.summary:
Baden-Württemberg stands under Germany's national framework, and no region-specific signal on trans visitor risk was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment applies.

Custody placement remains the sharpest documented exposure. Baden-Württemberg's own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, which operate on a binary men and women housing model. A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 reports that placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised: since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law is in force, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of Länder revised rules. Baden-Württemberg is not named among them.

The same analysis argues that no constitutional duty exists to anchor placement to the registered gender entry, since a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the gender entry; other Länder, implicitly or not at all, do so.

How placement is applied in practice has gone both ways. A July 2026 report concerns a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry who was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

10402087B44391416804171.name: Bremen
10402087B44391416804171.summary:
Bremen has no trans-specific statute or ordinance of its own. The city-state operates Germany's Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz) unchanged, and the federal criminal-law framework applies without local modification.

Under that act, adults over 18 may change their legal gender by self-determination rather than through the former medical and court pathway, with the change entered in the civil registry. In Bremen the entry is processed by the city-state's own registry offices, so the local administration of the procedure is a Bremen responsibility.

Prison placement is governed the same way. Bremen has no inmate-placement statute of its own; all German states tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender, section 6(1) of the Self-Determination Act allows state law to override the registered entry, and many states have enacted exception clauses. Where a Bremen inmate-placement question arises, the national framework is the operative standard rather than any local rule.

sources.summary: A 16 July 2026 France24/wire report covers the neo-Nazi prisoner in the 'Liebich' case, placed in a men's prison despite a legal gender change. The case drove Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The issue is framework-level for every Land, since prison administration and registry offices are Land competences.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of German state prison-placement rules under the Self-Determination Act: all Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender; § 6(1) SBGG lets state law override the entry, and many Länder have enacted exception clauses — some abstract (all inmates), some criticised as trans-targeted. Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions.

The article records that years of self-identification apply to adults without requiring the previous medical/court pathway, and that same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 October 2017. It confirms no Bremen-specific deviation: the city-state operates the unchanged federal act as of the article's coverage.

10402087B45896528657515.name: Hamburg
10402087B45896528657515.summary:
Hamburg stands under the federal framework of Germany. The Self-Determination Act (SBGG), in force since 1 November 2024, allows adults to change legal gender and first name in the civil registry by self-identification, without psychological evaluation or a court order; Hamburg's registry offices process the change, so a trans visitor's documents rest on that national regime rather than on any local instrument.

The Act replaced the earlier court-and-evaluation pathway, brought trans, inter and non-binary status regulation into a single statute, and revised the provisions of the Third Gender Act. Birth-register parent entries may still record the prior gender (for example, a trans woman listed as 'father'), though a 'parent' option is now available on birth certificates.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure, and prison administration is a Land competence, so Hamburg's prison service governs this directly. Under the Self-Determination Act, legal gender entry governs placement unless state law provides otherwise; constitutional doubts have been voiced about trans-targeted exception clauses in state correctional statutes. The July 2026 Neubrandenburg case, in which a court ordered male-prison placement despite a legal gender change, and the related placement of a prisoner in a men's prison despite a legal gender change reported on 16 July 2026, drove eastern Länder to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. No Hamburg-specific enforcement findings on trans prisoner placement are on file.

Prison administration is a Land competence.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of trans prisoner placement under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG, in force 1 Nov 2024): legal gender entry governs unless state law provides otherwise; constitutional doubts voiced about trans-targeted exception clauses. It anchors the July 2026 Neubrandenburg case (court-ordered male-prison placement despite legal gender change, DW/Telegraph 15-17 Jul 2026) that drove Länder action. No Hamburg-specific enforcement findings are on file.

10402087B60782008682549.name: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
10402087B60782008682549.summary:
The federal Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) governs legal gender recognition in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as in every other German Land. Approved by the federal cabinet in August 2023, passed by the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, and in force since 1 November 2024, it allows adults over 18 to change their legal first name and gender entry by self-declaration with three months' notice and no medical certification. No Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific trans statute, ordinance or placement reform is recorded in the sources; the federal framework applies here in full.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure in this Land. Under the Self-Determination Act, placement follows the prisoner's legal gender entry unless state law provides otherwise, and Länder prison statutes may contain either abstract exception clauses or clauses targeting trans prisoners specifically; which form is legitimate is actively debated. In July 2026 the Landgericht Neubrandenburg, sitting in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, ordered that a prisoner be held in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change. The case, known as the Liebich case and reported by France24 on 16 July 2026, prompted Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act.

Same-sex marriage with full marital and adoption rights has been available across Germany since 1 October 2017, under implementing legislation passed on 30 June 2017.

Legal gender recognition itself is straightforward on paper. The Self-Determination Act was approved by the federal cabinet in August 2023, passed the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, and has been in force since 1 November 2024. It lets any adult over 18 change their legal first name and gender entry by self-declaration with three months' notice.

Same-sex marriage with full adoption rights has held since 1 October 2017, under legislation passed 30 June 2017.

10402087B86022102756745.name: Nordrhein-Westfalen
10402087B86022102756745.summary:
North Rhine-Westphalia stands under the German federal framework. The Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, sets the default rule for housing a detained trans visitor: under § 6(1) the person's legal gender entry governs placement unless state law provides otherwise. Prison administration is dealt with at Land level, and the sources reviewed carry no trans-specific placement statute for North Rhine-Westphalia, so the federal default is the operative standard here rather than a local carve-out.

The Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 examines how the Länder apply that provision. Several states' exception clauses are criticised for singling out trans inmates specifically, while abstract clauses of the kind adopted in Rhineland-Palatinate are defended as compliant. North Rhine-Westphalia has enacted neither form, which leaves a trans visitor sentenced in the Land to be housed on the basis of registered gender unless an individual authority decides otherwise.

Placement outcomes under that default have not been uniform, and the federal Act itself is under political pressure: a Bundesrat initiative to tighten it was put forward by other states in July 2026. Any tightening would bind North Rhine-Westphalia as it binds every other Land.

North Rhine-Westphalia holds its own evidence base on trans residents. On 25 April 2025 the Land government published the study „Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*“, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans*, inter*, queer and non-binary people in the Land. It combined quantitative online surveys of more than 5,000 LSBTIQ* respondents, 775 relatives and over 5,000 professionals with qualitative focus groups and expert interviews.

The study covers discrimination, violence and safety; health, care and ageing; and integration, migration and flight. It was commissioned under Landtag resolution Drucksache 18/6360 to give the state's „Aktionsplan für Vielfalt und gegen Homo- und Transfeindlichkeit“ a broader data basis.

The Land has enacted no trans-specific statute, and its anti-homo- and transphobia action plan now rests on this dataset rather than on legislation.

10402087B42728698084544.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
10402087B42728698084544.summary:
Rhineland-Pfalz operates its own prison placement rule. A new § 17 of the Landesjustizvollzugsgesetz Rheinland-Pfalz took effect on 1 March 2026, anchoring inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry, with a general and abstract exception clause that is open to all prisoners rather than written specifically for trans people. An analysis published on Verfassungsblog on 18 March 2026 reads this as the model that other Länder should follow, and raises constitutional doubts about the alternative approach used elsewhere, in which states write trans-targeted exception clauses into their placement rules.

Rhineland-Pfalz is the Land that carried the count of states modernising placement rules past the absolute majority; the placement rules it replaced dated from the 1970s. The practical effect for a trans visitor facing detention in Rhineland-Pfalz is that placement follows the gender entry recorded in official documents, subject to an exception clause that can be invoked in an individual case.

Prison administration in Germany is a competence of the individual Länder, so the Rhineland-Pfalz rule governs detention in this state and not in neighbouring ones. Placement practice across the country remains unsettled: a wire report of 16 July 2026 covering the Liebich case, in which a neo-Nazi prisoner was held in a men's prison despite a legal gender change, drove the eastern Länder to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act.

10402087B83775792336645.name: Saarland
10402087B83775792336645.summary:
Saarland has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or prison-placement rule of its own. Placement of a trans prisoner in Saarland therefore stands under § 6(1) of the German Self-Determination Act, in force 1 November 2024, which follows the legal gender entry unless a state law provides otherwise; Saarland has enacted no such law. A legal commentary of 18 March 2026 adds that German constitutional law does not oblige authorities to follow the entry, so the default rule in Saarland is a statutory practice rather than a guaranteed outcome.

The same commentary cites Saarland's accommodation of trans inmates in single cells with en-suite showers as a positive practice model, which distinguishes Saarland's documented facility conditions from the complaints recorded elsewhere in Germany. Whether that accommodation is applied consistently across Saarland's prisons is not documented in the sources reviewed.

Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions name sexual orientation and gender identity explicitly, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is prohibited under that clause. This is a jurisdiction-specific difference: nationwide in Germany there is no general ban on hate speech of this kind, so a trans visitor in Saarland is covered by a constitutional protection that most of the country does not offer at Land level, alongside the federal prohibition on discrimination in employment, education, health services and goods and services.

Cites Saarland's single-cell-with-en-suite-shower accommodation as a positive practice model for trans inmates; framework-relevant to Saarland, which has no separate placement statute.

25490228B84620027724461.name: Canarias
25490228B84620027724461.summary:
Canarias stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 on legal gender recognition and LGTBI rights, and adds a regional layer of its own: Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 on non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognition of trans persons' rights (BOE-A-2014-11995), which gives a trans visitor a region-specific statutory basis against discriminatory treatment.

The community has permitted trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 Spanish autonomous communities to do so before the national statute of 28 February 2023 took effect. A visitor to Canarias therefore encounters self-identification as the operative regional practice, predating and now aligned with the national route.

Canarias is also listed among the Spanish communities banning conversion therapies, so the practice is prohibited within the region's own competence as well as under the national framework.

On relationship recognition, the Canary Islands created their same-sex couple registry in 2003, a regional instrument that predates the nationwide same-sex marriage regime in force since 2005.

It is also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies, and Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations. A trans traveler therefore stands under a regional anti-discrimination and self-identification regime alongside the 2023 national law.

25490228B81978515469630.name: La Rioja
25490228B81978515469630.summary:
La Rioja stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023), applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including La Rioja. Title II allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for adaptation of identity documents accordingly; transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Under Article 43 of the same statute any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, so a visitor's operative document is the basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Other operative provisions reaching a visitor include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime in Spain: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

La Rioja has its own regional layer alongside the national statute. It created a same-sex couple registry in 2010 and in February 2022 passed a regional trans-rights law allowing trans people to self-declare their legal gender; that regional law has applied since 2022 and remains in force alongside Ley 4/2023. La Rioja is also listed among the autonomous communities banning conversion therapies.

sources.summary: The Basque Parliament passed a law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people, dated 2013, which for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system. Institutional markers predating it include the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex. Osakidetza, the Basque health service, provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013. The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework.

25490228B27950689864224.name: Región de Murcia
25490228B27950689864224.summary:
Región de Murcia stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023) and applied uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities. Title II allows any person aged 16 or over to rectify the sex marker on their civil-registry entry by simple declaration before the Civil Registry, with no prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for the corresponding adaptation of identity documents. This replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 16 February 2023, placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition, while noting that the under-16 provision proved contentious.

Ley 4/2023 also mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force. Other operative provisions ban medically unnecessary normalising surgeries on intersex children before consent, expand access to assisted reproduction, enable parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthen sexuality education, and prohibit discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Spain rests on legal gender self-determination rather than biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Spain has no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022. Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level: in July 2026 a Tribunal de Instancia applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300, and in a case reported on 8 January 2026 a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them, with the only adult defendant receiving six months' prison and two minors judged separately.

Beneath the national layer, the Región de Murcia's own statute is Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170), which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics in public and private activity in the region and, within its scope, bars any requirement to prove declared gender identity by psychological or medical report.

The regional instrument sits within a wider pattern: autonomous-region LGTBI and trans-equality laws were approved across eight regions in the 2010s, with Murcia listed alongside País Vasco, Andalucía, Galicia, Extremadura, Madrid, Baleares and Aragón. Implementation of Ley 4/2023 falls to the regional government.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change; that ranking is a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

25490228B80227492032103.name: Cataluña/Catalunya
25490228B80227492032103.summary:
Catalunya stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGTBI rights, whose implementation in the region falls to the Generalitat de Catalunya, and under its own regional instrument, Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014, published in the Diari Oficial de la Generalitat de Catalunya (DOGC núm. 6730) on 17 October 2014.

Ley 11/2014 defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. A trans visitor treated less favourably on those grounds within Catalunya falls under this definition, and the statute obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms ensuring that administrative documentation reflects gender identity.

The regional statute extends protections across education, health, employment and sport, including broadening the Observatorio Catalán del Deporte to act against violence and discrimination in sport. It also guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures such as body identification, burial and handling of personal effects.

Sanctioning machinery exists at regional level. Article 35 of Ley 11/2014 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiència de Catalunya, between seven days' and three months' worth; Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, with the Síndic de Greuges able to instigate proceedings.

Catalunya holds several firsts inside the Spanish framework. The Ley de Parejas of 30 June 1998 was the first Spanish couples law allowing homosexual couples minimum legal provisions, and Ley 11/2014 prompted the 2010s wave of autonomous LGTBI laws across Spain.

Under the national framework as applied in Catalunya, legal gender recognition runs by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment; registered sex change is available from age 16 without medical reports or hormonal treatment, and from age 12 under conditions. The same national law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Human Rights Watch reported the Congress of Deputies' approval on 16 February 2023 and placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition; the under-16 recognition provision proved contentious.

Same-sex marriage has been in force across Spain since 2 July 2005, and legal gender change requires no surgery or sterilisation.

Spain's hate-crime machinery is being applied in practice. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. 25490228B94630301010512.name: Castilla-La Mancha
25490228B94630301010512.summary:
Castilla-La Mancha stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities, including this one, and the source inventory identifies no facility, expression or assembly restriction enacted at regional level.

Document-relevant provision is national and administrative. Adults may request rectification of the sex entry on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, without prior surgical reassignment, a gender-dysphoria diagnosis or two years of medical treatment; the right is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious during passage.

Because access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, that registry entry is the operative basis for facility rules in Castilla-La Mancha, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

The national statute defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the covered causes, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) recorded that the law strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Other operative provisions of the national statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, and strengthened sexuality education. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

19177384B98145761763330.name: Catamarca
19177384B98145761763330.summary:
Catamarca is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework set by Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743, which allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis, or approval by a doctor or judge. No Catamarca-specific legal restriction or separate provincial gender-recognition procedure was identified in the sources, so the national pathway is what a visitor should expect to apply here.

The national framework binding every province has weakened in practice. The Washington Blade reported on 10 April 2025 that activists describe Argentina's trans community as being in a 'chaotic, desperate situation' under the Milei administration: the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed in 2024. Violence, discrimination and poverty affecting trans people are reported to have worsened. Catamarca carries no separate reporting on how these national rollbacks are experienced locally, so the national picture stands as the baseline.

Nationally recorded violence bears directly on what a trans visitor in Catamarca should expect. The National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a 62% increase year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one crime every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis made up 62.5% of victims (142 cases) and gay men 22% (50). The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse. These are national figures; no province-level breakdown for Catamarca was located, and raw national counts are not adjusted for population.

Argentina's Supreme Court left standing on 5 April 2025 the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayan, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by a cassation court in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied in that case. Hate-crime data and this ruling indicate that legal protection against gender-motivated violence exists in statute but its application in practice is contested.

19177384B39000171219781.name: Córdoba
19177384B39000171219781.summary:
A visitor to Córdoba operates under Argentina's national legal framework, and nothing in the available sources records a provincial rule departing from it. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, while anti-discrimination protection runs through a combination of national and provincial statutes.

Emergency Decree 62/2025, issued in February 2025, amends the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment; Decree 61/2025 governs the placement of transgender people in the prison system. Both bind every province, including Córdoba. FALGBT announced legal action against the decrees, and constitutional experts described them as unlawful.

Violence data bear directly on this province. 17162690B9130125042960.name: Lower Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B9130125042960.summary:
Lower Silesian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, and the inventory records no local deviation in law or enforcement that would distinguish this voivodeship from the country as a whole. A trans visitor in Wrocław or anywhere else in the province meets the Polish national position on custody, entry and documents.

Detention is the clearest documented risk. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention published the case of a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, whom a Polish regional court placed in a guarded centre for male foreigners. Polish law bars such placement wherever a stay would threaten a person's life or health, and wherever the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that statutory bar, and she was freed only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander; the page was updated on 28 March 2024.

The March 2024 case sets the framework applied to trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention, and therefore bears directly on any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship. The statutory protection existed in writing and did not operate until a third party invoked it.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life under Article 8 of the Convention by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate.

The same judgment left the alleged breaches of Article 3 and Article 14 undecided. It binds Poland and governs healthcare for trans people in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, Lower Silesian among them, though placement decisions in custody remain individual and unpredictable in practice.

17162690B67719337891950.name: Opole Voivodeship
17162690B67719337891950.summary:
Opole Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and no voivodeship-level deviation from that framework has been documented.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars such placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence; the Border Guard refused to move or release her. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after the Association applied to the Border Guard Post commander and he ordered it. Her documented history of violence and sexual assault indicates that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while leaving the alleged Articles 3 and 14 breaches undecided; the refusal was held to have no reasonable legal grounds and to be disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland as a whole and sets the governing standard for trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including Opole. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

17162690B37876665907262.name: Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B37876665907262.summary:
Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. The sources identify no voivodeship-specific statute, court practice or detention-facility rule departing from it, so the national standards set out below are what a trans visitor here actually faces.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars placement in such a centre wherever a stay would threaten the person's life or health, or wherever the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that bar; she was released only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander, and the association updated its case page on 28 March 2024. The same case documented a history of violence and sexual assault. Because the case turns on national immigration-detention law, any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship is held under these rules and this pattern of enforcement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene on custody care. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court held the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate, and left the alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 14 undecided. The judgment binds Poland as a whole and is the governing standard for trans healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including Kuyavian-Pomeranian. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Krzysztof Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Adam Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Zbigniew Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

27671186B81745654473385.name: Cross River
27671186B81745654473385.summary:
Cross River State falls entirely under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 operates in full within the state: same-sex marriage or civil union, and the registration, operation or participation in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carry up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide, and the offence reaches anyone who assists, attends or promotes a same-sex relationship or an LGBTQ+ organisation. A visitor who accompanies a partner to a gathering, or who helps organise one, is exposed on the same terms as a resident.

The Criminal Code in force in Cross River separately criminalises sexual activity between men at 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency between men at 3 years.

Cross River is not among the twelve northern states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — where religious criminal law applies to same-sex acts and the maximum can be death. Within Cross River the exposure is secular and capped at 14 years; crossing into any of those twelve states materially raises it.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria, reported in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity, and of death-penalty risk under religious law in some northern states.

Nigeria offers no anti-discrimination protection to LGBTQ+ people, so there is no official complaint route when a visitor is refused service, threatened or extorted.

Dating apps and social venues carry documented entrapment risk. A nationwide 'kito' scheme lures gay men and trans women to meetings where they are assaulted, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police profiling produces arbitrary arrest and paid release. The pattern of mass detentions is national: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 held after a hotel raid in Delta in June 2018, 67 arrested in Warri in August 2023 and 76 detained in Gombe in October 2023.

Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion backed by threats and physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. The report is national in scope and describes the machinery a visitor perceived as gay or trans would meet.

sources.title: "Everyone's on the Game": Corruption and Human Rights Abuses by the Nigeria Police Force (Human Rights Watch)
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. 27671186B83907961412659.name: Ogun
27671186B83907961412659.summary:
Ogun State in south-west Nigeria has no protective statute of its own for transgender or gender-nonconforming people, and the sources reviewed record no Ogun-specific incident, enforcement action or divergence. The national framework applies in full.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers that they face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, with up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex unions under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, and death-penalty risk under Sharia criminal law in northern states. Ogun is a southern state and does not fall under Sharia provisions, but the 14-year exposure and the warning of attacks and blackmail apply to visitors in Ogun.

The only trans-specific killing documented in the sources is the case of 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender TikToker whose beaten body was found on a highway in Abuja on 9 August 2024, as reported by BBC News. She had posted about being transgender and working as a sex worker and had expressed fears for her life the previous year. Police stated that preliminary investigations revealed the individual was a man fully dressed in female clothing. The killing occurred in the federal capital, outside Ogun, and is carried here as national evidence of lethal violence against transgender people; no Ogun-specific incident is documented in the sources.

27671186B56513237316251.name: Oyo
27671186B56513237316251.summary:
Oyo State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies in full to visitors, including the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the imprisonment terms it carries.

Oyo is governed by the Criminal Code, which penalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. These are the state-level offences a visitor in Oyo would be charged under, alongside the national statute.

Oyo lies outside the Shari'a regime. The death-penalty exposure for male same-sex conduct reported in twelve northern Nigerian states does not apply within Oyo, where secular penalties ceiling at imprisonment.

Police in Oyo profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay, a practice known locally as 'kito'. The extortion demand is the point of the stop in many accounts, and victims do not report it to police for fear of being arrested themselves or attacked.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk in Oyo. A BBC Africa Eye investigation broadcast on 15 May 2023 documented criminal gangs posing as potential dates on popular apps, luring men to meetings where they are filmed, then extorted, beaten and kidnapped; the investigation interviewed 21 people about being 'kito'd'. The underground scene it filmed was Lagos-based, but the risk applies to gay and transgender app users in Oyo as elsewhere in Nigeria.

No anti-discrimination protection is available in Oyo. LGBTI people there face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under a framework that reaches LGBTI organisations as well as individuals, and the practical effect is that reporting a crime or seeking help can expose the person who reports.

27671186B25346211366833.summary:
Akwa Ibom stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, a maximum of 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity, no legal recognition of gender identity, and no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The state's position within that framework is the point on which the sources are explicit. Akwa Ibom lies in the part of the country outside the twelve northern states whose Shari'a-based criminal codes carry death-penalty provisions for same-sex conduct, so the death-penalty layer does not reach a visitor here.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) states that the death-penalty risk is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Akwa Ibom, and records no state-specific enforcement divergence for the country. The general country coverage of Nigerian LGBT rights records the same split, putting the maximum in the southern portion of the country, Akwa Ibom included, at 14 years' imprisonment. Neither source describes an Akwa Ibom police command, prosecutor, court or state authority acting on same-sex conduct or gender identity in either direction, and no Akwa Ibom arrest, charge, conviction or judgment appears in the material.

The sources record no Akwa Ibom state law or policy recognising gender identity, prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, or recognising same-sex relationships on any terms. For a trans visitor the practical result is that the state adds nothing to the national position: there is no state-level protective instrument to invoke, and no documented state-level escalation beyond the national statute's penalty range.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916. The Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. It criminalises all forms of same-sex unions and renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. The maximum penalty under federal law is up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes. In the southern portion of the country, which includes Akwa Ibom, the maximum punishment for same-sex sexual activity is 14 years' imprisonment. The death-penalty risk layer is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Akwa Ibom, which stands under the secular national framework of up to 14 years' imprisonment. No state-specific enforcement divergence is documented.

27671186B69086015704361.name: Delta
27671186B69086015704361.summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in the state with up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex unions, and no state-specific protective statute exists in Delta. Section 217 of the Criminal Code, applicable in Delta as a southern state, makes male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment. The death penalty attached to Shari'a provisions applies only in the twelve northern states, none of which is Delta.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of mass raids on social venues. On 27 August 2023 police from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan (Warri) at 9 pm, arresting 67 suspects at what police described as a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius, 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a cross-dresser's confession that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony; suspects fled on the officers' arrival and 67 were chased down and arrested. Police reported recovering drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses', kept the suspects and exhibits in custody, and continued efforts to arrest fleeing members for prosecution. One suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. Coverage of the incident framed the arrests alongside drug allegations.

The same raid is recorded differently across sources: the UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note, citing the USSD 2023 human rights report, describes a 27 August 2023 Delta State raid on a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community detaining more than 200 individuals, with police alleging a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records the Warri case as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court. Earlier, in June 2018, police in Asaba arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel on charges that they were gays and lesbians; by July 2018 the detainees were facing homosexuality-related charges in court.

A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the Home Office that 'kito' (predatory same-sex assault) victims under-report for fear of prosecution. State-level documentation for Delta is thin, which does not demonstrate safety for a trans visitor.

27671186B95832466049157.name: Rivers
27671186B95832466049157.summary:
Rivers State lies in southern Nigeria. The sources identify no Rivers statute, policy or enforcement practice of its own on same-sex conduct or gender expression; the state stands under Nigeria's national framework, which the sources confirm reaches a visitor to Port Harcourt and the rest of Rivers. The layer that varies by geography is the Criminal Code in force across southern Nigeria, and it applies here: sex between men carries penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years.

Rivers is not among the northern states where Sharia provisions apply. The penalties reported for those states, from lashing to death, do not reach a visitor in Port Harcourt. Exposure in Rivers comes from the secular Criminal Code and the national framework rather than from Zina provisions.

The only Rivers-specific event in the sources is an assault in Port Harcourt. In January 2015 a 21-year-old gay man travelled from Lagos to the city to meet a man he had contacted on Facebook, was attacked and sexually abused there, and did not report it to the police. Human Rights Watch recorded the case in its October 2016 report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe'. Meeting arranged online, assault by the contact, no recourse sought: all three are documented inside Rivers itself.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal and criminalises registering, operating or supporting gay organisations. The Nigerian Criminal Code in the south criminalises sex between men with penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act, and the court ruled them unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, removing those provisions as a basis for prosecuting LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals. No legal protections exist for LGBTQ people, and sharia-based states apply penalties from lashing up to death. None of these provisions names Rivers or Port Harcourt; the federal framework applies nationwide and covers a visitor to Rivers State.

sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the SSMPA, passed in January 2014, records that the law imposes 10 to 14 years' imprisonment on anyone who registers, operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. It documents that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the Act, including eight of the 21 young men arrested, but never charged, at a birthday party in Ibadan. It also records the case of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to Port Harcourt to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there, saying he did not report it to the police. The Port Harcourt incident and the nationwide abuse pattern substantiate the enforcement climate a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.

27671186B96047513549152.name: Kogi
27671186B96047513549152.summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, applies in Kogi in full: entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries 14 years' imprisonment, while registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carries 10 years.

The Criminal Code in force in Kogi separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

Kogi is administered under secular law rather than Shari'a. It is one of the states outside the twelve Shari'a-administering northern states, where penalties run higher; death penalties for lesbianism have been applied in two of those states. Kogi therefore sits under the 14-year maximum rather than a death-penalty regime.

The Constitution contains no protection on grounds of sexual orientation, and there are no federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Nothing in Kogi law gives a person refused work, services or accommodation on that basis a statutory claim.

In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country. That ruling reaches Kogi, and is recorded as effectively allowing LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise. No comparable ruling is recorded for the conduct provisions or the marriage prohibition, which remain enforceable.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

27671186B74554005070963.name: Nasarawa
27671186B74554005070963.summary:
Nasarawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the country, and the UK Foreign Office travel advisory of 19 August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, stating that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment. The federal law extends to people who arrange, attend or conduct same-sex weddings and to those involved with gay groups or organisations.

Nasarawa lies in Nigeria's north-central zone, close to the Federal Capital Territory; the advisory notes that some northern states operate Sharia law under which same-sex activity can attract the death penalty, and that breaching curfews or movement restrictions risks arrest and detention.

Violence against trans people in the capital region is documented. The beaten body of the 33-year-old Nigerian transgender TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama' was found along the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in Abuja on 9 August 2024, a suspected murder roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; an investigation was announced. Despite formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private and family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states.

27671186B91150779192485.name: Ekiti
27671186B91150779192485.summary:
Ekiti State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe' records enforcement and violence specific to the state. On 21 January 2014, days after the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened her with 'You will get 14 years in prison!'; the report states she was beaten at least twice over the period.

Debbie was unable to use Ekiti's health services safely and travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, indicating that trans and HIV-positive residents in the state face care access barriers that push them to seek treatment in Oyo State.

The report also documents police and official conduct in Ado Ekiti: in September 2014 a gay man was arrested at the Faguyi bar in the state capital, his third arrest, and was released after two days in detention once he paid 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend. In a separate 2014 incident, a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti.

27671186B90910891533368.name: Enugu
27671186B90910891533368.summary:
Enugu State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in full across the state, and Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe' documents its effects through testimony collected in Enugu State itself.

One Enugu-based woman, Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told the researchers that she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure, adding: 'For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married.' Her account shows the statute operating as pressure toward heterosexual marriage for people in the state who do not identify as straight.

An Enugu-based activist told Human Rights Watch that 'the major challenge in Enugu State is the rate of HIV and STIs among members of the community.' The same activist reported that there are no clinics in Enugu State where gay men and men who have sex with men can access services without fear of harassment, and that many people therefore travel to Lagos and other states for care.

65028918B98829509874887.name: West Nusa Tenggara
65028918B98829509874887.summary:
West Nusa Tenggara stands under Indonesia's national framework, and no sub-national deviation for this province is recorded: no enacted bylaw, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people in West Nusa Tenggara, and no protective legislation for the province. The province is assessed at the national risk level.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Parliament passed a new Penal Code in December 2022 that took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises consensual sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment and at up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside the national morality provisions. Aceh punishes homosexuality under sharia law by flogging or imprisonment, and its penalties apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. No equivalent provincial provision for West Nusa Tenggara appears in the sources.

Physical risk is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and August 2026 coverage reports growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community under the framework that governs West Nusa Tenggara. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. 65028918B99918739720671.summary:
Banten stands under Indonesia's national framework on gender identity and documentation. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue identity papers, including the electronic identity card (e-KTP), to transgender Indonesians, and Banten is named among the nine provinces where this has operated, alongside West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua.

A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

A presidential decree of October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy, and reporting of August 2026 ties the surge in attacks directly to that decree and to officials' public condemnations.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and screening carry exposure. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution does not address either.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. West Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework. No source addressing West Sulawesi province directly was identified, so the province is assessed against the national position; a visitor to West Sulawesi should expect the legal and enforcement conditions that apply across Indonesia.

Consensual same-sex relations are effectively criminalised nationally. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs attacked transgender women across Indonesia in a wave on 14-16 July 2026, in which more than 15 trans women in Bogor were doused, stripped and beaten, with footage circulated online. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to hardened official hostility, including an executive order of October 2025 that lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy.

Police raids on private LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside the national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother in Lima alleges police beat him and says authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections for LGBT people, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
