65028918B90323071856071.name: East Nusa Tenggara
65028918B90323071856071.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and East Nusa Tenggara stands under that national framework with no documented local deviation from it. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising across the country. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him, a claim Indonesian police denied.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. For East Nusa Tenggara specifically, no trans-specific statute, raid or service record is documented, so a visitor should expect the national pattern of selective prosecution, police raids on private gatherings and mob violence rather than any province-specific regime.

65028918B48178230554278.name: Maluku
65028918B48178230554278.summary:
Maluku stands under Indonesia's national framework. Both sources audited for this province are national in scope, and neither records a Maluku-specific ordinance, police operation, protection scheme or service, so the assessment rests on the national picture those sources document.

The penal code signed on 6 December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises sexual activity between adults outside marriage. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of two years' imprisonment, while the national overview gives up to one year where an immediate family member lodges a complaint; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within that outside-marriage restriction.

Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with no third-gender or X marker. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards in nine provinces as the document route.

National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections, and the Constitution is silent on sexual orientation and gender identity. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected 5-4 a petition to criminalise homosexuality; the Sharia-based criminalisation outlier is Aceh, not Maluku.

Reporting in August 2026 describes growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions. The page records that Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, and that a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage.

65028918B43243108525571.name: East Java
65028918B43243108525571.summary:
East Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. East Java has no provincial carve-out from this framework.

Physical risk is carried by the national regime rather than by any East Java-specific rule. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, with Amnesty International stating the gathering violated no law. The Diplomat's August 2026 reporting is national and does not describe East Java specifically.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger anywhere in Indonesia, East Java included. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and status: Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, so a trans visitor travelling on a foreign passport with a changed marker is entering a jurisdiction whose own standard of legal gender change is far stricter. Same-sex couples have no recognised legal relationship of any kind, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Indonesian law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on those grounds.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller in Indonesia. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

East Java specifics are thin but concrete on one point: nothing in East Java civil law barred authorities from placing the trans woman Isa Zega in a women's prison facility by identity, and with no anti-discrimination framework there is no statutory basis on which to contest such a placement. A trans visitor detained in East Java therefore faces custody conditions determined by local practice alone.

65028918B90123187256494.name: Riau Islands
65028918B90123187256494.summary:
The Riau Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The source inventory records the same amended penal code as carrying up to one year in prison when a complaint is lodged, and the two figures are not reconciled here.

No province-specific divergence from that framework was found for the Riau Islands: private same-sex conduct is not criminalised in the province, but it attracts no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection either. Two other provinces of Indonesia, Aceh and South Sumatra, do criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. A 2020 raid case elsewhere in the country illustrates how enforcement varies with local regulation: those held were released because no regional regulation existed.

Physical risk is documented at national level. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and in July 2026 mobs attacked trans women in several provinces including West Java with no prosecutions reported; civil society describes conditions as rapidly worsening. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism and drug addiction, placing it inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

65028918B68445169823185.name: East Kalimantan
65028918B68445169823185.summary:
East Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework, which applies in full to visitors in the province. Private same-sex conduct is not itself criminalised under national law, but it carries no protection: Indonesia has no national law prohibiting discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no hate-crime protection on those grounds.

The amended penal code, passed in December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026, penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment on complaint. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual relationships read as same-sex under birth-sex status; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Provincial criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity in Aceh and South Sumatra does not apply in East Kalimantan. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and bind anyone present within that province, including foreign visitors, and they have been carried out: two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025.

Expression offences are national and a visitor can trigger them. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Official hostility is explicit in national policy. A presidential decree of October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism and drug addiction, placing it inside national defence policy. A feature published on 14 August 2026 reports that civil society describes conditions as rapidly worsening.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. In July 2026 mobs attacked trans women in several cities, including West Java, and no prosecutions of the attackers were reported. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. No incident documentation was found for East Kalimantan itself.

65028918B52923737893214.name: North Kalimantan
65028918B52923737893214.summary:
North Kalimantan stands under the national framework of Indonesia, and no trans-specific safety finding is recorded for the province itself. It is assessed at the national score: a trans visitor in North Kalimantan faces the legal and physical risks carried by Indonesia as a whole.

Indonesia's penal code, signed in December 2022, took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual sex between unmarried adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not recognised, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Official hostility is now written into national policy. An October 2025 presidential decree lists 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' among nonmilitary threats, alongside terrorism and drug addiction. In July 2026 mobs attacked transgender women in several cities, including West Java, and no prosecutions of the attackers have been reported. Reporting dated 14 August 2026 records civil society assessments that conditions are rapidly worsening.

Protections are absent on paper. Indonesia has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity, no national law shielding a visitor or resident from harassment on those grounds, and no legal recognition of same-sex partnerships. Legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are available on Indonesian documents.

Provincial religious law adds a harder layer in one part of the country. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal in Aceh under Sharia, punishable by flogging or imprisonment, and those penalties apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. A proposed obscenity article explicitly naming 'same sex' is feared to trigger discriminatory regional bylaws, which would extend such reach to provinces including North Kalimantan.

Physical risk falls hardest on visibly gender-nonconforming people. Vigilante mobs attack transgender people with impunity, and the July 2026 assaults proceeded without prosecution. A trans traveller has also died in Indonesian custody: in August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an airport on drug charges and died in detention, with his mother alleging police beat him and police denying violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes writing or audio-visual material showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, the national broadcasting commission banned presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal on television and radio in March 2016, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related terms, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

15666254B97003483933575.name: Kuala Lumpur
15666254B97003483933575.summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct at the federal level. Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Section 377D's "gross indecency" offence carries up to two years. The federal territory of Kuala Lumpur stands directly under this Penal Code, with no local ordinance displacing it, and sodomy has been criminalised in the territory's governing law since 1871.

A second layer applies only to Muslims. Every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. All 13 states have passed such enactments since the 1980s, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. A non-Muslim foreign visitor is therefore outside this layer, but inside the federal one in full.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was still pending as of late 2014, filed after police arrested 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and publicly sanctioned. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out its enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the case of the trans public figure Nur Sajat, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Raid-based arrest is the documented pattern, and venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and Jawi raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media had been pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among those arrested were suspended. A magistrate rejected an extension of remand for lack of ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Human Rights Watch, working with Justice for Sisters, documented discrimination against LGBT people in August 2022 on the basis of interviews with 73 LGBT people conducted between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur; a Kuala Lumpur activist quoted there described regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the practical exposure is the Penal Code rather than the Sharia enactments. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

15666254B54729125478011.name: Putrajaya
15666254B54729125478011.summary:
Putrajaya is Malaysia's federal territory and administrative capital. It stands under the national framework: Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under the federal Penal Code 1936, and the territory's own Sharia code adds a second layer that reaches Muslims only.

Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Putrajaya maintains its own Sharia code, which like the codes of the other federal territories and all 13 states typically criminalises same-sex activity and gender nonconformity through a ban on cross-dressing. These Sharia offences apply only to Muslims; non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone. Penalties under such enactments elsewhere in Malaysia reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments. The enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the line between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and the Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes. A 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and is unaffected by reassignment surgery; the edict was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported across Malaysia, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Enforcement documented since the 2018 election includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August 2022 raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 Johor plans for conversion-therapy centres. Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had been attended by at least 1,733 people as of June 2021, based on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors; the nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay.

No Putrajaya-specific enforcement case against a transgender or gender-nonconforming visitor or resident is documented in the sources reviewed. The national framework governs what a visitor faces in Putrajaya.

Enforcement patterns elsewhere in Malaysia illustrate how the framework operates in practice: raids on social venues, arrests under section 377B, and Sharia proceedings against gender-nonconforming people. Arbitrary arrest of transgender people is documented over decades, including a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014 and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention.

Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence, not on the substance, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised.

US State Department travel advisory for Russia, which covers Altai Krai: foreigners found guilty of violating the 'propaganda' law may be arrested and detained for up to 15 days and then deported, displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and the advisory advises against all travel to Russia.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation; one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, and 17 cases remain pending or unknown. 28173009B16834140201491.name: Republic of Mordovia
28173009B16834140201491.summary:
The Republic of Mordovia stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full; the assessment is made at the national level, with no regional deviation identified for Mordovia.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers say so plainly.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (June 2025) records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years.

The same note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols since the 2023 Supreme Court designation, comprising about 98 administrative cases and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

No separate Mordovia-specific legal instrument, enforcement record, or service provision affecting transgender visitors was present in the inventory; the national figures above are the operative baseline for a visit to Saransk or elsewhere in the republic.

Kurgan Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full and with no identified regional deviation. The dedicated country record identified no deviation material enough to score separately (±0.02), so the oblast is assessed at the national score.

For a trans visitor this framework means that legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; gender-transition procedures are banned and gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Same-sex marriage is banned. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

The Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation operates nationwide, including in Kurgan Oblast: participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 of them administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The 2013 "propaganda" law, expanded in 2022 to cover any public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition, is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity: Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over the two preceding years.

Foreigners are explicitly at risk. The US State Department advisory for Russia states that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported, that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and it advises against all travel to Russia; the advisory stands at Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

The post-designation crackdown was immediate. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" law carries administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, rising to as much as four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them, and records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. 28173009B21210279674314.name: Komi Republic
28173009B21210279674314.summary:
The Komi Republic stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which extends in full. The sources record no republic-level variation in how these laws operate, and the jurisdiction is assessed at the national score. A trans visitor to Syktyvkar or anywhere else in the Komi Republic faces the same legal position as a trans visitor elsewhere in the country.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and foreign government warnings issued to LGBT travellers say so.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, among them three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. An independent media outlet reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, on 17 January 2024, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. A foreign broadcaster's report of 27 July 2024 followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The US State Department travel advisory advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war and arbitrary law enforcement. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

28173009B55422170414647.name: Khakassia
28173009B55422170414647.summary:
Khakassia is a republic within the Russian Federation and stands under the national framework of Russia. Khakassia is not among the subnational units singled out for the heightened North Caucasus finding, but the trans-specific finding is country-wide and reaches visitors and residents here.

The US State Department advisory for Russia advises against all travel. It warns that foreigners found guilty of violating the 'propaganda' law may be detained for up to 15 days and deported, and it states that displaying rainbow symbols is a crime. These are country-wide rules, and the advisory documents no sub-national variation in Khakassia.

Organising, participation, funding, public display of LGBT symbols including trans-related expression, and advocacy are punishable as extremist activity, carrying fines, administrative detention and imprisonment.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Khakassia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The propaganda law as expanded in 2022 applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and single-person foreign adoption is allowed only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. In a 30 September 2022 speech President Putin said teaching children about other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable, linking opposition to transgender rights to willingness to use all means against Ukraine. Officials cited protection of family values and draft evasion, claiming about 2,700 recent legal-gender changes and that many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 re-legalisation removing Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under Article 154-a and later Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples with no legal recognition offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and refuses to register LGBTQ organisations. A 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag, a 2010 European Court of Human Rights fine for systemic refusal of pride parade permits and an August 2012 Moscow City Court decision upholding a ban on Moscow Pride through 2012, and Chechnya detentions, torture and killings targeting persons based on perceived sexual orientation since February 2017 with over 100 men detained and OSCE confirmation in December 2018. Adoption is limited domestically to single persons regardless of sexual orientation and jointly only to married heterosexual couples, with foreign single-person adoption barred where the country recognises same-sex marriage.

28173009B46738131000378.name: Tatarstan
28173009B46738131000378.summary:
Tatarstan is an ordinary region of Russia and stands under the country's national legal framework, which the record for Russia carries in full. The findings below are limited to what is specific to the republic.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) assesses Tatarstan as an ordinary region. The elevated state-persecution exception, which covers trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and North Caucasus residents likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, is applied outside regions such as this one. A trans visitor or resident in Tatarstan is therefore assessed under the ordinary-country standard rather than the heightened exception.

The Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT public movement" as an extremist organisation, made on 30 November 2023 and entered in the federal extremist list on 22 March 2024, binds in Tatarstan. Participation in, financing of, and public display of LGBT symbols, including trans-related symbols, are punishable under administrative and criminal extremism law throughout the republic, and the ban on the movement's activity applies here as it does nationwide.

The sources document no Tatarstan-specific arrests, raids, prosecutions or incidents of violence against trans people, and no guidance issued by the republic's own prosecutors or courts on applying the extremism provisions.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025): documents the national framework governing this jurisdiction, under which same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection exists, with at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024. It places the elevated state-persecution exception, covering trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and North Caucasus residents likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, outside ordinary regions such as this one.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions by June 2025 for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols — 98 administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges (two sentenced to prison, seventeen pending or unknown); on 15 May 2025 three staff of two publishing houses were charged with 'running an extremist organization' (article 282.2) and face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols is punishable with up to four years in prison.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tatarstan (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Transgender people are not allowed to change legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned under a bill passed in 2023 and a July 2023 law prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. Russian children cannot be adopted by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions under a 2024 law, and a single foreign adopter is permitted only if their country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The military medical expertise statute provides that people 'who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences' can only be drafted during wartime, while authorities claimed about 2,700 legal gender-change decisions in recent times were sought to avoid conscription amid the special operation. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated 'Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us.' Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after homosexual acts between consenting males were re-legalised in 1993 with removal of Article 121, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years' imprisonment with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year in the Soviet era. The age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, and homosexuality was removed from the list of mental illnesses in 1999 with ICD-10, though new laws introduced 1 July 2023 effectively reinstate the classification. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage and no legal recognition available despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human-rights violation. The 2013 law criminalising distribution of 'propaganda' promoting 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated 'the international LGBT public movement' as an extremist organisation, formally listed 22 March 2024, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols including the rainbow flag a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections, has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, refuses to register LGBTQ organisations which are prohibited as extremist, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Anti-gay purges in Chechnya since February 2017 involved forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killings with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead, a further purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by EU economic sanctions on two Chechen officials in March 2021, while nationally an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals with 365 fatalities occurred between 2010 and 2020, tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with hate groups using dating apps to hunt homosexuals.

28173009B26811060113320.name: Tomsk Oblast
28173009B26811060113320.summary:
Tomsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal and physical risks for transgender visitors are severe. In 2023 the Russian government prohibited gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, effectively banning trans-specific healthcare; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression including anything that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official Russian government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the national framework as it applies to Tomsk Oblast: same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection is available to transgender people. The same note records 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024. It records no facts specific to Tomsk Oblast.

That note assesses that lesbian, gay and bisexual people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, transgender people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. For a trans visitor the practical consequence is exposure to the extremist-designation regime and to the propaganda statutes, under which display, advocacy or discussion can be charged as participation in a banned organisation.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions, with at least 20 people facing criminal charges from January 2024 onward. Three staff of a publishing house charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and repeated display of the banned symbols carries up to four years.

28173009B26811060113320.tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, with about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues raided the same night.

Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as a second-class citizen after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive practices targeting transgender people are documented at the parent-nation level: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mari El (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery and to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and foreign single-person adoption is permitted only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The article links legal gender change to conscription avoidance, stating that many young men have turned to private clinics to provide a sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation and that Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed 2,700 such decisions in recent times. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated "Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us." while invoking transgender rights in justification for action against Ukraine and willingness to use all means at disposal. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which had previously punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage in July 2020, no legal recognition is offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human rights violation, and only married heterosexual couples may adopt jointly though single persons regardless of sexual orientation may adopt domestically. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine organisations including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with estimates of 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, and group-organised hunting via dating apps including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. In Chechnya, authorities targeted persons based on perceived sexual orientation with forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killing, with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed from December 2018, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two officials.

28173009B55503329301013.name: Omsk Oblast
28173009B55503329301013.summary:
Omsk Oblast is one of the federal subjects of the Russian Federation and stands under the national legal framework. The sources reviewed record no oblast-level divergence in statute, enforcement or protection, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia, version 2.0 of June 2025, carries no oblast-level detail.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised under Russian law, while same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned. Gender-affirming healthcare was effectively prohibited in 2023, and in November 2023 the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation. That designation applies in Omsk Oblast as it does across the federation.

'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals, or up to 15 days' detention. The expanded propaganda provisions reach public expression that justifies gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention and deportation, and the US State Department's advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers.

Participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols is prosecuted as extremism, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 such convictions as of 30 June 2025, and the UK Home Office note records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded in January 2024, when masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling: about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The capital is cited as a single illustration of national practice rather than as evidence about Omsk.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 the case of a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The incident is recorded in a different oblast and indicates national risk, not an Omsk case.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Protection pathways outside Russia are being set by other governments. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under. As a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016), he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors', the city ban enacted in 2012 that the New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered. The page quotes his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when she visited the city. It also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview of LGBTQ rights in Russia supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. Ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. A July 2023 law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition. A 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fined Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Sakha Republic (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. In 2022 the 'propaganda' law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to 'rule out the possibility of changing a person's gender purely by changing the documents' and to ban reassignment without surgery on 'family values' grounds. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions; inside Russia single persons regardless of sexual orientation can adopt but a couple can adopt jointly only if a married heterosexual couple, and a foreign single adopter must live in a country that neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. In the draft-evasion context, authorities claimed many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation, with the Duma Speaker claiming some '2,700' such decisions, and Russian men were described as considering changing legal gender to avoid being drafted. On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin said teaching children that 'instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries' is 'unacceptable to us' while stating Russia would use 'all means at our disposal' against Ukraine. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited from operating. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which under Stalin from March 1934 as Article 154-a and from 1961 as Article 121 punished consensual sex between men with three to five years' imprisonment with a maximum of five years, with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year in the Soviet era; the age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, and homosexuality was removed from the mental-illness list in 1999 with ICD-10 but new laws on 1 July 2023 effectively reinstated classification as mental illness. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, the 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman, same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and Russia did not implement the 2021 European Court of Human Rights Fedotova ruling requiring legal recognition after leaving the court in 2022. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of 'propaganda' promoting 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors and was expanded in 2022 to anyone regardless of age; in November 2023 the Supreme Court designated 'the international LGBT public movement' as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting or repeatedly displaying symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings. Violence and custody include Chechen forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killings targeting perceived sexual orientation, with over 100 men detained and tortured since February 2017 and at least three dead, a December 2018 OSCE report confirming persecution ignored by authorities, another purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and March 2021 EU economic sanctions on two Chechen officials; nationally the government does not officially record hate crimes, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 including 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, increased premeditated group attacks in 2017-2019 using dating apps to 'hunt' homosexuals, and 205 cases by homophobic hate groups including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. Protection machinery is absent with no anti-discrimination protections based on sexual orientation and no hate-crime designation, illustrated by the January 2013 firing of television anchor Anton Krasovsky after announcing he was gay and the September 2013 firing of Khabarovsk teacher Alexander Yermoshkin after attack by neo-Nazi group 'Shtolz Khabarovsk' amid a campaign by 'Movement against the propaganda of sexual perversions.'

28173009B21415173479872.name: Saratov Oblast
28173009B21415173479872.summary:
Saratov Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Putin signed the law in 2023 prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The oblast's one region-specific enforcement datapoint is a Saratov court case: in February 2024 a Saratov court fined photographer Inna Mosina 1,500 rubles (about £13.97) for using rainbow-flag imagery in her artwork, recorded by the UK Home Office as the first criminal prosecution under the extremism law. Display of symbols associated with the designated movement is therefore prosecuted in this oblast, and imagery rather than conduct is sufficient to draw a charge.

National enforcement sets the baseline a visitor is measured against. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or display of its symbols since the November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison, and separately documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The UK Home Office note counts at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement across Russia in 2022-2024.

Document, relationship and care access are closed at national level. Same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were outlawed in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare is described as effectively banned. A trans visitor cannot obtain recognition of their documents in Russia and should expect entry screening, police checks and any interaction with medical services to be conducted against a legal order that treats their status as unlawful.

Physical harm accompanies the legal exposure. The Guardian reported that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, with about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two further venues raided the same night. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian documented a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

Protection machinery exists only outside Russia. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing the country, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

28173009B21415173479872.tangentialFactors:

Adjacent risks that a trans visitor may mistake for ordinary crime are in fact regime-driven. Detention on extremism grounds has proved lethal in pretrial custody, and forced confinement in conversion-therapy settings has been documented against transgender people held by their own families. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Udmurtia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. In 2022 the propaganda law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provides people who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences can only be drafted during wartimes, with officials stating non-standard orientation should not be revealed while serving because of risk of beating, while authorities claimed some 2,700 legal gender changes were made recently to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated it is unacceptable to teach children that instead of men and women there are supposedly some other genders and to offer sex-change surgeries, linking transgender rights abroad to willingness to use all means against Ukraine. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 with removal of Article 121, and the age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but same-sex marriages and civil unions are prohibited and a July 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. The 2013 law criminalising distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag designated as the movement symbol including earrings, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others. Documented violence includes an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities rising from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, premeditated group attacks often using dating apps to hunt homosexuals led by groups like Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions, and Chechnya purges since February 2017 with over 100 detained and tortured and at least three extrajudicial killings confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report leading to EU sanctions on two officials in March 2021.

28173009B2185273376578.name: Magadan Oblast
28173009B2185273376578.summary:
Magadan Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and every source consulted treats that framework as applying uniformly across the country. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out that framework, and none of its findings are specific to Magadan Oblast. A visitor to Magadan Oblast faces the same legal exposure as a visitor to Moscow or Vladivostok.

Consensual same-sex activity is not itself a criminal offence in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. The 2023 law prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year. The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded propaganda statutes criminalise any public expression, including anything explicitly justifying gender transition.

The practical consequence for a transgender visitor is that no document can be brought into alignment with their gender presentation. Any police stop, hotel registration, bank or transport identity check reads as a mismatch between presentation and papers. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Enforcement is documented at national scale. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The UK Home Office note records at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

Volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
