28173009B42697300509311.name: Ulyanovsk Oblast
28173009B42697300509311.summary:
Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full and offers no regional deviation material enough to score separately. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. For a visitor this means an identity document carrying an outdated marker cannot be corrected before or during travel, so any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute reaches public expression that 'justifies' gender transition, and foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention and deportation.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries 2 to 6 years and organising 6 to 10 years' imprisonment under Article 282.2. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The federal framework has been enforced inside Ulyanovsk Oblast itself. Citing an October 2024 OVD-Info report, the UK Home Office records that Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza in the Ulyanovsk region, was detained in August 2024 on charges of participating in the activities of the 'extremist' 'LGBT movement' (Part 2 of Article 282.2) and coercion of a person to a sexual act (Part 1 of Article 133). Human Rights Watch separately reports that in March 2025 a Ulyanovsk-region doctor facing a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the 'LGBT movement' and received a three-year sentence.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to provide protection. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

28173009B91128253561055.name: Vladimir Oblast
28173009B91128253561055.summary:
Vladimir Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and no regional deviation from that framework has been identified. The national law applies in full to a visitor in the oblast.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect. Any police, hotel or transport identity check therefore reads a mismatch that cannot be corrected.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded propaganda statute criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything 'justifying' gender transition.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as an extremist organisation, participation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising 6 to 10 years under Article 282.2. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, about 98 of them administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation.

Detention itself carries lethal risk. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

These are the national legal standards applied to Vladimir Oblast; no regional deviation has been identified.

28173009B38848907206629.name: Yaroslavl Oblast
28173009B38848907206629.summary:
Yaroslavl Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned outright, changes of gender marker on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. A transgender visitor therefore cannot obtain or amend documents reflecting their gender while in the oblast, and has no lawful route to gender-affirming care in the country.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' statute is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with a repeated offence escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement operates at volume. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty across 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. It assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection, and it affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

28173009B47279883421777.name: Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug
28173009B47279883421777.summary:
Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The federal statutes governing gender identity and sexual orientation apply within the okrug unaltered, and no regional deviation from the national position has been identified, so the national assessment governs what a visitor faces here.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned. Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, so a visitor's papers cannot be brought into line with their presentation: any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch that no supporting document can resolve, and no lawful route to obtain gender-affirming care exists during a stay.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, short detention and deportation, and the expanded law reaches public expression that justifies gender transition.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions arising from that designation as of 30 June 2025, of which about 98 were administrative and three criminal.

The volume of extremism cases is now substantial. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges connected to the designation, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment. A further 81 people were found guilty across 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, meaning symbol display alone has produced convictions.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution. Its assessment that the state is able but not willing to provide protection sets the standard applied to UK asylum claims, and it affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

The enforcement pattern is national rather than okrug-specific: convictions, raids and administrative cases are recorded across Russia since the 2023 designation, and nothing indicates that Yamalo-Nenets is insulated from federal policing priorities. The composition of the caseload shows how broad the designation has become. 28173009B41275184158050.name: Ivanovo Oblast
28173009B41275184158050.summary:
Ivanovo Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation. No regional deviation from the federal position has been identified, so the oblast is assessed at the national score: federal criminal and administrative statutes operate directly in the territory, and there is no local discretion over how they are applied.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage is banned and legal gender recognition was outlawed in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and gender change on official documents took effect. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year, and gender-marker changes on documents remain prohibited. Any police stop, hotel registration or transport identity check can therefore read as a mismatch between a trans visitor's paperwork and presentation.

The propaganda regime punishes public expression with administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation in that movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten years under Article 282.2. The expanded statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition.

Enforcement has escalated in volume as well as severity. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 of them administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years.

Physical risk is documented alongside the legal exposure. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state being able but not willing to provide protection. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kalmykia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions and applies to anyone regardless of age group. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if their country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. A 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provided that people "who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences" can only be drafted during war times, while Major-General Valery Kulikov stated the statute does not forbid people of non-standard sexual orientation from serving. Amid draft-avoidance claims, Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed some "2,700" gender-change decisions had been made in recent times, with reports that young men turned to private clinics for sex changes to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. Sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex is legal, after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121; prior law punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage after the 2021 Fedotova ruling found failure to offer any recognition violated human rights, though Russia left the court in 2022. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited. A 2013 law criminalised distribution of "propaganda" promoting "non-traditional sexual relationships" among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated "the international LGBT public movement" as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations and persons, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jailing for displaying the rainbow flag designated as the movement's symbol, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist including Centre T, Coming Out, LGBT Resource Centre, Irida, Kallisto movement, Moscow Community Center for LGBT+ Initiatives, Parni Plus, Russian LGBT Network and T9 NSK with founders convicted for leading an extremist organisation. Authorities have never approved Moscow pride requests, and in 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by refusing permits, while in August 2012 Moscow City Court upheld blocking yearly permits through 2012 citing public disorder. Documented violence includes Chechnya detentions since February 2017 of over 100 men with torture and at least three extrajudicial killings, a further purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities rising from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, including 205 cases by homophobic hate groups such as Occupy Pedophilia using dating apps to hunt homosexuals.

28173009B4400867918714.name: Kemerovo Oblast

Kemerovo Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which is assessed here through the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025). Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. The note contains no oblast-specific information beyond that national framework.

Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the federal propaganda statute by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and states that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 ruling, with sentences running up to 12 years in prison. Enforcement inside Kemerovo Oblast itself has produced prison time. RIA Novosti, citing the Federal Security Service, reported that a person already serving a prison sentence in the region received an additional six-year sentence in February for participating in the "LGBT movement" and "involving" other prisoners in its activities.

28173009B30250450380208.summary:

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025; page updated 12 August 2026) is the assessment framework for this division. Under the 'gay propaganda' law, public expression 'promising' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition, including displaying rainbow symbols, is punishable by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals or detention of up to 15 days. The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023. Between 2022 and 2024, at least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since that designation, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison. The 2013 'gay propaganda' law already made any positive or neutral depiction of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the 'propaganda' law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary:
The Free State province of the Republic of South Africa stands under the national framework set by the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, which prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. South Africa was the first country in the world to bar sexual-orientation discrimination, doing so in 1996, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly extends protection to gender identity and sex characteristics alongside sexual orientation.

Partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse. The Constitutional Court's judgment of December 2005 compelled Parliament to act, and the Civil Union Act was passed in November 2006 with a National Assembly vote of 229 to 41, legalising same-sex marriage nationwide.

Legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which permits a change of sex status in the population registry and therefore on identity documents and passports on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. The route nonetheless requires medical evidence, a pathologising standard that locks some people out of recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Detention carries elevated and now-litigated risk. On 10 November 2025 the High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge against the Department of Correctional Services. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate feminising attire and she/her pronouns, restricting her gender expression, and denying state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy constituted unfair discrimination, and that gender-affirming health care forms part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e). The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025, describing its OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty and the Department's argument that the therapy was cosmetic. Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling, but reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven and concentrated in the main cities, so trans people in the Free State must travel long distances to reach it; private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands and public waiting lists are long. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in access to gender-segregated bathrooms, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

The Justice Department's National Task Team, established in 2011, and the 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities address hate crimes against LGBT people. No Free State-specific trans source was surfaced, so this record rests on the national framework.

19338628B99642989531496.name: Pays de la Loire
19338628B99642989531496.summary:
Pays de la Loire stands under the French national framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal procedure, custodial oversight and marriage applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, and the sources document no regional deviation material enough to assess separately. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Custody is the principal exposure. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male (the vast majority, who have not had sex-reassignment surgery) are placed in men's facilities. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee recalling inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' alongside threats of violence.

The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, Adeline Hazan, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison. The same feature illustrates her finding with the case of Kara B., an American trans woman held in conditions she described as worrying.

The CGLPL, France's national custodial-inspection authority and preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It records the persistence of serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees in adult prisons, while noting that none were identified in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres.

That review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. The CGLPL examined roughly forty referrals from trans detainees since 2010 together with ministry and association input, and identified placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches as serious and persistent violations, with structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty; its stated reasons for a new opinion include changed terminology in the gender-recognition law and coverage now extending to intersex and non-binary detainees.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule beyond Article D248: where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in the BuzzFeed News feature describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

19338628B73800214047876.summary:

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees according to the sex inscribed on their identity documents, and each facility improvises around that rule. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'The Plight Of Trans Women In Prison', reports first-person accounts of placement in all-male facilities, including a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014 marked by detainee and staff hostility, and the story of an Argentinian trans woman's incarceration. The feature also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty states that transgender detainees are the group that suffers the most in prison.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021, issued by the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté, examines the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty. It rests on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections covering Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The opinion finds persistent serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees, including isolation and overcrowding risks, and recommends that the 2016 depathologising law, which removed the surgery requirement for civil-status change, be translated into prison regulations. Its scope explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

For partner recognition, France legalised same-sex marriage and full adoption in 2013, and civil solidarity pacts have existed since 1999. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore encounters a recognised legal baseline.

Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced 'sexual identity', protected since 2012. Homophobic hate speech has carried penalties of up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment.

On legal gender recognition, a bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017. It abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention.

Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale.

36201628B47773222326566.name: Zamboanga Peninsula
36201628B47773222326566.summary:
The Zamboanga Peninsula stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Consensual same-sex relations are legal and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but legal gender recognition is unavailable: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no national anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

The local legal floor in this division is set in part by Zamboanga City, the peninsula's regional center, which enacted its own anti-discrimination ordinance in 2020 and is named among the more than 20 local governments with such ordinances. Non-discrimination ordinances operate at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels across the country. The other provinces and cities of the peninsula are not sourced individually, so equivalent protection outside Zamboanga City is unresolved.

Violence against trans women is documented and recent. On 23 June 2025 Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman and student at Cagayan State University in Peñablanca, was found dead in a river in Cagayan province with visible signs of physical assault; a person who admitted picking her up the previous night surrendered to police and denied killing her. The same day Ali Macalintal, a trans activist and former journalist, was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos, and Shalani Dolina was killed in Caloocan earlier in 2025. The Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide. All three killings occurred outside this peninsula, but they are the clearest available indication of what a trans visitor to the country should expect.

Detention strips away most of what protection exists on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex. At Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and safety is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal 'weddings' with male inmates in what would be locally classed as same-sex relationships rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse' alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings housed there since the annex was established. These facilities are outside the peninsula; no jail practice specific to the peninsula is sourced.

Public space is governed by statute rather than by identity. The Safe Spaces Act 2019 criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs, with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority of Filipinos opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, a division of shared facilities a trans visitor may be challenged over. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly since 1999 and has never passed; campaigners cite its 25-year blockage as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy, and the latest version was filed in 2022 as House Bill 5551 and Senate Bill 1600.

sources.summary: Framework applying nationwide, including the Zamboanga Peninsula: same-sex relations are legal, there is no legal gender recognition, and LGBTI organisations can register; perception indices rank the country among the region's most accepting and surveys show strong support for an anti-discrimination law, although a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets; diversity-and-inclusion executive orders (2019, amended 2023) existed but were not implemented as of 2025; non-discrimination ordinances operate at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels, while national SOGIE legislation has been filed repeatedly since 1999 but never passed; the Anti-Bullying Act 2013 and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (2017, reiterated 2022) cover SOGI in schools; the Safe Spaces Act 2019 covers homophobic and transphobic slurs.

Bulatlat news (26 June 2025): an eighteen-year-old trans woman (Kierra Apostol, student of Cagayan State University, Peñablanca) was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025 with visible signs of physical assault; a person who admitted picking her up the previous night surrendered to police and denied killing her; the same piece records the killing of trans activist and former journalist Ali Macalintal by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos (23 June) and of Shalani Dolina in Caloocan earlier in 2025; a national LGBT alliance says the violence is 'proof that LGBT persons remain unsafe' and demands passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version filed 2022 as House Bill 5551 / Senate Bill 1600).

SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances cover eight provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo) and 32 cities and municipalities, alongside barangay-level ordinances, though none of the named provinces is in this peninsula.

Employment and service rules are specific. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty, and the Code of Professional Responsibility governing lawyers was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate. Because birth-certificate gender cannot be changed, trans service members serve under the marker assigned at birth.

Schools carry explicit duties. The Anti-Bullying Act 2013 and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy of 2017, reiterated in 2022, cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools. LGBTI organisations can register with the state. The Commission on Human Rights has publicly characterised the year's trans killings as transfemicide, and campaigners have demanded passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill as proof that LGBT persons remain unsafe without it.

36201628B29919658129037.name: Eastern Visayas
36201628B29919658129037.summary:
Eastern Visayas, six provinces in the eastern central Philippines, stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which applies uniformly across the region; the sources record no regional deviation from that framework, and the region is assessed at the national position.

Consensual same-sex relations are legal nationwide and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender; same-sex conduct has never been criminalised. An international overview updated 12 March 2026 confirms the position for the Philippines: same-sex conduct legal, and no legal gender recognition pathway of any kind.

Transgender visitors should expect their documents to be read as issued. No administrative legal gender recognition process exists: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A mismatch between presentation and the sex marker on a passport or birth certificate therefore has no domestic legal remedy during a visit.

Marriage equality does not exist. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage has no recognition in Philippine family law.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. National legislation on the subject has been filed since 1999 without enactment, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending in Congress since the 2000s. Protection instead comes from a patchwork of local anti-discrimination ordinances enacted at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels elsewhere in the country, alongside sectoral statutes: Republic Act 11166 bars discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression; the Safe Spaces Act, the Magna Carta of Women and the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalise SOGIE-based harassment and slurs with fines and, in the social-workers statute, up to one year's imprisonment. Visitors have no standing under local ordinances, and coverage in any given Eastern Visayas town cannot be assumed from the national picture.

Facilities remain contested. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority of respondents opposed transgender women's use of women's toilets, an attitude that shapes how establishments in the region are likely to treat a trans woman asking for gendered facilities.

Executive measures exist on paper without effect. Executive Order 100, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 of 2023 added a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025.

Violence against trans people is documented nationally and recent. On 23 June 2025 the body of 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, found with signs of physical assault, was recovered from a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan, after she had been reported missing on 22 June; her mother had reported the disappearance to local police. The case fell in Cagayan Valley rather than Eastern Visayas and is cited here as evidence of national climate. The national LGBT alliance Bahaghari's chairperson described the killing as part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill; the Commission on Human Rights has separately described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Detention carries acute risk for anyone remanded or arrested. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, where head-shaving on arrival can be mandatory and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; there is no gender-matched placement, and official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology.

Local ordinances elsewhere in the country restrict gender presentation in public: Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments with little or no legal consequence.

36201628B97761566458517.name: Northern Mindanao
36201628B97761566458517.summary:
Northern Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Same-sex relations are lawful and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but the country has no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity: the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress since 2000, roughly 25 years, and a comparable bill first filed in 1999 has not been enacted. The binding protections a visitor can rely on are therefore sub-national ordinances, sectoral statutes and the courts.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court's 2008 ruling in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; the Family Code confines marriage to a man and a woman, and Quezon City's 2023 Right to Care Card is a municipal health-decision mechanism rather than partner recognition.

Local protection across Mindanao is thin. Citing MindaNews of 24 June 2019, the national reference material reports that only four local government units across the entire island had passed pro-LGBT ordinances by mid-2019. Documentation for Northern Mindanao specifically is sparse, so the absence of a regional signal does not establish that no divergence exists. Lanao del Norte, within the region, has adjacent Muslim personal-law courts operating.

Executive machinery exists on paper. Executive Order 100 s.2019, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 s.2023 amended it to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither was implemented as of 2025. Anti-discrimination ordinances do exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels elsewhere in the country, which gives a visitor some sub-national recourse, but they are uneven.

Public attitudes constrain how protections are used. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, a divide that bears directly on which facilities a trans visitor can safely enter.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent at national level. On 23 June 2025 Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province, after going missing on 22 June; her mother had reported the disappearance to local police. The killing occurred in the Cagayan Valley region rather than Northern Mindanao, and Bahaghari's national alliance chairperson cited it as part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and as reason to renew calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill.

36201628B90061603712355.name: Davao Region
36201628B90061603712355.summary:
The Davao Region records no separate regional legislation. A visitor to the region stands under the national framework of the Philippines together with any local ordinance of Davao City, the region's administrative center, which passed a non-discrimination ordinance in 2012 covering LGBT people, minorities and persons with disabilities.

Same-sex conduct is legal nationwide, same-sex relations have never been criminalised, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores the capital at 69 of 100 for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 81 for HIV-positive travellers, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band rather than 'Generally Safe'.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route. A trans visitor's identity documents therefore cannot be brought into line with their presentation.

Marriage equality and civil unions have no national recognition. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been repeatedly filed in Congress without enactment, with national legislation on the subject pending since 1999.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force, and national protection runs only in the basic-education context. Local government non-discrimination ordinances fill part of the gap: anti-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels across the country, and Davao City's 2012 ordinance is among them.

Executive measures exist on paper without effect. Executive Order 100, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 of 2023 amended it to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025.

Public attitudes constrain day-to-day use of space. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22 per cent support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, which bears directly on restroom access for a trans visitor.

Detention carries acute risk and the region has its own practice. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, where there is no gender-matched placement, head-shaving on arrival is mandatory in the male dorm of Manila City Jail, and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy. In Davao, the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. A foreign national was arrested in May 2025 for raping a trans woman in Batangas, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Establishment practice can exclude gender-diverse people regardless of ordinance. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children, a provision in place since 2006.

Transphobic violence remains documented at national level. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

The national migration law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. 68945753B85747362819570.name: Gangwon
68945753B85747362819570.summary:
Gangwon province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, and gender identity and gender expression are not offences in civilian life. The criminalising provision that survives, Military Criminal Act article 92-6, reaches consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023.

Restroom access is governed by a national standard that reaches Gangwon directly. In July 2024 a Seoul appellate court finalised a 300,000 won damages award against the state, holding that police advice telling a person who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom forms part of the same standard. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to do so, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether.

Legal gender recognition without surgery is the operative rule in the province. In May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved registered-sex change from male to female for five applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria and that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity.

No Gangwon-specific ordinance, police practice, incident or enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors is documented in these sources, so the rules a visitor meets in the province are the national ones described above.

The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use. 68945753B5424648896322.name: South Jeolla
68945753B5424648896322.summary:
South Jeolla Province has no separate provincial ordinance on gender identity or gender expression. A visitor to the province therefore stands under South Korea's national framework, in which being transgender is not a criminal offence in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal.

The exception sits with the armed forces. Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted. In 2017 the military criminally charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a trans person concerns Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available without a surgical condition. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that gender change cannot be determined by surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity.

The Supreme Court ruled en banc on 24 November 2022 that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors. A 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the principal advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, although LGBTI organisations can register: an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government continued to appeal, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a documented live problem. On the ruling finalised on 22 July 2024, a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and made final a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink in order to do so, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that had prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom.

Schools are part of the same pattern. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed. A 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants; organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction. At Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters.

Everyday hostility is recorded in survey data. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, that 65.4% of those recommended reported harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the previous year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

A district court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the defence ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available without a surgical prerequisite. On 8 May 2024 a regional court approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that gender change cannot be determined by surgery, that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria, and that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. On 24 November 2022 the supreme court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors.

Restroom access is a live legal question. On 22 July 2024 an appellate court in the national capital dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right; the plaintiff had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020. A 2021 district court in another province awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. A 2021 survey by the national human rights commission of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to manage this, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. Research from an LGBTQ+ youth centre, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed, including a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school who reported holding it in and leaving school early.

1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
La Libertad region stands under Peru's national framework. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents requires restroom entry to be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Vague child-protection articles in that law, including a ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry; between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed. In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

La Libertad appears in the Public Ministry's Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people in Peru between 2012 and 2021, which recorded 84 criminal complaints involving 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. Fifty-eight per cent of the deaths were concentrated in six fiscal districts: Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). La Libertad therefore ranks second in absolute count, level with Lima Norte and behind Lima, making it one of the two highest-burden jurisdictions outside the capital.

The Regional Government of La Libertad adopted Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR of 6 September 2024, promoting labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in the region. It declares that every such person has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity and/or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in La Libertad.

The country does not criminalise trans identity, but the April 2025 law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents requires restroom entry to be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Vague child-protection articles in that law, including a ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. The national legislature voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving the country one of only three in its subregion, with two neighbouring jurisdictions, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and its co-author, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry; between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed. In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of a trans woman and LGBTI activist nearly 20 years after the attack. It was the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per a news outlet, the regional human-rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the subregion's history. Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 the national health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a constitutional court in the capital ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Fifty-eight per cent of the deaths were concentrated in six fiscal districts: the capital (12), this state/province (10), two capital-area districts (10 each) and two further districts (7 and 6 each), alongside a port district (6). 1875124B58976419670313.summary:
The Tacna region stands under Peru's national framework; the national layer of criminal law, anti-discrimination protection, identity documents and facility access is carried by the Peru record.

On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the Los 5 Titos hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel on a Sunday with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag; hostel staff discovered the body when the rental period expired.

By 21 May 2025 police were analysing surveillance footage from inside and outside the hostel to trace the suspect's escape route, and no suspect had been identified. The victim had initially been processed as an unidentified person and was identified only through the hostel's cameras. Relatives denounced the killing and demanded police action.

Wayka reported on 27 May 2025 that the case is being investigated as a possible hate crime, meaning an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. The family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
Atlántico department stands under Colombia's national framework. The department's own signal comes from the 2025 report "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", published by the regional LGBTI+ rights organisation Caribe Afirmativo and covered by Publimetro Colombia.

For Atlántico the report counts 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 69 threats, 12 discrimination cases, 8 cases of digital violence, 8 cases of lethal violence, and 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders during 2025. These are raw departmental totals; the report supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so they cannot be read as a ranking against other Colombian departments and no conclusion about relative danger follows from the counts alone.

The report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories carrying a "high" threat level for this population. Violence is described as expanding into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, with the state response judged insufficient.

Threat cases recorded in the report show near-total impunity: 99.8% never advance past the investigation stage. Whether that percentage is calculated for the department or for the country as a whole is not stated in the material available here.

The department's development plan and Barranquilla's development plan commit the local authorities to coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, the police and the judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

Bolívar is a department of Colombia, and its trans-related law and enforcement sit within the national framework. The department's documented record on trans safety centres on the killing of Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader, in Carmen de Bolívar on 22 May 2025. El Tiempo's data investigation classifies the case as a trans feminicide. Jiménez had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and had joined its sixth symbolic return march, which brought together more than 500 survivors of sexual violence. Her friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality.

More than 19 days after the killing, the circumstances remained unclear. No arrest, charge or explanation of the death is reported in that period, and the case is the department's documented instance of lethal violence against a trans person.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report, 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia', does not name Bolívar. It documents violence against LGBTIQ+ people expanding toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and places the department inside the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for that expansion and for the weakest state response. The department's risk picture therefore rests on cluster-level findings rather than on monitoring specific to Bolívar.

sources.summary: El Tiempo data investigation (2025): Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of more than 500 survivors of sexual violence, was killed - the article calls it a trans feminicide - in Bolívar on 22 May, in Carmen de Bolívar; more than 19 days later the circumstances remained unclear, and friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality. The piece exposes the gap between official and NGO figures: the Fiscalía's own data base records 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ between January 2010 and May 2025, 431 for 2024 versus about 160 reported by the NGO (267 fewer), and 39 homicides in one Fiscalía dependency's 2025 data versus 156 in the policies-and-strategies base; experts cited describe the information system as neither unified nor reliable.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia' records one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025. Violence escalates along a continuum from discrimination to intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases), threats (1,184 victims), homicide and impunity, and the report documents its territorial expansion toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, together with insufficient state response. The report does not name Bolívar explicitly. The department nevertheless sits within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for that expansion and weakest response, and the killing in Carmen de Bolívar is covered by the El Tiempo investigation.
