sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies include discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Since the March 2018 unanimous Supreme Federal Court ruling, transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial authorization or medical report, with registry-office gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender; in 2022 Álex Souza de Sá became the first non-binary person recognized, requiring rectification in Rio de Janeiro and six months of insistence plus intervention by the Public Defender's Office to obtain recognition in Manaus where the registry lacked a gender-neutral marker. For facilities, on 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. For care, in November 2023 the State Public Defender's Office opened monitoring of public health services for transgender and travesti people including hormones and surgeries, in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended the state formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualization services including sexual reassignment surgeries with deadlines for submission to the Ministry of Health, and on 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. For protection machinery, in 2021 the State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group focused on human rights violations and training security agents, and in August 2024 the State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes stating conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are described as underreported, with 43 cases registered according to Brazilian Public Security Forum data cited in research. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Amazonas since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, with a 328% increase between 2020 and 2025, 287 unions registered in 2024 and 98 in the first five months of 2025. Same-sex adoption was first authorized in Amazonas in November 2012 by a state court judge, with nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 state policies include discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Assembly and expression restrictions include State Law 6,469/2023 prohibiting participation of children and adolescents in pride parades with fines up to R$10,000, and the 17 October 2024 law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality, amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaça de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with prior bullying reported by area residents.

sources.title: Brazilian Supreme Federal Court ruling, March 2018 - legal gender change
sources.summary: In March 2018 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ruled that transgender people may change their legal name and gender marker on civil records without sex-reassignment surgery, hormonal treatment, or judicial authorization.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022
sources.summary: On 18 October 2022 Manaus sanctioned a municipal law prohibiting multigender/unisex restrooms.

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) Recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee integral health care to the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of 1 November 2023 the State Public Defender's health unit opened a collective procedure to audit SUS care for trans people covering access to hormonization, outpatient services, and lack of accreditation for gender-affirming surgeries including sexual reassignment, and in October 2023 the Manaus Municipal Health Secretariat committed to dispense standardized medications to trans people on prescription from the Codajás Outpatient Clinic that handles hormonization and to designate reference UBS primary-care units in each city zone, while the State Health Secretariat was ordered to report on equitable integral care including remedying hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under Federal Council of Medicine Resolution No. 2,265 of 2019.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 - gender-neutral language ban in schools
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas State Law No. 6,463 expressly prohibited use of neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of schools and public agencies statewide.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion are guaranteed under ECA Article 17 physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity and autonomy and under Constitution/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection from negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of children regardless of sexual orientation, with bullying criminalized under Law 14.811/2024 by fine to 4 years' imprisonment, homophobia criminalized per 2019 STF ruling as imprescriptible and non-bailable, conversion/"gay cure" therapy prohibited as illegal and ineffective, and legal support available through the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: DPE-AM Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office created the permanent Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship to identify LGBTQIA+ human-rights violations in public security, train public-security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ people, and issue recommendations and extrajudicial measures, while LGBTQIA+ victims in Manaus can obtain assistance via Disk 129 Monday-Friday 8am-2pm through the Specialized Human Rights unit, in a context where Amazonas led North and Central-West states with 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Nationwide criminalization of homophobia and transphobia - 2019
sources.summary: On 23 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia under Brazil's 1989 racism law punishable by up to five years' imprisonment until Congress enacts specific LGBT-discrimination legislation, to take effect after all justices voted on 5 June 2019.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security data + Fernando Vilaca de Souza homicide 5 July 2025
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022, crimes involving transsexual persons formed part of only 0.36% of total reported crimes in the capital and interior, police occurrence reports did not identify transfobia or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, trans victim data were few and badly structured with victims not infrequently inverted to accused through faulty BOs, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms left trans subjects invisibilized and without protection.

The Guardian investigation (30 July 2024) documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women. An activist quoted in it says the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. Colombia recorded 41 trans women killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. This national armed-group violence and displacement baseline applies to Sucre, where no specific information was found in the report.

13589884B54743798138783.name: Córdoba
13589884B54743798138783.summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is documented for Córdoba. A trans visitor here stands under Colombia's national framework and is assessed against the national position rather than against any local deviation.

Two national patterns bear on what a visitor might face. The first is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested: on 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon, police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper.

The second pattern is territorial violence and displacement of trans people by armed actors. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran a 'social cleansing' campaign in which flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

13589884B66570655136682.name: La Guajira
13589884B66570655136682.summary:
La Guajira stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America and is what a trans visitor in this frontier department meets directly. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The source inventory identifies no La Guajira-specific legal, document, entry, screening, facilities or care finding that departs from that national position, and no enforcement deviation material enough to score separately; the department is assessed at the national score.

What distinguishes La Guajira is who controls conduct on the ground. The department sits in the country's frontier belt where "orden público" regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct. In March 2024 armed groups in Guajira posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

A 2025 report by Caribe Afirmativo documents the territorial expansion of violence and the insufficiency of the state response, with trans women displaced from such departments because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others. National context reaching this department: the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count recorded 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

Targeted violence continues in ordinary urban settings as well. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a video of the assault went viral from 5 April showing her with fractured limbs in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

13589884B83777567082486.name: Valle del Cauca
13589884B83777567082486.summary:
Valle del Cauca stands under Colombia's national framework, among the more developed legal regimes for trans people in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Facilities access is protected by Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali, within Valle del Cauca) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk), which bar exclusion from public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Trans visitors married abroad in what would be locally classed as a same-sex marriage are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video circulated on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police questioned local residents but made no arrest even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. These incidents occurred in Antioquia and elsewhere, not Valle del Cauca, but the bearing for a visitor to Valle del Cauca is national: lethal anti-trans violence has occurred in daylight, has been filmed, and has gone unpunished.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed actors. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran a 'social cleansing' campaign with flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024, and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. The Guardian article offers no Valle del Cauca-specific finding; its bearing on Valle del Cauca is the pattern of territorial violence and displacement by armed actors.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

The formal framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; she died the following afternoon of a second cardiac arrest, with no arrests despite police interrogation of local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. The national toll of anti-trans killings is the context relevant to Putumayo; the Millerey case itself took place in Antioquia.

Organised armed-group targeting is documented in neighbouring departments. In Caquetá, three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she fled at night after hiding for a week. "Social cleansing" flyers appeared on Caquetá streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. The inventory contains no Putumayo-specific finding; the national armed-group violence, threats and displacement pattern is the claim this record relies on.

13589884B51885004571697.name: Guaviare
13589884B51885004571697.summary:
Guaviare Department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, and no Guaviare-specific legal or incident finding was identified in the source inventory. The assessment for a trans visitor therefore rests on the national framework and on national conditions, applied to a department where institutional reach is thin.

Armed-group violence against LGBTQ people is a documented national pattern that a visitor to Guaviare also faces. In Caquetá, three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she hid for a week and then fled at night. 'Social cleansing' flyers appeared on Caquetá streets and via WhatsApp naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers carrying kill lists threatening 'homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans' from March 2024.

Killing totals are high and accountability is low. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023; a CNN 'As Equals' investigation of 6 August 2025 recorded nearly 50 queer and trans people killed that year to date. Of 155 criminal investigations into LGBTQ killings, only 3 reached a verdict last year, about 2%, against a 9% overall homicide-conviction rate. These are national raw counts, not Guaviare figures, and no per-capita denominator is supplied.

Discrimination limits trans women in Colombia mainly to hairdressing or sex work, a labour pattern that constrains trans residents of Guaviare as well. The national legal baseline covers same-sex activity legal since 1981, discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds banned by a 2011 law, same-sex marriage legal since the Constitutional Court's April 2016 ruling, same-sex adoption since 2015, and legal gender change recognised since 1993.

13589884B16144547040567.name: Caquetá
13589884B16144547040567.summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia. The department-specific signal in the source inventory concerns organised violence rather than statute: The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups in Caquetá were running a 'social cleansing' campaign, distributing flyers on the street and via WhatsApp that named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets.

The campaign has produced forced displacement of trans residents. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week and then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend had been killed. The same reporting states that discrimination in Caquetá limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, narrowing the economic options that would otherwise let a resident or visitor remain independent of exposure.

Nationally the same reporting counted 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024, figures that give the Caquetá flyer campaign its wider context. A separate case, the killing of Sara Millerey in Bello, Antioquia on 4 April 2025, was filmed and circulated as a viral video on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon, and despite police questioning of local residents and an urgent investigation ordered by the president, no one was arrested. Thirteen trans people were killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. Both incidents fall outside Caquetá and are carried here only as evidence of the national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence a visitor to the department faces.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary: Puno is a department of Peru, and no region-specific signal was identified in the sources. Both records addressing the public-restroom restriction scope themselves to the national framework and record no Puno-specific application, exemption, local ordinance or enforcement practice; the national assessment carried by the Peruvian record applies to this department.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The measure stood at committee stage in February 2025 and, as national law, binds Puno.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) states that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The analysis addresses the national framework that governs Puno and records no Puno-specific finding.

1875124B61751373376494.name: Lambayeque
1875124B61751373376494.summary:
Lambayeque has no trans-specific ordinance, municipal rule or documented pattern of local enforcement on record; a trans visitor in this department is bound throughout by Peru's national framework.

The national framework restricts public restroom access. The Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity on 20 February 2025 a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting entry into public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argues the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The IDEHPUCP institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms, including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI, and notes that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive.

Violence against trans people is documented at the national level. Peru recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023 according to the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, with 19 killings in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of 19 in 2023. In February 2023 trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31) was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco (30) was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. These are national figures; the source provides no Lambayeque-specific breakdown, and the counts are raw totals without per-capita denominators.

The binding framework for trans visitors and residents of the state/province is the country's national legislation, and none of the sources examined contains state/province-specific content.

On 20 February 2025 the national congressional committee on women and family approved by unanimity a dictamen merging two bills, sponsored by two legislators, that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities, and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that point, and the reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at a major international airport. An activist argued the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the national identity document to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of the national Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of a law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The national human-rights institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under the national constitution and the regional human-rights convention, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms, including a 2022 administrative ruling dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a fitness chain, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the national identity document, and notes that gender-identity recognition in the country remains long, costly and invasive.

The country recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023 according to a university observatory. The homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of 19 in 2023. These are national raw counts, not per-capita rates, and the source provides no denominator for comparison across state/provinces.

In February 2023 a 31-year-old trans sex worker was kidnapped from the capital by an extortion gang and killed in a district on the city's periphery with some 30 gunshots; a 30-year-old woman was shot days earlier. Two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. In 2021 the Amazonas State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group to address human rights violations and train security agents, and in November 2023 it opened a process to monitor public health services for transgender and travesti people including provision of hormones and surgeries. In March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial document or medical report, with registry gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital services for the transsexualization process including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and presentation to the Ministry of Health. On 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under age 18. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender, and in 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person recognized in the state after rectification in Rio de Janeiro and intervention by the Public Defender's Office to secure recognition in Manaus after six months when the local notary lacked a gender-neutral marker. Homosexuality has been legal in Amazonas and Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, and same-sex adoption was first allowed in Amazonas in November 2012 by an Amazonas Court of Justice judge before nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. The August 2024 Amazonas Court of Justice booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes states that conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Research from the Brazilian Journal of Public Security states that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas are underreported. Data from the Brazilian Public Security Forum indicates cases of violence against LGBTQ people have increased, with 43 cases registered. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, and residents reported he had previously been bullied by other young people in the region. The Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, the Order of Attorneys of Brazil and federal deputy Erika Hilton expressed regret over the incident. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically so no such quote can be reproduced, and the above violence figures refer to LGBTQ people generally not to transgender people specifically.

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee comprehensive health care for the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Public Defender's Office of the State of Amazonas (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas in October-November 2023, trans access to SUS was under enforcement review for primary care, outpatient services, hormonization, and lack of local authorization for transexualizing surgeries including sexual reassignment, with the municipal health authority committing to dispense standardized hormone medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions and to designate a reference UBS in each city zone and the state health authority required to report on equitable integral care and hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under CFM Resolution No. 2.265/2019.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022
sources.summary: On 18 October 2022 the municipality of Manaus sanctioned a law prohibiting multigender/unisex bathrooms.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 on gender-neutral language ban
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas Law No. 6,463 prohibited the use of gender-neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression deviating from standard Portuguese in the curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public offices throughout the state of Amazonas.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas since August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion from home are affirmed as protected by ECA Article 17 guaranteeing physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity, autonomy and beliefs, by Constitutional/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection against negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of all children regardless of sexual orientation, by Law No. 14.811/2024 criminalizing bullying with penalties ranging from fine to 4 years' imprisonment, by the 2019 STF recognition of homophobia as an imprescriptible and unbailable crime, and by the prohibition of conversion/"cura gay" therapies as illegal and ineffective, with legal support available from the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: Amazonas State Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) Working Group - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) created the permanent Working Group "Diversidade Sexual, Identidade de Gênero e Cidadania" to defend LGBTQIA+ rights and identify human rights violations in the area of public security. Its mandate includes training public security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ persons and issuing recommendations and other extrajudicial referrals. Victims of LGBTphobia are served by the Specialized Human Rights Defensoria via Disk 129 in Manaus Monday to Friday 8h-14h, in a context where Amazonas led North and Center-West states with an average of 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security + 5 July 2025 homicide case
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022 trans persons faced persistent diverse violence intensifying each year while only 0.36% of crimes reported in the capital and interior involved homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual victims, police occurrence reports did not identify homophobia and transfobia motives or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, victim data were few and poorly structured with victims at times inverted to accused through faulty reports, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms produced invisibilization and lack of protection for trans victims.

1875124B60950944289640.name: San Martín
1875124B60950944289640.summary:
San Martín is a department of Peru. Neither source in the inventory contains San Martín-specific content, so the department carries no provision of its own and is assessed against the national framework as it stands across Peru.

The national framework is the operative one for a trans visitor. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

In February 2025 the Comisión de Mujer y Familia of the Congress approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex. The text carries narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where entry is required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. At that stage it still required plenary backing. Its reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, and that the measure is discriminatory.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes, enacted in April 2025, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The same legislative package mandates that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their gender identity, and bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity". The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. IDEHPUCP also documented dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the April 2025 provision does not meet on IDEHPUCP's reading.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

Legal gender recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation. That gap is what makes the DNI check the practical enforcement mechanism for the restroom restriction.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected; its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained by the same package. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

An activist argues that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the national identity card to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, and that the measure is discriminatory.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the report of the statute strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents, enacted in April 2025, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The same legislative package mandates that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their gender identity, and bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity". A university human-rights institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the national constitution and Article 1.1 of the regional human-rights convention, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute also documented dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of the national Congress by a legislator.

The regional human-rights court held in an advisory opinion that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the April 2025 provision does not meet on the institute's reading.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. A consumer-protection decision, reference 0735-2022, dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a national gym chain, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the identity card. On television, a presenter of a national channel publicly harassed a legislator, the first openly lesbian member of the national Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

Legal gender recognition in the country remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation. That gap is what makes the identity-card check the practical enforcement mechanism for the restroom restriction.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected; its co-author, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per a broadcaster's report, the regional human-rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the court through the regional human-rights commission.

The national Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new criminal code's hate-crime provisions, with two political blocs carrying the repeal after an April committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left the country one of only three states in the region, with two neighbouring jurisdictions, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 the country's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a constitutional court in the capital, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained by the same package. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. An international human-rights organisation states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

1875124B5969368354394.name: Huánuco
1875124B5969368354394.summary:
Huánuco stands under Peru's national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, such as accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities; venues are also barred from posting ambiguous restroom signs. The Comisión de Mujer y Familia had approved the merged dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, unanimously on 20 February 2025. The trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

Enforcement of the restroom restriction would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, according to activist Gianna Camacho. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. Documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms include SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, which dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit after the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in her DNI; gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive.

Recorded violence against trans people is rising and undercounts the reality. Peru recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023, according to the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of 19 in 2023. These are raw national counts without a per-capita denominator, so they rank volume of cases rather than comparative risk between jurisdictions.

The February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, followed the shooting of Priscila Aguado Huatuco (30) days earlier; two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

1875124B19837374654956.name: Pasco
1875124B19837374654956.summary:
Pasco department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern on record. It stands under the national framework of Peru.

Under that framework, Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, and the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction: its Article 5.1, approved by the plenary of Congress on 2 April 2025 with the second vote waived, prohibits entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than one's birth sex. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and Muñante of Honor y Democracia, also ban inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; the Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved the merged dictamen unanimously on 20 February 2025, with narrow exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities, and an obligation on venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

Human Rights Watch reports that the April 2025 law mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms, including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI, and notes that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. Activist Gianna Camacho argues enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

1875124B73300566086976.name: El Callao
1875124B73300566086976.summary:
El Callao, the department containing Peru's principal international gateway, stands under the national framework. No department-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources, so what a trans visitor faces in El Callao is what Peru's national rules deliver. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but its Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The governing instrument is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. The same package obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. A visitor who is visibly trans should expect to be refused entry to gendered facilities across the country, including at airports, hotels, shopping centres and public buildings.

The provision was fast-tracked. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, which still required plenary backing. On 2 April 2025 the plenary approved the dictamen and waived a second vote. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez international airport, the country's main port of entry for international visitors.

The Inter-American human-rights framework points the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5.1 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. Consumer-protection body INDECOPI dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit in Resolution 0735-2022, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the national identity card. Activist and journalist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement of the 2025 ban would rest on security staff checking the identity card to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so many trans people, including visitors, cannot obtain documents matching their presentation.

Hostility has been voiced from national platforms. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. A congressman, Lizarzaburu, made dehumanising comparisons on the floor of Congress, as recorded by IDEHPUCP.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBT people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, twelve of them trans women, and perpetrators were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Named cases illustrate the risk. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots. Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier; two killers were arrested in March 2023. Trans women engaged in sex work face elevated exposure to organised extortion and lethal violence.

Legal recourse is slow but not absent. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hate-crime coverage is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is now one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Ucayali stands under the national framework of Peru. The region has no distinct local regime governing trans people; the national rules on criminalisation, documents, facilities and protection apply directly to any trans visitor to Ucayali.

Peru's congressional Plenary approved, and exempted from a second vote, a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

The measure originated in bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, which the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved as a merged draft opinion in February 2025. Exceptions cover custody situations, cases where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12, or a person with disabilities.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

1875124B2667580847298.name: Madre de Dios
1875124B2667580847298.summary:
Madre de Dios has no distinct trans-specific law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement record in the material reviewed for this dossier; the national framework therefore governs what a trans visitor to the department faces. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, removed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women continues to rise.

Restroom access is restricted nationally. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously a merged dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. The text lists narrow exceptions for custody, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The bill followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the text and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex'. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same requirement into force for trans people, including trans youth, and the legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement is expected to rest on the judgement of individual security staff. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that access to restrooms would depend on staff discretion, including checks of identity documents, and notes that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television the presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that the restroom provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The institute states that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, and cites UN reporting showing that trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru for 2020-2023, with trans women accounting for more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints recorded in 2020. A 2024 report on rising hate crimes found trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stated that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One case sets a legal precedent for the region. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available to Peruvian residents. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions for residents. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases.

A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

1875124B63771233756824.name: Apurímac
1875124B63771233756824.summary: No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance, enforcement action or incident appears in the sources attached to this record. The department stands under the national framework of Peru, and the national assessment carried by the parent record applies to a trans visitor here.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The bills are national and contain no Apurímac-specific provision; they reach the region at committee stage as of February 2025.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) states that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues that this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The bill is national and carries no Apurímac-specific provision, so it governs the region as part of the national framework the analysis addresses.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024), covering the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty (multiple gunshots, stabbings), and the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination (61 denuncias in 2020). It recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. It contains no Apurímac-specific finding; for this record its value is the national hate-violence data the regional assessment relies on.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that Congress' Commission on Women and Family unanimously approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457 that would bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined to the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage; as of publication it still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and warning that security staff would effectively judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI. The bills contain no Arequipa-specific provision, and as national law they bind the department.

IDEHPUCP analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) reports that the Congress plenary on 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from second vote, the dictamen of the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes'. Its article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The authors argue the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination; they note that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage. The analysis makes no Arequipa-specific finding.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report: 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected and hate crimes rising. It recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano (31) in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang, the bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting that indicate extreme hate. No Arequipa-specific finding appears; the national figures describe the risk environment the department shares.
