The sources attached to this record are national in scope: congressional bills and plenary action, a university human-rights institute's legal analysis, and nationwide incident data, none of which contains a finding about Loreto, its departments, its capital or its authorities.

Loreto is a department of Peru and stands under Peru's national framework, which is carried in the national record and the parent bundle. As national law, Peru's rules on public facilities, non-discrimination and recorded violence against trans women apply within Loreto, but no source documents how, or whether, they are enforced there.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the Congress Commission on Women and Family unanimously approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457, which would bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined to the sex opposite to one's birth sex. Exceptions cover custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12, or a disabled person, and the measure would require unambiguous signage; as of publication it still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and warning that security staff would judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI. The bill contains no Loreto-specific provision, and as national law it applies in Loreto.

IDEHPUCP analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) reports the Congress plenary on 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from second vote, the dictamen of the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes', whose article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying/assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The authors argue the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination; they note Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage. No Loreto-specific finding appears; the source supports this record's critique claim.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report: 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, trans women the most affected and hate crimes rising; it recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano (31) in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang, with bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting indicating extreme hate. No Loreto-specific finding appears; the national data describe the risk environment that applies in the department.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) reports a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package that would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, including its so-called promotion, would bring up to three years in prison. Participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would bring up to four years; since same-sex marriage is not legal, such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. Gender-affirming care would be restricted, with the surgery age raised from 18 to 25 and permanent infertility made mandatory. Medical professionals would face fines or up to seven years, and transgender patients up to three years for care outside the new limits, forcing treatment into underground settings. The package contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific provision and stands as national law over visitors in the province.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy, documents six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. The counts come from media and civil-society reports because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics. It records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, together with 336 assembly and 313 liberty violations, a roughly 2.5-fold liberty increase consisting mostly of detentions, alongside event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. The report describes hostility institutionalised under Year of the Family instructions to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events as national practice. It contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific finding and describes the country-wide framework that governs the province.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) reports a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus '11th Judicial Package' that would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would bring up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years (same-sex marriage is not legal, so such ceremonies are by definition symbolic). Gender-affirming care would be restricted: surgery age raised from 18 to 25, mandatory permanent infertility, with medical professionals fined or imprisoned up to seven years and transgender patients up to three years for care outside the new limits, forcing treatment into underground settings. The package contains no Amasya-specific provision, and this national framework governs a visitor in the province.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', documents six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the counts are drawn from media and civil-society reports. It records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, plus 336 assembly and 313 liberty violations, a roughly 2.5-fold rise in liberty violations consisting mostly of detentions, with event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. Hostility is institutionalised through 'Year of the Family' instructions to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events, applied as country-wide practice rather than provincial choice. No Amasya-specific finding appears in the report.

Düzce stands under the national framework of Turkey. The source inventory for this province records no Düzce-specific incident, enforcement practice or local instrument, so the assessment rests on the national regime a visitor to Düzce is subject to.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Turkey since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. Turkish marriage law gives same-sex relationships no legal recognition and provides no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption. No comprehensive law bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ people are barred from open military service.

Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants, per Amnesty International.

25984515B21238382887484.name: Erzincan

Erzincan province stands under the Turkish national legal framework. No Erzincan-specific ordinance, incident or court decision was found on record, so what a trans visitor faces in the province is determined by national law and national policing practice.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited by law. Those provisions coexist with the absence of any legal recognition for same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions or same-sex adoption, and with a bar on LGBTI people serving openly in the military.

Since 2015 the Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia. In early 2026 the government was reported to be considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".

Freedom-of-assembly exposure extends to ordinary LGBT advocacy: ILGA-Europe reported on 7 December 2020 that 19 human rights defenders were prosecuted for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara in May 2019, and urged Turkish courts to acquit them and dismiss all charges. Even a campus Pride march can draw criminal prosecution in Turkey, and a visitor in Erzincan would be judged under that same framework.

Marriage is defined by law as a union between a man and a woman, making same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised; marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in a person's civil-registry record rather than on trans status.

Policing practice bears directly on a trans visitor's exposure. Police have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, deploying tear gas and water cannons; Amnesty International has documented restrictions and excessive force in 2015 and 2024. 25984515B47044460443496.name: Kütahya
25984515B47044460443496.summary:
Kütahya province stands under the national framework of the Republic of Turkey. No Kütahya-specific evidence of trans-targeted enforcement, violence or legal practice was located in the source inventory; the findings below are the national regime as it applies to a visitor in this interior province.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. There is, however, no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military, and same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised.

Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015, with Istanbul's 2015 to 2018 parades banned and dispersed. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

The 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 dropped provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, though these carry no legal marital status. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', which was ultimately not included in that year's package. In September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a 'Decade of Family and Population' crackdown.

25984515B19932594956901.name: Manisa
25984515B19932594956901.summary:
Manisa falls under Turkey's national legal and security framework. The sources behind this record contain no statute, incident, police action or court decision specific to Manisa province, so a trans visitor's exposure here is the national position as documented elsewhere in this map.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised; marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to 3 years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to 4 years; amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the gender-affirming care minimum age from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility requirements and government-approved hospital evaluation; and imprison care providers up to 7 years and trans patients up to 3 years. This is national legislation. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

A February 2026 press report described legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; that provision was not included in the 2026 omnibus, the 12th judicial package. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

Authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches in June 2025; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Since 2015 authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans.

In June 2025 Turkey's health ministry medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses.

In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49.

25984515B33535290178113.name: Mersin
25984515B33535290178113.summary:
Mersin province records no statute, police programme or administrative measure of its own directed at transgender visitors. No Mersin authority is recorded extending a safeguard that Türkiye's national framework withholds, and none is recorded adding a restriction of its own. Mersin therefore stands under the national framework of Türkiye as it is, with the country-level assessment carried in the national record rather than restated here.

What the Mersin sources do record concerns assembly. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025, covering 2024, documents that many cities across Türkiye impose bans on LGBT assembly, and that the same national ban pattern applies to visible LGBT assembly in Mersin-area cities. Istanbul Pride was banned for the tenth consecutive year, indicating the depth of the pattern Mersin-area cities follow. The Erdoğan government and religious conservative opposition parties regularly use discriminatory speech amounting to hate speech against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender communities on the pretext of promoting family values, which HRW finds puts LGBT people at great risk.

Legal-gender recognition is available nationally and applies in Mersin: Türkiye has permitted transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988, but only with sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are not available. Because Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, an individual who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, though it made symbolic same-sex weddings possible that carry no legal marital status.

25984515B57226385500606.name: Muğla
25984515B57226385500606.summary:
Muğla, the province containing Bodrum, Marmaris and Fethiye, stands under the national framework of Turkey. Turkey has permitted transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988, but only on condition of sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, so a visitor who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are not available in Turkey, and no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, though it made symbolic same-sex weddings possible that carry no legal marital status.

No region-specific signal was identified for Muğla itself. The enforcement patterns documented nationally reach resort-province institutions like Muğla's: authorities regularly and arbitrarily ban events by LGBT groups, local authorities around the country have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights, and the TV regulator RTÜK has justified fines on digital platforms for LGBT-related content as violating 'societal and cultural values.' These patterns colour what any visible LGBT assembly in Muğla can expect.

sources.summary: Muş province stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; no Muş-specific ordinance, incident or court decision is documented for the province. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTI people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' being leaked publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches; police used water cannon and tear gas on the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. Press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Amnesty also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

25984515B59741408878569.name: Niğde
25984515B59741408878569.summary:
Niğde Province stands under the national framework of Turkey. No Niğde-specific signal on trans or LGBTI+ legal exposure was identified in the source inventory; the findings below are national and apply in Niğde.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised. LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life.

Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court.

Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries.

25984515B15602000155844.name: Ordu
25984515B15602000155844.summary:
Turkey's national framework governs Ordu Province, and no local measure, enforcement programme or institution concerning trans visitors is recorded for Ordu in this edition's sources. What a trans visitor to Ordu faces is the national picture alone.

Homosexuality has been legal in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1958, and Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor, that requirement intersects with identity checks on the street: in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee's account captures the practical position: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded, and officers were already applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a draft legislative package then before the government would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague provisions protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that three draft law packages targeting LGBT people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but that they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly used the 'family' and 'public morals' framing to legitimise stigmatisation, and the reform sits within a broader authoritarian drift. Whether any package has since been reintroduced is unresolved in the sources.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 taken on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Hostility of this scale is best read as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

Amnesty International also records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. Comparable asymmetry recurs in custody: on 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

25984515B30494634933389.name: Sakarya
25984515B30494634933389.summary:
Sakarya is a province in Turkey's Marmara region and stands under the national framework of Turkey. No Sakarya-specific statute, enforcement programme, local ban or documented provincial incident concerning transgender visitors was identified in the sources assembled here; the national provisions set out below govern residents and visitors in the province alike.

The national baseline reaching Sakarya is that homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, while legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40, with the applicant at least 18, unmarried and holding a medical report from a state-designated hospital.

The most consequential visitor-facing development inside this framework is the 11th Judicial Package. Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet analyses a leaked 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws, leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025. Amnesty warns that it would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights, would raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition from 18 to 25 and add further conditions, and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare. As a nationwide proposal it would apply within Sakarya, so a trans visitor who needs medical care or a document change during a stay there is dealing with a governing framework under active, adverse revision.

25984515B33997294820892.name: Sivas
25984515B33997294820892.summary:
No Sivas-specific statute, enforcement programme, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled for this edition. The province of Sivas stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in Sivas is recorded adding prohibitions of its own.

That national framework, as set out in the sources, is as follows. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is, however, no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the Turkish military: a health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and the resulting 'unfit report' can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised; when the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the bill, leaving only symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. Early-2026 press reports recorded that the government considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'. Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches in Istanbul, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Blanket bans combined with case-by-case prosecutions under Law No. 2911 form the enforcement climate that provincial authorities in Sivas operate under, as across Turkey.

25984515B20532508270601.name: Tokat
25984515B20532508270601.summary:
Tokat province has no trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation of its own, and no region-specific signal was identified in the sources for this record.

The two sources that address Tokat do so only by placing the province inside Türkiye's nationwide regime of assembly bans. Any visible LGBT gathering in Tokat would be policed under the framework that has banned Pride in Istanbul and in other cities in most years since 2015, during which police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against those who attempt to assemble.

Provincial authorities and police in Tokat therefore operate inside a documented national pattern in which visible LGBT assembly is routinely banned and policed. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025, covering 2024, records Istanbul Pride banned for the tenth consecutive year and similar bans imposed by many cities across the country.

25984515B1589724669162.name: Trabzon
25984515B1589724669162.summary:
Trabzon province generates no trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation in the available record. What is recorded for Trabzon is the absence of any documented divergence from the national position, which is not a finding of safety: the Turkish national framework extends to Trabzon in full, and a visitor to the province should expect the same legal exposure, document checks and detention practice documented elsewhere in Turkey.

HRW reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus reform draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal code to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, mandate permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose both healthcare professionals performing such care and patients to criminal prosecution, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW calls for its withdrawal. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's Human Rights Report 2025, titled "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy, with instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected, 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (a striking increase over the prior year), 313 right-to-liberty violations — about 2.5 times the previous year — with 299 detention decisions, freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540, and 40 right-to-association violations including the first closure of an LGBTI+ association in many years. These figures are national totals reported without a provincial breakdown, so they cannot be attributed to Trabzon specifically; they indicate the enforcement climate a visitor to the province would enter.

Yalova is a province of Turkey and stands under Turkey's national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern, police practice or incident documentation specific to Yalova appears in the available sources. That gap is recorded as absence of documented divergence rather than evidence of local permissiveness: the national rules and the national enforcement climate apply in Yalova as they apply across Turkey.

The national enforcement climate a visitor enters is documented in Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People," which finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy. Instructions framed around "the Year of the Family" were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The review records 6 right-to-life violations over the year, including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; 313 liberty violations, about two and a half times the previous year, of which 299 were detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 passed the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention on 9 May 2012, was promulgated on 24 May 2012, and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. Emergency decree DNU 62/2025, published in February 2025, modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for people under 18, which Reuters reported as a ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Decree DNU 61/2025, published the same month, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere; it prohibits people who have legally changed gender from being held in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call both decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The national administration has eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a 62% rise on the previous year and a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026 shows that 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, that security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and that trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims, 142 cases. Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally. Activists from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is not applied in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration, even though anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.

19177384B49506124846693.tangentialFactors:
Two readings of the same national framework sit side by side. The United Nations called Law 26.743 a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so. An Outright International overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless returns negative assessments on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, which the monitor treats as evidence of deterioration.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Santa Catarina stands under the national framework of Brazil. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change, and joint and second-parent adoption were confirmed by the Supreme Federal Tribunal in RE 846.102 (2015). A visitor's entry, documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as any other traveller's.

Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punishable as equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989 following the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2019 ruling in ADO 26. Foreign spouses and partners of a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship are treated identically in visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign marriages read as same-sex under birth-sex status are recognised for immigration purposes.

Santa Catarina's own constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, yet as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Trans-specific protection in the state rests on the national constitutional and criminal provisions rather than on the wording of the state charter.

Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. The Superior Court of Justice has ruled that non-binary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity, and gender-marker changes proceed without surgery.

Courts in the state have applied family protection to foreign partners. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide.

The wider national environment remains contested. A deeply conservative Congress has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013, while constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions continue to apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina.

On health care, the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee in September 2025, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Santa Catarina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: State Law No. 12,534 enacted 4 April 2003 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity until repealed 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, while Complementary Law No. 527 signed 28 December 2010 also prohibited discrimination based on gender identity until partially overturned 11 October 2018 after a 2015 Supreme Federal Court challenge on labor-law grounds, followed by a 2019 Supreme Federal Court decision banning discrimination based on gender identity. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation, and in 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in Santa Catarina to judicially change documents to reflect a neutral gender, though judicial actions are still required without a state law recognizing it and legal sex is still required in birth certificates. In December 2023 the Constitution and Justice Committee of the Legislative Assembly approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of 18 August 2026, and a 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights with about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court. The Army provides that any person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and considered exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting Federal Constitution, Military Service Law, implementing regulations and 2024 General Conscription Plan requirements. On 21 January 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms, while the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signs from 18 June 2026 indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 Florianopolis shopping-mall case where a trans woman was denied access to the women's restroom, a lower court ordered 15,000 reais compensation for pain and suffering, the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina overturned it, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court voted 8-3 to reject her 2015 appeal as not involving a constitutional issue, followed in August 2025 by an extraordinary appeal to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts. Gender-neutral language was banned in state schools by decree of Governor Carlos Moises on 15 June 2021 until overturned 6 May 2025 by the Supreme Federal Court and banned in Joinville public office by law of 20 December 2021 until struck down 3 August 2022 by the Court of Justice, while on 1 April 2026 a law allowed parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics, and in 2024 three murders of trans people were recorded in the state. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830, same-sex unions were recognized as family units with same rights and responsibilities as heterosexual couples by the Supreme Federal Court in May 2011, and same-sex marriage was authorized statewide by General Inspectorate of Justice resolution on 29 April 2013. State Law No. 12,534 enacted 4 April 2003 prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation until repealed 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, while Complementary Law No. 527 signed 28 December 2010 also prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation until partially overturned 11 October 2018 after a 2015 challenge arguing only the federal government can legislate on labor law, followed by a 2019 Supreme Federal Court decision banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. As of 2025, 19 anti-LGBTQ bills had been introduced in the Legislative Assembly with 11 authored by the Liberal Party. On 1 April 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed a law published 6 April allowing parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics, while on 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck down a 2015 Tubarao law that had prohibited teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools. In 2024 the Brazilian Public Security Yearbook reported 85 cases of intentional bodily injury against LGBTQ individuals with low rates attributed to underreporting, and on 3 September 2026 the Court of Justice ordered parents of a gay teenager in Jaguaruna to pay 100,000 reais compensation after kicking him out and exposing his sexual orientation on social media.

sources.title: General Inspectorate of Justice of Santa Catarina - Resolution of 29 April 2013
sources.summary: On 29 April 2013 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Santa Catarina authorized notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses without observance of gender limitation, allowing same-sex couples where both partners reside in Santa Catarina to formalize civil marriage and expanding Article 629 of the CGJ Code of Norms beyond stable union recognized since 2011.

sources.title: Complementary Law No. 527 - Governor Leonel Pavan / STF challenge
sources.summary: Santa Catarina Complementary Law No. 527 of 28 December 2010 penalizes private legal entities and, where applicable, state public servants that promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation, defining as such violent, coercive, intimidating or vexatious acts, barring entry or stay in places of free public access, differentiated service not required by law, denying, preferring against or surcharging hotel/motel/pension lodging and rental/purchase/acquisition/lease/loan of movable or immovable property, and prohibiting expression of affection permitted to others, punishable by R$2,500 fine and R$5,000 on repeat plus 30-day suspension of annual license or revocation of monthly/daily/seasonal license with 30-day renewal bar with complaints to the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defense of the Citizen and fines to the State Civil Police Improvement Fund and up to 30-day suspension for state servants, while the Federal Supreme Court in ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018 unanimously declared Article 2 VI and VII formally unconstitutional.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court (STF) - 1 March 2018 gender identity ruling
sources.summary: In 2018 in ADI 4275 the Federal Supreme Court held that equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity or expression and allowed alteration of name and gender in the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization because gender identity is a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize, and in ADO 26 and MI 4733 it equated transphobia together with homophobia to the crime of racism until Congress enacts criminalizing legislation, and in ADPF 527 it determined that transgender women prisoners be transferred to women's prisons with later requirement that custodial placement be fixed by reasoned judicial decision after questioning the detained person's preference, and in ADPF 787 it required the Unified Health System (SUS) to guarantee transsexual and travesti persons full access to health services and actions consistent also with biological sex, biological apparatus and physiological needs.

sources.title: Court of Justice of Santa Catarina / Supreme Federal Court - Florianopolis shopping mall restroom case 2014-2024
sources.summary: In Florianópolis, Santa Catarina, a trans woman blocked by shopping-mall security from using the women's bathroom won moral damages at first instance under the Consumer Defense Code but lost on appeal before the TJSC, and on 6 June 2024 the STF majority dismissed her appeal pending since 2014 and withdrew its recognized general repercussion on procedural grounds that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages and not constitutional provisions, thereby issuing no binding constitutional ruling on trans bathroom access.

sources.title: Agencia Diadorim - research/report on Santa Catarina
sources.summary: From January 2019 to June 2025 Santa Catarina state deputies introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills versus 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills, including proposals to prohibit neutral language in official government communications and to bar minors from hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care, with 4 of the anti-LGBTQIA+ bills archived and none enacted.

sources.title: Office of Florianopolis Councilor Leonel Camasao (PSOL) - 2026 report
sources.summary: From January 2015 to October 2025 Santa Catarina's Legislative Assembly and its 295 municipal chambers approved or advanced at least 271 unconstitutional laws, bills and normative acts already declared unconstitutional by the STF, 41% attacking gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIA+ people, with 36% already in force and only 11% judicially annulled, concentrated in the Vale do Itajaí and accelerating in the last five years.

14911670B90188072957077.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013 under national judicial council resolution 175/2013, the national constitutional court removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change, and joint and second-parent adoption were confirmed by the national constitutional court in a 2015 decision. A visitor's entry, documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as any other traveller's.

Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punishable as equivalent to racism under the national anti-discrimination statute (7.716/1989) following the national constitutional court's 2019 ruling. Foreign spouses and partners of a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship are treated identically in visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign marriages read as same-sex under birth-sex status are recognised for immigration purposes.

The state/province's own constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, yet as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Trans-specific protection in the state/province rests on the national constitutional and criminal provisions rather than on the wording of the provincial charter.

Since 2020 people in the state/province have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. The national high court has ruled that non-binary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity, and gender-marker changes proceed without surgery.

Courts in the state/province have applied family protection to foreign partners. In the state capital, a judge of the 1st Civil Court blocked national immigration authorities from deporting a foreign citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a local lesbian. The ruling kept the couple together despite the partner's foreign nationality.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names the state capital among the parent nation's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas of the state/province may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide.

The wider national environment remains contested. A deeply conservative legislature has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the national constitutional court in 2013, while constitutional guarantees and national criminal provisions continue to apply nationwide and cover visitors in the state/province.

On health care, the national government reinstated the LGBTI+ health technical committee in September 2025, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy.

82249235B24619009834807.name: British Columbia
82249235B24619009834807.summary:
British Columbia stands under the Canadian framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation and hate-propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code, both carried by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia, and courts have applied these protections consistently. Sexual orientation has been a protected ground federally since 1996. No province or territory restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction for visitors.

British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation addressing trans people. It was the first jurisdiction in Canada to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code, in 1992, and is routinely assessed as the country's most progressive province on LGBT issues. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults; that ban applies in British Columbia.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Transgender people may change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial human rights machinery is available to visitors and residents who face discrimination in the province.

National hate-crime data shows a mixed picture. A Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 covering police-reported hate crime in 2024 records 4,882 incidents, up 1% from 2023 after a 34% rise between 2022 and 2023, and a 169% increase since 2018, with the population rate down 2% to 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. The release breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, and it contains no British Columbia breakdown, so trans-specific hate-crime volume in the province is not established by this dataset.

Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the record. Federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities according to their gender identity, and transgender prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Litigation has tested both placement and care: lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in a case over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns bear on a trans visitor only if the visitor is detained.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in British Columbia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, and as of 2017 all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly list gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in Charter section 15 to include transsexuality, with section 15 applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while complaints against private businesses proceed under the applicable federal or provincial human rights statute. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges blocked when the government passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 received royal assent, and the anal-intercourse provision in section 159 of the Criminal Code was repealed on June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75, setting the age of consent at 16 for all sexual activities, 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under Charter section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination as of 2017. Charter equality protections apply to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement but not directly against the private sector, are subject to reasonable limits under section 1 under the Oakes Test and to section 33's notwithstanding clause, which has never been used by the federal Parliament. Canada legalized same-sex marriage nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, becoming the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so, after court rulings between 2002 and 2005 struck down the opposite-sex common-law definition. Same-sex adoption is legal in all provinces and territories, beginning with British Columbia in 1996 and ending with Nunavut in 2011, and British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as defined by statute. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing RCMP, federal departments, and notified provincial, municipal police and courts to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions for living and deceased persons, distinct from a pardon or record suspension. Canada was ranked first in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023 indicating least dangerous, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessed same-sex marriage available throughout Canada since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt as heterosexual couples and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. The same poll documented transgender-specific tolerance, finding that "87.6% said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person."

47653553B5611469222723.name: RegiÃ³n de ValparaÃ­so
47653553B5611469222723.summary:
Región de Valparaíso stands under the national framework of Chile. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. People under 14 cannot use the statute, which nevertheless recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006. No legal ban exists on medically unnecessary interventions on intersex minors; the Health Minister published non-binding intersex-affirming guidance in 2023.

Transphobic violence remains documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, with an acquaintance perpetrator confessing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, and the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Regional conditions in Región de Valparaíso are not benign. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report records that the region concentrated 51.32% of national recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases in 2024, an increase of 80.93% over 2023. In 2025 recorded cases fell only in Valparaíso and Metropolitana while all other regions rose; Movilh reads this pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ themes have less visibility.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia stands under Colombia's national framework: the national rules on identity documents, recognition of marriages performed abroad, access to public and commercial premises, and the treatment of detainees apply in the department as elsewhere in the country, and the inventory identifies no Antioquia-specific statute, departmental decree or court ruling of its own.

The region-specific record is a killing in Bello, in the metropolitan corridor around Medellín. On 5 April 2025 a video circulated showing Sara Millerey González Borja, a 32-year-old trans woman, beaten and thrown into a waterway in daylight while onlookers filmed; her legs, arms and hands were fractured, she could not swim, and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon.

She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025, the two earlier victims being gay men. A clinic reportedly declined to treat her as an emergency, on the stated ground that she had not been shot. Bello city hall drew criticism for referring to her by her pre-transition name. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and protests followed in several cities.

sources.summary: El País English (14 April 2025), reporting from Bello, Antioquia: 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; the video went viral on 5 April, President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: 41 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024, national figures that also cover Antioquia. Armed groups in Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there fled after death threats. No Antioquia-specific source covers these national 2023-24 kill tallies or the southern-department flyers.

25490228B43154843394848.name: Comunidad de Madrid
25490228B43154843394848.summary:
Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres. The Chueca district anchors the city's LGBT life, the annual MADO Pride in late June or early July draws millions of attendees, and daily life offers substantial anonymity for LGBT visitors. The same source records that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in the city, and that marginalised groups including trans people and migrants face additional barriers.

Documents presented in Madrid stand under Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

The Comunidad de Madrid was among the first Spanish regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and following Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute was later amended by Ley 17/2023, and regional rules of this kind must comply with the national framework set by Ley 4/2023, which fixes the statutory floor a trans visitor to the region stands under.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. A Spanish criminal-law firm's analysis sets out what Ley 4/2023 does and does not do alongside the discrimination aggravating factor of Article 22.4 covering gender identity and expression motives and the hate offences of Article 510 as extended to trans and LGBTI people.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level, though the cases on record come from outside the region. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

The national statute also bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted reproduction rules, provides parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and imposes anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005.

Local support machinery recorded for the city includes COGAM, founded in 1986 and the city's most influential LGBT organisation, the municipal Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género, and Arcopoli, which works against discrimination and violence.

Human Rights Watch (Feb 2023): "Victory in Fight for Gender Recognition in Spain" - hails Spain's self-ID gender-recognition law as a hard-won victory after years of activism. National framework context.

Hauts-de-France has no regional statute of its own on detention, identity documents or anti-discrimination; the region stands under France's national framework, and the sources yield no region-specific legal signal beyond one documented custodial case.
