65028918B14696209246677.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
65028918B14696209246677.summary:
The Jakarta Special Capital Region stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Venue raids are a standing enforcement instrument. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Jakarta is the most heavily raided venue in Indonesia for LGBTQ+ gatherings, and the capital's raid series is the clearest documented instance of the national pattern. Police arrested 141 people over a "gay sex party" in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 with ten subsequently charged, and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 with six charged. All of those cases were pursued under the pornography law.

The same pattern continues in the current period. Police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025. Offences charged in these operations can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

Arrests in these raids are made without naming detainees and without judicial proceedings, according to Amnesty International's 24 June 2025 press release. Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy that exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia, and demanded the release of those arrested.

There is no LGBT-specific statute and no general anti-discrimination law in Indonesia, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific offence. A visitor therefore faces exposure through broadly worded national laws applied at the discretion of police, not through a named prohibition.

1811400B15614733245507.name: Mahārāshtra
1811400B15614733245507.summary:
As a state within India, Maharashtra stands under the national framework on transgender recognition. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, passed by Parliament in March 2026 and approved by both houses pending presidential assent, amends the 2019 law to remove the right to self-identification, limit legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex people, and require medical certification. Human Rights Watch reports the bill also creates offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender, provisions HRW describes as reminiscent of colonial-era laws criminalising transgender persons for appearing dressed as women. Lawyer N Kavitha Rameshwar has called the medical-certification requirement an attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual, while the government argues the narrower definition targets those facing extreme and oppressive discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking. Critics warn the bill could exclude many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits, and it reverses the 2014 Supreme Court ruling recognising third gender and self-determination.

India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, while only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for accessing social security. The practical effect of the narrowed scheme is that trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the recognised categories fall outside the recognition framework altogether.

1811400B23625213884851.name: Delhi
1811400B23625213884851.summary:
Delhi stands under India's national framework. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, passed by Parliament in March 2026, replaces the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals; trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the bill removes the right to self-identification, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise support systems, calling it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urging the president not to sign it. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security, a documentation gap that bears directly on a visitor's experience of document checks in the capital.

The bill has been approved by both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling on self-identification. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider, citing privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

At a press conference in Delhi, activist Grace Banu stated that the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation".

68945753B55100681051852.name: Seoul
68945753B55100681051852.summary:
Seoul stands under the national framework of South Korea. The national provisions on criminal law, documents, military service and legal gender recognition are carried in that country record; what follows is specific to the Seoul jurisdiction.

On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court, presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the state's appeal and made final a damages ruling in favour of plaintiff A against the state. The plaintiff was awarded 300,000 won of the 3 million won claimed. Neither party appealed, so the judgment stands without further review.

The court held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person in the middle of a legal gender transition, telling them to avoid public restrooms for a period, infringed personal rights. It stated that the right to use restrooms comfortably is a fundamental and universal human right.

The finding is documented judicial protection against official interference with restroom access in Seoul, including advice issued by police to a person whose transition is visible to the authorities.

The decision became final on 2 July 2024 after neither party appealed. The court held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights, stating that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 trans respondents found that 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. A 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling awarded 7 million won in damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National judicial-framework item (Yonhap, 8 May 2024): the regional court in the central county of Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to their gender identity. The national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The court sits outside Seoul, and the ruling bears on this jurisdiction as evidence of the national judicial trend cited for it.

31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary:
Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico, where extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure by that date, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco and Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans residents carrying documents permanently mismatched to their lived identity.

The same Human Rights Watch feature documents coercive detention and border scrutiny as risks for travellers whose documents contradict their presentation, hazards that fall hardest where recognition procedures are absent or obstructed. Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020, so a trans visitor's papers are not automatically a point of friction at the state level, although national reporting indicates that formal recognition does not guarantee consistent treatment.

Partnership and family rights are settled in Quintana Roo. Same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012: two marriages performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011 were annulled by the governor in April 2012 and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. The Quintana Roo congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009.

The state penal code punishes crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and Quintana Roo ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Quintana Roo banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023, following the example set by Morelos. Both legislatures approved initiatives prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies. Penalties run to two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value for those who carry out such practices, and the reform applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

Violence against trans people nationally gives the legal picture its context. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to the 100 recorded in another country in the region. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

15666254B89722251658211.name: Selangor
15666254B89722251658211.summary:
Selangor is a state of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework, including the federal Penal Code provisions that apply to all visitors. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records enforcement of these provisions in Selangor in recent years.

The Federal Court struck down provisions of the Selangor Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 in 2021 on the ground that they exceeded the state's legislative power, not on the substance of the cross-dressing prohibition. The federal Penal Code offences were unaffected.

Selangor authorities have pursued a transgender resident with significant resources. After Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in court in 2021 to answer a charge of "insulting Islam" based on her attire, the state religious department issued an arrest warrant and announced it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to locate her, then sought her extradition from Thailand. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters cited the deployment as evidence of how far authorities will go to enforce rigid gender norms.

A Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. As of June 2021, at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" under a crackdown on LGBT people that has been ongoing since the 2018 general election. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters found such programmes internalise discrimination and foster self-hatred.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile (last updated 16 December 2025) covering the national framework and Selangor enforcement. Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping; the provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, and are usable against trans people. Sharia state enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females". In Selangor, the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power (2021). State authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers (the Sajat case). A Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. At least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community ongoing since the 2018 election.

15666254B42356713390762.name: Johor
15666254B42356713390762.summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework: the federal Penal Code applies in full within the state, while Johor's own Sharia enactment reaches Muslims alone, leaving non-Muslim visitors to the federal provisions.

In November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The announcement is a formal statement of policy by the state administration and indicates official hostility toward gender-nonconforming and LGBT people in Johor, for residents and visitors alike.

The sources record no Johor-specific raid, arrest or prosecution. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting in August 2022 on state-conducted investigations, named Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah; Johor was not among the jurisdictions listed. Absence from that list is not evidence that enforcement does not occur in Johor.

15666254B45695250728659.name: Malacca
15666254B45695250728659.summary:
Malacca is one of the thirteen states of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework. A visitor to Malacca who is neither a Malaysian citizen nor a Muslim is exposed to the federal Penal Code alone; the state Sharia enactments reach only Muslims.

The Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile, last updated 2024, reports that sections 377A and 377B of the Federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years' imprisonment and whipping, and that section 377D, "outrages on decency", criminalises gross indecency in terms that can be used to target transgender people. State Sharia enactments additionally criminalise cross-dressing for Muslims. The profile records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years and a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election.

The same profile records a high-profile 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman fleeing the country following threats of arrest, and consistent reports of discrimination and violence, with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse.

An Human Rights Watch report published 10 August 2022, produced with Justice for Sisters, documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia. It cites the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. It details conversion and rehabilitation programmes, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of transgender woman Nur Sajat in western Selangor, and concludes that pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behaviour, and public discourse.

No Malacca-specific enforcement incident, arrest, or state-level provision was identified in the source inventory; the assessment for Malacca rests on the national framework as documented above.

27671186B76269877687363.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
27671186B76269877687363.summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory has no territorial variation from Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the criminal provisions it reinforces apply in the capital as they do elsewhere in the country, and the national assessment carries that layer in full.

1875124B65618634887963.name: Lima
1875124B65618634887963.summary:
Lima department and the metropolitan area stand under the national framework of Peru, and the national assessment carried by the parent record applies here. No separate departmental or municipal regime modifying that framework was identified in the sources.

The national norm approved by the legislature's plenary on 2 April 2025 bars entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated. In Lima, the international airport Jorge Chávez had installed signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity"; the text also prohibits signage of that kind as "ambiguous", so the inclusive signage already present in the capital's main airport falls within the ban. The Women and Family Commission had approved the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR unanimously on 20 February 2025, at which point the measure still required plenary backing.

LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, quoted by Infobae on 20 February 2025, called the measure discriminatory and described how enforcement would operate in practice: security staff judging for themselves whether a woman entering a restroom is trans, and demanding her national identity document (DNI) on that judgment. The rule therefore converts routine facility use in Lima into a documented-checkpoint risk for gender-nonconforming users.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in analysis of 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, characterises article 5 of the text as direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex", a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle. The authors note that trans people, though framed in the debate as aggressors, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination.

Recorded violence against LGBTI people in Peru, in counts that include Lima, is substantial and rising: the TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023. More than half of those killed were trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. The year 2023 saw the most homicides (19), and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. These are raw counts on a national denominator that includes Lima; the source provides no per-capita or city-level breakdown, so the figures cannot be read as a Lima-specific rate.

One of those killings occurred in central Lima: on 12 February 2023 the transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, was kidnapped from jirón Chancay by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang and killed with roughly 30 gunshots. Agencia Presentes, reporting on 22 July 2024, flags the state inaction around such cases: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

1875124B43998217738279.name: Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima
1875124B43998217738279.summary:
Lima stands under the national framework of Peru: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. The Metropolitan Municipality of Lima sets none of these rules itself; a trans visitor to the capital is governed by national statute and by the enforcement practice of national agencies and private security operating in the city.

On 20 February 2025 the Congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously, for plenary debate, a bill barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex that does not match their biological sex at birth. The same text obliges public premises to remove "ambiguous" signage of the kind Jorge Chávez international airport had displayed, wording such as "for all persons with female identity" and "for all persons with male identity". The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, extending the bar to trans youth, and the wider legislative package bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity".

Enforcement is expected to reach individuals at the door. Activist and journalist Gianna Camacho warns that the restriction will be applied through identity-card (DNI) checks carried out by security staff deciding who may enter a restroom, a screening practice she describes as discriminatory and grounded in prejudice rather than in any observed conduct.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and under-recorded. An Observatory report covering 2020 to 2023 counted 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reported rights violations, with trans women the most affected group at 30 of the 54 killed; 19 homicides were recorded in 2023 alone, and in 26 of the killings no suspects were identified. The state maintains no system recording the sexual orientation or gender identity of victims of killing, so official counts understate the pattern.

The capital illustrates that pattern. On 12 February 2023 members of the "Los Gallegos" gang kidnapped trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, from jirón Chancay in central Lima; she was killed with roughly 30 gunshots.

1875124B43998217738279.tangentialFactors:
Peru remains without LGBT coverage in its hate-crime law: Congress voted in 2017 to strip those protections from the new Penal Code, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking such coverage. Hate-crime reporting in Lima therefore has no specific statutory hook.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The bathroom statute and the removal of inclusive signage sit in tension with that binding regional standard, and the same Court has jurisdiction over cases arising from Lima.

In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Speech and association are constrained nationally: vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including a ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

25984515B47806653651907.name: Ankara
25984515B47806653651907.summary:
Ankara stands under Turkey's national framework: the sources record no Ankara-level law or municipal measure, and the city's distinct exposure is institutional, since the presidency, the Ministry of Family and the drafting machinery for national legislation sit there. The penal-code package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 is drafted, and would be enforced, through institutions operating in Ankara.

The leaked draft, known as the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct treated as contrary to biological sex and general morality, punishable by up to three years in prison, and to punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, attach mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, expose health professionals performing such interventions to fines and up to seven years in prison and trans people receiving care the authorities deem illegal to up to three years, and allow courts to order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, which had not been enacted as of the reporting date.

Kaos GL's 2025 annual report concludes that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, centred on the presidency and implemented through the Ministry of Family, both of them Ankara institutions. It records censored broadcasts, artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years, with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

The same report counts six violations of the right to life over the year, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the most affected group, alongside a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year. Turkey compiles no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on the organisation's own monitoring; with no general homicide or violence denominator in the sources, the six deaths cannot be expressed as a rate or compared with the risk borne by the general population.

25984515B12971548112787.name: Eskişehir
25984515B12971548112787.summary:
Eskişehir stands under the national framework applicable in Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than residual prejudice. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes with articles criminalising behaviour "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and its "promotion", carrying up to three years' prison through an amendment to the indecent-acts provision. The same package would impose sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care, including a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements, and could expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges, all justified as protecting "the family and public morals".

Eskişehir itself has a documented record of suppression. In June 2021 police blocked the city's first Pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have moved against the local Pride event. Duvar English reported that officers reached the assembly area hours before the scheduled start time and carried out identity checks; organisers were not permitted to hold a press conference or conduct the march, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of "violating the ban on the march". The intervention followed similar police action against Pride events in Istanbul and Ankara days earlier. Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years, citing security concerns and public order.

On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries.

In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex", a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. Kadir Has University surveys recorded public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

25984515B63001774148772.name: Gaziantep
25984515B63001774148772.summary:
Gaziantep stands under Turkey's national framework on LGBT rights in full, with no documented local divergence: a visibly trans visitor to the province faces the same legal exposure, the same document checks and the same enforcement climate as elsewhere in the country, applied by provincial authorities under national law.

The most serious pending threat is a leaked 11th Judicial Package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal and civil codes with articles criminalising behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion', carrying up to three years' prison through an amended indecent-acts provision, alongside sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care including a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements. Charges could reach trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists, justified publicly as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

The statutory baseline is otherwise unchanged: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change legal gender since 1988 subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries.

Enforcement against public visibility is documented. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. This evidences the state-level hostility and case-by-case prosecutions under the same meeting-and-demonstrations law that a visibly trans visitor would face anywhere in Turkey, including Gaziantep.

In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'; that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. A visibly trans visitor's exposure in the province is the national one, locally enforced.

The state/province stands under the national framework on LGBT rights in full, with no documented local divergence: a visibly trans visitor to the state/province faces the same legal exposure, the same document checks and the same enforcement climate as elsewhere in the country, applied by provincial authorities under national law.

The most serious pending threat is a leaked judicial package reported by a human-rights organisation on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal and civil codes with articles criminalising behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion', carrying up to three years' prison through an amended indecent-acts provision, alongside sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care including a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements. Charges could reach trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists, justified publicly as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

The statutory baseline is otherwise unchanged: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the historic-era penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change legal gender since 1988 subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. In a 2026 regional Rainbow ranking the country placed 47th of 49.

Enforcement against public visibility is documented. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under the national assembly law and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks.

In December 2025 a court in one city ordered the dissolution of a young LGBTI+ association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. This evidences the state-level hostility and case-by-case prosecutions under the same meeting-and-demonstrations law that a visibly trans visitor would face anywhere in the country, including this state/province.

In early 2026 national media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'; that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. A visibly trans visitor's exposure in the state/province is the national one, locally enforced.

The dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association in December 2025 signals judicial willingness to act against organisations on 'moral values' grounds, which narrows the space for local civil-society support that a trans visitor in difficulty might otherwise rely on.

25984515B18786507826220.name: İstanbul
25984515B18786507826220.summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records state-policy hostility toward LGBTI+ people operating in the city directly, including intensified practices of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ residents that obstruct access to housing. The same monitoring counts six violations of the right to life across Turkey in 2025, three recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the group most affected; torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled to 89 from 51; one LGBTI+ association was closed with criminal cases opened against 11 members; and the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

Street-level policing in İstanbul targets trans women specifically. On 31 July 2025 police in Beyoğlu stopped around 20 trans women for ID checks while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station, recorded their names and took videos of them; bianet's report characterises the operation as profiling.

The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned pride parades in the city since 2015 on security and public-order grounds, with the 2016 to 2018 bans stated explicitly and water cannon used on 29 June 2015. Police suppression escalated in the years that followed: blockades and tear gas in 2021 with 25 people arrested; 373 arrested in 2022 as public transport to Taksim Square was shut down; 113 arrests in 2023; and 11 arrests in 2024, three of them minors, after organisers moved İstanbul Pride to non-Taksim public spaces and issued fake meeting calls to thwart police. The 2014 march drew over 100,000 participants, the largest LGBT event in Turkey's history.

On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the Pride march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the nearby Cihangir neighbourhood, shut down public transport to the square and detained 373 people, including AFP photojournalist Bülent Kılıç, who were released after a night in custody according to Kaos GL. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all Pride Week events for seven days.

25984515B59477790330217.name: İzmir
25984515B59477790330217.summary:
İzmir stands under the national framework of Turkey. No İzmir-specific signal on trans legal status, policing or facilities was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment applies, and İzmir's own exposure should be read through the documented national pattern of street identity checks. On 31 July 2025 police in a large-city entertainment district conducted mass identity-document roundups of trans women, recording names and filming them without giving any official reason, a practice bianet links to profiling concerns.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would amend civil code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing deemed-illegal interventions would face fines and up to seven years' prison, and trans people receiving such care up to three years, with courts able to order pretrial detention. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment into unregulated underground settings. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. It records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, citing detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants as the main reasons; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations; and six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected. For the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy.

66186276B86072070009793.name: Puerto Rico
66186276B86072070009793.summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised in Puerto Rico. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, and Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico enacted Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, which bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and punishes violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Article 4 of the law directs the prohibition at medical institutions and health professionals, forbidding surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment. Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause: it expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and sets the age of the protected class at under 21.

The drafting leaves an unresolved gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers, while Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. What the ambiguity produces instead is exposure to questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

Opposition to the measure was registered across the island's professional bodies before signature. The ACLU of Puerto Rico urged Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, stating that it criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. The Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico all opposed it.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples in Puerto Rico was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge filed in March 2014, the Ada Conde Vidal case, drew intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and New York in 2012.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.

sources.title: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025 (LexJuris de Puerto Rico) — primary legal text
sources.summary: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, 'Ley para la protección de la salud y el bienestar de los menores de edad en Puerto Rico' (primary legal text, LexJuris). Article 4 — the operative prohibition — is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments altering the sex biology of a minor 'bajo el pretexto de una transición de género o como parte de un tratamiento de disforia de género'. The Article 3 definition of banned 'chemical and surgical mutilation' is drafted broader than the prohibition: it expressly includes 'el uso de bloqueadores de pubertad y hormonas sexuales (incluyendo bloqueadores androgénicos, estrógenos, progesterona o testosterona) utilizados con el propósito de tratar la disforia de género' — the USE itself of puberty blockers and sex hormones for gender-dysphoria treatment — and defines 'niño o menor de edad' as any person under 21. Article 6 then penalises 'toda persona que viole las disposiciones de esta Ley' with a fixed 15-year term, plus permanent licence loss for professionals and a $50,000 per-violation fine for juridical persons. Legal analysis of this drafting notes a structural tension: the definition speaks of patient 'use' while the operative clause restricts only providers, and the penalty catch-all says 'any person'. Under standard criminal doctrines (definitions create no offence by themselves; a protected class cannot be prosecuted as the perpetrator of its own victimisation; the principle of legality bars analogy; and travel with lawfully prescribed personal medication), a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own prescribed hormones — or of their parents for enabling it — would almost certainly fail, and the statute is a textbook void-for-vagueness candidate. But the textual ambiguity is precisely what legal advocates flag as its chilling effect: it leaves interpretive room for hostile officials to question, detain or investigate trans youth and their families on the ground, with the answer coming only after the fact. For a travelling under-21 trans person the practical reading is: carrying and using prescribed HRT in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of banned practice, enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. The ACLU of Puerto Rico had urged a veto before signature, stating the bill 'criminalizes doctors and parents' and creates 'two distinct categories of children' divided by sex-assigned-at-birth identity, and the island's College of Physicians and Surgeons, Psychology Association, College of Social Work Professionals, Bar Association and LGBTQ+ Federation all registered opposition.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): Gov. Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit in PR (filed March; Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening - one couple married in Canada 2007, another in New York 2012; former National Guard member among plaintiffs. Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

For a trans visitor the ban closes off all gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the deliberately vague facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

sources.title: ACLU of Puerto Rico Urges Governor to Veto Senate Bill 350 (ACLU-PR press release)
sources.summary: The ACLU of Puerto Rico called on Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, 'which criminalizes doctors and parents and aims to prohibit gender-affirming medical treatments for individuals under the age of 21'. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated the bill 'creates two distinct categories of children: one that allows parents to access and authorize treatments if the child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth, and another that prohibits parents the same right if their child's identity is different'. The release records that the bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned 'do not remedy the violation of fundamental constitutional, civil, and human rights', and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. It states the bill's 'text is clearly and exclusively aimed at minors whose identity does not correspond to the sex assigned to them at birth' and that it disregards the specialist consultation process that precedes parents authorising puberty blockers or hormonal treatments, 'and instead, criminalizes them'. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona: the measure 'directly discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth, whose very lives may be at risk'. The release lists local opposition from the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

SYN-ASM.name: American Samoa
SYN-ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applicants. The policy is challenged in federal courts, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; trans and nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad.

Same-sex marriage remains formally contested in the territory. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it. In 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory whose attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. In January 2016 a district court judge confirmed by the Senate told legislators he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date; the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar, then the United States Department of the Interior. As of mid-2024 the local ban was still treated on-island as operative, with its constitutional durability an open question under academic study.

Trans-specific violence and protection machinery are documented. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case against the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local cultural context shapes daily expectations. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, frames fa'afafine as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture; reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and homosexuality is widely accepted within Samoan culture compared with neighbouring Pacific states.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Lambda Legal's FAQ sets out passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under the current federal policy change: which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the current status of document updates.

HRC (updated 2025): since Jan 2025 executive order, new/renewed US passports show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change; the 'X' marker (available since 2022) eliminated; policy challenged in federal courts -- current passport posture for trans US travelers.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025) reports that the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

sources.summary: The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should only be altered to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption. The Office of Vital Statistics has interpreted this ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals. The Office will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order. The Office may change the gender marker on a birth certificate with medical documentation of the sex change. The first criminal law against sodomy was enacted in 1963 and made male homosexual and heterosexual sodomy illegal, but did not address lesbian sex. In 1979 the Fono revised criminal law so that consensual sodomy was no longer illegal unless it involved public acts, prostitution, minors or people unable to give consent due to mental illness, with the law taking effect in 1980. The age of consent is set at 16 years, regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation. The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to the age of "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and as "daughter," and a 2003 bill to ban same-sex marriage was voted against by the House Judiciary Committee and then the full Senate. Same-sex marriages are currently not licensed in American Samoa, with the Attorney General in July 2015 reviewing applicability of Obergefell v. Hodges and the Governor stating the ruling does not apply due to preamble, constitution, Christian values and unorganized and unincorporated political status. Under the Respect for Marriage Act passed by the 117th United States Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, all territories including American Samoa are required to recognize, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The article states American Samoa remains the only part of the United States along with select Native American tribal jurisdictions to enforce a ban on same-sex couples marrying, while same-sex couples married legally in other jurisdictions are recognized and must be treated equally under US federal law since 13 December 2022. The article states "American Samoa, like the neighboring country of Samoa, tends to be tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities." It notes a long-standing tradition of raising some boys as girls to play an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, with such individuals known as the fa'afafine. It states nevertheless American Samoan society is highly religious and conservative attitudes regarding gender and sexuality tend to dominate. It states open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. The main LGBTQ organization is the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (S.O.F.I.A.S.) which annually organizes events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions, beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are quite popular, and families generally turn up en masse to support candidates.

sources.title: 2003 Same-Sex Marriage Ban Bill by Rep. Sua Carl Schuster
sources.summary: On 20 March 2003 the American Samoa Senate rejected Representative Sua Carl Schuster's bill to outlaw same-sex marriage after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed, with fa'afine witness Tiffany Poutasi testifying that fa'afine are men who express femininity through dress and speech and oppose marriage with other men as against Christian upbringing.

sources.title: Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale - July 2015 Review Statement
sources.summary: As of July 10, 2015, American Samoa had not authorized same-sex marriage and no same-sex marriage license applications had been filed while Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale reviewed the U.S. Supreme Court marriage-equality ruling for applicability to the territory, which maintained a tradition of embracing faafafine — males raised as females taking on feminine traits — alongside dominant conservative Christian churches.

SYN-ASM.tangentialFactors:
American Samoa's 2015 position was exceptional within the United States territories: its attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still being reviewed, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. No licence application had been made at that point.

Samoan cultural norms place behavioural expectations on everyone regardless of orientation. Reserved public conduct is expected across the board, so public affection or gender-nonconforming presentation may draw comment for reasons of custom rather than statute, even where homosexuality is widely accepted in comparison with neighbouring Pacific states such as Fiji.

Practical guidance for trans and nonbinary travelers under the current federal document rules is published by Lambda Legal, which sets out which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records and the current status of document updates, and by the Human Rights Campaign, whose 2025 travel and passport guidance covers the sex-assigned-at-birth requirement for new and renewed passports.
SYN-ASM.localsOnly:
Territorial employers have faced federal consequences for anti-trans conduct: the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case against the American Samoa Government in September 2023 over harassment of a transgender employee, and a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the territorial government over her gender identity.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 through the merger of the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, and re-anchors fa'afafine to cultural pride. Fa'afafine are defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, described as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, within a wider narrative of colonial suppression and contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Marriage recognition remains unused in practice. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa records that no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence in the territory, and sets out a litigation route beginning in the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar and continuing to the United States Department of the Interior. In July 2024 Samoa News reported an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether the territory's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment alongside questions on collectivistic and individualistic orientation.

The territory's own legislative history on marriage is on record. The Fono Senate rejected a ban bill in March 2003 introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it; at that hearing the fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing.
SYN-ASM.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source any American Samoa statute or administrative procedure for changing gender markers on territorial documents such as local identification or driver's licences; the marker rules established here are federal passport rules. Whether the territorial government issues any local document reflecting a changed gender marker is unresolved on this record.

The effect of EO 14168 and EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding within American Samoa is not sourced at the service level. The orders and their funding reach are documented; concrete reductions in available care on-island are not, and this remains unresolved.

No American Samoa provision on hate-crime enhancement for anti-trans violence, and no local penalty schedule for the conduct described in the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge, appear in the inventory. The charge itself is documented; its outcome is not.

The ACLU's challenge to the federal document policy was pending as of the source material, so the current passport posture rests on a policy under active federal litigation with no final ruling recorded here. Whether any court will restore the X marker or other non-binary markers is unresolved.

SYN-GUM.name: Guam
SYN-GUM.summary:
Guam stands under the United States federal framework as an unincorporated territory, and its own local law adds specific protections and specific conditions for trans visitors.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression is prohibited locally. In August 2015 the Guam Legislature passed Bill 102-33 unanimously, banning discrimination in private employment on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, and separately forbidding discrimination against government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity.

Legal gender recognition requires surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a trans person must give the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery. The Motor Vehicle Division issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed. A 2018 bill that would have permitted legal gender change on judicial permission with a supporting letter from a licensed professional and no surgery requirement failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote after the Legislature postponed action on 13 December 2018, so surgery remains the condition.

On partner recognition, chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

A January 2025 executive order banning transgender troops from serving openly applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence; the order directs the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days and frames trans identity as "radical gender ideology."

sources.summary: NPR (28 Jan 2025): a Trump executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs SecDef Hegseth to submit an implementation plan within 30 days; the order frames trans identity as 'radical gender ideology'. The order applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent US military presence.

Guardian/AP (5 Jun 2015): chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's same-sex marriage prohibition after an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero denied a licence; ruling effective 8am Tuesday 9 June — Guam became the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Guam (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In August 2015 the Guam Legislature unanimously passed Bill 102-33 which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression in employment. Discrimination against government employees based on sexuality or identity is also forbidden. Federal law has covered hate crimes based on gender identity since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act. To change legal gender on a birth certificate transgender people must provide the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician that they have undergone sex reassignment surgery after which the Office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended drivers license upon receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicants sex has been surgically changed. In May 2018 Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill to permit legal gender change with judicial permission and a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist social worker therapist or other licensed professional with no surgery required. On December 13 2018 the Legislature postponed a vote on the bill until medical and law enforcement process issues were addressed and the bill failed on December 17 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Private adult consensual and noncommercial homosexual acts have been legal in Guam since reform of the Criminal Code in 1978. The 1933 penal code ordained by the Naval Governor and identical to Californias prohibited sodomy fellatio and cunnilingus whether heterosexual or homosexual with between one and ten years imprisonment. The only reported sodomy case in Guam occurred in the early 1950s in Pennington v Government which resulted in victory for the defendant solely on procedural grounds when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held the trial court had been without authority to try Pennington without a jury. Bill 102-33 passed unanimously in August 2015 bans employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and discrimination against government employees based on sexuality is also forbidden. Federal law has covered hate crimes based on sexual orientation since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The article states "The Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people." It further describes Chamorro society as very sexually tolerant but specifies for sexuality that homosexuality was never viewed as taboo but "was taken for granted as part of life". For contemporary conditions the article states Guam is regarded as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment which is a general LGBTQ finding not a transgender specific finding. It reports a visible LGBTQ social scene since the 1990s with a handful of nightclubs and social functions and annual Guam Pride held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. It notes Guam is a member of the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association and has begun commercializing itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people and these contemporary observations are framed as LGBTQ general findings rather than transgender specific findings.

SYN-GUM.tangentialFactors:
Federal law has covered hate crimes motivated by gender identity since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act.

Guam is regarded as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people, with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment; this is a general LGBTQ finding rather than a transgender-specific one. The Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people, and homosexuality was never viewed as taboo in Chamorro society.

A visible LGBTQ social scene has existed since the 1990s, with a handful of nightclubs and social functions and annual Guam Pride held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. Guam is a member of the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association and has begun commercialising itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people; these are general LGBTQ observations, not trans-specific findings.
