Local employment protections under Bill 102-33 cover Guam residents in private employment and separately bar discrimination against government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity.

Legal gender recognition for residents requires surgery: the Office of Vital Statistics amends a birth certificate only on a sworn physician statement confirming sex reassignment surgery, and the Motor Vehicle Division issues an amended driver's licence on the same condition. The 2018 reform bill (introduced in May 2018 by Senator Fernando Esteves) would have allowed legal gender change on judicial permission with a supporting letter from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional and no surgery requirement, but the Legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 pending medical and law-enforcement process issues and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by 6 to 7.

Private adult consensual and non-commercial homosexual acts have been legal in Guam since the Criminal Code reform of 1978. The 1933 penal code ordained by the Naval Governor, identical to California's, prohibited sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus whether heterosexual or homosexual with one to ten years' imprisonment. The only reported sodomy case in Guam occurred in the early 1950s in Pennington v Government, which the defendant won solely on procedural grounds when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held the trial court had been without authority to try Pennington without a jury.
SYN-GUM.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not document any trans-specific violence incidents, enforcement actions under Bill 102-33, or hate-crime prosecutions in Guam motivated by gender identity; the absence of such reports is not sourced as evidence that none occur.

Whether Guam's local employment non-discrimination protections have been tested in practice, and how the surgery requirement for legal gender recognition is applied at present, are unresolved on the available sources.

SYN-VIR.name: United States Virgin Islands
SYN-VIR.summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework governs what a trans visitor meets at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a visitor arriving on United States documents carries an identification that does not match their presentation at entry.

Airport screening follows federal procedure. Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and lead to secondary screening and pat-downs; travellers may request alternative screening and may decline the scanner. The agency's know-your-rights guidance extends to United States nationals travelling to and from the territory on the same terms as mainland travellers, including what may and may not be carried in hand baggage under the federal screening framework.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

Territorial law adds a layer of protection. The U.S. Virgin Islands human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending that protection explicitly into the education setting.

Relationship status is settled. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later federal recognition settled the question nationwide, so a married couple can rely on their marriage in the territory. The historic sodomy statute, applicable to the territory since 1957, has been replaced and is no longer in force.

The Attorney General's 2017 interpretation is an official reading of existing anti-discrimination law rather than a new statute, which makes its scope in practice beyond the education setting a matter for enforcement rather than text.

Parent-nation travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by an executive order in January 2025, so a visitor arriving on parent-nation documents carries an identification that does not match their presentation at entry.

Airport screening follows national procedure. A national transport-security agency's body scanners can flag trans bodies and lead to secondary screening and pat-downs; travellers may request alternative screening and may decline the scanner. The agency's know-your-rights guidance extends to parent-nation nationals travelling to and from the state/province on the same terms as mainland travellers, including what may and may not be carried in hand baggage under the national screening framework.

The January 2025 executive order halting national funding for gender-affirming care reaches nationally funded institutions in the state/province, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

State/provincial law adds a layer of protection. The state/province human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the national justice department issued an official interpretation that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending that protection explicitly into the education setting.

Relationship status is settled. In 2015 the state/province Superior Court struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later national recognition settled the question nationwide, so a married couple can rely on their marriage in the state/province. The historic sodomy statute, applicable to the state/province since 1957, has been replaced and is no longer in force.
SYN-VIR.blindTangential:
Reporting from July 2017 on the LGBTQ community in the state/province describes setbacks alongside reasons for hope, indicating a contested local climate rather than a settled one; the account does not set out a discrete trans-specific legal finding.

The state/province's position within the parent nation means national screening, document and funding rules operate alongside local anti-discrimination law, so a visitor may face restrictive national rules on entry and care while holding statutory protection against discrimination once inside the jurisdiction.

The national justice department's 2017 interpretation is an official reading of existing anti-discrimination law rather than a new statute, which makes its scope in practice beyond the education setting a matter for enforcement rather than text.
SYN-VIR.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents of the state/province are covered by the local human-rights statute, which prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and by the March 2017 national justice department interpretation holding that the law applies to transgender students in schools.

Same-sex marriage has been available in the state/province since the 2015 Superior Court ruling, and marriages performed there are nationally recognised.

The historic sodomy statute applied to the state/province from 1957 has been replaced and is no longer in force.

National know-your-rights guidance on airport security applies to residents on mainland routes on the same terms as other parent-nation nationals, covering scanner refusal, alternative screening, and hand-baggage restrictions under the national framework.

The January 2025 national funding restriction on gender-affirming care reaches nationally funded institutions in the state/province, which bears on residents' care access as well as visitors'.
SYN-VIR.blindOutOfScope:

Whether the anti-discrimination statute's protections extend beyond education to public accommodations, housing, or restroom access in the state/province is unresolved in the available sources.

The current statute replacing the 1957 sodomy provision, and its text, are not specified in the inventory; only the fact of replacement is sourced.

Hate-crime provisions covering gender identity in the state/province are not sourced, and no local violence data against trans people appears in the inventory.

The July 2017 reporting on setbacks and prospects for the LGBTQ community does not yield a discrete trans-specific legal claim and is left as context rather than a finding.

SYN-MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
SYN-MNP.summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth and stands under the national framework of the United States for travel documents, immigration and airport screening. United States passports and entry documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker option was eliminated by the January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents presents a gender marker that may not match presentation at the port of entry.

Screening at the airport follows federal procedure, and the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to such care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges; the first same-sex marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015.

Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes: CNMI Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence.

Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, which means identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement.

Wider protection remains thin. As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a Negative gender-identity score. There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity; recourse beyond federal EEOC complaint channels is limited, and commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only.

SYN-MNP.tangentialFactors:
The Movement Advancement Project comparison places the Northern Mariana Islands among the weakest jurisdictions in its assessment set on gender identity policy, where a score of minus 2 of 25 is classified as Negative while marriage recognition scores a full 1 of 1. Recognition of a relationship therefore runs well ahead of protection from discrimination.

The gap between the two layers of government shapes practical recourse. Federal law supplies nondiscrimination machinery through EEOC complaints, but the commonwealth layer adds protection only for government employees, leaving employment and services outside that category dependent on federal channels alone.

Public visibility exists at community level: the commonwealth's first Gay Pride event was held at the GIG Discotheque in Garapan with about 60 people attending, and organiser Sharmaine Casquero described it as a success. Attendance at a single event is a limited indicator of the wider social climate.
SYN-MNP.localsOnly:
Residents may change legal gender in the Northern Mariana Islands on condition that the applicant has undergone the specified medical process; the requirement is part of the local procedure rather than an option waived for residents.

Same-sex couples have been able to adopt since 2015, and same-sex marriage has been available since the Obergefell v. Hodges ruling, with the first ceremony on Saipan performed on 27 July 2015.

Discrimination protection at commonwealth level covers government employees only. Residents who fall outside that category rely on federal EEOC complaint channels; no comprehensive commonwealth statute addresses gender identity.

CNMI Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, gives prosecutors a basis to seek enhanced sentencing where a crime is motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity.
SYN-MNP.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports prosecutions or sentences obtained under CNMI Public Law 22-32, so its use in gender-identity-motivated cases is unverified here.

The medical process required for legal gender change is referenced but not specified in the sources, and no information is available on its availability, cost or waiting time within the territory.

The composition of the Movement Advancement Project's negative gender-identity score is not broken down in the inventory, so the specific policy failures driving it are unresolved.

No sourced material addresses restroom or facilities rules, identity screening procedures at Saipan International Airport, or partner and next-of-kin recognition beyond marriage and adoption; those points remain not sourced rather than confirmed absent.
